title: Bus collides with truck in eastern Pakistan, killing at least 11 people
summary: Officials say a passenger bus has collided with a truck in eastern Pakistan, killing at least 11 people and injuring 33 others
story: Officials say a passenger bus has collided with a truck in eastern Pakistan, killing at least 11 people and injuring 33 others
MULTAN, Pakistan -- A passenger bus collided with a truck in eastern Pakistan on Thursday, killing at least 11 people and injuring 33 others, police and rescue officials said.
The crash occurred in Pakpattan district in Punjab province, said Dr. Ahmad Raza, a hospital official.

Rescuers used cranes and other heavy machinery during a three-hour operation to free passengers trapped in the wreckage, police said. Authorities declared an emergency at the hospital and called in additional doctors and medical staff to treat the injured, Raza said.
President Asif Ali Zardari expressed sorrow over the deaths in a statement, offered condolences to the victims’ families, and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Road crashes are common in Pakistan, where poor road conditions, inadequate enforcement of traffic laws and unsafe driving practices contribute to frequent collisions. Last month, a bus collided with a van in southwestern Balochistan province, killing at least 12 people and injuring about two dozen others.

title: Belarus sentences Catholic priest to 3 years after he opposed the Ukraine war
summary: A Roman Catholic priest, who has opposed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and helped Ukrainian refugees, has been sentenced to three years in prison in Belarus
story: A Roman Catholic priest, who has opposed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and helped Ukrainian refugees, has been sentenced to three years in prison in Belarus

TALLINN, Estonia -- A Roman Catholic priest, who has opposed Russia's invasion of Ukraine and helped Ukrainian refugees, has been sentenced to three years in prison in Belarus, the latest move in the authorities' crackdown on critical voices, a rights group said Thursday.

A court in Belarus convicted Anatoly Parakhnevich, 66, on charges of “insulting the authorities” and “extremism” during a closed-door trial last month, said the Viasna Human Rights Center, which designated him as a political prisoner. It said Parakhnevich rejected the charges and would appeal the verdict.

Belarus' authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko has governed the nation of 9.5 million with an iron fist for more than three decades, and Belarus has been sanctioned repeatedly by Western countries — both for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing Moscow to use its territory in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.

Lukashenko’s rule was challenged after a 2020 presidential election that kept him in power, when tens of thousands of people poured into the streets to protest a vote widely seen as rigged. In an ensuing crackdown, tens of thousands of people were detained, with many beaten by police. Prominent opposition figures either fled the country or were imprisoned.

Viasna said that Parakhnevich, the parish priest in Alkovichy in northwestern Belarus, had openly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and condemned Belarus’ role in it, while calling for peace and repentance.
He was among the local leaders who organized the collection of aid for Ukrainians. In one of his sermons about the war, he asked his parishioners: “Will our own consciences ever forgive us?”
Parakhnevich has been in custody since his arrest in March and suffered a heart attack behind bars, according to Viasna.

“The authorities are aggressively persecuting, threatening and intimidating those who shape public opinion within the country, and Parakhnevich is a very popular priest whose sermons were heard by thousands of Belarusians,” Pavel Sapelka, a lawyer for Viasna, said.
“The trial of the clergyman took place against the backdrop of long-standing, large-scale pressure exerted by the authorities on all religious communities.”

Dozens of clergy — Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant — have been jailed, silenced or forced into exile for protesting the 2020 election. Clergy who supported the protests and sheltered demonstrators at their churches were particularly targeted in the repression.
Orthodox Christians make up about 80% of Belarus’ population. Just under 14% are Catholic and 2% are Protestants.

The legal framework for religious organizations in the country has become even more restrictive following Lukashenko’s signing of a new law that mandates the reregistration of all religious communities. The document prohibits the use of civic symbols during religious services and bars individuals listed as “extremists” from leading parishes.
Belarusian opposition leader-in-exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya condemned the verdict against Parakhnevich as “heartbreaking” and “politically motivated.”
“The repression continues, and the authorities are filling the vacancies in prisons with new political prisoners,” Tsikhanouskaya told The Associated Press.
According to Viasna, Belarus currently has 884 political prisoners.

title: American national sentenced to life in prison for murders of partner and infant daughter in Rome
summary: An Italian court has sentenced an American citizen to life in prison for the murder of his partner and their infant daughter
story: An Italian court has sentenced an American citizen to life in prison for the murder of his partner and their infant daughter

ROME -- An American man was found guilty by a Rome court Thursday of murdering his partner and their infant daughter, whose bodies were found naked in a city park, the LaPresse news agency reported. He was sentenced to life in prison.

Francis Kaufmann, 47, fled to the Greek island of Skiathos after the killings in June 2025 and was extradited by Italy to face trial for the murders of Anastasia Trofimova, 28, and their daughter Andromeda, who was nearly a year old.
Kaufmann denied killing them.

The bodies were found in Rome’s Villa Pamphili park. Trofimova, whose body was found under a black bag, had been killed several days before the infant, who was found in nearby undergrowth. Neither had identification.

Kaufmann, a self-described filmmaker using the alias Rexal Ford, had secured $1 million in Italian tax credits for a film that was never made. The scandal prompted the resignation of the head of the Culture Ministry’s film department.

title: Nigerian court nullifies presidential contender’s candidacy 2 months before election
summary: A Nigerian court has disqualified a leading presidential candidate, complicating the electoral process two months before the election
story: A Nigerian court has disqualified a leading presidential candidate, complicating the electoral process two months before the election
LAGOS, Nigeria -- A Nigerian court disqualified a leading presidential candidate Thursday, complicating the electoral process two months before the election.

A Federal High Court judge in Abuja, the country's capital, ruled that the leadership of the African Democratic Congress, one of the three major parties contesting the January 2027 election, was illegally constituted and therefore voided the candidacy of Atiku Abubakar.

Earlier in the year, a court ordered the party deregistered for failing to meet constitutional requirements, but an appeals court overturned the ruling. The party and government critics say the case was orchestrated by the ruling party.

Nigeria is set to go to the polls next year against the backdrop of a troubled economy and escalating insecurity. Incumbent President Bola Tinubu faces a splintered opposition, mainly from Abubakar and Peter Obi, setting up a rematch of the 2023 presidential election.
Abubakar and Obi came second and third in 2023, respectively.
The campaign has gotten off to a slow start since August, as opposition parties remain mired in legal battles, boosting Tinubu's chances at the polls.

“The timing of this ruling is no coincidence," Abubakar said Thursday in a statement. “It is part of a strategy to weaken my support in the north and frustrate a campaign whose message is resonating across the country.”
The party said it would be appealing the judgment.

title: Small eastern Caribbean archipelago seeking slavery reparations holds general election
summary: Grenada and other eastern Caribbean islands are voting in general elections
story: Grenada and other eastern Caribbean islands are voting in general elections

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Grenada and other eastern Caribbean islands were voting Thursday in general elections in which Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell, who has called for slavery reparations and an apology from Britain, is seeking a second term.
Mitchell, of the National Democratic Congress, faces Peter David, a former foreign affairs minister running with the Democratic People’s Movement.
Mitchell has pledged to modernize the island’s economy, strengthen healthcare services and lower youth unemployment.
He and other leaders across the Caribbean have long been pushing for an apology and reparations for slavery from Britain.

In early September, Jamaica took its case for reparations to King Charles III, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. It was an unprecedented legal maneuver, even though the British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
David has promised to generate more jobs, improve medical care and create a robust local food supply system.
More than 97,000 people are registered to vote in Grenada, Carriacou and Petite Martinique.
Fifteen seats in Grenada’s House of Representatives are up for grabs. The Senate, meanwhile, is represented by 13 appointed members.
Grenada obtained independence in 1974, after being under French and then British rule.
In 1983, the U.S. invaded Grenada after a radical faction executed Marxist Prime Minister Maurice Bishop, three members of his Cabinet and four other people.
While the U.N. and several countries condemned the invasion, Grenada celebrates its anniversary every year on Oct. 25, dubbing it “Thanksgiving Day.”

title: UN's peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara enters liquidation phase after mandate expires
summary: The U.N. peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has entered a “liquidation phase” and is beginning to vacate positions and dispose of equipment following a U.S.-Russia standoff at the Security Council last week
story: The U.N. peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has entered a “liquidation phase” and is beginning to vacate positions and dispose of equipment following a U.S.-Russia standoff at the Security Council last week

LAAYOUNE, Western Sahara -- The U.N. peacekeeping mission in the disputed territory of Western Sahara will start repatriating personnel, closing a dozen facilities and disposing of equipment as part of a “liquidation phase” following a U.S.-Russia standoff at the Security Council last week.

The mission’s abrupt end after 35 years raises questions about security and stability in the region. Western Sahara is a vast desert nearly the size of Colorado and rich in fisheries and minerals. The contested resource corridor once ruled by Spain is now claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.

U.N. peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix said late Wednesday that the department dealing with operational issues of the U.N.’s far-flung peacekeeping missions wants to ensure an “orderly'' retreat. “And we count, of course, on the full cooperation of all the parties.”
The U.N. mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front and organize a referendum on self-determination.

But the vote never materialized, as the two sides failed to agree on who would be eligible to participate. The ceasefire collapsed in 2020, and the U.N. says the region remains marked by tensions and low-intensity hostilities.

During the mission, 20 U.N. personnel lost their lives. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.

Morocco’s royal palace, which oversees the country’s foreign policy, welcomed the mission’s end, saying it had failed to monitor the ceasefire. The Polisario Front and Algeria, meanwhile, regretted the decision not to renew its mandate.

Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesperson for the Secretary-General of the U.N., said the liquidation will include “the repatriation of approximately 160 military observers, the drawdown of 180 civilians and affiliated personnel, and the closure of about 13 mission facilities and team sites.”

In Laayoune, the capital of Western Sahara and home to MINURSO’s headquarters, U.N. and Moroccan flags continued to fly side by side on Thursday. U.N.-marked vehicles still move through the disputed city’s streets, where Moroccan flags and portraits of King Mohammed VI are a constant presence. Above the entrance to the mission’s headquarters, a sign reads: “Welcome to the United Nations.” For now, there is no visible indication that the mission is preparing to leave.

The closure serves Morocco’s push for full sovereignty over Western Sahara, while further isolating the Polisario Front, whose international support has dwindled in recent years. But it also leaves the future of the region’s fragile ceasefire uncertain.

“MINURSO peacekeepers helped to keep a lid on escalation,'' Hamish Kinnear, a U.K.-based analyst focusing on North Africa, told The Associated Press. Its "on-the-ground presence meant there was a stronger international stake in maintaining the peace in Western Sahara, even if its key purpose — to arrange a referendum — was becoming increasingly unlikely due to the shifting diplomatic position of key powers.''
The withdrawal gives Morocco “a freer hand'' against the Polisario, Kinnear said. He predicted that Sahrawis will increasingly call for alternative strategies.
Lederer reported from New York.

title: British man being treated for Ebola in Congo is being evacuated to the UK
summary: A British man being treated for Ebola in Congo is being evacuated to the U.K., the government said Thursday
story: A British man being treated for Ebola in Congo is being evacuated to the U.K., the government said Thursday
LONDON -- A British man being treated for Ebola in Congo is being evacuated to the U.K., the government said Thursday.
The man, believed to be a healthcare worker, is the first British patient evacuated from the current outbreak of the deadly virus, and the third person to have tested positive to return to Europe.

The patient is expected to be taken to the Royal Free Hospital in London, which has a high level isolation unit that was used to treat patients from an Ebola outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.
The Foreign Office said the U.K.’s procedures for dealing with infectious diseases had been activated and the risk to the public from Ebola is low.

France confirmed a case in June in a doctor — since recovered — who had returned from a humanitarian mission in Congo. A Swiss woman believed to have contracted the virus in Uganda was medically evacuated to Geneva for treatment last month and her husband, a diplomat, was held in isolation in Zurich.

The disease spreading in some of Congo’s remotest provinces has infected 10,600 people, more than 5,100 of whom have died. It’s spread to 67 health zones across eight provinces, from three zones when it was first declared in May.

“The infection of a British healthcare worker with Ebola is deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected,” said Dr. Damien Tully, an infectious disease expert at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. “Healthcare workers are on the front line of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur.”

title: Mugabe's son faces assault charges linked to luxury car smuggling case
summary: The son of the late Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe faces assault charges after allegedly attacking an anti-corruption official
story: The son of the late Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe faces assault charges after allegedly attacking an anti-corruption official

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- A son of the late Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe appeared in a court in Harare on Thursday accused of assaulting an anti-corruption agency official during an operation linked to the alleged smuggling of two luxury vehicles into the country.
Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe arrived at the Harare Magistrates Court with four other men who were arrested with him at a lodge.
Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said Bellarmine, 29, and the four others were arrested Tuesday and face assault charges.

An anti-corruption commission spokesperson told state media Wednesday that officers had gone to the lodge to seize a Lamborghini and a Mercedes-Benz when one of the officials was assaulted. The spokesperson said the vehicles were in the country illegally.
Neither vehicle has been linked to Bellarmine, who is Mugabe’s youngest child with his second wife, Grace.
The arrest is the latest in a series of legal troubles involving members of the former president’s family in Zimbabwe and neighboring South Africa.
Bellarmine appeared in a Harare court in October on drug possession charges, but prosecutors withdrew them after his co-accused accepted responsibility for possessing cannabis.
Other cases involving Bellarmine and his older brother, Robert Jr., in recent years have largely centered on allegations of cannabis possession, assault and property damage.

In April, Bellarmine was deported from South Africa after pleading guilty to brandishing an object “likely to lead a person to believe it is a firearm” and being in the country illegally. He was ordered to pay fines totaling about $36,000 or serve two years in prison. A magistrate also ordered his immediate deportation as part of a plea deal.

Their mother, Grace Mugabe, became embroiled in a high-profile legal dispute in South Africa in 2017 after allegedly assaulting a young model she found in the company of her sons at a Johannesburg hotel. South African authorities initially granted Grace diplomatic immunity, but the country’s High Court overturned that decision in 2018 following a legal challenge.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being ousted in a military-backed coup in 2017. He died in 2019 at age 95.

title: Gas deposits off Cyprus are an opportunity for the EU, president says
summary: Cyprus's president says natural gas deposits off the country's coast offer the European Union a chance to boost energy security by diversifying supply
story: Cyprus's president says natural gas deposits off the country's coast offer the European Union a chance to boost energy security by diversifying supply

NICOSIA, Cyprus -- Natural gas deposits off the southern coastline of Cyprus are an opportunity for the European Union to bolster its own energy security by diversifying its supply, the island nation's president said Thursday.

President Nikos Christodoulides told The Associated Press in an exclusive statement that the first of a number of natural gas fields discovered off Cyprus, dubbed Cronos, is expected to start production in the first half of 2028.

“Cyprus is part of the energy equation, with Europe benefiting with added diversification and with the Union’s autonomy being anchored. This is the first step in a path that is bright,” Christodoulides said.

Europe is looking for alternative sources of energy after turning its back on Russian oil and gas following Moscow's full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while consumers are being lashed by rocketing fuel prices compounded by the Iran war.

Italian energy company Eni last month signed development contracts with eight main contractors to develop Cronos, estimated to contain around 3 trillion cubic feet (85 billion cubic meters) of the hydrocarbon.
The contracts involve subsea production systems and pipelines, a floating control unit and drilling rig services.
“The conclusion of these agreements, which trigger the commitment of billions of euros in investment, provides for a clearly defined path towards production,” said Christodoulides.

Once the gas is extracted from the field situated some 185 kilometers (115 miles) southwest of Cyprus, it will be conveyed by pipeline to Egypt’s Damietta facility where it will be liquefied and exported to international markets, primarily Europe.
The Cypriot president said production capacity is expected to reach up to 500 million standard cubic feet (14.16 million cubic meters) per day at peak production.

Christodoulides said that for the EU, the significance of Cronos “lies precisely in the opportunity to diversify its sources of supply through the development of a field in a member state and in cooperation with the region.”

Apart from Cronos, there are six other natural gas deposits found within Cyprus’ exclusive economic zone that are being considered for development, including ExxonMobil’s Glaucus and Pegasus fields situated south of Cronos.

ExxonMobil's vice president of global exploration, John Ardill, said in June that natural gas could start flowing from those two deposits by 2033. He said the gas would most likely be piped to Egypt, where it can be liquefied for export.

Christodoulides said Cronos is a “substantive step” toward the country’s first natural gas production which intersects with Europe’s broader need for “the diversification of natural gas supply sources and the enhancement of energy security.”

title: Russian captain among 2 crew found guilty by Finnish court of damaging Baltic cables
summary: A Finnish court has convicted the captain and another crew member of a cargo ship of damaging undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea last year
story: A Finnish court has convicted the captain and another crew member of a cargo ship of damaging undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea last year
HELSINKI -- A Finnish court on Thursday convicted the captain and another crew member of a cargo ship of damaging undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea late last year.

The Helsinki District Court found the two guilty of aggravated sabotage and gave them prison sentences. The captain was sentenced to three years and six months, and the boatswain to two years and 10 months. National broadcaster Yle reported that the captain is Russian and the boatswain Azerbaijani.
The court also ordered them to pay compensation for the costs of examining and repairing the cables.

The ship, the Fitburg, was flagged in St. Vincent and the Grenadines and was sailing from Russia to Israel when the incident occurred on Dec. 31. It was subsequently seized and inspected. Police said at the time that the ship had been dragging its anchor for hours when it was discovered in Finland’s exclusive economic zone.

The ship dragged its anchor along the seabed for about 130 kilometers (80 miles), damaging two telecommunications cables, according to a court statement. The statement said the anchor’s locking mechanism had been working properly and the anchor had been raised when the ship left St. Petersburg the previous day.
The indictment did not allege that the captain had explicitly ordered the anchor to be lowered, but the court found that both defendants must have known it was dragging.
Both defendants denied wrongdoing, Yle reported. The court dismissed a charge of aggravated interference with telecommunications, saying it was covered by the aggravated sabotage charges.

The cable damage was one of a string of incidents in the Baltic Sea involving ships linked to Russia. More broadly, The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe that Western officials have blamed on Russia since its invasion of Ukraine.

title: Security officer attacked and killed near Sri Lankan Embassy in Jordan's capital
summary: An assailant has attacked and killed a security officer near the Sri Lankan Embassy in Amman, Jordan, in what authorities describe as a terrorist act
story: An assailant has attacked and killed a security officer near the Sri Lankan Embassy in Amman, Jordan, in what authorities describe as a terrorist act
CAIRO -- An assailant attacked and killed a security officer near the Sri Lankan Embassy in Jordan’s capital Amman on Thursday, in what Jordanian authorities described as a terrorist act.
The attack comes weeks after gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in southern Jordan, killing nine people and wounding dozens more.

Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said that a member of its forces was assaulted with a sharp object and died “in a cowardly terrorist attack.” It said a preliminary investigation indicated the attacker had been “planning to commit the terrorist act against the officers of the General Security Directorate.”

Jordan’s state-run Al-Mamlaka TV reported that the assailant, who has been arrested, attempted to seize the weapon from the security officer who was killed. A second security officer intervened, and both the assailant and the second officer sustained injuries, Al-Mamlaka said.
The Sri Lankan Embassy confirmed the attack took place in its vicinity, but didn't elaborate.

Jordanian government spokesperson Mohamed al-Momani wrote on X that the prime minister was “closely monitoring the response of the security services to this incident.” Attacking security personnel while on duty is an “assault on the dignity of the state,” he added.

title: Russia and Ukraine trade airstrikes as reconstruction and security talks resume
summary: Russia and Ukraine have traded damaging airstrikes as talks resume in Brussels to discuss Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees
story: Russia and Ukraine have traded damaging airstrikes as talks resume in Brussels to discuss Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees

KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia and Ukraine exchanged airstrikes overnight as talks were set to resume in Brussels on Thursday on Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and security guarantees once the fighting ends.
The latest Russian aerial barrage underscored the scale of the rebuilding task, as did the ongoing search for people missing beneath rubble after a deadly airstrike in southern Ukraine on Monday.
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at Russian targets. The Russian Defense Ministry said that its forces shot down nearly 500 drones overnight.
A Ukrainian attack killed five people and wounded 13 others on Thursday in Ukraine’s Russia-occupied Luhansk region, Kremlin-installed officials said.
The strike hit a bus traveling between the regional capital, Luhansk, and a nearby town, said Leonid Pasechnik, the region’s Moscow-backed leader. Further details weren't immediately available.
Meanwhile, rescue teams continued to search for more than 30 people believed trapped in the wreckage of a former school and a nearby shelter hit by Russian guided bombs on Monday.

The attack in Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, struck as residents waited for humanitarian aid. It was one of the deadliest strikes in the region since the full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 43 people have been confirmed killed. Efforts to identify some of the victims using DNA samples from relatives were continuing. Zelenskyy said in a message on X that one person who had been reported missing was found alive.

Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said that talks were continuing for a second day at NATO headquarters in Brussels focused on postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government's Western allies.

Umerov said that the discussions with officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the European Union and NATO were also being attended by the World Bank and the U.S. investment group BlackRock.
“We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote in an online post.

The Brussels meetings are taking place days before negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at trying to end the war. Late Wednesday, Zelenskyy said that he had held a 90-minute conversation with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

“The negotiations must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. “Ukraine is ready to take the necessary steps. Our proposals are clear, and we have given them to the American side.”
Kushner posted on X that talks are focused not only on “ending this terrible war, but on the broader security architecture needed to ensure that when the fighting stops, it never starts again.”
He paid tribute to Zelenskyy and his team's “constructive engagement and commitment to finding a path forward.”

In excerpts from an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, to be aired in full on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed hope that the Democratic Party's win in the U.S. midterm elections could usher in a new era of support for Ukraine.

“We have support from two parties — support from both parties. I am also grateful to the Republicans,” Zelenskyy said. He added that the Democrats “speak of renewing the ties between the U.S. and Europe, which have been somewhat lost in recent years. And that is very important to us.”
The European Commission on Thursday sent Ukraine 4.36 billion euros ($4.9 billion) as part of a 90 billion-euro ($101 billion) loan agreed in April by EU leaders to support the embattled nation.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the money will help Ukraine fund essential spending on defense and public services.

“As Russia continues its relentless attacks, Ukraine is about to start its fifth wartime winter,” she said. “And as efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine continue, so too does the EU’s unwavering support.”

Zelenskyy took to X to thank Europe, saying the money will help fund pressing needs “such as strengthening Ukraine’s energy resilience and procuring drones, electronic warfare, and air defense assets.”

Ukraine’s air defenses shot down or suppressed 105 of 128 Russian attack drones overnight and into early Thursday, while Russian strikes wounded four people in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv regions, Ukrainian officials said.

Russian drones struck six areas in the Dnipropetrovsk region, wounding three people in the city of Dnipro, regional administrator Oleksandr Hanzha said. A Russian attack on logistics infrastructure west of the capital, Kyiv, caused a fire and wounded a man, the State Emergency Service said.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that its forces shot down 496 Ukrainian drones over 13 Russian regions overnight, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which was annexed by Russia, and the Black and Azov Seas.
More than 200 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, wounding one person, local governor Pavel Malkov said.

Malkov said that falling debris from the attack damaged power lines and sparked a fire at an industrial site. Russian media outlets later reported a blaze at Ryazan oil refinery, sharing pictures of plumes of smoke and the night sky glowing red.
Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, and Katie Marie Davies in Manchester, England, contributed to this report.

title: Japan's Sony reports a hefty profit on the back of its blockbuster 'Spider-Man' movie
summary: Japanese electronics and entertainment company Sony has reported a 44% surge in its profit in July-September, largely on the box office success of its movie, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”
story: Japanese electronics and entertainment company Sony has reported a 44% surge in its profit in July-September, largely on the box office success of its movie, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”

TOKYO -- Japanese electronics and entertainment company Sony reported Thursday a 44% surge in its profit for the July-September quarter, largely on the box office success of its movie, “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”

Sony Group Corp.’s profit in the last quarter totaled 449.6 billion yen ($2.8 billion), up from nearly 311 billion yen in the same period a year earlier. Quarterly sales edged up 10% to 3.4 trillion yen.
Apart from its hit film, continuing strong demand for Sony’s PlayStation game consoles helped boost the Tokyo-based company’s bottom line.

Sony sold 2.6 million PlayStation 5 consoles in the second quarter, compared with 4 million a year ago. The PlayStation 5 went on sale starting in 2020, and sales for such machines tend to decline with time.
Like other technology companies, Sony is facing the problem of a computer chip shortage because of the artificial intelligence boom.
But, as with other Japanese giant exporters, it has benefitted from the weakness of the Japanese yen, which raises the value of the company’s overseas earnings when converted into yen.
The U.S. dollar has been trading at about 158 Japanese yen lately, up from about 154 yen a year ago.
By business segment, Sony said its operating profit and sales rose for the latest quarter in its games, music and pictures operations.

Sony, which makes the Walkman portable audio player, Xperia smartphones and Bravia TV sets, raised its profit forecast for the full fiscal year through March 2027 to 1.3 trillion yen from an earlier 1.2 trillion yen.
The new projection would mark an improvement from Sony's 1 trillion yen net profit in the previous fiscal year.
Sony's shares closed 7% higher in Tokyo trading, shortly before its financial results were announced.

title: More than a dozen flights in Europe receive bomb threats that an official calls 'malicious' hoaxes
summary: Authorities say that bomb threats have targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases
story: Authorities say that bomb threats have targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases

MILAN -- Bomb threats targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe on Thursday, leading to a slew of emergency landings and military escorts in some cases, authorities said. No hazardous or suspicious materials have been found in what a British official called “malicious" hoaxes.

Several similar threats targeted planes earlier this week, prompting searches and diversions. Europe has experienced a slew of other disruptions recently, such as attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions  and mysterious triggers to alert apps.

While fake bomb threats are relatively common, it is unusual to see so many in a single day. They come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.
It wasn't known whether this week's threats were linked, who sent them or what they hoped to achieve.

An email containing the threat to Rome-bound planes was sent on behalf of a group that described itself as anti-feminist, according to a copy provided by an airport official and reviewed by The Associated Press. An official from another European airport said the threat they received also came from a group calling itself anti-feminist, and used some of the same language. It wasn't clear if the same group sent the two threats. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to share the information.
At Rome's airport, travelers whose flights weren't affected seemed to take the threats in stride.

“As of now, I am not scared of being in an airport or getting on board a plane," said Alessia Strada, a 19-year-old Italian returning from Kenya. "Probably this idea I have about traveling in Europe will change in the near future, but let’s see how it goes.”
Alex Langenkamper, a 38-year-old German headed to Munich, said “crazy people” exist and will in the future.
Meanwhile, Michael Romano, a 54-year-old traveler headed to Colombia, expressed concern about the world moving toward war.
“These things never used to happen here in Europe,” he said. "This is all new, so it is a little bit scary.”

Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels, said the threats were “stress-testing” how European governments and airport officials respond, and whether their responses were coordinated.

The idea behind the threats “appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe” and could have “cascading effects” — like economic damage and costs related to inspection, investigation and cleaning aircraft.

Joji Waites, who heads flight safety at the British Airline Pilots’ Association, said the industry has put in place “proved mechanisms” for dealing with such threats, including a team of assessors to grade the level of threat in a red-amber-green color-coding system, quick notification of flight crews, and the evacuation of planes on the ground.

Each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000, on a par with the possible costs of dealing with an unruly passenger, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.

“And that’s because you might end up with the crew going out of hours. You might need replacement crew. You have got passengers that miss their flight connections," Baum said. "It knocks everything out of sync for the rest of the day for the airline in question.”
Military escorts cost money, too, which would be borne by governments rather than airlines, he added.
Britain's transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told British broadcasters that flights across Europe have been hit by “malicious hoax threats.”
European Union Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas told reporters in Dublin that it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked.”
“National investigations remain ongoing,” he said, adding that an EU information-sharing mechanism on aviation security had been activated.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in France after receiving a threat, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux, which was under high alert, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.
Lecornu ordered warplanes to intercept the plane because the pilot “didn’t cooperate as expected with the authorities,” his office said. It declined to comment further.
Hours after the flight landed, the plane was sitting on the tarmac with a Red Cross vehicle nearby while explosive experts with dogs examined it.
An investigation was opened by French aviation security authorities. The regional prosecutor, Remi Coutin, said in a statement that the pilot and co-pilot were questioned about what happened.

Italian air force fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight that departed Helsinki bound for Rome after a threat was received by email, the air force said in a statement. Croatia's defense ministry said one of its fighter planes first intercepted the commercial jet in Croatian airspace before handing it off to the Italians.

Finnair said that two of its flights, including the one that received the military escort and landed safely in Rome, “faced unfounded hoax bomb scares.” The other flight, operated by Jettime from Helsinki to Vienna, landed safely at its destination, and was expected to return to service after an inspection, Finnair said.

Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, meanwhile, also received military escorts and made emergency landings after bomb threats, officials said. Two of the flights — one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid — landed safely in Sofia, airport officials told reporters. The third, from London, was diverted and landed safely in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second-largest city, Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshev said.
Several flights across Europe received bomb threats earlier this week, officials said.

The flights included ones operated by Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary upon receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured.
A slew of other flights were disrupted Thursday. Among those incidents:

— Czech police said searches of four planes that landed in Prague after being targeted by bomb threats turned up nothing. They haven't given details on where the flights originated, and said they took precautions despite not finding the threats credible.
— A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said.
— A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in the Romanian capital following a bomb threat, airport spokesman Teo Postelnicu said. Checks turned up no bomb.

— A flight to Warsaw landed in Vienna after Polish authorities received a threatening email, said Stefan Loidl, a police spokesperson in the Lower Austria province. Nothing was found and the plane continued to Warsaw. He said there was also an abstract threat to Vienna Airport concerning four other flights, which he declined to identify, but operations weren't disrupted.
- Air Serbia said a flight from Belgrade to Bucharest received a bomb threat that turned out to be a hoax. The plane landed in Bucharest, underwent checks and resumed operating.
Charlton reported from Paris and Biller from Rome. Associated Press writers throughout Europe contributed to this report.

title: French unions unite for nationwide strikes, piling pressure on Macron's government
summary: Hundreds of thousands of trade union members have joined nationwide strikes and demonstrations in France to demand higher wages and support the high school protest movement
story: Hundreds of thousands of trade union members have joined nationwide strikes and demonstrations in France to demand higher wages and support the high school protest movement

PARIS -- Hundreds of thousands of trade union members joined nationwide strikes and demonstrations on Thursday to demand higher wages and support the high school protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.
After more than a month of large, recurring protests across France, major rallies took place again in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and elsewhere.

An official close to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that by early afternoon around 270,000 people had joined the union action in 180 rallies outside of the capital, and that most of them were peaceful.
The official, however, noted some violence in the cities of Lyon, Nantes, Pau, Orléans, Rennes and Toulouse.

Students also held fresh protests. About a third of France’s high schools were closed or unable to operate, some because of student blockades and others because teachers were on strike. Public transportation was heavily disrupted. Police in the northeastern city of Strasbourg urged people to exercise extreme caution near certain schools.
The Eiffel Tower was also closed.

The atmosphere was joyful and relaxed despite heavy security at the capital’s Place de la République, where Thursday’s march was due to begin in the early afternoon. Rioters had clashed with police there during protests marred by looting on Oct. 17.
Protesters carrying trade union flags gathered as hundreds of musicians played string, brass and percussion instruments, accompanied by singers.
Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers were being deployed, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters. Police have been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics.
Many demonstrations have been marred by violence, much of it committed by masked rioters who do not support the students’ or workers’ demands.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said “masked individuals” tried to block roads in Rennes on Thursday. They said young people, often accompanied by adults, committed “serious acts of violence,” including throwing steel balls at police.

France’s main unions warned that the country is on the brink of recession and that layoff plans are multiplying. “Fuel, food products, rent, gas, electricity … everything’s going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement.
France is mired in debt and is one of the worst economic performers in Europe, along with Italy and Belgium.
The unions put President Emmanuel Macron’s government and employers on notice.
“Anger is immense,” they said. “The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay.”
Fabien Villedieu, national secretary of the SUD-Rail union, took aim at the government and the French rail company, SNCF.

“When the government is not reasonable, when the head of the SNCF is not reasonable — bosses in general are not reasonable — and when they’re not reasonable, we simply do what we’ve always done in France, which is to go on strike,” he told The Associated Press at the Gare de Lyon station in Paris.

Before the strike action, the government had been negotiating with unions — a familiar scenario in French politics — in hopes of limiting the rioting, which has resulted in France's worst civil unrest in years.

The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.

The rallies come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political parties seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favorite to win.

Some candidates, including veteran far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, propose radical solutions that appear difficult to implement, said Paul Smith, an associate professor of French history and politics at the University of Nottingham in England.

“There is a sense of absolute frustration at the government’s failure to operate,” Smith said in an interview. “Whoever wins the presidential election is going to have a stack of problems to cope with.”
“It’s very difficult to see exactly where things go,” he said.
Lorne Cook contributed to this report from Brussels.

title: Toyota raises profit projection for the year as sales hold up
summary: Toyota has reported a 19% drop in fiscal second-quarter profit but raises its full-year forecast
story: Toyota has reported a 19% drop in fiscal second-quarter profit but raises its full-year forecast
TOKYO -- Japan’s top automaker Toyota reported Thursday that its fiscal second-quarter profit fell 19% from a year ago but raised its full-year profit forecast.
Toyota Motor Corp.’s July-September net profit fell to 759.4 billion yen ($4.8 billion) from 932 billion yen for the same period a year ago.

Quarterly sales rose to 13.4 trillion yen from 12.4 trillion yen, despite headwinds from U.S. tariffs, as well as supply disruptions and rising raw material costs caused by the war in the Middle East.

Toyota is now projecting a 3.57 trillion yen profit for the full fiscal year through March 2027, up from an earlier forecast for 3.25 trillion yen. Its profit for the previous fiscal year totaled 3.8 trillion yen.
Toyota, which makes the Prius hybrid and Lexus luxury models, sold 4.76 million vehicles in the first fiscal half, down from 4.78 million the previous year.
It expects to sell 9.7 million vehicles globally for the full fiscal year, up from nearly 9.6 million sold the previous fiscal year.

Like other Japanese exporters, Toyota benefits from a weak yen, which raises the value of its overseas revenue when translated into yen. The U.S. dollar has been trading at about 158 Japanese yen, up from 154 yen a year ago.

By region, Toyota’s China vehicle sales have suffered, partly because of surging gasoline prices. Toyota’s sales remained strong in the U.S., while holding up in Japan, its main global markets, as well as Europe.

In Japan, the models that sold well recently included the RAV4, bZ4X and Land Cruiser FJ sport-utility vehicles. In the U.S., the Camry and RAV4 hybrids were popular, according to Toyota. Overall sales in Asia remained flat, but sales grew in Indonesia and Thailand.
Toyota officials said the company mitigated the impact of rising raw material prices by optimizing its global supply network and maintaining strong sales.
For the first half of the fiscal year, Toyota reported a 2.2 trillion yen profit, up from nearly 1.8 trillion yen, on revenue of 26.96 trillion yen, up from 24.6 trillion yen.
Toyota shares jumped in Tokyo trading after the earnings results were announced to about 3,500 yen from about 3,200 yen.

title: The leader of a German conservative party is found dead at a Berlin hotel
summary: Hubert Aiwanger, leader of a conservative party influential in Bavarian politics, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel
story: Hubert Aiwanger, leader of a conservative party influential in Bavarian politics, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel
BERLIN -- Hubert Aiwanger, the leader of a conservative party that has become a mainstay of Bavarian politics and sought to expand its influence across Germany, has been found dead at a Berlin hotel.

Berlin police and prosecutors said the body of Aiwanger, who was Bavaria's deputy governor and the southern state's economy minister, was found in his hotel room in the center of the capital on Wednesday evening. An investigation into the cause of death was opened.

German news agency dpa reported, without naming sources, that the 55-year-old Aiwanger had planned to make a speech Wednesday afternoon at the opening of a Berlin office of his party, the Free Voters, but pulled out of the event for health reasons.
Aiwanger had been the party's leader in Bavaria since 2006 and its national leader since 2010.

The combative politician with a strong regional accent and a populist touch made his party a serious rival to Bavaria's long-dominant Christian Social Union, which is part of the center-right bloc that currently leads Germany. On his watch, it entered the state legislature in Munich in 2008. Ten years later, when the CSU lost its majority in the state legislature, it entered Bavaria's government as the junior coalition partner.

Shortly before Bavaria's 2023 election, Aiwanger faced a furor that started with allegations — denied by the politician — that he was responsible for an antisemitic flyer when he was a high school student 35 years earlier. The Free Voters emerged unscathed from the election, gaining support and remained part of the state government.
Aiwanger's party has made only limited inroads outside Bavaria and he wasn't able to lead it into the national parliament.
Bavarian governor Markus Söder wrote on X that “the sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy.”
Aiwanger is survived by his partner, Free Voters politician Tanja Schweiger, and two children.

title: Troops deployed to secure Jakarta trial as tensions remain high over wiretap scandal
summary: Indonesian authorities have tasked thousands of police and military personnel to secure a court appearance of former President Joko Widodo, as tensions remain high in the capital over a wiretapping scandal involving senior police officers
story: Indonesian authorities have tasked thousands of police and military personnel to secure a court appearance of former President Joko Widodo, as tensions remain high in the capital over a wiretapping scandal involving senior police officers

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesian authorities tasked thousands of police and military personnel to provide security Thursday for a trial involving former President Joko Widodo, as tensions in the capital remained high over allegations that top officers had been involved in intercepting the current president's telephone conversations.
Three senior generals have already been detained in the wiretapping scandal, including Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who had been named chief of staff to President Prabowo Subianto last month.

Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, though the former president has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation. There are allegations that Cabinet officials, politicians, journalists, civil society leaders and business executives were also subjected to unauthorized surveillance.

After losing two presidential races to Widodo, Prabowo aligned himself with the popular leader and campaigned as his successor, choosing Widodo’s son as his running mate in a move that fueled concerns about a growing political dynasty in Indonesia’s young democracy.

Widodo and Prabowo were once close political allies, with Widodo backing Prabowo’s successful 2024 presidential bid, but their relationship has come under increased scrutiny amid signs of a growing rift since Prabowo took office.
Neither has commented on the wiretapping case.

Retired police Gen. Oegroseno, a former deputy national police chief, told the Forum Keadilan TV podcast on Wednesday that investigators should examine all possible lines of command behind the wiretapping, including whether any directives originated from Widodo.

“Investigators should not hesitate to question a former president if necessary,” Oegroseno said. “The motive behind the alleged wiretapping operation must be fully uncovered under the leadership of the current police chief.”

The wiretapping operation could also constitute a serious human rights violation and could be used to intimidate critics and weaken civil liberties, said Usman Hamid, Amnesty International's executive director in Indonesia.

“This is not merely about the alleged wiretapping of the president,” Hamid said in a statement. “Authorities must disclose who else may have been targeted and investigate the full impact of the operation.”

Police allege the unauthorized wiretapping took place between 2025 and 2026, after Prabowo had been elected and while Listyo was still national police chief. National Police Legal Division head Sonta Nasution and Eko Hadi Santoso, a senior instructor at the National Police Education and Training Institute, were also detained.

Authorities have called in more than 20,000 troops to Jakarta, and on Thursday said that 6,770 police and military personnel had been deployed to secure Widodo's hearing. Widodo was called to testify in a defamation trial stemming from allegations that he used a fake university diploma. The trial is unrelated to the wiretapping case and Widodo denied the diploma allegations.
As he arrived Thursday morning at the East Jakarta District Court, the former president was welcomed by hundreds of his supporters chanting messages of encouragement.
The presidential palace has said the wiretaps were being considered an “act of treason” that endangered state interests, but has not linked the deployment of troops to Jakarta to the case.

East Jakarta Police chief Alfian Nurrizal said that the deployment for the hearing was a precautionary measure due to potential security risks and large crowds, and that most of the forces were being held on standby.
Indonesian military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Muhammad Nas previously said that the deployment of the 20,000 marines and other personnel to Jakarta was a “normal occurrence."

Despite the number of troops sent to Jakarta, there has also been no visible military presence on the streets and authorities have said most are being held in reserve in barracks and other facilities.
Associated Press writer David Rising in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Bank of England welcomes energy price falls since US midterms after first hike in nearly 3 years
summary: The Bank of England is raising interest rates for the first time in more than three years in an effort to tackle an inflation shock stoked by the Iran war
story: The Bank of England is raising interest rates for the first time in more than three years in an effort to tackle an inflation shock stoked by the Iran war

LONDON -- The Bank of England indicated Thursday that the sharp decline in energy prices after the U.S. midterm elections — if sustained — could limit the prospect of further interest rate hikes in the coming months.
After raising its main interest rate for the first time in more than three years to 4% from 3.75%, the bank said the outlook for U.K. borrowing costs largely hinges on what happens with the Iran war.

“We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours," Bank Gov. Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing following the first interest rate hike since August 2023. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.”

The heavy losses suffered by the Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections have been followed by a sharp drop in energy prices. Many believe that it’s now less likely that U.S. President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran, with Democrats gaining control of Congress early next year following their big wins this week. Many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday, blamed the war for the party’s poor performance at the ballot box.
Though Brent crude is down around $15 a barrel this week, trading at $96, that is still more than $30 more expensive than it was at this time last year.

If the decline in oil and gas prices is sustained over the coming weeks, then the expected peak in inflation next summer — which the bank anticipates will reach 5% — could be lower. That could temper the need for future rate hikes, and not just by the Bank of England.

Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently in response to the higher inflation stoked by the Iran war, and their interest rate strategies are largely contingent on what happens to energy prices.
Bailey said Thursday's hike “shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes” but stressed that the outlook depends on what happens in the war with Iran.
“Unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.
For hard-pressed households facing higher mortgage rates and businesses paying more to access capital, the hope is that Thursday’s rate hike will be the last for some time.
“The path for interest rates is hanging in the balance, with U.S.-Iran hostilities holding the key," said Suren Thiru, ICAEW's chief economist.
The decision to raise interest rates was unanimous given the pickup in inflation this year, though one of the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed an even bigger increase, to 4.25%.

The pressure on rate-setters has grown steadily in recent months. When inflation hit an 11-month high of 3.5% in September — well above the bank's 2% target — it cemented market expectations of a rate hike this month, with potentially more to come in 2027.

The main cause of the spike in inflation this year has been the sharp rise in fuel costs resulting from the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies and pushed prices at the pump and household energy bills higher.
“There is now enough inflationary pressure in the pipeline caused by the rise in energy prices that an increase in Bank rate is warranted," Bailey said.
Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.

title: A still-recovering pope will head home to Latin America and his beloved Peru for a 12-day trip
summary: Pope Leo XIV is embarking on the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate three weeks after lung cancer surgery
story: Pope Leo XIV is embarking on the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate three weeks after lung cancer surgery

VATICAN CITY -- Three weeks after lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV is embarking on the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate: a 12-day, three-nation tour of Latin America that carries more personal and historic weight than any of his voyages to date.

The U.S.-born Leo is returning home to Peru, where the former Robert Prevost lived for two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be the pastor he is today. Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and is so attached to Peru’s people he gave them a shoutout in Spanish from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica on the night of his election.

Leo is also going to Argentina, the home of his predecessor, Pope Francis, to whom Leo owes his pontificate. It will be a homecoming of sorts there, too, since Francis never returned to Argentina after his 2013 election, leaving a complicated legacy that Leo will now have to navigate.

Leo starts his trip Friday in Uruguay, the least Catholic, most secular country in all of Latin America, where not even the big Catholic feast days get their due: Christmas in Uruguay is officially “Family Day” and Holy Week is “Tourism Week.”

Leo is nevertheless expected to draw huge crowds throughout his trip and will likely raise issues of concern to his still-young pontificate: economic injustice, the plight of Indigenous peoples and the Amazon, and the church’s dreadful legacy of clergy sexual abuse.
But many eyes will be on Leo himself for having confirmed this grueling trip at all so soon after surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

When doctors announced that Leo required no further treatment, they also said there was no reason why he couldn't make the Nov. 6-17 trip. It includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides covering 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), the longest of Leo’s pontificate.

While popes always travel with ample medical care, the Vatican said no special or additional provisions are planned for Leo, including when the 71-year-old travels to Cusco, Peru, at an altitude of 3,400 meters (11,200 feet).
“We’re not talking of a permanent condition,” said Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni. “We’re talking about something that you heal from, because it is surgery.”

No leg of the trip is more anticipated than the final stop in Peru, with Leo’s arrival in Lima, and after that Chiclayo, his beloved former diocese that he headed from 2015-2023, when Francis summoned him to Rome.
“He is so excited. He personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief.

Leo told the region’s bishops in September that it was in Peru where he “came to know firsthand the faith of a people from whom I received so much, and I came to understand better what it means to be a shepherd.”

Alvarado said Peru “opened his eyes” to the diverse needs of the church and how the church encounters its flock. “This is a place that gave him his ministry and inspired who he is as a pastor,” she said.

Alvarado predicted that Leo will speak off-the-cuff in Spanish throughout the visit and will show his true feelings much in the same way he did in June during his visit to Spain, where the world saw a much more relaxed and happy Leo than the reserved, quiet one often on display in Rome.
“You will see that again but in a totally different way because he knows these streets,” she said.

Francis befuddled friends and foes alike for the duration of his 13-year pontificate, because he never returned home. He had plenty of opportunities, including during his first trip as pope to Rio de Janeiro, and subsequent trips to the region, including to neighboring Chile and Bolivia.

“How many times, I and other people asked him,” confided one of Francis’ closest friends at the Vatican, Guzmán Carriquiry, the former head of the Vatican’s pontifical commission for Latin America. “But it was useless, useless! He’d respond with jokes, by staying silent or getting irritated if you insisted.”

Carriquiry said Leo was coming to Argentina to “fill a void that has remained,” much in the same way Leo has undertaken trips to Spain and France — two once staunchly Christian European countries that Francis stubbornly refused to visit, preferring instead more far-flung “peripheral” places.

María Marcela Mazzini, an Argentine theologian who participated in Francis’ 2015 big meeting on the family, attributed Francis’ reluctance to return to Argentina’s complicated political polarization during his pontificate.

“We understand,” she said. “Things are contextual. I believe the people never doubted the pope’s affection. They always felt he was close to them and now we’re also watching with great joy as Pope Leo” continues his legacy.
“So we’re waiting for him with open arms,” she said.

The Argentine leg of the trip, however, is likely to be the most politically delicate, given the clear differences of priorities and styles of the reserved, pensive Leo and those of President Javier Milei, a self-described “anarcho-capitalist” who once described Francis as a “filthy leftist” and “representative of evil on Earth."

Leo Guardado, associate professor of theology at Fordham University, said he expected Milei’s push to attract AI investment and data centers to Argentina will be a point of discussion, given Leo’s concern about AI’s impact on humanity and the environment.

The visit begins in Uruguay, the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.

More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation over the strong opposition of the Catholic Church, evidence of Uruguay's entrenched, church-state separation that prohibits any mention of God in oaths of office.

“Uruguay is by far the most secularized nation in Latin America. It’s pretty much like a Western European nation,” said Andrew Chesnut, chair of Catholic studies and an expert in the Latin American church at Virginia Commonwealth University.

All of which begs the question of why Leo would bother spending three days of a 12-day trip in a country of 3.5 million people, only a third of whom identify as Catholic and a fraction of whom actually goes to Mass regularly.
Alvarado had a ready reply: ”Why not?”

Leo is expected to make clear church teaching on abortion and euthanasia. But he is likely to also recall Uruguay's strong Catholic roots from the Spanish colonial era, most significantly on Sunday when he marks an important Catholic feast day that is intrinsically connected to Uruguay's 1825 declaration of independence and nationhood.

“He is going to meet people and meet hearts and hopefully inspire them to look again for the places where the church was big and now is small," Alvarado said. His message to today's religious “nones,” or nonbelievers, is: “Reconsider.”
