title: Lured into an online scam network, an African man spent almost a year in Cambodia trying to go home
summary: In Cambodia, workers carried out online scams against people worldwide from inside massive fortified buildings they weren't allowed to leave
story: In Cambodia, workers carried out online scams against people worldwide from inside massive fortified buildings they weren't allowed to leave

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- The 33-year-old man, lured to Cambodia with the offer of a receptionist job, endured daily beatings for a month, locked in a dark room somewhere in the Southeast Asian country. He didn't know where he was, but he knew the price of his freedom: $6,000.

He had arrived from Ghana in November 2025 with the promise of a $1,000-a-month job — way more than he could make back home. At a training session he was taught to promote work-from-home “jobs” to people online, dangling the prospect of easy money.
He soon realized it was a scam, he said, and wanted out. That's when the beatings began.

“It’s not a joke the way they threaten you, they’ll beat you to your core,” the man told The Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution from the scam enterprise — which, he said, seized his passport — as well as the recruiter who got him into it.

For the next month, he said he endured beatings with fists, sometimes a bat and was shocked with tasers until the scam center was raided by Cambodian police in January as part of a nationwide campaign to shut down the criminal operations. Months later, he still cannot grip with his left hand after his wrist was broken during the abuse.

Online scam operations have flourished in Cambodia, as well as in Myanmar and Laos, since the COVID-19 pandemic, a multibillion dollar industry where workers carried out web-based scams from inside massive fortified complexes, living in dormitories they weren't allowed to leave. Some came knowing they were signing up for something illegal. But many, like the Ghanaian man, were baited with false promises of high-paying jobs through complex human trafficking webs. Cambodia was home to at least 182 confirmed scam locations, according to data collected by CyberScamMonitor, a watchdog that tracks them, though it has evidence of roughly 300.

Facing international pressure in late 2025 after the death of a South Korean student forced into such an operation and the U.S. indictment of the Chinese-born founder of a Cambodian conglomerate behind a massive cryptocurrency scam, Cambodia kicked its crackdown into high gear.

But even as it closed down dozens of scam centers, Cambodia has not prosecuted the criminal operatives behind the schemes or the elites who helped them flourish by providing financing, facilities and connections to the highest echelons of Cambodia's government — including senior politicians and relatives of Prime Minister Hun Manet, according to the U.S. Congress, which has called for sanctions.

After the raids ramped up in January, tens of thousands of former workers ended up in the capital, Phnom Penh, many sleeping in the streets. Some faced police harassment and arbitrary detentions. More than 10 months later, hundreds remain stranded.

“The government generally treats migrants found trapped in scam centers as offenders, and we have seen no evidence of adequate efforts to screen them for internationally recognized indicators of human trafficking,” said Li Ling, of the Eos Collective, a nonprofit dedicated to investigating human trafficking, which has helped 220 stranded workers return home.

Cambodia said in September, that it had dismantled all the larger compounds, and was prosecuting court cases linked to the scams. Last month, it said it seized assets worth $1 billion from one alleged scam network and called on Interpol to help track down 29 ringleaders. But it provided no evidence it was taking action against the Cambodian political and business elites behind the operations.

“They need to begin holding accountable evidenced elite perpetrators, not concocted, mid-level token investigations, but the ... Cabinet-level members, senators and members of the prime minister's family,” said Jacob Daniel Sims, a transnational crime expert and visiting fellow at Harvard University’s Asia Center.

Cambodian Information Minister Neth Pheaktra did not respond to detailed AP questions sent via Telegram for this report concerning Cambodia's treatment of scam workers, the calls for prosecutions of its senior politicians, or further information about any criminal cases it is carrying out.

In response to AP questions earlier this year about the treatment of former scam workers caught up in the crackdown, Pheaktra said Cambodia “rejects claims that it is failing trafficking victims or tolerating abuse linked to scam compounds.”

"All individuals are screened to separate victims from perpetrators, with victims receiving protection, shelter, medical care and assistance for safe return,” he said, without providing evidence of any such process.

The Ghanaian man, a university graduate who speaks English fluently, couldn't find a job in his special education field and, struggling to support his family of four, was working as a farmer. Then an acquaintance told him about what sounded like a dream opportunity: A Chinese company was looking for an English-speaking receptionist with IT skills in Cambodia.

“He told me I will be paid $1,000. The company is going to provide me with accommodation and with food,” the man said. He interviewed online and within days had a job offer, a visa and a flight paid for by the company.

There were early warning signs once he arrived in Cambodia: He was driven several hours from the airport to an unknown location, where he said his cellphone and passport were seized. He was given a two-year contract instead of one year like he'd agreed to. When he hesitated to sign, burly men threatened him.
He signed, and soon was training to be a “chatter.”

While scams differ from operation to operation, a “chatter's” job is to solicit as many people online as possible, with a simple text message like “hello,” or something more targeted, like “are you able to work weekends?” Then comes the pitch, often using a script.
Once the victim engages in a back-and-forth, a supervisor experienced in emotional manipulation takes over to build a relationship and entice the victim to hand over their money.
The Ghanaian man said he refused to work when he realized what the job was. But he didn't have the $6,000 demanded in repayment for bringing him to Cambodia.

After Cambodia's crackdown, workers who had money to buy a plane ticket home got out quickly. Others went on to find similar work in other countries. But thousands wanted to go home, couldn't afford it and got no help from their home countries.
The Ghanaian man headed to Phnom Penh, where he slept on the streets and went without food for two or three days at a time.
Henry Kyeyune, from Uganda, also slept on the street for months.

He eventually sought shelter at Caritas, a Catholic-run charity that was the only refuge for the ex-workers after the government issued a ban on providing them housing. It was full, but he slept on the ground outside in hopes of getting a spot.

While there are no comprehensive figures for how many workers left the compounds, reports from nearby countries provide a glimpse into the size and diversity of the workforce. China said in June it had repatriated more than 20,000 workers linked to scam centers, according to state broadcaster CCTV. One border province in Vietnam said it received more than 1,700 ex-workers in the first half of 2026. The Indonesian Embassy said in September it had received requests from 12,940 Indonesians for help getting home and that another 700 remain stuck in the country.

Betty O. Bigombe, Uganda’s ambassador to Malaysia, said she has helped more than 1,000 former workers navigate the complexities of getting out, mostly Ugandans like Kyeyune, but also Africans from other countries as more workers were lured into the operations from the continent.

Changing government policies were a major obstacle for the ex-workers. Many no longer had their passports and faced fines for remaining in Cambodia without proper visas. The government also started requiring interviews with immigration authorities to leave, said Li of the Eos Collective.
There were roundups by police in which ex-workers were taken to detention centers, where they'd be stuck until they could get a ticket home.

Kyeyune said he'd been sleeping outside the Caritas shelter for a week when he and others were detained. He was held for two weeks at a police station, then taken to a detention center known as Mango 2.
He spent another week there, sleeping on the floor, crowded with other workers before Bigombe helped him get a flight home.
“They keep it like a prison, we weren’t allowed to go outside,” Kyeyune said.
The Cambodian government did not respond to AP questions about why workers were taken into detention and the treatment they faced there.

The Ghanaian man was also detained in Mango 2. He was held for two weeks before he was suddenly removed by authorities in handcuffs and taken to the airport on Oct. 14. He boarded a plane to Ghana with a ticket provided by the Eos Collective.
Almost a year had passed since he arrived in Cambodia.

At times he'd thought about not going home, he said, so ashamed by what he'd gotten mixed up in and not wanting to face his family's disapproval. His father died while he was in Cambodia, and he said he failed in his duty to help bury him.

Now back in Ghana, he said he worries about how he will rebuild his life. He doesn't have the money to travel to his family's home, far from the capital. He can't even afford to buy data for his phone.
“I’m still not with my family yet, because I couldn’t transport myself there," he wrote in a text message. "I'm still not safe yet.”

title: Former Chinese Politburo member Ma Xingrui charged with taking bribes
summary: China's state media say a former member of one of China’s top decision-making bodies has been formally charged with accepting bribes a week after Communist Party leaders confirmed his expulsion from the party
story: China's state media say a former member of one of China’s top decision-making bodies has been formally charged with accepting bribes a week after Communist Party leaders confirmed his expulsion from the party

BEIJING -- A former member of one of China’s top decision-making bodies has been formally charged with accepting bribes, state media reported Thursday, a week after Communist Party leaders confirmed his expulsion from the party.

Prosecutors in Yichang, a city in the central province of Hubei, accused Ma Xingrui of using his leadership positions to accept “exceptionally large” bribes and to secure benefits for others, while also accepting financial assets himself, Xinhua state news agency said.

Ma had been named to the Politburo in 2022 and his downfall became public in April, when authorities said he was being investigated for severe violations of party discipline and national laws, without providing details.

He had served in leadership positions for China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, a state-owned company in charge of aspects of China's space program, as well as the party secretary of Shenzhen, China's technology hub, as well as the Politburo. Prosecutors accused him of using the benefits and powers afforded to him in these positions to carry out his crimes, according to Xinhua, without providing more detail on how he did so.

He was the latest senior official to fall in Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s long-running anti-corruption campaign, a policy reinforced at last week’s closed-door meeting of the Central Committee’s fifth plenum, where the leaders adopted a resolution on strengthening discipline and combating corruption.
The leaders also ratified the expulsions of more than 30 senior officials from the party, including Ma and one who was until early this year the army’s top general.
The Politburo had 24 members before three were recently purged — Ma and two military generals.
Analysts have said that the campaign is a way to enforce loyalty to Xi as well as root out corruption.

Ma was the Communist Party chief of the Xinjiang region until 2025, and before that the governor of Guangdong province, the manufacturing powerhouse bordering Hong Kong in China’s south. In the Chinese system, the party leader outranks the governor in a province or region.

title: Hong Kong's Joshua Wong is spending years of his adult life in prison
summary: Joshua Wong, once a rising political star in Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, has been sentenced again under Beijing's national security law
story: Joshua Wong, once a rising political star in Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, has been sentenced again under Beijing's national security law

HONG KONG -- Some 15 years ago, then-high school student Joshua Wong was a rising political star in Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement. Now 30, he has been sentenced for the second time under a Beijing-imposed national security law that effectively crushed the movement he once championed.
Critics say Wong’s imprisonment reflects the authorities’ determination to keep prominent dissidents behind bars. But Beijing views him as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence.
Here is what to know about the activist.

Wong became a household name in the city as a teenage activist in 2012 when he and his now-dissolved group, Scholarism, protested against the introduction of national education in schools. Thousands of people gathered outside the government headquarters, some launching hunger strikes.
Wong, then 15, already spoke like an experienced politician.

Louis Lee, a former Scholarism member, recalled sleeping on the streets for days as a high school student during their protests, fearing that their demonstrations might end like the deadly crackdown on the 1989 Tiananmen Square student-led movement in Beijing, which involved hunger strikes.
But the Hong Kong government eventually shelved its plans, and Lee felt their efforts made things a little better.
Lee described Wong as a demanding leader who kept a close eye on the group’s work. He still remembers Wong’s phone number because Wong had called him too often.
“Back then, the Scholarism members always joked that he was a merciless boss,” Lee said.

Wong was a poster boy of the 2014 Umbrella Movement, in which protesters used umbrellas to fend off police pepper spray. During the protests, also known as Occupy Central, demonstrators occupied major thoroughfares for 79 days in an ultimately unsuccessful push for direct election for the city’s leader.
Scholar Chan Kin-man, a leader of the 2014 movement, had mixed feelings about Wong back then.
Although he wasn’t a key decision-maker in the movement, Wong’s speeches stirred crowds with a political energy rare for his age, and his activism was viewed as “David taking on Goliath,” Chan said.

Chan also felt Wong acted on his beliefs, though sometimes without telling others in advance. Wong stormed into a fenced-off forecourt in front of government headquarters days before the planned start of the Occupy protest, without first informing Chan. The turnout swelled beyond what Chan had planned.

Another student group was also caught off guard when Wong and other Scholarism members launched a hunger strike near the end of the movement, Chan said. Some were concerned at the time about Wong's political calculations, he said.
When Beijing didn't budge during the 2014 movement, some young activists began advocating for Hong Kong’s independence.
Wong took a different path and co-founded a political party called Demosisto in 2016, advocating for self-determination and striving for a referendum on the city's political future.
But later, a Chinese official said “self-determination” equates to Hong Kong independence.

During the leaderless anti-government protests in 2019, Wong played a less prominent role on the streets but worked on seeking overseas support. He urged U.S. politicians to pass the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act.
Beijing criticized him for “begging for interference."
As the national security law loomed, he urged the U.S. to sanction China. But Demosisto disbanded when the law took effect.
Beijing said the law was necessary for the city’s stability.

Wong has been arrested and jailed repeatedly for his activism over the years. In 2024, he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison for a separate national security case over his role in an unofficial primary in 2020.
On Thursday, he received a prison term of 10 years after pleading guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security.

Chan said Wong once asked him to send “Letters to Olga,” a collection of letters Czech dissident Václav Havel wrote to his wife from prison before becoming president. Wong told him in a letter that he reflected on being not just a politician, but a better person, including a better son.
“He was a political machine,” Chan said. “But through our correspondence later, I feel he is someone who is very reflective, and an increasingly mature politician."

Lee, Wong's former Scholarism colleague, visits him regularly in prison and exchanges letters with him. He said Wong kept reading books, taking university courses and teaching himself guitar, always striving to improve himself. The two grew closer, with Wong softening behind bars, caring more about others’ personal lives and sending Lee cards on special occasions.
Before his arrest for the collusion-related offense in June 2025, Wong had been expected to be freed in January next year.

“The message he gave me is that the most important thing is to not forget why you first stepped forward," Lee said, relaying what Wong told him in 2021. "He also believes that what we learned in the organization will continue to be useful today and will keep helping us grow."
Although Scholarism ended a decade ago, Lee still keeps a book about the group. In it, Wong, then 16, wrote to his future self.

“I truly believe that having space as a student to participate in social movements and to contribute a little more to Hong Kong, I can at least tell everyone that I have lived vibrantly and meaningfully,” he wrote.

title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist faces sentencing in 2nd national security case
summary: A Hong Kong court has sentenced activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years in prison under a national security law imposed by Beijing
story: A Hong Kong court has sentenced activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years in prison under a national security law imposed by Beijing

HONG KONG -- A Hong Kong court sentenced prominent activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years in prison Thursday under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say underscores the crackdown on the city’s once-thriving pro-democracy movement.

Wong, 30, first led student protests as a teenager and engaged in international advocacy efforts for Hong Kong's democracy movement. He was already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term after pleading guilty in the city's biggest national security case, and had been due to be freed in January.
But he was further charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, an offense under the security law imposed by Beijing in 2020.
Judge William Tam said Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law colluded with foreign officials and other foreign actors and sought measures against China and Hong Kong.

The judge pointed to the U.S. revocation of the city’s preferential treatment as a special administrative region and U.S. sanctions imposed on Chinese and Hong Kong officials, saying these were the kinds of sanctions or hostile measures Wong and Law had called for.

“The punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed,” Tam wrote. “It is also necessary for this court to express the community’s abhorrence of the defendant’s scheme and acts together with others to collude with foreign forces.”
Wong, who appeared at the High Court in a dark shirt and dark-framed glasses, appeared calm and nodded to his supporters and pro-democracy activists in the public gallery.
The United States strongly condemned the sentencing and called for Wong's immediate release.

The U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that Wong has been “unjustly imprisoned” since late 2020, showing that “Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong.”
Wong pleaded guilty to the offense earlier this year. Tam said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong’s guilty plea and mitigation.
Tam said Wong would serve the remaining two months of the sentence for his first national security conviction concurrently with the new sentence.
Wong appeared serious but calm as the judge read out his sentencing remarks. Before leaving the courtroom, his supporters waved to him. “Thank you all,” he said to them in Cantonese.
Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism movement once led by Wong, was in tears after the sentence was delivered.

With limited seating available, some took turns entering the courtroom. Dozens had lined up outside the court to secure a seat in the public gallery, some as early as Tuesday. One resident, ET Wong, said Wong walked a difficult path for Hong Kong’s future, human rights and the student movement. “He should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment,” she said.

In a statement written in prison, Wong said he thought he was acting within the law and was not directly advocating for sanctions when he reposted others' social media posts or called on foreign companies to consider ceasing business with the Hong Kong police. He said he later realized his judgment was wrong.

He said during his nearly six years in prison, he enrolled in university courses and read many books. He said he devoted himself to becoming a better person, and he hoped he would regard the experience as having helped forge his character when he looks back one day.

Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society. But after huge anti-government protests rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for reporting critical of the government shut down and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible.

Eric Lai, a research fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law, said the national security law charges “can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary.”

Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities argue the security law is crucial for the city’s stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.
The prosecution alleged that Wong and Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination.

After the security law was enacted, Law, who left for the U.K., and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw international attention and bolster the request for sanctions, a blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
Wong's lawyer Derek Chan had urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing that Wong had pleaded guilty in the face of overwhelming facts and evidence and that the central government supports Hong Kong in upholding national security.
He said “relevant parties” should stop making irresponsible remarks about the city's judicial proceedings and stop interfering in its judiciary.
Hong Kong leader John Lee said Wong, Law and their accomplices are among the “primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability.”
Steve Li, chief superintendent of the police’s national security department, welcomed the court's ruling and said he hoped Wong would reflect on his wrongdoing.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Though he's held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern for the pro-Beijing camp.

In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for “beautifying” his crimes. The city’s security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
The documentary then topped Netflix’s most-watched list in Hong Kong.

title: Authorities say multiple grizzlies may have attacked mother and daughter found dead
summary: Authorities in British Columbia say more than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead along the province’s central coast
story: Authorities in British Columbia say more than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead along the province’s central coast

More than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead in Bella Coola along the province’s central coast, the Conservation Officer Service in British Columbia said.

The service’s Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video message that the second body had been found in a search by Royal Canadian Mounted Police and conservation officers on Tuesday afternoon that followed the discovery of the first set of remains a day earlier.
He said it’s “not yet clear if more than one bear was involved,” and any bears captured in the area will be assessed.
Family members of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, had reported them missing on Sunday.

Balcarras' brother, Matthew Balcarras, said Wednesday that his sister was “incredibly strong” and had lived in many difficult, remote places, including Alaska, before moving to Bella Coola on B.C.’s central coast a few months ago.
“She was a beautiful artist and was an inspiration for me and my brothers,” Matthew Balcarras said of his sister.

Authorities have imposed a curfew on the community, about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, as the search for the animal or animals behind the attack continues. If the “offending bear” is captured it will be killed to protect public safety, Tyre said.
A fundraiser set up by relative Mary Melissa Smith said Reed was 20, “with her whole life ahead of her,” while Balcarras leaves behind three young adult children, as well as a grandchild.

Balcarras left behind a son, two daughters and a grandson who now are “faced with the devastating loss of their mother,” while navigating the financial burden of arranging funeral services, Smith said.

The Central Coast Teachers’ Association said on social media that Balcarras had joined their school community as a counselor in August, and she devoted “countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being.”
The attack comes nearly a year after a grizzly attack on a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area, which left one adult and three children badly hurt.
The animal involved in that attack last November was never captured.
Kim Titchener, founder of Bear Safety & More Inc. based in Calgary, said she was concerned when she saw reports about the women on Facebook hiking groups.
“When I saw that they were missing and in the area that they were missing, my heart just dropped because I just kind of knew this could be a bear attack,” Titchener said.
“This community and area have suffered so much last year,” she said, referring to the grizzly attack on schoolchildren.
Bella Coola is well-known for its large population of grizzly and black bears, and Titchener said it’s common for people in Bella Coola to see bears walking near their homes.

Titchener said there have been “concerning pressures” on bear populations in British Columbia because of the loss of habitat, food stress caused by drought and climate change, setting off more conflicts with people.
“I don’t know if Bella Coola suffered from any drought issues, but certainly other parts of the province of B.C. did,” she said.

title: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% to tackle higher inflation
summary: The Bank of England is raising interest rates for the first time in more than three years in an effort to tackle an inflation shock stoked by the Iran war
story: The Bank of England is raising interest rates for the first time in more than three years in an effort to tackle an inflation shock stoked by the Iran war

LONDON -- The Bank of England indicated Thursday that the sharp decline in energy prices after the U.S. midterm elections — if sustained — could limit the prospect of further interest rate hikes in the coming months.
After raising its main interest rate for the first time in more than three years to 4% from 3.75%, the bank said the outlook for U.K. borrowing costs largely hinges on what happens with the Iran war.

“We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours," Bank Gov. Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing following the first interest rate hike since August 2023. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.”

The heavy losses suffered by the Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections have been followed by a sharp drop in energy prices. Many believe that it’s now less likely that U.S. President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran, with Democrats gaining control of Congress early next year following their big wins this week. Many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday, blamed the war for the party’s poor performance at the ballot box.
Though Brent crude is down around $15 a barrel this week, trading at $96, that is still more than $30 more expensive than it was at this time last year.

If the decline in oil and gas prices is sustained over the coming weeks, then the expected peak in inflation next summer — which the bank anticipates will reach 5% — could be lower. That could temper the need for future rate hikes, and not just by the Bank of England.

Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently in response to the higher inflation stoked by the Iran war, and their interest rate strategies are largely contingent on what happens to energy prices.
Bailey said Thursday's hike “shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes” but stressed that the outlook depends on what happens in the war with Iran.
“Unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.
For hard-pressed households facing higher mortgage rates and businesses paying more to access capital, the hope is that Thursday’s rate hike will be the last for some time.
“The path for interest rates is hanging in the balance, with U.S.-Iran hostilities holding the key," said Suren Thiru, ICAEW's chief economist.
The decision to raise interest rates was unanimous given the pickup in inflation this year, though one of the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed an even bigger increase, to 4.25%.

The pressure on rate-setters has grown steadily in recent months. When inflation hit an 11-month high of 3.5% in September — well above the bank's 2% target — it cemented market expectations of a rate hike this month, with potentially more to come in 2027.

The main cause of the spike in inflation this year has been the sharp rise in fuel costs resulting from the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies and pushed prices at the pump and household energy bills higher.
“There is now enough inflationary pressure in the pipeline caused by the rise in energy prices that an increase in Bank rate is warranted," Bailey said.
Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.

title: How one bank’s collapse is upending Paraguay, trapping savings and threatening its president
summary: The collapse of Ueno Bank has left savers scrambling for their money and Paraguay’s president facing calls for impeachment
story: The collapse of Ueno Bank has left savers scrambling for their money and Paraguay’s president facing calls for impeachment

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- Hours after Paraguay’s central bank seized Ueno Bank, a major digital lender that went from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, President Santiago Peña was facing impeachment, protesters were clashing with riot police and the bank's executives had been detained.
The swift collapse of a bank that claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers has sent shock waves through the country’s financial system.

By Thursday morning, a rebellion by several members of Peña's own conservative Colorado Party had become a party-wide revolt. Both of the ruling party’s main factions in the lower house pledged to back impeachment, with a debate scheduled for Thursday, after former President Horacio Cartes, the party’s powerful leader, withdrew his support for Peña.

Impeachment requires a two-thirds majority of lower house lawmakers present to send the case to the Senate, where another two-thirds vote would be needed to remove Peña, a 47-year-old former International Monetary Fund economist.

On Wednesday, before his own party turned against him, Peña had sought to move past the scandal in a video message, accepting no blame and promising to protect depositors’ savings. He also approved emergency payouts to depositors Wednesday and named a new central bank chief.
“Paraguay needs institutions that provide answers and protect our people’s resources,” he said.

The political upheaval and promises of relief leave a bigger question unanswered: how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

For many Paraguayans, the answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees’ savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers’ accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what’s left.

Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
“The banking system is sound,” insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña’s request.

Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.

Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank’s parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.

“We want your head, Peña!” they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña’s impeachment, called him “the enemy of savers” and pleaded “Give us back our money.” Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.

Many demonstrators saw Ueno’s collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
“This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor,” said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno’s name, the bank’s logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.
DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina.

title: The average US 30-year mortgage rate falls to 7.18% this week, its third straight decline
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate fell for the third straight week, offering some relief to prospective homebuyers facing higher home prices
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate fell for the third straight week, offering some relief to prospective homebuyers facing higher home prices
WASHINGTON -- The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate fell for the third straight week, offering some relief to prospective homebuyers facing higher home prices.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. declined to 7.18% from 7.24% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.22%.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also fell again this week. That average rate dipped to 6.57% from 6.60% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.50%.
Lower mortgage rates relieve some of the pressure on prospective homebuyers facing higher borrowing costs on home loans.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.

Until the past few weeks, mortgage rates had been on the rise since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher. The run-up in rates also reflected heightened bond market volatility, which led to rising yields on U.S. Treasurys.

However, the 10-year Treasury yield has been mostly easing for the past month after climbing to its highest level since 2002. That’s caused the average rate on a 30-year mortgage to come back down after reaching 7.4% early last month, its highest level in nearly three years.

The yield was at 4.84% at midday on the bond market Thursday, its lowest level since early September. It had surged to more than 5.30% in early October and remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

U.S. home sales remain stalled this year mostly due to elevated mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home.

In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The rise in rates since then has added roughly $300 to $350 to the monthly cost for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan.
Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average.

The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low.

title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
summary: French authorities have thwarted a cyberattack on blood banks that aimed to dangerously raise storage temperatures
story: French authorities have thwarted a cyberattack on blood banks that aimed to dangerously raise storage temperatures

PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday.
French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said the temperature, which was usually set to minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit), went up to 110 C (230 F).
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident.

“The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

This week’s cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros.

“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings.

The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.
AP journalist Kelvin Chan in London contributed to the story

title: JetBlue raises baggage fees for a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
summary: JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year
story: JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year
JetBlue has raised its checked baggage fees for the second time this year, making it more expensive for travelers to check luggage just as the busy holiday travel season gets underway.

The new fees for tickets purchased on or after Nov. 3 mean most economy passengers flying within the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean will pay at least $50 each way for their first checked bag, up from $39 previously.

The price climbs to $55 during peak travel periods, including Thanksgiving and the winter holidays, if passengers pay at least 24 hours before departure. Those who wait until the final 24 hours will pay $60 during off-peak periods and $70 during peak periods.

At the start of the year, the first checked bag on most economy domestic JetBlue flights cost $35 during off-peak periods. But that was before the Iran war started in late February with U.S.-Israeli strikes and sent jet fuel prices swinging.

The fee for a second checked bag has also increased, starting at $70 each way during off-peak periods and $75 during peak travel. Passengers checking their bags at the airport can pay as much as $85 for a second bag.

JetBlue, which has its flagship terminal at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, previously raised checked baggage fees in March. That increase helped set off a broader round of baggage fee hikes among major U.S. airlines, including Delta, United, American and Southwest.

The airline said in the spring that the increases are intended to help offset higher operating costs while allowing the airline to keep its base fares competitive. The Associated Press sent the airline emailed requests for comment Wednesday on the latest fee increases.

The war with Iran remains unresolved, keeping traffic largely restricted through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route for global oil supplies. The disruption has kept jet fuel prices elevated.

JetBlue executives said last week during the airline's third-quarter earnings call that demand has remained resilient even as fares have risen in response to higher jet fuel prices. JetBlue said its average fuel price reached $3.91 per gallon in the summer, up 57% from a year earlier, and is expected to climb to $4.64 during the final three months of the year, up 85% from the same time last year.
JetBlue said some travelers, including eligible co-branded credit card holders and members of JetBlue’s loyalty program, can still check bags for free.

title: Kenya’s mining ambitions raise fears for farms and ancestral graves
summary: Farmers and community elders in coastal Kenya fear a proposed mining project could threaten their livelihoods and a sacred forest where their ancestors are buried
story: Farmers and community elders in coastal Kenya fear a proposed mining project could threaten their livelihoods and a sacred forest where their ancestors are buried

MRIMA, Kenya -- Farmers fear losing the land that feeds them. Community elders worry about damage to a forest where their ancestors are buried. Both are demanding answers about Kenya's plans to mine valuable minerals beneath Mrima Hill, a forested area rich in niobium and rare earth elements.

The proposed development comes as countries race to secure supplies of rare earth minerals used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and defense technologies, seeking alternatives to China’s dominance of mineral processing.

Residents near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast and the Tanzanian border say they have received little information about where mining would take place or how it could affect their farms, livelihoods and a sacred site.

“We haven’t been informed about the process at all," said Justus Mwero, chairman of the Mrima Farm Owners Community-Based Organization, which has about 500 registered farmers. “We don’t know how people are going to be looked after, or what impact the project will have.”
On a recent morning, farmers gathered in a circle beside the main road in Mrima, discussing the mining plans as the wooded hill rose across the street.
“We are waiting to see what is going to happen,” Mwero said.

Kenya's Mining Minister Hassan Joho told The Associated Press earlier this week that a technical committee was evaluating five proposals and that an announcement would follow within two to three weeks.

While the ministry has not disclosed the nationalities of the bidders, citing confidentiality, Australian company RareX said its consortium with Iluka Resources — another Australian company — submitted a technical and financial proposal on Oct. 21.
Another company, Nasdaq-listed Critical Metals Corp., said in July that its consortium had been shortlisted for the final stage of bidding to develop the Mrima Hill rare earths and niobium project.

In a Sept. 28 interview with Semafor, a U.S.-based news outlet, Joho said the Kenyan government views mining and local mineral processing as a way to expand Kenya’s economy and create jobs. He said Kenya aimed to increase mining’s contribution to gross domestic product from about 1% to 10% within a decade. That target covers the entire mining sector.

In 2013, projections put the project's potential gross revenue at about $62 billion over 23 years, according to mining news website Extractives Daily. The estimate was based on commodity prices at the time, excluded development and operating costs and did not indicate how much Kenya would receive.
For members of the local Digo community, Mrima Hill’s value cannot be measured by its minerals alone. It contains a sacred forest known as a kaya, where residents say their ancestors are buried.

“Our traditions and practices are organized around the forest," said Masoud Suleiman Mwarizo, chairman of the Mrima Hill Digo Community Trust, formed in 2025 to defend the community's interests in the project. "All our ancestors are buried here. We will refuse any digging of the hill.”
The Mrima Hill Sacred Grove forest reserve was designated a national monument in 1992.
The National Museums of Kenya did not respond to a request for comment.
Farmers around the hill fear that relocation could leave them with less productive land, though it remains unclear whether the project would require residents to move.
“We all rely on farming to survive. This land is fertile, and if we are relocated to less fertile land, hunger could strike us,” Mwero said.

Rama Bindo, treasurer of the Digo Community Trust, said residents without formal ownership documents were particularly vulnerable. “Not all farmers have title deeds to prove ownership of their land, and that makes it easy for land grabbing to happen,” Bindo said.

Joho, the mining minister, told the AP in an interview that the ministry consulted with the community before advertising the tender for developing Mrima Hill, and that once a winner is chosen, the ministry will formally introduce the company to the community so they can reach agreements.

Under Kenya’s Mining Act, a mining licence holder must sign a community development agreement with the community where mining takes place, and cannot start mining until landowners have been compensated.

Harry Kimtai, principal secretary at Kenya's Mining Ministry, said that once a company is awarded the project, “communities will be encouraged to engage directly with the winner.” If disputes arise, he said, the government will explain residents’ rights and monitor whether the company complies with the law.
The Centre for Litigation Trust, a Kenyan civil society group, has challenged a proposed Kenya-U.S. agreement to develop Mrima Hill’s minerals. Details of that agreement have not been disclosed.

In a June 22 petition, the group said it asked the High Court in Kwale, a coastal town near Mrima Hill, to suspend the agreement until residents and their leaders are consulted. It argued that the bidding process lacked transparency and public participation. The government has not publicly explained how the agreement relates to the tender.

Kenya's attorney general challenged the court’s jurisdiction, according to the group’s lawyer. The group says a ruling on that objection is scheduled for Nov. 6 and that no court order currently blocks the implementation of the agreement.
Meanwhile, residents and advocates want details about how the minerals would be extracted.

“We don’t know anything about the extraction method. Will it be open-pit mining, and what will be the impact on the environment and on health?” said Fakii Omar of the Kwale Mining Alliance, an advocacy group for mining-affected communities.
The National Environment Management Authority did not respond to questions from The Associated Press about environmental assessment, public consultation and the approval process.

RareX, the Australian rare earths exploration company, said its consortium’s proposal called for securing community support before mining begins and protecting residents, the environment and cultural heritage. It also said it proposed further study to determine whether the deposit could support underground mining.
Mwero said residents want a voice in decisions about their future.
“We want an open forum to discuss our concerns. We are the custodians of this land, and we should be the ones negotiating over it,” he said.

title: Gas deposits off Cyprus are an opportunity for the EU, president says
summary: Cyprus's president says natural gas deposits off the country's coast offer the European Union a chance to boost energy security by diversifying supply
story: Cyprus's president says natural gas deposits off the country's coast offer the European Union a chance to boost energy security by diversifying supply

NICOSIA, Cyprus -- Natural gas deposits off the southern coastline of Cyprus are an opportunity for the European Union to bolster its own energy security by diversifying its supply, the island nation's president said Thursday.

President Nikos Christodoulides told The Associated Press in an exclusive statement that the first of a number of natural gas fields discovered off Cyprus, dubbed Cronos, is expected to start production in the first half of 2028.

“Cyprus is part of the energy equation, with Europe benefiting with added diversification and with the Union’s autonomy being anchored. This is the first step in a path that is bright,” Christodoulides said.

Europe is looking for alternative sources of energy after turning its back on Russian oil and gas following Moscow's full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while consumers are being lashed by rocketing fuel prices compounded by the Iran war.

Italian energy company Eni last month signed development contracts with eight main contractors to develop Cronos, estimated to contain around 3 trillion cubic feet (85 billion cubic meters) of the hydrocarbon.
The contracts involve subsea production systems and pipelines, a floating control unit and drilling rig services.
“The conclusion of these agreements, which trigger the commitment of billions of euros in investment, provides for a clearly defined path towards production,” said Christodoulides.

Once the gas is extracted from the field situated some 185 kilometers (115 miles) southwest of Cyprus, it will be conveyed by pipeline to Egypt’s Damietta facility where it will be liquefied and exported to international markets, primarily Europe.
The Cypriot president said production capacity is expected to reach up to 500 million standard cubic feet (14.16 million cubic meters) per day at peak production.

Christodoulides said that for the EU, the significance of Cronos “lies precisely in the opportunity to diversify its sources of supply through the development of a field in a member state and in cooperation with the region.”

Apart from Cronos, there are six other natural gas deposits found within Cyprus’ exclusive economic zone that are being considered for development, including ExxonMobil’s Glaucus and Pegasus fields situated south of Cronos.

ExxonMobil's vice president of global exploration, John Ardill, said in June that natural gas could start flowing from those two deposits by 2033. He said the gas would most likely be piped to Egypt, where it can be liquefied for export.

Christodoulides said Cronos is a “substantive step” toward the country’s first natural gas production which intersects with Europe’s broader need for “the diversification of natural gas supply sources and the enhancement of energy security.”

title: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan
summary: Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
story: Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low

Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low and didn't take into account the company's long-term earnings potential under its new CEO.
The Dublin, Ohio-based burger chain also said Thursday that its board had adopted a “poison pill” plan designed to make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.

Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.

But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results. Wright, who is the fourth CEO to lead Wendy's since 2024, was previously the president and CEO of Potbelly. He has also held senior leadership roles at Wendy's, Checkers and Domino's Pizza.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose less than 1% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance in the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.

Wendy's shareholder rights plan — commonly known as a “poison pill" plan — grants all shareholders except a hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares and dilute the hostile bidder's ownership stake. It is automatically triggered if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said.

Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. Peltz served as chairman of Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024. His son Bradley Peltz still serves on the company's board and is a Wendy's franchisee.
Dine Brands, the parent company of Applebee's and IHOP, adopted a similar one-year poison pill plan last week to fend off a takeover bid by two investment firms.

Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy’s is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.

But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

The industry has also been seeing lower U.S. traffic, especially from lower-income customers, as high gas prices and affordability concerns eat into household budgets. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.

Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.

Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Under Wright, Wendy's has launched a turnaround plan dubbed Dave's Way, which calls for improving food quality, more distinctive marketing and improved digital ordering and restaurant operations.

Wright said Thursday that Wendy's has begun testing quality improvements, including thicker and crispier bacon, creamier Frosties and whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches. The company is removing lower-volume items from its menus to reduce complexity in its kitchens and making breakfast optional, allowing franchisees to focus on their most profitable times of day.

Wendy's on Thursday reported revenue of $547 million in the July-September period. That was better than the $531 million Wall Street had forecast, according to analysts polled by FactSet. Wendy's same-store sales, or sales at locations open at least a year, fell 5.2%, which was also better than the 6.4% drop analysts forecast.
Wendy’s had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.

title: Asian shares mostly advance following US midterms, though Kospi falls
summary: World shares are mostly higher though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections
story: World shares are mostly higher though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections
World shares were mostly higher Thursday, though heavy selling of artificial intelligence-related stocks offset gains for some markets following the U.S. midterm elections.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 5% and the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo lost nearly 2%. Oil prices were mixed after the Dow industrials jumped more than 3% on Wednesday following the Republicans' loss of control of the U.S. Congress.
In early European trading, the German DAX rose 0.6% to 26,598.03, while the CAC 40 in Paris surged 1.2% to 8,276.55. The United Kingdom's FTSE 100 gained 1% to 10,935.08.

The future for the S&P 500 was nearly unchanged, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.4%. On Wednesday, the S&P 500 jumped 1.6%. The Dow surged more than 1,500 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4%.

U.S. stocks usually climb following midterms, regardless of who wins. But technology shares have taken a hit as investors mull the potential impact on the boom in AI from a Congress led by Democratic Party lawmakers from January.
The Kospi, which has gyrated through waves of selling and buying driven by the AI frenzy, tumbled 5.3% to 5,383.80.
Shares in Samsung Electronics sank 7.6%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix lost 9.4%.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 fell 1.8% to 61,077.90. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group shed 6.9%, while computer chipmaking equipment company Tokyo Electron skidded 9.5%. Testing equipment maker Advantest tumbled 15%.
Taiwan's Taiex lost 3.2%.
Asian markets less heavily exposed to the AI industry mostly climbed Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng jumped 3.7% to 24,796.98. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher, to 3,689.91.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 rose 2.6% to 9,065.10, while India's Sensex gained 2.8%.

“Global equity markets mostly welcomed the strong win by Democrats, with European and Chinese markets surfing on hopes that the Democratic shift in Congress could increase pressure to undo some tariffs and restore stronger trade ties with the U.S.,” Ipek Ozkardeskaya of Swissquote said in a commentary.

However, she noted, with regard to AI, “The Democratic victory is expected to become a potential obstacle to an investment story already facing questions over massive spending, future returns and financing.”
On Wall Street, stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally on Wednesday following the U.S. nationwide losses for Republicans.

Overall, the election may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. But investors generally prefer split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the U.S. economy.
But investors see risks ahead for U.S. President Donald Trump’s social media company, the AI industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.
Trump Media & Technology Group was one of the market’s bigger losers Wednesday, down 24.5%.
Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it’s dropped to $4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is best known for Trump’s postings on the platform.
Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3%, and SpaceX sank 3.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress.

A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the Iran war, and that hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military. Lockheed Martin sank 6.9%; Northrop Grumman fell 4.5% and General Dynamics lost 2.6%.
The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war also sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, plunging 8.7% to $94.62.
Early Thursday, Brent crude rebounded, gaining 0.4% to $95.04 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude fell 0.3% to $87.86 per barrel.
In other dealings early Thursday, the U.S. dollar slipped to 158.22 Japanese yen from 158.41 yen. The euro rose to $1.1241 from $1.1228.

title: UK government tasks regulators to scrutinize proposed tie-up between Sky and ITV
summary: British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has asked regulators to scrutinize Sky's proposed takeover of ITV’s media and entertainment arm
story: British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has asked regulators to scrutinize Sky's proposed takeover of ITV’s media and entertainment arm

LONDON -- British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy asked regulators Wednesday to scrutinize the proposed 1.6 billion-pound ($2.3 billion) takeover of ITV’s media and entertainment arm by Sky, the U.K.-based TV, internet and mobile phone provider owned by U.S. company Comcast.

Nandy announced her decision to issue a so-called Public Interest Intervention Notice, paving the way for the Competition and Markets Authority, or CMA, and media regulator Ofcom to probe the takeover.

The pair will report back to her on the impact of the deal on the media landscape in the U.K. and its impact on free speech by Jan. 27. Following their reports, she may then decide to refer the deal to the CMA for a further in-depth investigation.
Nandy also said she will bring forward new streaming legislation in view of her “specific concerns” over the tie-up.

ITV, the U.K.'s largest commercial broadcaster, struck a deal in July to sell its media and entertainment division to Sky, in a move that would create a major competitor to the global streaming giants. The proposed deal includes ITV's terrestrial television channels and streaming service. ITV’s production arm, ITV Studios, known for shows such as the “I’m A Celebrity’’ series, will remain an independent company.

Sky said it believes the tie-up "is in the public interest, with clear commitments already made to protect ITV’s identity, public service broadcasting obligations and the distinct editorial voices of Sky News and ITV News.”
And ITV said it looks forward to “co-operating fully” with the investigation.
The combined Sky-ITV entity, if approved, is set to become part of NBCUniversal following the completion of its split from Comcast.

title: Unemployment claims drop to 189,000, the fewest since mid-July
summary: Fewer Americans applied for unemployment benefits last week as layoffs remain scarce and most workers enjoy job security
story: Fewer Americans applied for unemployment benefits last week as layoffs remain scarce and most workers enjoy job security
WASHINGTON -- Fewer Americans applied for unemployment benefits last week as layoffs remain scarce and most workers enjoy job security.

The Labor Department reported Thursday that 189,000 people sought jobless aid last week, the fewest since mid-July and down from 195,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week ups and downs, dipped to 194,750.
Applications for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed.
Claims have remained at historically low levels in the year to date, never topping 230,000 in a single week. They’ve come in at or below 200,000 for eight straight weeks.

So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have been adding an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement on a lackluster 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Consumer spending has remained resilient and a surge in investment in artificial intelligence has lifted economic growth.

The Labor Department will release hiring numbers for October on Friday. They are expected to show that the economy added 65,000 jobs this month, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet. Unemployment is expected to remain at a low 4.2%.

title: Turkey’s solar boom shines ahead of a UN climate summit but coal and other fossil fuels loom large
summary: Turkey is spotlighting its renewable energy efforts as it hosts the upcoming U.N. climate summit
story: Turkey is spotlighting its renewable energy efforts as it hosts the upcoming U.N. climate summit

KARAPINAR, Turkey -- Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity — and helping Turkey, the host of the upcoming U.N. climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.
Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Turkey's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.
Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Turkey’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

The town of Karapinar in Konya is home to the Kalyon Karapınar YEKA-1 Solar Power Plant, which boasts more than 3 million solar panels perched on a terrain equivalent to the size of 2,600 soccer fields.
Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7% of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press — evidence, he says, of how Turkey has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.
Turkey’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.
Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Turkey has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Turkey's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Turkey is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Some 265 kilometers (165 miles) away from Konya, the Nov. 9-20 summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit — officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.
Many experts have recently argued that a key mission — combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions — has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after U.S. President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from global climate negotiations.
And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.
Turkey’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.
To that aim, Turkey will push a “climate implementation bridge,” an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.
“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.
COP31 will also prioritize electrification and reduction of waste and methane emissions, Kurum has said.
However, the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, has described Turkey’s climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to the early 1800s, directing countries to develop policies that would help meet that goal.
Meanwhile, human rights groups accuse Ankara of dismissing environmental concerns and frequently arresting activists.

Earlier this year, a court annulled an environmental impact assessment for a planned expansion of a coal-fired power plant at Afsin-Elbistan in southeastern Turkey. The ruling was hailed by environmentalists as a major victory.
But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Turkey faces mounting risks from heat waves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Turkey was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.
Climate advocates have slammed the summit for being awarded to coal-reliant Turkey; coal-exporter Australia has also come under criticism.

But U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.
With “Turkey and Australia leading this process, there is every opportunity to deliver a very strong outcome," he said.
Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey. Associated Press journalists Serra Yedikardes in Trabzon, Turkey, and Ayse Wieting in Istanbul contributed to this report.
