title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
summary: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish
story: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish

MONTAUK, N.Y. -- Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.
Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.

“I’m part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon,” said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.
Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren't showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.

Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.

Factors like years of warming waters — a prime concern cited by many scientists — poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.
See a visual essay featuring anglers who were fishing the shores of Long Island earlier this month here.

“Stripers” are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine's coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.

Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they're measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action — including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s — is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.

“They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned,” said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. “People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass.”
Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms — it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U.S. alone.
And it relies on a fish whose future looks grim.

“Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse,” said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.
“Sometime around 2029, 2030 it’s going to go off a cliff,” he said, “and it’s going to be ugly.”

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them — specifically, cool, wet springs.

Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.
Conditions have been poor in recent years, and fewer fish have entered the population going back to 2019, said Chris Batsavage, chair of the commission's striped bass management board.
“Low precipitation and waters that warm quickly result in weak year classes,” Batsavage said. “It seems like it's environmentally driven.”
The conditions have led to a “slump of bad years” that have made it especially difficult for the fish to maintain their population in the Chesapeake, Versak said.

John Skinner, who wrote a book about striped bass fishing and runs a YouTube channel on the subject that has more than 100,000 followers, has been fishing off Long Island for more than 50 years and says once-reliable spots have completely dried up.
“I'm not saying the fishing is bad. I’m saying when you go there in perfect conditions, you catch nothing,” Skinner said. “Absolutely nothing.”

Many other striped bass fishermen across the Northeast shared a recurring story this summer and fall — the fish's once-plentiful schools are dried up, and the individuals that remain are clearly older, meaning years of reproduction failure are starting to take their toll.

Some fishermen said stricter rules or a fishing moratorium could be the only ways to prevent the fish’s population from becoming dangerously low. And they lament what they’re seeing on the waters — smaller schools of fish, many of them older and larger, with few young fish entering the population to provide a future.

They also see more factors than just the warming environment at play. Some see years of heavy fishing on striped bass becoming apparent today in the form of a lower population. Others blame the resurgence of sharks buoyed by years of conservation efforts, as a reintroduction of competition for the fish.

The Atlantic States commission considers the stock to be overfished, although it says overfishing is not occurring at the moment. The fish are caught commercially as well as recreationally, but recreational fishing is much larger.

Most of the recreational catch is tossed back into the ocean alive. Still, some fish don't survive the encounter. Regulators have historically expected 9% to die after release, while newer data shows the number could be less than 5%.

Limits on how large a striped bass can be caught and kept are typically in the range of 28 to 31 inches (71 to 79 centimeters), with rules varying by state and location. Striped bass are popular with catch-and-release fishermen, and these days, it’s more common to catch larger bass, many well over 31 inches.
Paquette, the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association coordinator and a longtime angler himself, said that without drastic action he fears the end of striped bass fishing.
“If you’re a guy who thought he was going to retire and striped bass fish, and you’re planning on retiring soon, get a different plan,” Paquette said.
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine. Associated Press video journalist Mingson Lau contributed.

title: Dow plunges 1,800 points, wiping out gains from midterm results rally
summary: The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
story: The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, putting the tech-heavy index into correction territory.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down more than 1,800 points on Thursday, wiping out all of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.
The S&P 500 finished trading down 4.3%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.5%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.
The Dow closed down 1,833 points, or about 3.4%.

The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.

Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, closed down 9% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fell 17%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 22% in value by market close.
The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.

Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price close down more than 3%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.
The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.

On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.
Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.

"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.

Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.
OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.

The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post.

title: Voter frustration about the economy went beyond gas prices, Voter Poll shows
summary: Three-fours of voters described the economy as not good or poor, polls showed.
story: Three-fours of voters described the economy as not good or poor, polls showed.
A monthslong surge of inflation. A national average gas price well above $4 a gallon. Thirty-year mortgage rates north of 7%.

Economic woes helped fuel a Democratic takeover of the U.S. House and Senate in the midterm elections as voter frustration spanned from gas and grocery prices to healthcare costs and utility bills, according to ABC News Voter Polls, which are based on surveys of voters conducted on and before Election Day.
Three-quarters of House voters nationally described the economy as not good or poor, according to the Voter Poll.

A blue wave on Tuesday catapulted Democratic Senate candidates to victories in Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Texas. As of Wednesday, Democrats were projected to win 54 seats in the Senate, with competitive races yet to be called in Alaska and Mississippi.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber. ABC News has projected Democrats will win the House.

The Iran war sparked a rise of inflation earlier this year, squeezing household budgets and dampening consumer sentiment. A survey of consumer sentiment conducted by the University of Michigan every month for more than seven decades showed its second-lowest level ever in October.

Similarly, midterm voters nationwide voiced their discontent about inflation on Tuesday. About 8 in 10 House voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship over the previous year, according to the Voter Poll.
By contrast, 21% of House voters said inflation had caused them and their family no hardship at all over that period.
On Election Day, the national average price of a gallon of gas stood at $4.14 a gallon, which marked a rise of 1.16, or 38%, since the outbreak of the Iran war, AAA data showed.
The U.S. average price of diesel registered at $6.28, an increase of more than $2.50 from a year earlier, according to AAA.
About 6 in 10 House voters said they were very concerned with gasoline or diesel prices, according to the ABC News Voter Poll (59%).
The same share also expressed frustration with grocery and food prices: 59%.

The sense of strain on voters' budgets extended to costs like healthcare and utility bills: 59% said they were very concerned about healthcare costs and 53% said the same about utilities, according to the Voter Poll.

Those who get their health insurance through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) saw their average monthly benchmark premium jump from $497 per month in 2025 to $625 in 2026, according to KFF, particularly after enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of last year.
Trump's signature "One Big Beautiful Bill" included a range of tax reductions for both individuals and businesses, but the measure also slashed some people's Medicaid benefits.

Over half of House voters said that the Trump administration's policies have made their healthcare costs worse and by a 20-percentage point margin they said they trusted the Democratic Party more to handle healthcare, according to the Voter Poll. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the federal government to play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare, according to the Voter Poll.

Utility bills also drew attention during midterm campaign season as some candidates, mostly Democrats, criticized artificial intelligence data centers, citing potential strain on local water systems and high residential utility bills as a result of increased demand.
ABC News' Mary Kekatos contributed to this report.

title: Russell Brand found guilty in UK rape, sexual assault trial
summary: Brand, 51, denied the charges, pleading not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of attempted indecent assault.
story: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty by a London jury Thursday on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Brand had faced a total of seven charges against six women, pleading not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
He is scheduled to be sentenced on Nov. 9 after a trial that began in mid-October.
The jury of four women and eight men deliberated for more than eight hours before delivering their verdict, according to The Associated Press.
The U.K.'s Metropolitan Police said detectives began investigating Brand in 2023 after allegations against the actor were reported by multiple U.K. news outlets.

In April 2025, Brand was initially charged with one count of rape and one count of oral rape, one count of indecent assault, and two counts of sexual assault in connection with alleged incidents from around two decades ago, according to the Metropolitan Police.

Brand responded to the initial charges on social media that same month, saying, "I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family ... I was a fool, man, I was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord. I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile. But what I never was, was a rapist. I've never engaged in nonconsensual activity. I pray that you can see that by looking in my eyes."
He then thanked his supporters, adding that he was "incredibly grateful" to defend the charges in court.
Several months later, in December 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service announced it had authorized further charges against Brand concerning two additional women.

Following Thursday's verdict, David Roberts, senior Crown Prosecutor in the London Rape and Serious Sexual Assault Unit, issued a statement, saying in part, "Russell Brand was predatory and used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes. ...Although his tactics varied, at the centre of every assault was an abuse of power and sexual greed, with a complete disregard for the impact of his actions."
Roberts added, "I would like to thank all the women in this case for their courage in coming forward and seeing this sexual abuser brought to justice."

In a separate statement on Thursday, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police Service said, "I want to pay tribute to the team of detectives and specialist staff who worked tirelessly on this investigation. Their professionalism, determination and compassion for the victims represent the very best of the Metropolitan Police."
He added, "Finally, I would urge anyone who may have been a victim of rape or serious sexual assault to speak to us. You will be listened to, supported and treated with dignity and respect."
In addition to acting and comedy, Brand has worked as a political commentator and wellness influencer.
He was previously married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 until their divorce in 2012.
In 2017, Brand married Laura Gallacher, who appeared with him in court throughout the trial. The couple has three children.
ABC News has reached out to Brand's attorney for comment.

If you or someone you know is in need of help, the National Sexual Assault Hotline -- 800-656-HOPE -- is free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. You can also use the hotline's online chat option.

title: 'Extinction-level event': How Republicans eyeing 2028 are taking midterm losses
summary: Republicans considering a presidential run offered their assessment of the party's performance in the midterm elections.
story: "It's the political equivalent of a meteor strike," DeSantis said.

Following Republicans' poor midterm election performance -- which not only saw Democrats win back the House and the Senate, but also win Senate races in deep-red states -- several Republicans considering a 2028 presidential run have offered their evaluations of the party's performance in the midterm elections with all of them saying the GOP needs to find a way to move forward.
Sen. Ted Cruz: 'It was a Watergate-level repudiation'
Sen. Ted Cruz called Republicans' performance in the midterm elections a "Watergate-level repudiation" of the Republican Party.

"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a---kicking. It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation. What happened, and why? What are the consequences, and where on earth do we go from here?” Cruz said during his podcast out Wednesday.
He then turned to his state of Texas, where Republicans lost every statewide election, leaving Democrats in power.

"Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter. But Texas, today at least, is blue. As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That’s not something I ever thought I would say," Cruz said.
Cruz said that the dismissal of the rising cost of living led Republicans to be unsuccessful this election cycle.

"The top issue, cost of living, is very real. Too many in politics dismissed it. They didn't understand," Cruz said. "They pointed to the macro numbers showing the stock markets soaring, median income at record highs, and poverty at record lows. Those data are true, but they don’t tell all of the story."
Cruz said in his podcast that the Republican Party needs "to rebuild, getting behind policies that directly benefit the constituents we lost."

Cruz hasn't outright said he is pursuing the presidency, but the Texas Republican, who ran for president in 2016, told ABC News' Linsey Davis in September that he was focused on the midterms and that "there'll be plenty of time to worry about [2028] after the midterms."
Gov. Ron DeSantis: 'Close to an extinction-level event'
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis described Tuesday's election results as a "meteor strike," arguing that even a "wave" fails to capture the scale of the Republican losses.

"To call it a wave, I don't think would be fully accurate. It's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States, blue states, red states, everything in between, and the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida,” DeSantis said Wednesday in Florida.
DeSantis did not mince his words about the election results for Republicans across the country, calling it a "close to an extinction-level event" for the party.
"But let's just be clear about what happened last night. This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country, as we have seen, probably in the last 100 years."
DeSantis said it will take time for the Republican Party to rebuild, but he offered Florida as an example of how the national party can start to move forward.

"Now it's going to take a lot of time and effort to rebuild. It will not happen in just one election cycle. But Florida shows how you can build a coalition, not only to convert on all your promises in good times, but also to withstand the bad times," he said.

During his Wednesday press conference, DeSantis was asked about seeking higher office in 2028 and responded that he's currently focused on the end of his term as governor and will discuss his future once he's out of office at the beginning of 2027.
"We'll talk about anything I'm doing on the other side of this. You know, I still got more work to do. We'll work till the lights are out and cross that bridge when we get to it," he said.
Vice President JD Vance: 'The reason we lost is the war'
In a lengthy social media post on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance said his party lost because of the war in Iran, saying, "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance said.

Although Vance said the war led Republicans to suffer losses, ABC News' Voter Poll of House voters found that voters nationally were more focused on other factors, including the cost of living, than the Iran war.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest,” he added. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
President Donald Trump, though, has taken no responsibility for Republicans' poor performance in this year's election, maintaining that the party would have won if he were on the ballot.

"No, look. I mean, if I were on the ballot, we would have won. You saw the people that were packed, thousands and thousands of people at every rally, and if I was on the ballot, we would have won, but they just -- you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies; it was incredible. We weren't able to transfer the love to candidates," Trump said on Wednesday.

Vance conceded that immigration enforcement may have played a role, saying he is "open" to changing it, but said that "establishment politicians" will be gaslighting voters into offering amnesty for migrants.
Vance told NBC News in an October interview that Republicans' showing in the midterms could impact his decision on whether to run for president in 2028.

"You make these decisions by collecting as much information and trying to make a wise decision. And yeah, I mean, regardless of what happens over the next 35 days, there will be new information, new things you have to make a decision over," Vance said at the time.

title: Election 2026 live results: Karen Bass concedes LA mayoral race to Nithya Raman
summary: Raman is poised to become the 44th mayor of the nation’s second-largest city.
story: Raman is poised to become the 44th mayor of the nation’s second-largest city.
Democrats won several key races in the high-stakes midterm elections -- with ABC News projecting that Democrats will take control of the Senate and the House.
Key Headlines

1 hour and 22 minutes agoDem Colom discusses tight election vote count, grassroots campaign as Mississippi awaits final results1 hour and 47 minutes agoScalise tells GOP to prepare for Dem investigations2 hours and 7 minutes agoKaren Bass has conceded to Nithya Raman in LA mayoral race
1 hour and 22 minutes agoDem Colom discusses tight election vote count, grassroots campaign as Mississippi awaits final results
1 hour and 47 minutes agoScalise tells GOP to prepare for Dem investigations
2 hours and 7 minutes agoKaren Bass has conceded to Nithya Raman in LA mayoral race
Dem Colom discusses tight election vote count, grassroots campaign as Mississippi awaits final results

Democrat Scott Colom spoke with ABC News on Thursday at a diner in Jackson, Mississippi, as race between him and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith remains tight -- with around 1,000 votes separating the two, according to the current vote count.

Colom tells ABC News that his campaign didn’t get much attention or resources outside of Mississippi until about a month ago because some in his party couldn’t fathom that Democrats could flip a Senate seat in deep-red Mississippi.

He says that forced him to build a ground game that took him to many areas of the state and put him face-to-face with a lot of voters. Many of those voters gravitated toward him, he says, because they were tired of broken promises in Washington.
"The voters were betrayed. That gave us an opportunity to compete everywhere," he said.
-ABC News' Faith Abubey, Oren Oppenheim and Brendon Baur
'I was caught up in the Trump tsunami': Sen. Susan Collins reflects on not being able to distance herself enough from Trump

Outgoing Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who conceded her Senate race to Democrat Troy Jackson, told The New York Times on Wednesday that she was “caught up in the Trump tsunami” that also took her Republican colleagues this election cycle, which saw Democrats pick up seven seats with the chance of possibly adding two more depending on the election results in Alaska and Mississippi.

“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” Collins told The New York Times.
Collins has survived tough races before, but 2026 proved different, as President Trump's unpopularity and agenda affected Republicans down the ballot.
And although Collins emphasized her breaks with Trump during the election cycle, it proved not to be enough for Maine voters.

"Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” Collins said. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”
-ABC News' Hannah Demissie
Scalise tells GOP to prepare for Dem investigations
Rep. Steve Scalise, who is seeking to become House minority leader, told Republican committee chairs in a letter Thursday to prepare for Democratic investigations in the next Congress.
The letter comes ahead of House GOP leadership elections scheduled for Nov. 10. Scalise is going up against Rep. Jim Jordan, the current Judiciary committee chairman, for the top position.

"They will use their oversight authorities to harass the President, his family, cabinet officials, and they will seek to destroy our allies,” Scalise wrote of House Democrats in the letter. “You all will be a key line of defense in this fight, and we must maximize our remaining days in power to prepare for what is coming."

Scalise said GOP chairs should "take inventory" of what Democrats will focus their oversight efforts on, identify administration officials and allies that are likely on Democrats’ target list and consider "how recent Supreme Court decisions and the August 2026 opinion issued by the White House Office of Legal Counsel will factor into oversight going forward."
-ABC News' Lauren Peller
Karen Bass has conceded to Nithya Raman in LA mayoral race
ABC News reports that Nithya Raman is the winner in the Los Angeles mayoral race, based on the concession of incumbent Karen Bass.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote in a statement.
With Karen Bass' concession, this is the first time an LA mayor has lost reelection in more than 20 years.

Raman entered the race back in February in a last-minute bid, making the announcement just hours before the filing deadline closed. Her entry caused a major shakeup in the race, partially because she had endorsed Bass just two weeks before; the move soured their political allyship.

Raman is a Los Angeles city councilmember overseeing District 4 as the first Asian American woman and first South Asian in the role. She has also served as chairwoman of the Housing and Homelessness Committee.

Raman is poised to become the 44th mayor of the nation’s second largest city. She immigrated to the U.S. from India when she was 6, grew up to study urban planning and has degrees from Harvard and MIT.
She also will make history: Raman is the first South Asian and Asian American mayor of Los Angeles.
-ABC News' Clarissa Gonzalez and Juhi Doshi

title: Appeals court weighs Trump's challenge to 2024 criminal hush money conviction
summary: Two and a half years after a jury convicted Donald Trump of 34 felony counts in his hush money case, the president's lawyers are seeking to have the verdict overturned.
story: Trump's attorneys are seeking to get the conviction reversed.
Two years after a jury made Donald Trump the first president to enter office as a felon, a New York appeals court is considering his bid to throw out his criminal hush money conviction.

Across more than an hour of oral argument Thursday, five justices of New York's Appellate Division wrestled with Trump's claims that prosecutors misused the law to target him, and that some of the evidence elicited at trial should have been protected by presidential immunity.
"This case was infected by multiple fatal errors under New York and federal law," argued Trump attorney Robert Giuffra.

Prosecutors in the 2024 case alleged a scheme to conceal a $130,000 hush money payment from Trump's then-lawyer to adult film actress Stormy Daniels ahead of the 2016 presidential election. A jury convicted Trump on 34 criminal counts of falsifying bushes records in the first degree -- one for each of the payments Trump made to reimburse his lawyer, which prosecutors say were falsified to conceal their true purpose.

Giuffra's main argument to the court was that prosecutors improperly used a federal law -- the Federal Election Campaign Act -- in state court to secure a conviction. During the trial, jurors were told that to convict Trump for falsifying business records in the first degree, they would need to conclude that the crime was done in furtherance of one of three other illegal acts -- by violating tax laws, state campaign finance laws, or the Federal Election Campaign Act.

"The reason why this case is so important, there's never been a case where a local district attorney -- there's 2,300 of them in the United States -- has ever prosecuted a candidate, a federal candidate, much less a presidential candidate, for a violation [of] FECA," he said.
But the panel of judges questioned whether that argument was enough to justify throwing out the conviction, since FECA was only one part of the state's overall case.

"That's the issue. The defendant was not convicted of violating federal election laws. He was convicted of falsifying business records of a New York enterprise, right?" said Associate Justice Troy Webber. "It's not that he was convicted of violating any type of federal election."

Steven Wu, an attorney for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, who brought the case, argued that Trump's argument about FECA has already been rejected twice by a federal court, that the jury had a choice of three violations, and that the federal law only played a "minor role" in their case.

"They were given a menu of options and said from any of these you can draw the inference," Wu said. "The people are not required to establish particular unlawful means under that statute ... it is enough to come in with general evidence of criminal behavior."

Wu also pushed back against Trump's argument that some of the evidence at trial -- including the testimony of former White House Communications Director Hope Hicks, part of Trump attorney Michael Cohen's testimony, and a series of Trump's tweets -- should have been protected by presidential immunity.

At least one the justice's appeared receptive to the argument related to Hicks. Prosecutors had described her testimony about Trump's reaction to the Stormy Daniels story coming out in 2018 as the final "nail" in Trump's coffin.
"I think Mr. Trump's opinion was it was better to be dealing with it now, and that it would have been bad to have that story come out before the election," Hicks testified at trial.
Associate Justice Martin Shulman noted that the testimony "certainly seems to fit within the outer perimeters" of presidential immunity.

"We're talking about certain functions and communicating with Hope Hicks, who was his communication director, on a particular matter that concerned his role as a president and the perception of the public as his role as a president," he said.
Wu argued that Trump's lawyers were overextending presidential immunity to protect his actions, and that the evidence in question was a small part of the case.

"It is just not correct that anything that a president says publicly will qualify as an official act, even within the presumptive outer sphere," he said. "They object to four tweets from the defendant out of five of 500 trial exhibits. This is a drop in the bucket of the evidence that was against the defendant."

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, he was sentenced to an unconditional discharge -- due to the extraordinary circumstances of him being days away from his inauguration -- and later made his lead defense attorney from that trial, Todd Blanche, the attorney general of the United States.
"It's been a political witch hunt. It was done to damage my reputation so that I'd lose the election, and obviously that didn't work," Trump said during his sentencing.

title: 3rd place Mississippi Senate candidate says he did not spoil tight race for Democrat
summary: The independent third place candidate in Mississippi's tight Senate race, Ty Pinkins, says he did not spoil the race.
story: The race remains uncalled as of Thursday morning.

Independent Ty Pinkins, the third-place candidate in Mississippi's surprisingly tightly contested Senate race, says he does not believe he spoiled the race for the Democrat, and may have ultimately helped him in the final tally.

With only around 1,700 votes separating Democrat Scott Colom and incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the hotly contested race, Pinkins, who currently holds around 20,000 votes, said Wednesday he hopes Colom wins the race, and said he may have actually boosted the Democrat's performance.
"Now, there's a fight, and he's in the lead, and I hope he wins," Pinkins told CNN on Wednesday, when the margin was 65 votes.
Pinkins claimed that a majority of his votes came from traditionally Republican counties in the state.
"What we did in this race as an independent campaign, we did the opposite of a spoiler if you look at the data coming out of this race," Pinkins said.
Pinkins said throughout the summer his campaign believed a large amount of his support was coming from Republicans.
"You can't assume that all of those votes would have went right back to Scott Colom," he said, citing the state's history of electing Republicans.
Pinkins said, "I'm happy that we drew votes from Cindy Hyde-Smith."
With 96% of the expected vote reporting as of Thursday, Democrat Scott Colom slightly leads with 49.0% of the vote (466,226), followed by Republican Hyde-Smith with 48.9% of the vote (464,502).

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a Wednesday afternoon update that, at the time, there were around 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could be received within the next five business days, and that there are "an unknown number of affidavit ballots that will be processed within the 10-day window counties have to certify their results."
Mississippi's Secretary of State Office confirmed to ABC News this week that the state has no formal recount process.
According to the secretary of state's office, candidates cannot request a recount, and a recount cannot be automatically triggered in Mississippi.

The office did share, however, that a candidate can perform "a ballot box exam" and examine ballot materials after the election is certified. If they see issues, they can file a legal challenge, the office said.
ABC News has not projected the race.

title: What to know about recounts in Mississippi with razor-thin margin in Senate race
summary: The Senate race between Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom remains uncalled. Mississippi election law does not provide for automatic or requested recounts.
story: The Senate race between Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom remains uncalled.

While razor-thin election margins in American politics typically spark anticipation of recounts, there is no such process in place in Mississippi, where the Senate race is currently within a margin of a few dozen votes as of Wednesday morning.

As the Democratic challenger Scott Colom and incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith remain neck-and-neck with 96% of the expected vote in, Mississippi's Secretary of State Office confirmed to ABC News that the state has no formal recount process.
According to the secretary of state's office, candidates cannot request a recount, and a recount cannot be automatically triggered in Mississippi.

The office did share, however, that a candidate can perform "a ballot box exam" and examine ballot materials after the election is certified. If they see issues, they can file a legal challenge, the office said.
As of Wednesday night, Colom had 49% of the vote followed by Hyde-Smith who had 48.9% of the vote with 96% of the expected vote reporting.
Independent challenger Ty Pinkins held 2.1% of the vote
Colom, with 464,926 votes votes, had 1,138 more votes than Hyde-Smith, with 463,788. Pinkins had 19,934 votes.

Mississippi allows mail ballots to arrive up to five business days after the election, according to the Secretary of State's office, which sets that day as Nov. 10, 2026. However, the ballots had to be postmarked on or before Election Day.

It is possible there are mail ballots or provisional ballots -- called "affidavit ballots" in Mississippi, which allow a resident to vote even if their address cannot be found in the poll book at their precinct-- still left to be counted, although it is unclear how many there may be.

Colom's campaign manager said on Tuesday night that the campaign thinks there could be around 15,000 provisional ballots left to be counted; the office of the Mississippi Secretary of State told ABC News there is no definitive number they can give.

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a Wednesday afternoon update that there are around 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could be received within the next five business days, and that there are "an unknown number of affidavit ballots that will be processed within the 10-day window counties have to certify their results."
The certification deadline is Nov. 13.

The slim margin comes as a shock in deep-red Mississippi, which voted for President Donald Trump with 61% of the vote in 2024 and elected Hyde-Smith to the Senate with 54% of the vote in 2020, two years after she took office by appointment in 2018.

Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982.
President Donald Trump rallied with Hyde-Smith last month, attempting to shore up support for the incumbent candidate before the election.
"My opponent, Scott Colom, is the most radical Senate candidate to run for Mississippi, literally, in our lifetimes," Hyde-Smith said, speaking ahead of Trump at the rally.
Colom, speaking at a press conference ahead of the rally, said, "A lot of folks ain't gonna be able to make this rally because they can't afford the gas to get up here."

title: Who won the redistricting war? So far, it looks like Democrats
summary: Dems were able to keep seats that Republicans redrew to make them GOP-friendly.
story: Dems were able to keep seats that Republicans redrew to make them GOP-friendly.

Texas Republicans touched off a battle of mid-decade redistricting efforts when they embraced a plan pushed by President Donald Trump for the GOP-controlled legislature to redraw congressional districts to make them more friendly to Republicans.
California retaliated with its own gerrymandering in an effort to flip five seats held by Republicans to counter the effort to redraw five seats in Texas.
Other states got into the fight, either choosing to redraw their maps ahead of the midterm elections or taking advantage of court rulings that gave them an opportunity to.

While Republicans redrew 15 congressional seats to try to flip over the past two years, as of Thursday afternoon they are projected to lose more than two-thirds of them. Meanwhile, California's Proposition 50 ballot initiative that redrew five seats to make them more friendly to Democrats appears to be paying off for them.
Here's where things currently stand:
Alabama Second District: Democrats hold -- Rep. Shomari Figures is projected to hold onto his seat.
Florida 9: Not yet projected.
Florida 14: Democrats hold -- Rep. Kathy Castor is projected to keep her seat.
Florida 22: Democrats hold -- Democratic candidate Pia Dandiya is projected to win.
Florida 25: Democrats hold -- Rep. Jared Moskowitz is projected to win in this district.
Louisiana 6: Not yet projected.
North Carolina 1: Democrats hold -- Rep. Don Davis is projected to win.
Ohio 1: Democrats hold -- Rep. Greg Landsman is projected to win.
Ohio 9: Democrats hold -- Rep. Marcy Kaptur is projected to win.
Tennessee 9: Republicans flip -- Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson conceded to Brent Taylor in this seat that opened up when Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen announced he was retiring.
Texas 9: Democrats hold - Democratic candidate Leticia Gutierrez is projected to win this open seat.
Texas 28: Democrats hold -- Rep. Henry Cuellar is projected to win.
Texas 32: Republicans flip -- Republican candidate Jace Yarbrough is projected to win this seat that is open after Democratic Rep. Julie Johnson opted to leave Congress.
Texas 34: Democrats hold -- Rep. Vincente Gonzalez is projected to win.
Texas 35: Democrats hold -- Democratic candidate Jonny Garcia is projected to win.
California 1: Democrats flip -- Democratic candidate Mike McGuire unseated GOP Rep. James Gallagher.
California 3: Democrats flip -- Rep. Ami Bera won this seat held by Republican-aligned independent Kevin Kiley, who is projected to lose in the new 6th District.
California 6: Democrats flip -- Democratic candidate Randy Villegas unseated Rep. David Valadao
California 41: Democrats flip -- Democraitc candidate Linda Sánchez is projected to win this seat held by Republican Ken Calvert, who ran in a different district.
California 48: Democrats flip -- Democratic candidate Marni von Wilpert is projected to flip the seat held by Republican incumbent Darrell Issa, who is retiring.
Utah 1: Democrats flip -- former Rep. Ben McAdams is projected to win in this redrawn district that favored Democrats and caused shuffling and retirements among Utah incumbents.

title: How Democrats flipped the Senate blue: The ABC News Voter Poll tells the story
summary: ABC News projects that the Democratic Party has won a majority of seats in the U.S. Senate. Here’s how Democrats won some key races to get there.
story: ABC News projects that Democrats will take control of the House as well.

Democrats rode a wave of discontent -- both for the economy and President Donald Trump -- and gained control of the Senate once again, making gains in places that just two years ago would have been unthinkable.

From Georgia, South Carolina and Texas in the South to Ohio, Kansas and Iowa in the Midwest, insurgent Democrats not only won but did so with significant margins -- with notable shifts in key demographic groups and voting blocs.
Here's how we got here:

Democrat Jon Ossoff is projected to win reelection to the U.S. Senate, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Ossoff, who narrowly won his Senate seat in a runoff election in 2021, earned more support from Georgia voters in this year’s race, winning the support of around 6 in 10 voters across the state.
Ossoff was able to improve his vote margins among white voters by about 10 percentage points compared to Democrat Raphael Warnock’s victory in 2022.

Younger voters helped propel Ossoff to victory in the 2026 Georgia Senate race, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Voters under 30 widened their support for a Democrat, from 21 points in 2022 to 72 points now. While 45- to 64-year-olds supported the Republican candidate by 8 percentage points in 2022, they supported Ossoff by 11 points this year, according to ABC News Voter Polls.

Ossoff was able to win solidly among independents, who make up 3 in 10 voters in the Georgia electorate, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Two-thirds of independents voted for Ossoff over his Republican challenger, Mike Collins.
Ossoff built support among white voters in the 2026 election compared to Warnock in 2022. Four in 10 white voters backed Ossoff in this year’s race, while 29% supported Warnock back in 2022.

About 3 in 10 Georgia Senate voters say they are angry about the way things are going in the country today according to ABC News Voter polls. Around 9 in 10 Georgia gubernatorial voters who said they were angry about the country’s state of affairs supported Ossoff.

According to ABC News Voter Polls, about three-quarters of Georgia Senate voters rate the economy negatively, including about a third who say the economy is poor. Roughly 9 in 10 voters who describe the nation’s economy as poor voted for Ossoff in the 2026 Senate election.

According to ABC News Voter Polls, about 6 in 10 Georgia Senate voters disapprove of the way Trump is handling his job as president, including about half of voters who strongly disapprove. Roughly 9 in 10 voters who disapprove of Trump backed Ossoff in this year’s race.
Democrat Annie Andrews is projected to have defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who held the seat after her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham, died in June.

Black voters in South Carolina supported Andrews over Graham by an 85% to 12% margin and made up 18% of the electorate, according to ABC News Voter Polls, wider than the margin that Democrat Krystle Matthews had over Republican Tim Scott in 2022 when Black voters made up 22% of the electorate.
But white voters shifted heavily toward the Democrat this year. In 2022, white voters supported Scott by 54 percentage points. This time they supported Graham by only 14 points.

Women backed Andrews over Graham by 13 percentage points, according to ABC Voter Polls. In 2022, women backed Scott by 18 percentage points. While Graham won men this year, her margin was in the single digits -- compared to a 34-point margin in favor of Scott four years ago. Among white men, in particular, Graham’s margin was around 19 percentage points -- down from a 58-point margin for the Republican in 2022.

Roughly 4 in 10 South Carolina voters are 65 and older, and they backed Graham by 9 percentage points over Andrews, according to ABC Voter Polls. That margin is much narrower than the 32 point margin that Scott held among these older voters in 2022.
One in 10 voters who said they backed Trump in 2024 crossed over to vote for Andrews this year. Almost none of Kamala Harris' 2024 voters supported Graham, according to ABC News Voter Polls.

College graduates backed Andrews by a margin of 18 points, according to ABC News Voter Polls. That was a flip from 2020 when 57% of college graduates voted for Lindsey Graham. In 2022, Scott won college graduates by 23 percentage points.

Suburban voters in South Carolina broke toward Andrews by 7 percentage points according to ABC News Voter Polls. In 2022, suburban voters favored Scott by 24 percentage points. Urban voters backed Andrews by a 27 point margin, more than double the margin from 2022.

Josh Turek is projected to win the Iowa Senate race, becoming the first Democrat to represent Iowa in the upper chamber since Tom Harkin was elected in 2008. His victory was propelled by strength among independents and by peeling off enough Trump 2024 voters.

Self-identified independents in Iowa preferred Turek by around 20 percentage points, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Party-switching among Democrats and Republicans was relatively muted, though Turek captured more Republicans (7%) than Democrats who voted for GOP candidate Ashley Hinson (1%).
About 1 in 10 Iowa Senate voters who backed Trump in 2024 crossed over to Turek, while few Harris voters supported Hinson, according to ABC News Voter Polls.

Male voters in Iowa backed Hinson by 8 percentage points, while women supported Democrat Turek by 15 points, according to ABC News Voter Polls. In 2022, Republican Chuck Grassley carried men by 24 points and women by 3 points.

In 2022, Iowa Senate voters under 30 were the only age group to back Democrat Michael Franken over Grassley by 9 percentage points. This year, voters aged 18 to 29 supported Turek by around a 2-to-1 margin, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Voters aged 30 to 44 also preferred Turek by about 13 points, those aged 45 to 64 backed Hinson by 8 points and voters 65 and older were roughly evenly split between the candidates.
Democrat Sherrod Brown is projected to win the Ohio Senate seat over Republican John Husted and retake the seat he lost in 2024. Here’s how he built a winning coalition.

Ohio voters were negative about the state of the economy, frustrated with Trump’s tariffs and concerned about high costs, which a majority blamed on Trump, according to ABC Voter Polls. And Brown won big among the more economically disenchanted. He was also able to capitalize on the roughly 6 in 10 who said Husted was too supportive of Trump, gaining ground relative to his 2024 margins among most key demographic groups.
Brown won female voters in Ohio by 14 percentage points over Husted, according to ABC Voter Polls. In 2024, women split about evenly between Brown and Republican Bernie Moreno.

Brown won voters under 30 by more than 40 percentage points, according to ABC Voter Polls -- a sharp reversal from 2024 when voters under 30 backed Moreno by 4 percentage points. He also won voters ages 30 to 44 by roughly 30 points, compared with his 2-point margin in 2024. The two candidates split the vote of those ages 45 to 64 -- a group Brown lost by 10 points two years ago. This year, though, Brown lost ground among voters ages 65 and older compared with 2024.

Independents backed Brown over Husted by 25 percentage points, according to ABC Voter Polls. This is a sizable increase over his margin with this group in 2024 (+9) and 2018 (+12), according to Edison. Brown also won nearly all Democrats and around 1 in 10 Republicans.

White Ohio voters supported the Republican Senate candidate by at least 10 percentage points in each of the last two cycles. But tonight, white voters broke nearly evenly according to ABC Voter Polls -- returning to margins last seen in the 2018 midterms.
Brown’s margin among Black voters also increased from 71 points in 2024 to 81 points this year, according to ABC Voter Polls.

Ohio voters with a college degree backed Brown by about 22 percentage points, according to ABC News Voter Polls. This is an improvement over his 14-point margin with this group in both 2024 and 2018. While he lost voters without a college degree to Husted by single digits, this improved substantially over the 14 points by which he lost this group in 2024.
Democrat Adam Hamilton is projected to become the first Democrat to be elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. Here’s how he beat incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall to win the seat.

Four in 10 Kansas Senate voters say they are angry about the way things are going in the country today, according to ABC News Voter Polls, and they supported Hamilton over Marshall by an 80-point margin. Another roughly third are dissatisfied and they roughly split their vote according to ABC News Voter Polls.
Nearly 6 in 10 Kansas Senate voters disapprove of Trump, including about half who strongly disapprove and they widely supported Hamilton over Marshall, according to ABC News Voter Polls.

About 4 in 10 voters in Kansas are Republicans and over 8 in 10 of them voted for Marshall, according to ABC News Voter Polls -- but 12% of them split off to vote for Hamilton and nearly all Democrats supported Hamilton. Independents split for the Democrat by a more than 2-to-1 margin, according to Voter Polls.

Women supported Hamilton by a 10-percentage point margin and men supported Marshall by a 2-point margin, according to ABC News Voter Polls. In the 2022 election, both men and women supported Republican Jerry Moran by double-digit margins and he won his third term to the U.S. Senate by a wide margin. In 2020, when Marshall beat Democrat Barbara Bolinger for the U.S. Senate, men supported Marshall by 22 points, but Kansas women were about evenly split.

Essentially all of the Kansas voters who voted for Harris in 2024 supported Hamilton, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Trump voters were not as united around Marshall, with 9% of them peeling off for Hamilton.

Democrat James Talarico, an educator and member of the Texas House of Representatives, was projected to defeat Republican Ken Paxton. Talarico was propelled to victory by younger voters. Roughly 8 in 10 voters ages 18-29 (79%) supported Talarico in this year’s race, compared with about half of 18 to 29-year-olds who supported Democrat Collin Allred in 2024.

In the Texas Senate race, 58% of female voters supported Talarico, while men were roughly evenly split in their vote, according to ABC News Voter Polls. In the 2024 Texas Senate race, male voters favored Republican Ted Cruz by an 18 percentage point margin over Allred while women were about evenly split between candidates.

Talarico gained among Black and Hispanic Texans during his 2026 Senate victory, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Nine in 10 Black voters and about two-thirds of Hispanic Texans supported Talarico over Paxton. This is roughly 10 percentage points higher than the shares Allred received from these groups during his 2024 candidacy for Senate.

Roughly 7 in 10 Texas Senate voters (72%) rated the economy negatively, including 34% who rated the economy as poor according to ABC News Voter Polls. Among voters who evaluated the economy negatively, 73% voted for Talarico.

About 4 in 10 Texas Senate voters (40%) said the economy was the top issue facing the country, while 29% said the state of democracy, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Voters who viewed democracy as the most important issue favored Talarico by a roughly 3-to-1 margin, while Talarico won economy-focused voters by a double-digit margin.
Nearly 6 in 10 Texas Senate voters disapproved of Trump, including 51% who disapproved strongly, and those voters supported Talarico by wide margins.

About twice as many Texas Senate voters said they were worse off (44%) than better off (20%) compared with two years ago, according to ABC News Voter Polls. Among voters who said their financial situation has worsened, 77% voted for Talarico.
-ABC News' Sofi Sinovich, Bianca DiJulio, Alauna Safarpour and Will Lennon contributed to this report.

title: Vance blames Iran war for GOP's midterms defeat. Trump says he would 'do it again'
summary: ABC News Voter poll found 34% of voters say the war was "crucial" to their vote.
story: ABC News Voter poll found 34% of voters say the war was "crucial" to their vote.

Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the Trump administration's ongoing war with Iran was to blame for Republicans' massive losses in Tuesday's midterm election, during which Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress.
But President Donald Trump, asked about Vance's comments, remained committed to the ongoing military action despite "largely" agreeing with Vance about the impact of the war on the election.
The vice president wrote in a lengthy social media post that "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said of the Trump administration's ongoing conflict with Iran. "The president himself said so last night."
Vance said he spoke with pollsters who told him that many people who voted for Trump in 2024 switched to the Democrats in this election because they were "angry."
The ABC News Voter Poll found about 4 in 10 House voters nationally said they were angry about the way things were going in the country today and a similar share were dissatisfied.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance wrote.
The vice president in the past has publicly been supportive of the war and slammed the president's critics over the issue.
Trump often suggested on the campaign trail that the war, and inflated gas prices, were "a small price to pay" to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon.
Asked about Vance's comments during an event at the White House on Wednesday, Trump called them "largely true," however he defended his decision to attack Iran, which he has done in the past.
"If I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long term, it's the only answer," Trump told reporters. "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
Trump said he knew Vance's view of the war from the beginning.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine. Yeah, I thought it was good," Trump said of Vance's social media post. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Asked if he felt the war was worth it, Trump said he did.
"I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice," he said, later adding, "I can tell you that, as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing differently."
ABC News' Voter Poll of House voters found that voters nationally were more focused on other factors, including the cost of living, than the Iran war.

Nationally, 34% of U.S. House voters said that the war in Iran was "crucial" to their vote, while 49% said the same about the cost of living and 55% said government corruption was crucial to their vote.
Although the Iran war has led to rising gas prices, voters have said that their concerns over the cost of living weren't just limited to their receipts at the pump.
The Voter Poll found 59% of House voters nationally saying they were "very concerned" about the cost of healthcare.

About 6 in 10 U.S. House voters said that the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare and 55% said the Trump administration's policies have made their healthcare costs worse. Just 10% said the Trump administration has improved their healthcare costs, according to the Voter Poll.
Trump's tariffs have also been costing the typical American household almost $1,000 a year.
Vance said in his X post that an unidentified pollster told him that their "economic messaging wasn't sharp enough down the stretch."

Vance argued that Republicans were not failed by turnout among Trump 2024 voters, saying they "showed up," but that those Americans, according to a pollster, were "pissed and planning to vote for the other guys."
He also claimed of Republican turnout that "in no state was it catastrophic."
"The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," the vice president said.
-ABC News' Elizabeth Schulze contributed to this report.

title: DOJ again moves to dismiss Steve Bannon's contempt of Congress conviction
summary: The DOJ has filed another push to have a judge dismiss Trump ally Steve Bannon's conviction over his defiance of a subpoena from the House panel that investigated Jan. 6.
story: Bannon was convicted in 2022 for defying a subpoena from the House Jan. 6 panel.

The Justice Department on Thursday filed a renewed push to have a federal judge dismiss Trump ally Steve Bannon's conviction for criminal contempt over his defiance of a subpoena from the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Bannon was convicted in 2022 on two counts of contempt of Congress for defying a subpoena from the congressional committee that investigated the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. He served four months in prison in 2024.

In August, the Trump-appointed federal judge who presided over Bannon's case, Carl Nichols, rejected the DOJ's motion to dismiss the conviction after determining prosecutors didn't provide sufficient justification for the move.

In their filing Thursday, the DOJ explained its argument was rooted "in an exercise of its prosecutorial discretion" and that the administration "does not believe that it is appropriate to pursue contempt of Congress charges against a former advisor to the President who did not comply with a subpoena investigating the events of January 6, 2021, based on an asserted belief that he was protected by executive privilege."

"That is especially so because the United States harbors significant doubts about the fairness of Defendant's trial and whether D.C. Circuit precedent improperly foreclosed Defendant from raising a defense that he did not "willfully" violate [the contempt of Congress statute] in light of his belief that compliance with the subpoena was unnecessary due to executive privilege," the filing said. "In these circumstances, the United States no longer wishes to pursue this prosecution."

The filing further points to President Trump's "grave concerns" about the Biden administration's prosecutions that stemmed from the Jan. 6 assault on the Capitol and Trump's sweeping commutations for nearly all of the pro-Trump rioters charged in connection with the attack.

"In light of those actions by the Chief Executive, the Department has determined that it is inconsistent with this Administration's enforcement priorities to seek affirmance of a criminal conviction of a former advisor to President Trump who did not comply with a subpoena related to January 6 based on an asserted belief that executive privilege applied," the DOJ said.

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
summary: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations
story: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations

MEXICO CITY -- Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country's Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.

No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.

Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City's main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.

But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.

In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.

In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island's community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery's perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: Heavy rains cause flash flooding, water rescues on Georgia-Tennessee border
summary: Thunderstorms with heavy rain have caused record flooding in two towns straddling the Georgia-Tennessee border
story: Thunderstorms with heavy rain have caused record flooding in two towns straddling the Georgia-Tennessee border

McCAYSVILLE, Ga. -- Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused record flooding overnight in twin towns straddling the Georgia-Tennessee border, submerging some buildings to their rooflines on Thursday as emergency responders rescued dozens of people.

The storms dropped 3 to 5 inches (8 to 13 centimeters) of rain in a mountainous area where the Toccoa River flows between McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, causing life-threatening flooding and flash flood warnings on both sides.
McCaysville is home to about 1,000 people, while Copperhill has fewer than 500 residents.
The Toccoa River reached a record high Thursday morning of 18 feet (5.5 meters) after the overnight deluge, according to a river gauge in Copperhill.
The river was 2 feet (0.6 meters) above the level where forecasters call for a catastrophic flood that tops bridges and cuts off Copperhill and McCaysville as well as requiring massive evacuations.

“It’s over the rooftops in several different areas. Right here in our downtown business district it’s about 6-7 feet high,” McCaysville Police Chief Michael Earley told Fox5 Atlanta. “I have one of my police cars that’s floating down the river right now. Don’t know where it’s at, but it’s somewhere down there.”

Photos shared with local media showed some buildings submerged up to their rooflines. Local news video footage showed rescue crews in red boats and motorized rafts navigating through deep, rushing water flowing through downtown streets. Earley said more than 30 rescues were conducted overnight.

Robert Poole, spokesperson for the Fannin County Emergency Management Agency on the Georgia side, estimated that about 20 people had been rescued, with no reported injuries or deaths. The water had begun receding by late Thursday morning, he said.

“The calls have slowed down as far as people stranded that need rescues, so we’re probably going to end up utilizing a helicopter and possibly some drones just to do an aerial survey and see if there’s anybody out there that needs our help,” he said.

“Please do not let the rain stopping give you a false sense of security,” the agency said on social media. “Floodwaters remain extremely dangerous, and conditions can continue to worsen even after the rain has stopped.”

title: Postal employee shot 2 coworkers at an Iowa post office before being captured, police say
summary: Authorities say a female postal employee shot two colleagues at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city before being captured nearby
story: Authorities say a female postal employee shot two colleagues at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city before being captured nearby
DES MOINES, Iowa -- A female postal worker shot two fellow employees at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city Thursday before being captured nearby, authorities said.
A third employee was injured in a fall while trying to escape. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, police said.
“They’re all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now,” Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims, two women and a man. All were in stable condition.
The shooting happened on the facility’s second floor, in an area not accessible to the public. Witnesses reported hearing 10 to 12 shots, he said.

Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured the suspect, who was detained along a nearby bike path without resistance. Police began receiving calls about the shooting around 9:10 a.m., and the suspect was detained at 9:21 a.m., he said. Authorities didn’t immediately identify the alleged shooter.
The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in an email that it was investigating the shooting along with local, state and federal law enforcement.
Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting.
“We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved," she posted online. "Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.”

Des Moines Public Schools said the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center temporarily barred anyone from entering or leaving the facilities due to the shooting. Those restrictions were lifted after police told them the suspect was in custody.
Past shootings at postal facilities have prompted the Postal Service to study employee safety.

In 1986, a disgruntled postal worker went on a deadly rampage at a post office in Edmond, Oklahoma, shooting 14 fellow workers before killing himself. After that shooting and others over the next decade, postal officials commissioned a study released in 2000 to examine workplace violence around the time that the term “going postal” was becoming conversational.
The report issued several recommendations to flag violent tendencies while concluding that “going postal” is a myth and that postal employees are less violent than the national workforce.
Associated Press writers R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.

title: College students found dead in mountains fell to deaths when climbing anchor broke
summary: Authorities say the two Colorado college students whose bodies were recovered last week died when an anchor they were using to climb failed and they fell a “substantial distance."
story: Authorities say the two Colorado college students whose bodies were recovered last week died when an anchor they were using to climb failed and they fell a “substantial distance."

The two college students whose bodies were recovered last week in the Colorado mountains died when an anchor they were using to climb failed and they fell a “substantial distance,” authorities said Tuesday.

Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, died instantly from multiple blunt force injuries, an autopsy found, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office and coroner’s office. Their bodies were found in a snow-filled basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Aspen.

It was not known why the anchor failed, but the heavy snowstorm was not a direct factor, according to the statement, which commended the college students for their love of the outdoors and preparation for the climbing trip.

“In most similar cases that have led to a devastating conclusion we find it easy to pick apart what was done wrong,” said Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich. “That was not the case with Kaden and Jackson.”

The pair had set out from Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus for what was supposed to be a weekend trip. While they were originally aiming for Ice Mountain, a 13,958-foot (4,254-meter) peak, Rohrich said they appeared to switch to the 13,597-foot (4,144-meter) West Apostle Mountain.

Donlon was starting to rappel from an anchor point on a rock when it had a “catastrophic failure," despite being backed up by a metal spike in the rock and a secondary anchor, according to the statement. Matsuda was attached to the same anchor points.
They both fell a long distance, although officials said the exact length was not known, according to the statement.

“While their lives were far too short, they spent their final moments together surrounded by the majestic beauty of Chaffee County’s high peaks that they loved,” Rohrich said. “There is also relief knowing neither of them suffered.”

Colorado Mountain College, which has campuses throughout the Colorado Rockies, is known for its programs focusing on the state’s robust outdoor recreation economy, including mountaineering, ski patrol and guiding careers.

Matsuda, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Donlon, of Queensbury, New York, became fast friends at the small campus in Leadville, which bills itself as America’s highest city at 10,119 feet (3,084 meters) above sea level. Located about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Denver, the city is home to about 2,600 people and is flanked by some of Colorado’s tallest mountains.
Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter. Donlon, an avid climber and skier, was studying outdoor recreation leadership and had come to Colorado to pursue his love of the mountains.
It was raining when they started hiking, according to the sheriff’s office, and later a severe storm arrived, dumping up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of snow.

title: 3 executions scheduled for the same day in Indiana, Florida and Alabama
summary: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two young children in a house fire has been executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S. Jeffrey Weisheit's time of death was 12:45 a.m. Thursday
story: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two young children in a house fire has been executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S. Jeffrey Weisheit's time of death was 12:45 a.m. Thursday
An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
It will be Florida’s 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis — matching a record set by the state in 2025 — but the first this year in Indiana.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said that it's confident “in our ability to humanely carry out” the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit’s case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
“These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence,” he said. "Today, Weisheit’s sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court.”

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty.”

In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said that Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.

Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.

Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.

“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
Fischer reported from Fort Lauderdale, Florida and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: Gov. Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in state to life without parole
