title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
summary: Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.
story: Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.
Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.
Raman released a video statement on Thursday afternoon saying she is deeply honored to be the next mayor of LA.

"Thank you to the thousands of people who knocked on doors, sent texts, made phone calls, convinced their neighbors to believe in the promise of this big, beautiful, joyful city that we get to call home," the video said.
Raman spoke directly to people who voted for Bass or didn't vote at all, saying she is "going to City Hall to work every single day to earn your trust, and to earn your trust in this city again."
In the video, Raman also paid tribute to Bass, thanking her for her decades of service and highlighting her as the first woman mayor of LA.

"She has served Los Angeles for so many decades and I know so many people, not just across this city but across this country, are grateful for her dedication to the promise of Los Angeles," Raman said.
Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.
Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.
A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.
Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Spencer Pratt.
Councilmember Nithya Raman
Raman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.
During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Spencer Pratt to face Bass in the general election.
Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.

One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hoped to undertake similar work to help small businesses.
Mayor Karen Bass
After serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office.

Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.

She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.

Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November.
"For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."
He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."

title: Did Republican efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 24 seats and Democrats had won 14 seats, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Seven Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night, and CBS News estimates another district is likely Democratic. Republicans have only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Wednesday, four Democrats had won and CBS News estimated that another four were toss-ups. Another district, North Carolina's 8th District in the southern part of the state, is likely Republican.
If Democrats ultimately win any of the undecided races, North Carolina will be a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 6th District is a toss-up and the 5th District race will go to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 16 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were five districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Wednesday, Democrats won in 42 districts, while CBS News estimates another six are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won seven seats, Republicans won two and two are considered toss-ups.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

Gabriella  Biello

Democrats won control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projects, with victories in battleground districts across the country. The decisive wins came as President Trump's approval rating hit 38%, historically low for a president in the midterms, in an election where 89% of voters said cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their votes.

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson announced in a call with his staff Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader when the new Congress is seated. Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise told Republicans they want the job.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said he expects his party to win at least 255 seats after all the votes are counted. He also said no one in the caucus has raised the idea of impeaching President Trump. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability," he told reporters.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election. Democrats, who had 214 seats going into the midterms, flipped a number of GOP-held seats and proved to be competitive in battlegrounds and in some unexpected places.

Democrats won in battleground districts nationwide, in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky and Colorado, among other states. Several races still remain to be called, two days after the election.
Republicans in several states, including Texas and Florida, had redistricted to try to gain an edge in the elections, but redrawing ultimately did not stave off their losses.

title: Trump's lawyers argue appeal in "hush money" case
summary: President Trump was convicted in 2024 of 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
story: President Trump's lawyers on Thursday urged a New York appellate court to throw out his conviction on 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to an adult film star.

They argued that the jury was given flawed instructions, allowing them to consider violations of federal election law as part of their determination in the case, calling it an "obvious ground for reversal." Mr. Trump has long argued that the federal law, known as FECA, preempts state prosecution.

"All of the payments that are issued in this case, whether it be the payments to [adult film star Stormy Daniels], other payments to two other folks, those were payments that were deemed to be illegal contributions or expenditures under FECA," said Mr. Trump's attorney, Robert Giuffra.
Steven Wu, a lawyer for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, countered that a federal court has twice rejected the claim that FECA preempted New York's prosecution of Mr. Trump.
"This court should reach the same conclusion here," Wu said.
Giuffra and Wu were interrupted frequently by a five-judge panel that pelted them with questions picking apart their arguments.

A unanimous jury convicted Mr. Trump in May 2024 for his part in a scheme to falsify business records related to reimbursements made to Michael Cohen, his attorney at the time. Cohen had paid $130,000 to adult film star Stormy Daniels, days before the 2016 election, in exchange for her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Mr. Trump years earlier. Mr. Trump has denied the allegations.

The jury was asked to consider if Mr. Trump falsified business records, counts that by themselves would have been misdemeanors, and if he intended to commit any other crime in doing so, including bank fraud, tax fraud or the violations of FECA — any of which elevated the charges to felonies. They did not have to be unanimous in what other crimes they thought he intended to commit.
Giuffra, the powerful co-chair of the white-shoe firm Sullivan & Cromwell, argued that they should have been required to be unanimous on that element of the felony.

Wu noted that the trial judge in the case asked Mr. Trump's defense attorneys about that, and they indicated they did not believe it was required under the law. Instead, they asked the judge to include that directive "in his discretion because of the importance of the case," Wu said, paraphrasing Emil Bove III, who was one of Mr. Trump's trial lawyers.
The trial judge, Juan Merchan, declined.
"What you're asking me to do is change the law, and I'm not going to do that," Merchan said at the time.

Mr. Trump's attorneys in the case have changed since the 2024 trial — one former defense attorney, Todd Blanche, is now U.S. attorney general, and Bove is now a federal judge — but his new team of personal lawyers has continued to echo the arguments he made throughout the trial.
An Oct. 16 filing by Giuffra began with a line that Mr. Trump himself frequently said and posted on social media: The case, "should have never been brought."

A spokesman for Mr. Trump's legal team said a 2024 Supreme Court decision related to presidential immunity, "the federal and New York state Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan D.A. be overturned and dismissed."
"President Trump will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn," the spokesperson said.
Lawyers for Bragg have characterized the 2016 "hush money" plan as "a conspiracy to defraud the American public and government regulators."
"The criminal charges here arose from [Mr. Trump's] unofficial, non-presidential conduct—as multiple courts have already found," they wrote in a July brief.
The arguments came a week after the death of a judge who was presiding over a yearslong parallel effort by Mr. Trump to move the case from state to federal court.

The judge, Alvin Hellerstein, repeatedly rejected Mr. Trump's arguments, and was particularly scathing in his response to Mr. Trump's claim that the reimbursements to Cohen were related to his official work as president.

"Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to [Stormy Daniels] cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty," Hellerstein wrote. "Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty."
On Thursday, the two sides also argued over whether tweets shown at trial and testimony of former White House communications director Hope Hicks fell under presidential immunity.

One judge on the panel said Hicks' testimony, which described a conversation about the Stormy Daniels allegations after they became public, may have fit in the "gray area of what's in the outer sphere of presidential duties."
Asked for his thoughts after the arguments, Giuffra said, "I think it went well."
"We should definitely win," he said.

title: Harmeet Dhillon, DOJ's controversial civil rights chief, resigns
summary: Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, resigned from the Justice Department on Thursday.
story: Washington — Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She overhauled a division that had long prioritized fighting discrimination against some of the nation's most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.

Since taking over the division, often lauded as being the "crown jewel" of the DOJ, she has reoriented it to focus instead on other priorities that have included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

In her resignation letter to President Trump, which was seen by CBS News, Dhillon said that she told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in early October that she intended to step down after the midterm elections.

Two sources familiar with the matter, however, told CBS News that Mr. Trump demanded she be fired after he watched her Oct. 18 appearance on "60 Minutes" discussing the government's election integrity efforts.

In that interview, Dhillon touted the Justice Department's efforts to prosecute noncitizens who unlawfully voted in prior elections, noting that the Biden administration had only prosecuted 13 people while the Trump investigation was investigating "thousands" of such cases.
One of the sources said Mr. Trump felt that Dhillon should have been more forceful in her explanation.
Despite the president's demands, Justice Department officials were able to stall for time and allow her to proceed with her plans to resign after the election was over, the sources added.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said that Dhillon did a "fantastic job" in her role and the White House is "very grateful for her dedicated service at the Department of Justice."
Dhillon's tenure

In her resignation letter, Dhillon touted her efforts to end "unlawful and discriminatory DEI practices" and to protect "women and girls' sports from biological males, including through lawsuits against Minnesota and California," among other accomplishments.
"While I am leaving this post, I will continue fighting for our country in the years ahead," she added.

During her tenure, the Justice Department closed many of its cases involving discrimination targeting Black Americans and announced it had dismissed more than 50 decades-old consent decrees with public schools, many in the Deep South, that were in place to protect Black students from unlawful discrimination.

Dhillon nixed two pending consent decrees last year with the Minneapolis and Louisville Police Departments over systemic abuses that were investigated in the wake of the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, and rescinded the investigative findings of misconduct into six other police departments.

Earlier this year, after immigration agents shot and killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis as they were protesting the administration's immigration crackdown, the Civil Rights Division did not move to open any criminal civil rights investigations, in violation of longstanding practice for such high-profile officer-involved shootings.

The division ultimately got involved in the Pretti case after the Justice Department faced staunch criticism and questions about why Homeland Security Investigations — and not the FBI — was leading the probe into its own agency.
To date, no charges have been filed in the Pretti case, which is also separately under investigation by state officials.

Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who founded the nonprofit advocacy group Justice Connection, called Dhillon "the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history" in a statement on Thursday.
"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it."
Dhillon, a staunch ally of President Trump who for years ran her own law firm in San Francisco, is a frequent guest on conservative podcasts and a very active poster on social media.

Unlike her predecessors, she frequently took to X to post videos about the work that her division was undertaking. She acknowledged in media interviews that she often generated ideas for civil rights investigations based on various posts she encountered on social media.

She has sometimes announced the opening of civil rights investigations online, a stark departure from historical practice. She also handed out challenge coins to fellow DOJ attorneys with the term "FAFO" ("f--k around and find out") printed on them.
Among the areas where she has been the most vocal has involved voting rights issues.
Under her leadership, the Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits against primarily blue states and the District of Columbia in an effort to gain access to unredacted voter rolls.

Lawyers from the division repeatedly argued that they needed the information to ensure states were complying with two federal voting laws that require them to maintain clean voter lists. However, they later admitted in court that the Justice Department intended to share the information with the Department of Homeland Security so they could use it for criminal and immigration enforcement purposes.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 27 of those cases.

During the midterm elections on Tuesday, the Civil Rights Division sent out more than 1,000 monitors to polling sites across the country, a record number that required the Justice Department to solicit volunteers from unusual parts of the DOJ, including the Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
However, in more recent weeks, Dhillon has been noticeably less involved in the effort.

She did not appear at an election integrity briefing that was held at DOJ for journalists, and the Office of the Deputy Attorney General, who does not have oversight authority on civil rights, solicited election monitor volunteers, according to a Sept. 10 memo seen by CBS News. That program has historically been run by the Civil Rights Division.

A senior Justice Department official denied that the election integrity work had been taken away from Dhillon when asked about it directly at the briefing, saying they were spreading around resources due to the increase in the workload.
"I don't agree that anything has shifted away from Harmeet. I think she's as busy as the rest of us. We're spreading the wealth," the said.

Nicole  Sganga
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Democrats prepare to take Congress as GOP grapples with stunning losses
summary: After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, the party is laying out how it plans to wield power, while President Trump and Republicans react to their midterm losses.
story: Latest updates on 2026 midterm election results:

After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, Democratic leaders are laying out how they plan to wield power with President Trump in the White House while Republicans are preparing for their time in the minority.Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats after upsets in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and more. The Alaska and Mississippi races remain unresolved. House Democrats will control 251 to 268 seats, CBS News projects, after flipping dozens of districts and staving off major losses from redistricting. In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, won the highly watched mayor's race, defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, CBS News projects. Find updates on key House races here, Senate battleground races here and all election results in the CBS News Election Center.

After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, Democratic leaders are laying out how they plan to wield power with President Trump in the White House while Republicans are preparing for their time in the minority.

Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats after upsets in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and more. The Alaska and Mississippi races remain unresolved. House Democrats will control 251 to 268 seats, CBS News projects, after flipping dozens of districts and staving off major losses from redistricting.
In Los Angeles, Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, won the highly watched mayor's race, defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, CBS News projects.
Find updates on key House races here, Senate battleground races here and all election results in the CBS News Election Center.

title: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences
summary: The move does not repeal California's death penalty or prevent prosecutors from seeking it in future cases.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute every current death sentence in California to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Newsom announced the decision Thursday in an open letter, saying he will use his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences of 548 people currently facing the death penalty.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom wrote.
The move does not repeal California's death penalty or prevent prosecutors from seeking it in future cases. Newsom said those decisions will remain with prosecutors, juries and courts.
"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," Newsom wrote.
California voters, however, have repeatedly chosen to keep the death penalty.

Voters rejected Proposition 34, which would have abolished capital punishment, in 2012. Four years later, they again rejected repeal with Proposition 62 while narrowly approving Proposition 66, which sought to speed up death penalty cases.
Newsom imposed a moratorium on executions shortly after taking office in 2019. California last carried out an execution in 2006.
Under the commutations announced Thursday, every current death sentence would instead become life without parole, which Newsom called the most severe punishment he can impose through clemency.

Some cases will require review by the California Supreme Court because the state constitution requires court approval before a governor can grant clemency to someone convicted of more than one felony.

title: Gluesenkamp Perez wins competitive Washington race
summary: The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun in a district President Trump has won three times.
story: Washington — Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won a third term in Washington's 3rd Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Gluesenkamp Perez's victory, in a district President Trump has won three times, comes as she's flexed her independence over party loyalty. Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives in January, with stunning wins across the country.

The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun to win reelection in the rural district in the southwestern corner of the state. Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate, was a more mainstream Republican than Gluesenkamp Perez's prior opponent, far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Mr. Trump's counterterrorism chief before resigning in protest over the Iran war. But Braun, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump, also distanced himself from the president on some issues, including on tariffs, the Iran war and affirming that Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Though Gluesenkamp Perez angered her Democratic colleagues in September by helping Republicans on two party-line procedural votes that were struggling to pass, her win is a relief to Democrats, who needed to hold the highly competitive seat in their quest to retake the House majority.

Though House Democratic leaders initially called the split "a significant breach of trust" that "necessitates a serious response," the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — which is controlled by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York — continued to back Gluesenkamp Perez. In a coordinated ad with the DCCC in October, Gluesenkamp Perez said, "I don't answer to any political party or any president. I answer to you."
At a district event in September, Gluesenkamp Perez emphasized her loyalty to her community as she referenced her occasional defections.

"We have no form of representative democracy if we do not represent our districts, if we don't stand for a working waterfront, if we don't stand for people working in the trades, if we don't stand for right-to-repair, if we don't stand for our Ukrainian countrymen, we have nothing," she said. "All of democracy is predicated on representative government. That's the point."
Braun also sought to put space between himself and GOP leaders during the campaign.

While not criticizing the president directly on his handling of the Iran war, Braun said during an Oct. 13 debate, "I will not and I do not support a war without clear objectives and without a clear ending point."
"I think Congress has a very important role here — one they should exercise," he said.
Braun also lamented Congress ceding its powers to the president, especially its control over federal government spending and the ability to declare war.
"We have to take power back," he said.

On tariffs, Braun said, "with our allies, indiscriminate use of tariffs is not helpful and ultimately lead to an increase of prices for manufacturers and consumers." He called the administration's handling of immigration enforcement  a "mixed bag."

title: Black candidates for governor make history with midterm victories
summary: Americans elected the country's first Black woman, and four other Black candidates, into gubernatorial roles during Tuesday's record midterm races.
story: Americans elected their first Black woman into a gubernatorial role during the 2026 midterms, alongside four other Black candidates who won races for governor around the United States on Tuesday.

The races culminated, respectively, in victories for Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, in Georgia; Byron Donalds, a Republican, in Florida; David Crowley, a Democrat, in Wisconsin; Aaron Ford, a Democrat, in Nevada; and Wes Moore, also a Democrat, who was reelected to serve a second term as governor of Maryland. He became the state's first Black governor when he was elected in 2022.

Including Moore, only three Black Americans have previously been elected to serve as U.S. governors. Former New York Gov. David Paterson, who is also Black, became governor when Eliot Spitzer resigned in 2008.
Once Bottoms and Crowley were projected the winners in their races, Moore reflected on their wins to CBS News on Tuesday, calling the victories "incredibly important."

"This is exciting, because up until this moment, I was the only Black governor in America. And I was very clear that that's a title that I did not want to hold onto for very long," said Moore. "I'm only the third African American ever elected governor in the 250-year history of this country, and, now, in one cycle, we have at least doubled that number. I just think it's incredibly important. It's a historic moment."

Bottoms has been hailed as a trailblazer for more reasons than one, as she will become the first Black woman elected to a gubernatorial position in U.S. history. She will also be the first woman to serve as governor of Georgia when she joins the ranks of a record-high number of women — 17 — in governor's offices nationwide.
She told "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King on Wednesday that she had been trying to tune out the results when she learned that she won.

"I had put in my AirPods to work on my speech, and my husband was on the sofa near me, laying near me, and he kicked me," said Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor. "I went like, 'What?' He said, 'They called it.' And I said, 'Called what?' And so that's how I knew."

Donalds, who served as U.S. representative for Florida's 19th District after his election to that spot in 2020, is now also slated to become Florida's first Black governor. He is also the first Black Republican elected governor in the nation.

In Wisconsin, Crowley, a moderate Democrat, defeated Republican challenger Tom Tiffany in the culmination of a governor's race that played out in one of the country's most purple states. Tiffany, a U.S. representative, is also one of President Trump's top allies.

Ford, who was elected as Nevada's attorney general in 2018, won his state's gubernatorial race against Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, CBS News projected on Thursday. He will become Nevada's first Black governor and the first Black governor ever elected west of the Mississippi.

title: Aaron Ford beats GOP incumbent in Nevada governor's race
summary: GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo struggled in Nevada as the economy struggled because of tariffs and a decline in tourism.
story: Democrat Aaron Ford won the Nevada governor's race, CBS News projects, defeating incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo as the state struggled because of tariffs and a decline in tourism.
Ford, who has been elected statewide twice as attorney general, will be Nevada's first Black governor and the first Black governor elected in a state west of the Mississippi.

Lombardo, a moderate Republican who was first elected in 2022, had a massive war chest, but was unable to overcome the challenges stemming from the state's economic woes. Nevada's largest city, Las Vegas, is driven by tourism and has seen a dropoff in international tourists under President Trump, particularly from Canada. Nevada has also been hit hard by tariffs.
Mr. Trump won Nevada by three points in 2024, the first Republican presidential candidate to win the state since 2004.

Although Lombardo touted his successes with the Democratic-led state legislature, Ford successfully tied him to national Republicans and Mr. Trump. According to an October poll by Noble Predictive Insights, 58% of Nevada residents disapprove of Mr. Trump's performance.
Democrats racked up stunning wins across the country on Tuesday, including Nevada, where Democrats flipped the 2nd District that encompasses the northern part of the state.

title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Thursday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. By midday Thursday, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,700 votes.
Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."
The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: CBS News exit polls show how Democrats won in the midterms
summary: Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
story: Note: Poll percentages may have updated since this was published.
Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
Fueled in part by economic frustration, parts of the Democratic coalition that Mr. Trump made inroads with in 2024 swung back toward Democrats this year.
Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats for the House, according to CBS News exit polls.

This was the second straight election most voters told us inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.
This election was clearly a referendum on Mr. Trump and largely a rejection of his policies.
Nationally, most said his tariffs hurt the economy, his administration's immigration efforts went too far and the decision to take military action against Iran was the wrong one.
Groups coming back to the Democrats

In 2024, Mr. Trump made gains nationally with young voters, Latinos and women, but majorities of all these groups backed Democrats for the House this year. Democrats' margins with women were similar to what they were in 2018 when Democrats won control of the House during the president's first term.
And majorities of each of these key groups said the cost of living was crucial in their vote.
Democrats made inroads with Republican-leaning groups
Historically, men have generally backed Republicans in both presidential and midterm elections, but they largely split their votes this year.
Mr. Trump won men by double digits in 2024. Today, most disapprove of the job he is doing, and those who do backed Democrats.
White women historically mostly vote Republican, but they narrowly backed Democrats in this election, according to exit polls.

The national electorate was slightly more Democratic than the most recent two elections, which helped Democrats. But their lead with independents was critical in putting them over the top. They also led with those who did not vote in the 2024 presidential election.
This electorate was a pessimistic one — unhappy about the state of the country and the economy and not very hopeful for the next generation.
So the Democrats may have their work cut out for them.
Just over half of voters had an unfavorable view of the party. Voters did give the Democrats an edge over Republicans on the economy, so they likely expect results.
Joe Williams contributed to this report.

title: The biggest races Democrats won in the midterms
summary: Democrats won pivotal races in Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Michigan and elsewhere. Here are the biggest victories of the 2026 midterms.
story: Washington — Voters across the country delivered a stinging rebuke to Republicans in Congress and President Trump's agenda in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, with Democrats capturing House and Senate seats that had seemed out of reach just a few months ago.

CBS News projects Democrats will take control of both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January, with wide margins in each. Democrats are projected to control at least 54 Senate seats, with two races still unresolved. In the House, CBS News estimates the party could control between 251 and 268 when all the votes are counted.

Out of 11 Senate races that CBS News considered battlegrounds, Democrats were projected to win 10. The 11th race, in Alaska, is still rated a toss-up, with a lengthy ballot-counting process expected. The Mississippi Senate race is also unresolved and is unexpectedly close, with Democrat Scott Colom leading incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by only around 1,000 votes. CBS News has rated that race as a toss-up.
The victories weren't just limited to House and Senate races, either. Democrats captured the governor's mansion in Texas, a feat they haven't accomplished since 1990.
Here are the major races that propelled Democrats to victory on Tuesday, according to CBS News' projections:
Texas Senate: James Talarico
In the most expensive Senate race in Texas history, and one of the closest-watched matchups of the election cycle, Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who was elected to serve in the Texas House of Representatives in 2018.

Talarico's campaign focused on corruption and lowering costs. He told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that his victory sent a message to Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the race, that "Texas is not for sale."
"The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way," he said.
Paxton was backed by Mr. Trump, who endorsed the Republican attorney general over Sen. John Cornyn in the GOP Senate primary earlier this year.

Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary runoff in May, setting the race against Talarico. Paxton had weathered numerous controversies and was impeached by the state House in 2023 on allegations of bribery, obstruction of justice and abuse of trust. He was acquitted by the state Senate.
Texas governor: Gina Hinojosa

Hinojosa, a state lawmaker, bested Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democrat to win the governor's mansion in more than 30 years. Hinojosa will be the third woman to lead the state.

Abbott had been in office for more than a decade and was seeking a fourth term as governor, and the race against Hinojosa narrowed in the months leading up to the election. Hinojosa focused her campaign on affordability and public education. The fight over data centers also emerged as a major issue in the governor's race.
South Carolina Senate: Annie Andrews
Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Andrews, 45, made healthcare access and affordability the focuses of her campaign.

Graham was appointed to finish out the remainder of her late brother's Senate term following his unexpected death in July. President Trump swiftly threw his support behind Graham and campaigned for her in South Carolina in the lead-up to the midterms.
It has been nearly 30 years since a Democrat won the Senate in South Carolina, a state Mr. Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
Kansas Senate: Adam Hamilton

Hamilton, a fifth-generation Kansan, is the leader of the largest United Methodist church in the country and is a well-known author and speaker. The 62-year-old defeated Roger Marshall, a Republican, who was seeking his second term in the Senate.
Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 16 points in the last presidential election.

In the closing weeks of the Senate campaign, Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, came under scrutiny after the New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of his patients over outstanding medical bills, and 81 were arrested.
Georgia governor: Keisha Lance Bottoms

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will make history as the nation's first Black woman governor. The former Atlanta mayor and senior adviser in the Biden administration defeated Republican Rick Jackson and Libertarian Chase Oliver, CBS News projects.
With 99% of the vote counted, Bottoms had 54.3% of the vote, compared to 45.7% for Jackson.
Bottoms told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that she was surprised that the race was called as early as it was on election night.

"I thought that it was going to be a very long night. I knew that we had done the work, but Georgia has always, for the past few years, been a purple state, so I thought it would be much closer," she said.
Michigan Senate: Abdul El-Sayed
Michigan was viewed as Republicans' best chance to flip a Senate seat, but El-Sayed's victory over GOP opponent Mike Rogers keeps it in Democrats' hands.

The Senate race emerged as one of the most contentious of the midterm election cycle. Top Republicans, led by Mr. Trump, repeatedly leveled anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed, calling him a "jihadist" and claiming that he is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
El-Sayed told Fox News in an interview last month that he has "never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."
El-Sayed also came under scrutiny for his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and views on Israel raising questions as to whether he could win support from Jewish and Black voters.

There was a late twist in the Senate race in Michigan when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who sought the Democratic Senate nomination, endorsed Rogers and appeared alongside him at a Detroit church Sunday.
Maine Senate: Troy Jackson
Jackson was facing off against GOP Sen. Susan Collins, the only Republican running for reelection in a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.

Collins was first elected to represent Maine in the Senate in 1996 and had touted her ability to bring home benefits for the state as part of her pitch to voters. While she had survived difficult campaigns in the past, Collins was not able to fend off the challenge from Jackson.

Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who jumped into the Senate race late after Graham Platner, who initially won the Democratic Senate nomination, withdrew from the race after allegations of sexual misconduct. The former president of the Maine Senate unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for governor earlier this year.
Dozens of House seats across the country
Democrats are on track to flip dozens of House seats.
In Iowa, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats had a sweep of the most competitive seats.

Democrats defeated GOP incumbent Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, Zach Nunn of Iowa, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Brian Steil of Wisconsin and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin. They also flipped an open Iowa seat that is currently held by the GOP.

Redistricting helped Democrats win California's 1st District and Utah's 1st District. Redistricting was expected to hamper Democrats' chances in Texas' 15th District and 23rd District, but Democrats pulled off upsets.

In Ohio, embattled GOP Reps. Max Miller and Mike Carey both lost reelection, as did Tom Kean in New Jersey, Ann Wagner in Missouri, Gabe Evans in Colorado, Victoria Spartz in Indiana and Jen Kiggans in Virginia.
Democrats also flipped open seats in Kentucky's 6th District, Nebraska's 2nd District and North Carolina's 11th District.

title: Trump library plans on collision course with Democratic Congress
summary: President Trump is expected to spend time on plans for his presidential library, but Democrats in Congress have some questions about how it's being financed.
story: As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."
With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.
"The donors bankrolling his personal vanity project will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told CBS News.

In March, Mr. Trump shared renderings of a 47-story tower on a donated plot in downtown Miami. It showed golden escalators, a full-size Air Force One and a giant statue of him raising his fist, as he did after surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. But then he told reporters he does not "believe in building libraries or museums" and that the building is "most likely going to be a hotel," a departure from the traditional library his foundation described to the IRS last year.

The Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit, registered in Florida and run by Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, will fund the project. The foundation says it expects to raise $950 million by the end of 2027, including $600 million in 2027 alone, according to its October 2025 IRS application, obtained by CBS News. That far outpaces what Mr. Trump's predecessors had raised at this stage.

Tens of millions of dollars have already come from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. The nonprofit is also collecting donations through a payment processing company that has Donald Trump Jr. on its board, according to a fundraising portal page. And Mr. Trump has said the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave the U.S. last year — now in use as Air Force One — would go to the library, though Eric Trump and the White House have since said that plan is not final.

Some of the most recent money has come from people trying to stay in Mr. Trump's good graces. After the president threatened to cut ties with his top political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their consulting work for a pro-Russian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two men donated their fees from that work to the library, The New York Post reported.

A week later, The New York Times reported that Mr. Trump had told aides and allies that his former personal lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, should donate part of a contract worth more than $50 million to his library or another Trump-related entity. Habba Mildon's contract was with a company tied to the family of a Venezuelan businessman Mr. Trump pardoned in January, the outlet reported.

Asked by CBS News whether she planned to donate some of her fees to the library, Habba Mildon responded to the text message with a "haha" reaction. (She removed the reaction seconds later and declined to comment.)

A former Trump adviser, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the library is now where the fundraising action is, with the midterms over and donors already tapped for the America 250 celebrations and the White House ballroom. MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by Mr. Trump's allies, started September with more than $400 million to spend on Republicans in the midterms. Its filing due in December will show how much left it has in cash on hand.
"The library is one of the last few places he can squeeze people for money," the former adviser said. "That's what a businessman does. He just creates opportunities."

Fresh scrutiny of the library is expected after Democrats swept the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Starting in January, Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word warning on X to the administration after the election results: "Lawyer up."

"Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," Warren told CBS News, adding that she will be investigating the library "and any wrongdoing will be held accountable."

The library has already drawn scrutiny over Mr. Trump's stated plan to display the gifted jet. The plane's memorandum of understanding, signed in 2025 by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Qatar's Minister of State for Defense Affairs Soud bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, called it an "unconditional donation." But when questions were raised about the U.S. accepting and using the Qatari plane as Air Force One, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi concluded that the gift could be conditioned on transferring the plane to the library foundation by Jan. 1, 2029, about three weeks before Mr. Trump leaves office.
In August, Eric Trump told NBC News that displaying the plane was "not the plan at the moment," saying a retired Air Force One would be shown instead.

A Qatari official, speaking to CBS News on the condition of anonymity, said what happens to the plane after Mr. Trump leaves office is not Qatar's concern. "This is something the Americans need to deal with," the official said.
The White House referred questions about the library and whether any final decisions have been made about the plane or a hotel to the foundation, which did not respond to requests for comment.

"The Trump Presidential Library will be one of the most magnificent buildings in the world and a living testament to the indelible impact President Trump has made on America and its people," Davis Ingle, a spokesman for the White House, said in a statement.
Tens of millions from companies Mr. Trump sued

There have been two iterations of the library's nonprofit funding structure. The first, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund, was incorporated in Florida in December 2024, days after ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward the library to settle a defamation suit over anchor George Stephanopoulos' inaccurate on-air claim that Mr. Trump had been found civilly liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found him liable for sexual abuse.

Other settlements followed. Meta agreed to pay $22 million toward the library over the suspension of Mr. Trump's accounts after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Elon Musk's X paid $10 million to settle a similar suit by Mr. Trump and other plaintiffs. And Paramount paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.

By then, the current foundation had been incorporated in Florida in May 2025, listing Eric Trump, Boulos and James Kiley, an attorney who has represented Mr. Trump, as trustees. The original fund was dissolved that September after failing to file a required annual report. Jacob Roth, an attorney who incorporated the first fund, declined to comment.

In March, Sens. Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Melanie Stansbury asked the four companies for details of their payments. ABC said its $15 million was still in an escrow account held by a law firm representing Mr. Trump, where it had been since December 2024, awaiting release to the foundation. Paramount said it had paid $16 million but did not say to whom. Meta said $22 million had been "designated" for the library but did not say whether or where it was paid, and X, citing confidentiality, did not say how much of its $10 million settlement went there.

Mr. Trump's financial disclosure, filed in June, lists $56.5 million in settlement money from ABC, Meta and Paramount as paid to the foundation. It lists $8 million from X as paid to Mr. Trump himself, without saying whether some funds reached the foundation. The foundation's October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, which it labeled a proposed budget, projected $50 million in revenue and about $6 million in spending.

Meta and ABC declined to comment. X did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Skydance referred CBS News to the company's July 2025 statement announcing the settlement, which said the $16 million included the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs and that the remainder would go to Mr. Trump's future presidential library, with nothing paid to him personally.

The settlements are not the only large gifts. SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant, told Congress in July that it gave the foundation $50 million in January to support a library exhibit highlighting U.S.-Japan relations. Two months later, Mr. Trump's Energy Department announced it would lease federal land at a former uranium enrichment plant in Ohio to an affiliate of SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for a data center campus that the company says will be the world's largest for artificial intelligence.

A spokesperson for the Energy Department said the agency signed its lease agreement with the company on Feb. 26, about a month after SoftBank's donation to the library foundation. They added that a local development group first proposed the project in October 2024, before SoftBank acquired the lease rights in the fall of 2025. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment.
A library or a hotel?

The library foundation's filings offer few other details about how it operates. When it registered as a charity in Florida, the foundation said its officers did not expect to be paid. But in its application to the IRS, the foundation said it would pay its leaders. It projected spending $400,000 on compensation in 2025, rising to $1.2 million in 2027. The foundation's bylaws say trustees can't be paid, but other roles can come with compensation. Eric Trump is both a trustee and the foundation's president.
The foundation told CBS News it expects to file financial disclosures covering fiscal 2025 by Nov. 15. It did not respond to a question about whether Eric Trump will be paid.
Fundraising for the library is led by Meredith O'Rourke, who has worked with Mr. Trump since 2016.

The foundation also raises money through PSQ Impact, a donation platform run by PublicSquare, a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr. The foundation's donation page says contributions will "help preserve important archives, promote civic education, and inspire generations to come." Trump Jr. began receiving $42,000 a month in consulting fees from PublicSquare in August 2024, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he was not aware of the fundraising page and had no involvement in it. PublicSquare did not respond to questions about how much has been raised through the donation page or what fee, if any, it is charging for processing.

"This is just one example of many where the Trumps are set to possibly profit off something connected to Donald Trump's presidency," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen.

It remains unclear what form the library will ultimately take. Mr. Trump's suggestion that it could become a hotel is cited in a lawsuit filed in May by Miami residents, a local nonprofit and a Miami Dade College student. They argue that Florida's gift of the 2.63-acre parcel, a former college parking lot, violates a U.S. constitutional provision that bars states from giving the president financial benefits.

The land was appraised at more than $67 million, but the suit cites real estate experts who say its true market value is over $300 million. The plaintiffs note that the state's terms require only that the site include "components of a Presidential library, museum, and/or center" within five years, and do not preclude a hotel.

Other presidential libraries have been built on donated public land. Chicago leased parkland for Mr. Obama's center for $10, and Little Rock used eminent domain to assemble the site for Mr. Clinton's. But Florida conveyed its parcel outright.

The Justice Department has argued that Mr. Trump is immune from the suit. In September, U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II, a Trump appointee, halted discovery, writing that the defendants' arguments for dismissal, including presidential immunity, "may prove to be successful." He has not yet ruled on motions to dismiss the case, and a ruling may not come until March, according to Gerald E. Greenberg, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.
If the suit is dismissed, Greenberg said the plaintiffs are likely to appeal.

"This case is really about one of the core anti-corruption provisions," Greenberg told CBS News, saying the founders "understood the dangers of people currying favor with the sovereign by giving him gifts."
"It is extremely disturbing to think of our skyline and our downtown being blighted by this monument to corruption," he added.

title: Indiana carries out first of 3 U.S. executions set for Thursday
summary: An Indiana man was executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for Thursday in the U.S., which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. were put to death on the same day.
story: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13.
It would be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, but was the first this year in Indiana.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said.

Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit's case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," he said. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty."
The execution on tap in Florida

In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a "full and fair" hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.

Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama's scheduled execution

Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.

"If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today," said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

title: 2 Native American women make history in midterms
summary: In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
story: Two Native American women made history Tuesday night in the 2026 midterm elections, winning a Senate seat and a governorship — both firsts for Native women — as Democrats swept races across the country.

In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo, was already the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. She defeated Republican Gregg Hull, former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the race for governor.
Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and conservative commentator.
Who are they?

Haaland has notched many firsts. She became the first Native American woman to chair a state political party in 2015 when she was elected to lead the Democratic Party of New Mexico. In 2018, she became one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, alongside Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas, who was reelected Tuesday. Haaland later served as former President Joe Biden's Interior secretary from 2021 until January 2025.
On the trail, she spoke about raising her daughter alone, selling homemade salsa and relying at times on food stamps.
"My story is a lot like many New Mexicans — humble beginnings," she told a Rio Rancho congregation in October.

Flanagan got her start as an organizer, then served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children's Defense Fund Minnesota. She was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2015 and has been lieutenant governor since 2019, where she has helped reshape Minnesota's relationship with the state's 11 tribal nations.
Raised by a single mother in Section 8 housing, Flanagan had childhood asthma that kept her in and out of hospitals. She's been an outspoken supporter of Medicaid, saying that it "saved [her] life."
What do they stand for?

Haaland ran on the cost of living, protecting New Mexico's Universal Child Care program and overhauling its child welfare system. She also blamed President Trump for cuts to federal safety net programs. She has promised to issue an executive order on day one to pause the construction of new large-scale data centers until the state Legislature passes guardrails.
Flanagan drew on her own upbringing to connect with voters who are feeling financially squeezed. She ran as a progressive, backing "Medicare for All" and national paid family and medical leave.
"Minnesota, you just beat Donald Trump again," Flanagan told supporters on Tuesday night at her election watch party in St. Paul, where White Earth leaders played a victory song on a drum.
Why does it matter?

The National Congress of American Indians, the country's oldest and largest association of tribal governments, called the wins historic milestones for Indian Country. Native American women make up approximately 1% of the U.S. population, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, but have long been underrepresented in elected office.

"Long before Native women were welcomed into the halls of government, they were leading our Nations, protecting our families, and shaping the future of Indian Country," NCAI Executive Director Larry Wright Jr. said in a statement to CBS News.

"For young Native girls across Indian Country, these victories send an important message: their voices matter, their leadership is essential, and they belong wherever possibilities are reimagined," said Wright.

He added that he hopes that representation translates into "meaningful progress," in particular, protecting tribal lands and honoring treaty obligations between the U.S. government and tribal nations.

A third Native American woman could soon join Haaland and Flanagan in making history this midterm election. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, is in a Senate race with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan that remains a toss-up, according to CBS News estimates. The outcome may not be decided until ranked-choice tabulation later this month.

title: DFL trifecta 2.0: Democrats win full control of Minnesota government
summary: Democrats flipped the Minnesota House and won the governor's race, returning the DFL to a trifecta after two years of divided government. The results, however, remain unofficial.
story: Minnesota Democrats won back control of both chambers of the Legislature on Tuesday, delivering the second "trifecta" in state government in four years, according to unofficial results.

The Associated Press called at least 37 state Senate seats for the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, which is an improvement over their one-seat majority in the 67-member chamber. DFL leaders are claiming victory in 39 districts; two races where Republicans prevailed by single digits are headed towards an automatic recount.
In the House — which was previously tied between Democrats and Republicans — the DFL has at least 77 seats, according to the AP.

With the election of DFL U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar to be the next governor, Democrats have total control of state government. They first won back a trifecta in the 2022 election, but their margins were much tighter.

"We are very sure that we will have a large majority — the largest majority in the House since the Obama era," said DFL House Leader Zack Stephenson late Tuesday night when votes were still being counted.
"I think it's an overwhelming display of frustration that people had with the Trump administration and with Republican governance," he said of the blue wave in Minnesota and nationally.

In 2023 and 2024 — the last time the Democrats controlled the Capitol — they passed a slate of progressive priorities, including universal free school meals, legal marijuana, abortion rights protections, paid family and medical leave, gun safety bills like a red flag law and expanded background checks and more.

The agenda for next year is still in the works and will come into sharper focus soon after each caucus meets. But both Stephenson and Senate Majority Leader Erin Murphy said affordability, especially when it comes to health care, is top of mind.

"The first thing we have to do is to address the cost of living for people, and that's not going to happen in one bill," Murphy told reporters. "We have a lot of work to do for the people of Minnesota in health care, in housing, and in child care. And those issues are going to take some time."
But when it comes to gun regulations, Democrats have already promised to pass a package that includes a ban on assault-style weapons and high-capacity magazines to Governor-elect Klobuchar's desk.

That bill passed the Senate but failed to clear the House earlier this year and it is a push from some families of Annunciation Catholic School, where a gunman killed two children and injured more than two dozen others during school mass last summer.

Klobuchar said she spent time with the parents of Harper Moyski, who was killed in the shooting at just 10-years-old, on Tuesday night before she joined the DFL Party on election night. It was what would have been her 12th birthday.

"I think the gun safety bill is going to get passed and I am so excited to be working with the leaders on this. And it certainly should be one of our top priorities," Klobuchar told reporters Wednesday.

Republicans were disappointed with the results. They believed the fraud scandal plaguing social services programs would help them break their 20-year losing streak statewide office and earn the trust of voters to lead at the Capitol.

"With another trifecta on the horizon, Senate Republicans remain committed to holding state government accountable and putting Minnesotans first," said Sen. Mark Johnson, the Republican minority leader, in a statement.

Klobuchar's election means a new negotiator at the table with lawmakers when they work to pass the next state budget next legislative session. She said she already talked to all four legislative leaders — including Republicans.
She vowed to include the minority in negotiations, even if Democrats can pass bills without GOP votes.

"I was No. 1 for bipartisan bills, No. 3 for passing bills into law — you don't get to that stage in the U.S. Senate if you don't understand the value of working with people both on the Republican side and in the same caucus that you maybe don't always agree with," she told reporters. "And I am going to put a huge priority on this as we set our priority going forward, because I believe for our state, the stakes couldn't be more high right now."

Klobuchar also said she knows she will spar with members of her own party who may be further to the left than she is. Some progressives want to raise taxes, like on social media companies, when they get power back in January. Klobuchar has said she does not want to raise any taxes.

"I see every day in my own caucus in the U.S. Senate, you're going to see people with different views," she said. "And the most important thing to me is that people know where I am coming from and the fact that I have been consistent from the beginning, including last night, in front of the entire celebration — which was an ongoing and never-ending celebration for the Democratic Party nationally and in the DFL — I actually said, spoiler alert, you're not going to like everything I do."
When asked what he thinks his caucus may not like, Stephenson said the focus Tuesday was on the celebration for Democrats commanding victories.
"We're focusing on affordability. We got a lot of things that we know we can do," he said.
