title: Why did Republicans lose the midterms?
summary: Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong, and a brewing blame-game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.
story: Washington — Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.
The war in Iran

Throughout the country, as Republicans tried to rally support around their accomplishments over the last two years, the president's war in Iran loomed large. And in this week's elections, its impact on the economy and prices appeared to overshadow most everything else.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vice President JD Vance said in a candid post on social media that was among the first efforts from a top Republican to unpack the party's losses.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay," said Vance, who is widely seen as a possible presidential contender in 2028. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Asked about the comments, President Trump told reporters that it's "largely true" that Republicans lost the House and Senate because war led to higher energy prices, agreeing with Vance. But he also argued that the war has been worthwhile.
"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," Mr. Trump said.

Early in the war, Mr. Trump acknowledged that the vice president was "philosophically, a little bit different than me," and was "less enthusiastic about going" into Iran. Still, Vance has largely stood by Mr. Trump on Iran.
GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation," also cited the war, saying, "the Iran war has dragged on too long."
"It should have been brief, decisive, and over — it needs to end," said Cruz, who has vocally supported the war.
But Cruz pointed more broadly to the war's impact on prices, citing gas and diesel, along with the impacts of the president's trade policy, saying, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive."

Former Vice President Mike Pence also criticized Republicans' handling of the Iran war, but from the opposite direction, writing that the "unfinished war against Iran became an albatross around the necks of Republicans because Washington stopped short and pursued appeasement rather than allowing our troops to finish off the threat posed by the Iranian regime, once and for all."
Cost of living takes center stage
More so than the war in Iran, voters nationally said cost of living was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polls.

Cruz said many GOP candidates this cycle seemed "like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living. He said there's a "very real economic disconnect: Our K-shaped economy is a yawning divide," referring to the idea that some Americans' fortunes are on the upswing while others are pointing downward.

The Texas Republican cited Elon Musk becoming the world's first trillionaire, while at the same time, millions of Americans struggled to feed their families. And as data centers were constructed and the wealthiest people became even wealthier, he said Americans saw their electricity bills go up significantly in recent years.
"Understandably, people were pissed off," he said. "And elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain."

Democrats hammered Republicans over the cost of living, as economic populism became a key tenet of the cycle, while some candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, billed the fight as top-versus-bottom, rather than left-versus-right. Texas Republicans suffered one of the most striking routs of the midterms: Starting next year, Cruz will be one of the only Republican statewide elected officials in a state that was once viewed as almost imperviously red.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, whose seat Talarico will take in the new year after Cornyn lost his primary to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lamented that after voters trusted Mr. Trump and the GOP to "protect their pocketbooks" in the 2024 elections, the president "misread his mandate."

"Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary 'Liberation Day' tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring," Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed. "Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement. The Iran conflict came with no attempt to persuade the public. And Mr. Trump signaled disconnection by focusing on sideshows like swimming-pool liners in the Reflecting Pool."
Cornyn added, "Americans elected the Donald Trump who put on the apron of the Golden Arches and got a plan for a Triumphal Arch instead."

Cornyn, who was formerly the No. 2 Senate Republican, also pointed to how corruption surged to a top issue for voters, "thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington."

Democrats like Talarico worked hard to tie corruption to cost-of-living concerns expressed widely. And roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote.

"Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks," Cornyn wrote. "Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle — or voters will continue to police it for us."
Focus on culture wars
Beyond the cost-of-living concerns, some Republicans also pointed to an over-emphasis on culture war issues.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the midterm outcomes as "close to an extension-level event for Republicans as we have seen probably in the last hundred years," said he knew Republicans were in trouble when he saw they were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads centering transgender issues.
"That was not the issue motivating voters, and it was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote," DeSantis said at a news conference.

By late October, more than $180 million had been spent on ads that centered transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to the Associated Press, reminiscent of the "Kamala is for they/them, Trump is for you" ads that blanketed the airwaves in the 2024 presidential election.

DeSantis — who has staked out conservative positions on transgender issues — argued the issue is no longer as potent, saying: "Four years ago, we were in the peak-woke era." But now, he argued, "the issues are different."
"Republicans, it seemed like — in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending — they really were fighting yesterday's battles," he said.

As Republicans turned their attention to transgender and other culture-war issues, Democrats didn't give the attacks traction, shifting the focus at nearly every turn to affordability concerns. Some moderate Democrats in battleground states also voiced opposition to transgender athletes' participation in girls' sports, which may have neutralized some attacks.

But DeSantis also argued the election wasn't the result of voters having positive views of Democrats — exit polling shows voters had unfavorable opinions of both parties, though Republicans' favorability (40%) was lower than Democrats' (47%).

Instead, DeSantis said, it was a "rejection of Republicans in Washington." And that rebuke wasn't only aimed at the president, he argued, but also the GOP-controlled Congress, as voters became "frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate."
"So it's really both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue," DeSantis said. "It's not just one."

title: U.S. gas prices on track to fall below $4 a gallon, experts say
summary: Fuel prices have dropped in recent weeks amid hopes that the midterm elections would increase pressure on the U.S. and Iran to reach a peace deal.
story: Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving, he said.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was largely due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Other factors pushing down gas prices
Other factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.

The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual.

"Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. "A more normal markup would be 40 cents a gallon, and that means that even if futures prices and physical markets hang around present levels, we should see lower pump prices for the foreseeable future."

The Trump administration has used various tools to ease gas prices. That includes expanding access to tax-free red-dyed diesel, opening the door to Russian diesel imports, and waiving what's known as the Jones Act, a federal statute that requires goods shipped between U.S. ports to be moved on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed.

The decisive wins came as President Trump's approval rating hit 38%, historically low for a president in the midterms, in an election where 89% of voters said cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their votes.

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson announced in a call with his staff Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader when the new Congress is seated. Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise told Republicans they want the job.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said he expects his party to win at least 255 seats after all the votes are counted. He also said no one in the caucus has raised the idea of impeaching President Trump. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability," he told reporters.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election. Democrats, who had 214 seats going into the midterms, flipped a number of GOP-held seats and proved to be competitive in battlegrounds and in some unexpected places.

Democrats won in battleground districts nationwide, in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky and Colorado, among other states. Several races still remain to be called, two days after the election.
Republicans in several states, including Texas and Florida, had redistricted to try to gain an edge in the elections, but redrawing ultimately did not stave off their losses.

title: Trump's lawyers argue appeal in "hush money" case
summary: President Trump was convicted in 2024 of 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
story: President Trump's lawyers on Thursday urged a New York appellate court to throw out his conviction on 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to an adult film star.

They argued that the jury was given flawed instructions, allowing them to consider violations of federal election law as part of their determination in the case, calling it an "obvious ground for reversal." Mr. Trump has long argued that the federal law, known as FECA, preempts state prosecution.

"All of the payments that are issued in this case, whether it be the payments to [adult film star Stormy Daniels], other payments to two other folks, those were payments that were deemed to be illegal contributions or expenditures under FECA," said Mr. Trump's attorney, Robert Giuffra.
Steven Wu, a lawyer for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, countered that a federal court has twice rejected the claim that FECA preempted New York's prosecution of Mr. Trump.
"This court should reach the same conclusion here," Wu said.
Giuffra and Wu were interrupted frequently by a five-judge panel that pelted them with questions picking apart their arguments.

A unanimous jury convicted Mr. Trump in May 2024 for his part in a scheme to falsify business records related to reimbursements made to Michael Cohen, his attorney at the time. Cohen had paid $130,000 to adult film star Stormy Daniels, days before the 2016 election, in exchange for her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Mr. Trump years earlier. Mr. Trump has denied the allegations.

The jury was asked to consider if Mr. Trump falsified business records, counts that by themselves would have been misdemeanors, and if he intended to commit any other crime in doing so, including bank fraud, tax fraud or the violations of FECA — any of which elevated the charges to felonies. They did not have to be unanimous in what other crimes they thought he intended to commit.
Giuffra, the powerful co-chair of the white-shoe firm Sullivan & Cromwell, argued that they should have been required to be unanimous on that element of the felony.

Wu noted that the trial judge in the case asked Mr. Trump's defense attorneys about that, and they indicated they did not believe it was required under the law. Instead, they asked the judge to include that directive "in his discretion because of the importance of the case," Wu said, paraphrasing Emil Bove III, who was one of Mr. Trump's trial lawyers.
The trial judge, Juan Merchan, declined.
"What you're asking me to do is change the law, and I'm not going to do that," Merchan said at the time.

Mr. Trump's attorneys in the case have changed since the 2024 trial — one former defense attorney, Todd Blanche, is now U.S. attorney general, and Bove is now a federal judge — but his new team of personal lawyers has continued to echo the arguments he made throughout the trial.
An Oct. 16 filing by Giuffra began with a line that Mr. Trump himself frequently said and posted on social media: The case, "should have never been brought."

A spokesman for Mr. Trump's legal team said a 2024 Supreme Court decision related to presidential immunity, "the federal and New York state Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan D.A. be overturned and dismissed."
"President Trump will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn," the spokesperson said.
Lawyers for Bragg have characterized the 2016 "hush money" plan as "a conspiracy to defraud the American public and government regulators."
"The criminal charges here arose from [Mr. Trump's] unofficial, non-presidential conduct—as multiple courts have already found," they wrote in a July brief.
The arguments came a week after the death of a judge who was presiding over a yearslong parallel effort by Mr. Trump to move the case from state to federal court.

The judge, Alvin Hellerstein, repeatedly rejected Mr. Trump's arguments, and was particularly scathing in his response to Mr. Trump's claim that the reimbursements to Cohen were related to his official work as president.

"Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to [Stormy Daniels] cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty," Hellerstein wrote. "Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty."
On Thursday, the two sides also argued over whether tweets shown at trial and testimony of former White House communications director Hope Hicks fell under presidential immunity.

One judge on the panel said Hicks' testimony, which described a conversation about the Stormy Daniels allegations after they became public, may have fit in the "gray area of what's in the outer sphere of presidential duties."
Asked for his thoughts after the arguments, Giuffra said, "I think it went well."
"We should definitely win," he said.

title: Harmeet Dhillon, DOJ's controversial civil rights chief, resigns
summary: Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, resigned from the Justice Department on Thursday.
story: Washington — Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She overhauled a division that had long prioritized fighting discrimination against some of the nation's most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.

Since taking over the division, often lauded as being the "crown jewel" of the DOJ, she has reoriented it to focus instead on other priorities that have included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

In her resignation letter to President Trump, which was seen by CBS News, Dhillon said that she told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in early October that she intended to step down after the midterm elections.

Two sources familiar with the matter, however, told CBS News that Mr. Trump demanded she be fired after he watched her Oct. 18 appearance on "60 Minutes" discussing the government's election integrity efforts.

In that interview, Dhillon touted the Justice Department's efforts to prosecute noncitizens who unlawfully voted in prior elections, noting that the Biden administration had only prosecuted 13 people while the Trump investigation was investigating "thousands" of such cases.
One of the sources said Mr. Trump felt that Dhillon should have been more forceful in her explanation.
Despite the president's demands, Justice Department officials were able to stall for time and allow her to proceed with her plans to resign after the election was over, the sources added.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said that Dhillon did a "fantastic job" in her role and the White House is "very grateful for her dedicated service at the Department of Justice."
Dhillon's tenure

In her resignation letter, Dhillon touted her efforts to end "unlawful and discriminatory DEI practices" and to protect "women and girls' sports from biological males, including through lawsuits against Minnesota and California," among other accomplishments.
"While I am leaving this post, I will continue fighting for our country in the years ahead," she added.

During her tenure, the Justice Department closed many of its cases involving discrimination targeting Black Americans and announced it had dismissed more than 50 decades-old consent decrees with public schools, many in the Deep South, that were in place to protect Black students from unlawful discrimination.

Dhillon nixed two pending consent decrees last year with the Minneapolis and Louisville Police Departments over systemic abuses that were investigated in the wake of the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, and rescinded the investigative findings of misconduct into six other police departments.

Earlier this year, after immigration agents shot and killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis as they were protesting the administration's immigration crackdown, the Civil Rights Division did not move to open any criminal civil rights investigations, in violation of longstanding practice for such high-profile officer-involved shootings.

The division ultimately got involved in the Pretti case after the Justice Department faced staunch criticism and questions about why Homeland Security Investigations — and not the FBI — was leading the probe into its own agency.
To date, no charges have been filed in the Pretti case, which is also separately under investigation by state officials.

Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who founded the nonprofit advocacy group Justice Connection, called Dhillon "the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history" in a statement on Thursday.
"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it."
Dhillon, a staunch ally of President Trump who for years ran her own law firm in San Francisco, is a frequent guest on conservative podcasts and a very active poster on social media.

Unlike her predecessors, she frequently took to X to post videos about the work that her division was undertaking. She acknowledged in media interviews that she often generated ideas for civil rights investigations based on various posts she encountered on social media.

She has sometimes announced the opening of civil rights investigations online, a stark departure from historical practice. She also handed out challenge coins to fellow DOJ attorneys with the term "FAFO" ("f--k around and find out") printed on them.
Among the areas where she has been the most vocal has involved voting rights issues.
Under her leadership, the Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits against primarily blue states and the District of Columbia in an effort to gain access to unredacted voter rolls.

Lawyers from the division repeatedly argued that they needed the information to ensure states were complying with two federal voting laws that require them to maintain clean voter lists. However, they later admitted in court that the Justice Department intended to share the information with the Department of Homeland Security so they could use it for criminal and immigration enforcement purposes.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 27 of those cases.

During the midterm elections on Tuesday, the Civil Rights Division sent out more than 1,000 monitors to polling sites across the country, a record number that required the Justice Department to solicit volunteers from unusual parts of the DOJ, including the Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
However, in more recent weeks, Dhillon has been noticeably less involved in the effort.

She did not appear at an election integrity briefing that was held at DOJ for journalists, and the Office of the Deputy Attorney General, who does not have oversight authority on civil rights, solicited election monitor volunteers, according to a Sept. 10 memo seen by CBS News. That program has historically been run by the Civil Rights Division.

A senior Justice Department official denied that the election integrity work had been taken away from Dhillon when asked about it directly at the briefing, saying they were spreading around resources due to the increase in the workload.
"I don't agree that anything has shifted away from Harmeet. I think she's as busy as the rest of us. We're spreading the wealth," the said.

Nicole  Sganga
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: LIV Golf shutting down after debtors bail and players head for exits
summary: Bankrupt LIV Golf, which sought to disrupt professional golf, will wind down its operations after failing to secure funding.
story: LIV Golf is in the water hazard — forever. The bankrupt Saudi Arabia-backed venture, which shook up the professional golf world after launching in 2022, said Thursday that it is shutting down.
An attorney for LIV said in a New Jersey bankruptcy court that the fledgling golf league's debtors have decided against a proposed reorganization and will instead wind down the business.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which had bankrolled LIV, announced earlier this year that it would yank funding for the league after the 2026 season, ending its investment after sinking more than $5 billion into LIV since its launch, CBS Sports reported.

The league, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8, thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable "LIV 2.0."
But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren't interested. Brooks Koepka, another major golf name that had signed with LIV, opted to return to the PGA Tour.

"BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement. "While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players' last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O'Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn't going forward.
LIV suffered two big setbacks, before and after filing for bankruptcy.
The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the commercially known DP World Tour in Europe.

Then, European tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.

But the biggest setback was in April, two weeks after the Masters and two months after the start of the Iran war. PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.

LIV was originally run by Greg Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as "Golf, but louder" with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.
But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.

title: Hostages share tales of terror, heroism during Trader Joe's standoff
summary: Hostages recount the chilling details about what actually happened inside the California store and how they were able to get out alive
story: This story first aired on Feb. 16, 2019. It was updated on Dec. 14.
"I don't know what's going to happen," Lynne Westafer said of the moment she heard gunshots. "None of us know what's going to happen."
"A hundred-percent, I thought it was a mass shooting,"  Arta Gjonbalaj told "48 Hours." "We're all going to die."

Gjonbalaj and Westafer were trapped with approximately 30 other people inside a Trader Joe's in Los Angeles, when a beautiful July 2018 Saturday afternoon was shattered by the sound of a car wreck and gunshots. Gene Atkins, who police say had shot his grandmother and then kidnapped his girlfriend, had led police on a chase when he crashed his car outside of Trader Joe's and exchanged gunfire with arriving officers as he entered the store. The store manager, Melyda Corado, was caught in the crossfire and killed by a police bullet. Those left in the store scrambled for cover.
"The gunshots had gotten louder," MaryLinda Moss recalled. "Somebody yelled, 'The gunman is in the store.'"
"It looked like a murder scene. There was blood everywhere," said Gjonbalaj.

Members of the Los Angeles Police Department surrounded the store, including the SWAT team, which took strategic positions on buildings in the sight lines of the entrances. Then the alleged gunman spotted a sharpshooter on the roof of the cheese store next door. The gunman, on the phone with police, demanded the sniper move.
"He says, 'If you don't get them off the roof, I'm going to shoot somebody," said Westafer. "I'm going to shoot somebody in 5, 4, 3, 2 …'"
A SUNNY SATURDAY TURNS DARK
Lynne Westafer: Saturday, July 21st, was a really nice summer day.
Cory Page: It was sunny, just like every single day has been since I moved here (laughs).

WOMAN [ON PHONE]: Hello? 911 DISPATCHER: …Is everything OK? We got a 911 call from your phone. WOMAN: Yes, um, the – that front house in front of me – I think it's my aunt's grandson just shot her. 911 DISPATCHER: Oh, my goodness! 911 DISPATCHER: OK – WOMAN: Now he's leaving in her car… 911 DISPATCHER: What kind of car? Tell me what kind of car, ma'am. WOMAN: It's a blue – a dark blue Camry…
Richard Winton | Los Angeles Times crime reporter: The gunman … shot his grandmother …  multiple times.
KCAL REPORTER: That just goes to show you how dangerous the suspect is.
KCAL ANCHOR: And then leading police on a pursuit from South L.A.
KCAL REPORTER: He had a female with him.  We believe that that may be his girlfriend.
Lynne Westafer: And I was just doing my usual Saturday thing.  I went to my yoga class in the morning, and then ran a couple errands…
KCAL REPORTER: Police started searching for that car.  They found it in the Hollywood division…
Arta Gjonbalaj:  My friend was letting me stay at her place and I was like, "OK …  I'm gonna go get groceries for us for the week." I love grocery shopping.  It's like my hobby!
Lynne Westafer: I was coming right up on the Trader Joe's.  I thought, "Oh I'll just go in there."
Cory Page: Whenever you go into that Trader Joe's, there are always like hundreds of people inside of it.
Richard Winton: On this given Saturday … this is where the eyes of the world turned.
POLICE VIDEO | OFFICER 1: Oh, s--t. Shots fired. Broadcast.
POLICE VIDEO | OFFICER 2: 6A67, shots fired. Shots fired. Officer needs help.  West Silver Lake Drive …

MaryLinda Moss: My daughter and I were having an afternoon together.  We were getting her ready for high school. It was midafternoon when we got to the Trader Joe's.  … My daughter didn't have her shoes on, so I said, "I'm gonna go in right now, and you can follow me in."
POLICE VIDEO: The gunman's car crashes into a pole right in front of Trader Joe's.
Richard Winton: He ends up crashing his car, 15 to 20 yards, from the front of a Trader Joe's supermarket.
Lynne Westafer: I was in the cheese section and I heard this loud screech – boom of a car crash.
Arta Gjonbala: It was like, "Eeerk" [imitating the sound].
MaryLinda Moss: Huge sound of impact, of crunching metal.
Lynne Westafer: And I looked at the other people who were around me and we were like, "What was that?  And then we heard gunfire… boom, boom, boom, boom, boom…
Arta Gjonbala: …boom, boom, boom, boom.  And that's when everyone was either running out, taking cover.
Lynne Westafer: Someone started shouting, "Get down!  Get down!  Get down!"
POLICE VIDEO | OFFICER 1: Hey! Shots fired, get down!
MaryLinda Moss: When I threw myself to the ground, I was … calling my daughter at the same time. … I said … "Stay in the car. … Get down.  Hide in the bottom of the car.  There's a shooter."
MaryLinda Moss: The gunshots had gotten louder.  Somebody yelled, "The gunman is in the store."
POLICE VIDEO | OFFICER: Watch out! Oh s--t!
Cory Page: I'm sort of like rerunning every single previous mass shooting in my head … over and over again because that's what I thought was happening…
MaryLinda Moss: And then, I hear the assailant start counting down…
"WE HAVE AN ACTIVE SHOOTER"
KCAL ANCHOR: This situation still unfolding right now here at the Trader Joe's …
KCAL REPORTER: We have an active shooter …
Lynne Westafer: Oh god!
KCAL ANCHOR: He went into the back of Trader Joe's and took hostages.
KCAL ANCHOR: This is just a very tense situation…
Inside the store, strangers from all walks of life would find themselves united with one desperate goal: to get out alive.
Lynne Westafer: I don't know. I don't know what's going to happen. Like, none of us know what's going to happen here.

Lynne Westafer is a promotions producer for the CBS station KCAL, Arta Gjonbalaj is a student and model, Cory Page is an environmental associate for the Walt Disney Company and MaryLinda Moss is an art consultant.
MaryLinda Moss: I'm between these two counters … I was exposed on two sides.
MaryLinda was in the front of the store.
MaryLinda Moss: I was terrified. I didn't know what I should do … So I just stayed there.
KCAL ANCHOR: We're still waiting to see what is going on inside the store.
Lynne Westafer: There was a lot of commotion that I could not see but I could hear.
In the back of the store was Lynne.
Lynne Westafer: Screaming, the sounds of pushing and shoving and running feet.
Arta Gjonbalaj: A 100-percent, I thought it was a mass shooting.
Next to Lynne was Arta.
Arta Gjonbalaj: The first thing I thought was that we're all going to die.
Cory Page: It was mass chaos getting into the closet. People were pushing each other out of the way.
Also, in the back of the store hiding in a closet with a glass window, was Cory.
Cory Page: The closet was actually pretty small. … My knees were like, you know, almost in my mouth.
Cory Page: I took pictures while we were in there. … They are kind of like a direct reflection of what I was experiencing.
Cory Page: Inside the closet there were 21 people. … We are fully exposed. We are sitting ducks.
MaryLinda Moss: And then I saw the assailant. The gun is in his right hand and his left arm was bleeding profusely – just blood was flowing out of it.
Lynne Westafer: Every person had their phones out and they were texting. … They were all texting, texting, texting. … And I did not have my phone.
Arta Gjonbalaj: The shooter told us … "Get off your phones or you're gonna get killed." … I quickly messaged all my family members. … I thought that was the last time I was gonna talk to anybody.
Arta's mother Naze Gjonbalaj was home in New York watching the story unfold on television.
Naze Gjonbalaj [crying]: I wish I can help her.
KCAL ANCHOR: The situation, still very dangerous. An active hostage situation with an active shooter.
Naze Gjonbalaj: I didn't know what to do.
Lynne Westafer: I am not gonna die here today. There's no way. No!
Lynne Westafer: Do I run or do I stay here? When … the guy's threatening to shoot you, that's a life or death decision … I couldn't make a decision. I just was paralyzed.

Cory Page: This may be it. I'm like, "I've, you know, lived 22 years on this earth." And I was like, "that might be all that I have." … And that's when I started texting people. I texted my mom. I texted my friend who lived close by.
Lexi Kavanaugh: "Lexi, call the cops. There's a shooter inside. … Help!"
Lexi Kavanagh, 24, is Cory's best friend.
Cory Page [reading texts]: "Lexi, please do something. I'm so scared…"
Lexi Kavanaugh: He did send me several text messages that really tugged on my heartstrings.
Cory Page [reading texts]: "I love you with all my heart."
Lexi Kavanaugh: He was reiterating that he loved me continuously … That was really what started to scare me.
Cory Page [reading texts]: "Lexi, I'm terrified…"
Lexi Kavanaugh: He was terrified enough to talk to me in this way…
MaryLinda Moss: The assailant was clearly weak from the wound … but he kept on looking out to the door obviously aware that the police were out there.

What the hostages did not know was that about two hours earlier, the gunman had shot his grandmother seven times. He also injured his 17-year-old girlfriend, but because she was a minor, her name and details about her injury have never been released.
Richard Winton: What happened is the -- the gunman had a -- essentially a domestic dispute with his girlfriend and his grandmother had been involved.
Richard Winton covered the story for the Los Angeles Times.
Richard Winton: You can't have a more dangerous kind of gunman than someone who's already shot their nearest and dearest.
KCAL ANCHOR: An unknown number of people are still being held hostage …
Richard Winton: Everyone was trying to assess where this was going … how many people will he kill?

MaryLinda Moss: He looks to me and he said, "Come over here and massage my hand."… And it felt very uncomfortable. It's not what I wanted to do … but -- he has a gun, he's asking me to come over, so that's what I did.
Richard Winton: He was very obsessed with talking to those he'd already done harm to.
The gunman made frantic phone calls and learned his grandmother was still alive.

MaryLinda Moss: He then started going into shock and was shivering … He said, "There are some jackets down there" and so I very specifically said, "Would you like me to get them?" And he said, "Yes." … And as I went, I saw a woman lying behind the manager's counter. … As I walked by her, she didn't move. … I looked down and that's when I saw that she was lying in a pool of blood and it was devastating.

MaryLinda Moss: So, I said to him, "There's a woman who's been shot. And she probably needs help." And he yelled back at me, "That was the cops not me!" … And I said, "Can we get her help? Can we take her outside?" And he said, "OK."
A Trader Joe's employee brought the dying woman outside and then ran to safety. The hostages would later learn her name was Melyda Corado, known as Mely, the store manager. She was 27 years old.
MaryLinda Moss: She was doing what she was doing, running out to help somebody, because that's the kind of person that she was.
Mely was caught in the crossfire between police and the gunman -- hit by an officer's bullet.
MaryLinda Moss: And then his phone rings. It's the police. … The police officer introduced himself. He was encouraging him to let everyone go.
The gunman was told his girlfriend was also alive and headed into surgery. Then he made a demand.
MaryLinda Moss: "You get her on the phone with me, I'll turn myself in." … And then he hung up.
MaryLinda Moss: He was getting really amped up.
MaryLinda Moss: He then, within the next couple minutes, said, "How many people are in the store? Bring them here."
Lynne Westafer: Oh sh--!
A WAITING GAME

Lynne Westafer: We're in a single file, hands up. And we walk from the bread aisle down … and there is stuff scattered -- baskets overturned and there is [becomes emotional] abandoned purses and there is things knocked off the shelves and it's so empty.
Arta Gjonbalaj: I see blood all over the floor. … It looked like a murder scene, it was blood everywhere.
Arta and Lynne were among 13 hostages who were brought to the front of the store.
Arta Gjonbalaj: You look at the register and he's sitting right there. … And I saw my shopping cart that I left right in front of him.
Lynne Westafer: There's the gunman who's covered in a sweatshirt. It's got a hood up. And there's several people around him.
Arta Gjonbalaj: You see his gunshot wound in his arm.

Lynne Westafer: So, I'm trying to… take him in … and I think I see a young female Trader Joe's employee holding his hand. … I see there's this other woman who is rubbing on his back a little bit. …What is going on? Like, grab the gun for Ch----'s sake!
MaryLinda Moss: I had been massaging his shoulder … I was trying to help ground him.

MaryLinda felt she understood the gunman. She says she had a troubled childhood and began using alcohol and drugs before getting sober at the age of 18. She spent years in therapy in order to pull her life back together.

MaryLinda Moss: Over the years I have been with people who have … made … bad choices in their life … I have learned how to be present with them without judgment. … That allowed me to be present with the assailant in a way that perhaps I wouldn't have been able to be.

MaryLinda Moss: He said to me, "You have nothing to do with this. I don't want to hurt you. I don't want anybody to get hurt." … I then reached over and I put my hand on his heart … and I looked at him in his eyes, and I said, "I know you have a good heart and I know you don't want to hurt anybody." And he said, "You don't know what I did this morning." And my hand, still on his heart, I said, "It doesn't matter, I know you have a good heart, and I know you don't want to hurt anybody."

Lynne Westafer: He was a guy in so far over his head and I'm glad that that woman was able to help him. At the time I had mixed feelings about it because I just wished that someone would grab the gun and end this. That's what I kept thinking, like, "grab the gun." To be fair … if I had been sitting next to him I don't know if I could have grabbed the gun.  … I wanted someone to do that, but I don't know if I could have done that. That's the truth.
Arta Gjonbalaj: When we first got to the front … he asked the Trader Joe's employee … to pick somebody from the crowd.
Lynne Westafer: I heard that young guy say, "You want me to choose?" and I thought, "Choose what?"
Arta Gjonbalaj: And I sort of put my head down because I was like, he's maybe he's trying to ask him to pick someone that he wants to shoot next.
Lynne Westafer: And he turned and he pointed at this boy who was like 13, 14. And he said, "I choose you," and I thought, "choose him for what?"
Lynne Westafer: I wanted to just like grab him … and say, "No don't choose him! What is happening?" … And then the Trader Joe's guy said, "He's letting you go," and I thought "Oh" [sighs in relief].
Arta Gjonbalaj: "You can go out with your hands up."
Lexi Kavanaugh: I have never seen so much of a police presence in my life.
While waiting for texts from her friend Cory, Lexi who lived about 5 minutes from the Trader Joe's, was glued to the television coverage.
KCAL ANCHOR: Police are getting into position, they are on tactical alert …
Lexi Kavanaugh: I saw multiple helicopters above my house, there was the S.W.A.T. team, there was a tank on the street … It looked like an apocalyptic event.

Cory Page: I definitely could hear people crying in the closet. I couldn't really pinpoint who because I couldn't see people's faces. …It's sort of like this wave. It would get super quiet and then it would get louder, people would get more comfortable and, you know, they'd whip out their phone again and start having a conversation with a loved one or the police. And then we would hear stuff from the front of the store. And so then we would all get really quiet. And it went on like that.

Cory Page: The reason why I was pushing myself further and further back under the sink was because I was convinced that there was not only one, but multiple active shooters, and it was only a matter of time before they were gonna find us.
MaryLinda Moss: We were just waiting for the phone call with the girlfriend.
Arta Gjonbalaj: We just sat there waiting. … Surprisingly, no one was like crying or screaming or yelling.
But even in the quieter moments, it was never completely silent.
Cory Page: The crazy part about being inside a grocery store is … this underlying soundtrack to the whole – the whole event.
Lynne Westafer: There was a moment when … the song that was playing was Stevie Wonder, "My Cherie Amour."
Lynne Westafer: So, Stevie Wonder then becomes the soundtrack for your nightmare. ... It was just like -- perfectly horrifying.
By now, approximately an hour had passed. In addition to the boy, other hostages had been allowed to go. A Trader Joe's employee was trying to keep up morale.
Lynne Westafer:  He turned around and he said to us in the calmest voice, "It's gonna be OK. He's letting people go. I'm gonna be the last one out."

MaryLinda Moss: There was this woman, around 30 years old, she was clearly terrified.  So, I asked him if he would let this woman go. … Within a minute or two, he said yes. …When she gets right in front of the door, the automatic door opens and the assailant yells, "Stop!"
Arta Gjonbalaj: As she was standing at the door, the door kept opening and closing and he said, "Do not walk out."
Lynne Westafer: "Come back here." And she took a step back towards him, and the doors opened again. He said, " Stop opening the doors."
MaryLinda Moss: She looks at me like, what am I supposed to do? … so I shook my head, "yes."
Arta Gjonbalaj: And she just jetted. She ran out of there.
Lynne Westafer: And I thought, oh great, now we're all gonna get shot.
MaryLinda Moss: He said, "She left! I told her to stop and she left!"
MaryLinda Moss: Then he asked the Trader Joe's employee who was standing there, "do you have the keys?"
Lynne Westafer: He said, "Lock the damn door."
THE COUNTDOWN
Lynne Westafer: When that front door locked, it was like, wham, you know, it's game over.
Outside, the SWAT team made its next move.
MaryLinda Moss: The assailant looks out the door and he says, "What is that sniper doing on the roof?"
Lynne Westafer: And sure enough there was … a sniper on the roof of the cheese store, next door to the Trader Joe's.
MaryLinda Moss: The gun aimed right at us.
MaryLinda Moss: The assailant starts yelling to the police on the phone, "What is that guy doing there? Get the guy off the roof!"
Lynne Westafer: And they're screaming … "Get that guy off the roof, you've got to get him off the roof!"
What they couldn't see was that there were three sharp shooters on the roof.
MaryLinda Moss: I'm yelling to the sergeant. And the sergeant's like, "Let me see if I can reach them."
Lynne Westafer: "Why won't you get the guy off the roof? Get him off! Get him off! Why won't you do it?"
MaryLinda Moss: We were in danger in a way we had not been before that.
Lynne Westafer: This yelling … went on for five minutes. Do you know how long five minutes is in hostage time?
Arta Gjonbalaj: I was ready to run.
Lynne Westafer: Finally the gunman is so aggravated that he says, "If you don't get 'em off the roof, I'm gonna shoot somebody."
Arta Gjonbalaj: And that's when he starts counting down from five.
Lynne Westafer: I'm gonna shoot somebody in FIVE…
Arta Gjonbalaj: FOUR…
MaryLinda Moss: And I'm saying , "GET HIM OFF THE ROOF!" … THREE …

Lynne Westafer: When he got to two … the sniper climbed off the roof. Do you know how he got off the roof? Another officer climbed up and tapped him on the arm. … Like, did his walkie talkie not get charged? … How did that happen? … It almost was IT for somebody.
Lynne Westafer: After the sniper got off the roof, there was this silence. It was like the most scary sound of nothing.
Arta Gjonbalaj: We're like, OK. There's no hope in here. There's no hope.
MaryLinda, who had been trying to keep the gunman calm, also acted as an intermediary between him and the LAPD during their many phone calls.
MaryLinda Moss: And so I said into the phone to the sergeant, I said, "You need to know that we are all very, very, very scared and it is because of what just happened."

Lynne Westafer: Do you know what it feels like to be sitting on the floor of a grocery store … and you get increasingly afraid that the people who are there who are supposed to save you, are -- are making it worse for you?
Lynne Westafer: It gives me no pleasure to beat up on the LAPD, but I would not be doing my job as a witness … if I didn't say what happened here.
Richard Winton | Los Angeles Times: The hostages see the incident in one way and SWAT officers see it in a different way.
The LAPD declined to comment citing an ongoing investigation. Richard Winton says in the age of mass shootings, police are pressured to act quickly.

Richard Winton: The protocols are very different these days post Columbine. No one waits. … It's try and rush in. … Here I think at the end they ultimately decided it wasn't a mass shooter scenario that he was more of a man who has some history of mental struggles. … And that's where I think they make the fine line decision. Don't rush in, let's try and talk him down.
But Winton says the LAPD didn't know what to make of MaryLinda.

Richard Winton: SWAT negotiators are used to dealing with the person directly.  They want to hear their voice, they want to know what their tone is, they want to understand what's going on exactly from them.
Back in the closet, the hostages watched snippets of the drama in silence.
Cory Page: I think when you are surrounded by 20-plus people in a room that is no bigger than like an average closet, everyone's deepest and darkest personalities will come out.

Cory Page: This guy, there were, like five or so knives on a magnet on the wall cause it was the food prep area for where they give out the samples … and he and another person grabbed a knife and they were like, "If things go south, like we're gonna, we're gonna take him down." And it immediately terrified me. Because I knew … we needed to stay as quiet and as undiscovered as possible.
In the front of the store, a new LAPD negotiator called to say an officer was being sent to the hospital to talk to the gunman's girlfriend.
MaryLinda Moss: It was starting to feel like they were just delaying and he was getting more frustrated.
Arta Gjonbalaj: Our lives are on the line for a phone call.
Then, more pressure from the LAPD.
MaryLinda Moss: The assailant looks towards the door … "What is that truck doing there?" And I look … and there is a SWAT truck, right in front of the door.
MaryLinda Moss: And he starts with the new negotiator, "What are you doing, what's that SWAT truck doing there, get it out of there." … And so they back it up, like a foot [laughs]. And then stop.
MaryLinda Moss:  And I think he realized that there was not gonna be a better way out of here. …  He said, "Get me my call with my girlfriend …"
LAPD OFFICER: OK that – that – that works for me. Just – OK. Do me a favor, just hang tight.
MaryLinda Moss:  "… send handcuffs in ..."
LAPD OFFICER: He says, "If you guys could – would – would throw a – throw a set of handcuffs in…"

MaryLinda Moss: "…I will let myself be handcuffed and give over my gun and I will turn myself in." And then he hung up the phone. … And I was like, "that was it, that was the solution. …We've got our way out!"
AN EXIT STRATEGY
As the frightening standoff continued, the frustrated gunman repeated his demands to the police negotiator.
KCAL REPORTER: The suspect is barricaded.  Police are trying to get him to surrender…
MaryLinda Moss: So the assailant said … "send in the handcuffs, get my call with my girlfriend, and I'll turn myself in."

Lynne Westafer: The gunman believed that if he walked out handcuffed he was less likely to be shot by the police. So there was a long negotiation to try to get the police to give a pair of handcuffs. … Finally, they agreed.
Lynne Westafer: And a young man who has been a customer in the store – Mike … was gonna walk to the front door and he was gonna get the handcuffs.
Mike D'Angelo had been quietly assisting MaryLinda from the beginning.
MaryLinda Moss: Mike had already been going and getting things for the assailant.
Mary Linda Moss: I mean we really … depended on each other.
MaryLinda Moss: I told the negotiator … "Mike is coming out. … He's coming to get the handcuffs."
Lynne Westafer: So Mike starts to walk towards the door.
MaryLinda Moss: The Trader Joe's employee unlocks the door…
Chris Ritzen | "48 Hours" producer: Were you scared?
Mike D'Angelo: Yeah, we didn't know what was gonna happen next.
KCAL CHOPPER AUDIO: This is NOT the suspect.  Now this is NOT the suspect.

MaryLinda Moss: And then I see the SWAT team member … start gesturing strongly for Mike to come out. …And both Mike and I at the same time start yelling, "No, no, no, no-no-no-no-no-no-no!" I'm like, I'm into the phone, "No, no, no, no.  … Throw the handcuffs in."
Lynne Westafer: Now Mike, bravely, is standing at the doorway saying, "Give me the handcuffs." … All the while officers are trying to get him to leave.
Mike D'Angelo: And I said, "There's no way I'm leaving these people here."
Lynne Westafer: The gunman was saying …  "Don't you go out that door, you better bring those handcuffs back here."
MaryLinda Moss: He'd already said, "I'm going to get myself handcuffed … I'm gonna turn myself in. …The trust that we had developed was key in him following through with what he had said.
Lynne Westafer: After many more minutes of yelling, screaming… that panic, just that screeching losing your voice kind of shouting…
MaryLinda Moss: No-no-no-no. … No-no-no-no-no! "Throw the handcuffs!  Throw the handcuffs!"  I'm yelling out the door.  I'm yelling into the phone…
Lynne Westafer: There was this "thunk" [claps her hands] as the handcuffs hit the linoleum.
MaryLinda Moss: And the assailant jumps and tenses. And I – and I'm like, "It's the handcuffs."… And I say, "Mike, pick up the handcuffs!  Show him it's the handcuffs!"
Lynne Westafer: And then Mike walked back in…
MaryLinda Moss: And then we have the handcuffs.
Lynne Westafer: What a hero.
Mike D'Angelo: I didn't want to let the people down or anybody to get hurt. So I stayed.

Richard Winton: There was a lot of reluctance on the part of the police to give him the handcuffs. He could take the handcuffs and handcuff himself to a hostage and make them a human shield.  So, they had to really buy into this idea that he would handcuff himself.
KCAL CHOPPER AUDIO: They've got the suspect on the phone.  But they're trying to get the girlfriend to talk to him or something…
MaryLinda Moss: He then is getting more and more frustrated with them not getting his girlfriend on the phone.
MaryLinda Moss: The assailant said to me, "They're not trying to get her."  I said, "Of course they are." … This is our way out.
MaryLinda Moss: This is a guy who's saying he's gonna let himself out if you get him a f---ing phone call!  Right?
MaryLinda Moss: When we were waiting to hear about his girlfriend … he said, "It's all over. It doesn't matter what happens to me. … I'm in for life."
MaryLinda Moss: I said to him I had known people who had been in prison for many years, and who had made lives for themselves inside prison. … And that there was always hope.
MaryLinda Moss: And he said to me, "I wish I had met you earlier.  I just needed somebody to talk to."
At just about that time, the negotiator called.  The police had finally contacted the gunman's injured girlfriend.  She recorded a short message.

MaryLinda Moss: And she said, "I'm OK. Go outside. I'm OK.  Go outside." … She said it three times. … And that clearly gave him the relief that he was looking for. … He never asked again for a phone call. That was enough.
With his demands met, he released more hostages.  Arta noticed a mother and daughter were about to be let go.
Arta Gjonbalaj: At that point, something told me, pretend she's your mom. … So I grabbed her hand and she grabs mine back.
The gunman then asked, "Is this also your daughter?"
Arta Gjonbalaj: And she said, "Yes, this is my daughter."  And he said, "You can get up and go with your sister."
And just like that, Arta was free and allowed to leave with her "sister."
Arta Gjonbalaj: I just walked out as fast as I can.
Moments later, the woman who risked her life pretending to be her mom was also released.
Arta Gjonbalaj: I gave her the biggest hug in the whole world.
And then Arta called her real mom.
Naze Gjonbalaj: Everything is OK because I got my daughter alive.
Arta Gjonbalaj: It was just a lot of tears at that point. … It was relief, but it was also, "Wow, that was the closest I've ever been to death."
Next, it was Lynne's turn.
Lynne Westafer: Most of the other hostages, when they were leaving, turned to him and they said [she whispers], "Thank you. Thank you." … I was just getting madder and madder.

Lynne Westafer: And when I stood up, I very intentionally did not look at him … because I thought, if I turned around to say anything to him, I wouldn't be saying, "thank you."  I'd be saying, "f--- you."  And that would be bad for everybody. … So I just looked straight ahead … and out I went.
The police had negotiated a plan with the assailant to leave the store and surrender safely.  But he was still there with four hostages and still holding the gun.
MaryLinda Moss: He was afraid to walk down the long aisle to the door where they could see him. … He was afraid he was gonna get shot.
MaryLinda Moss: I actually turned to him. I took his face in my hands. … I said …  "Do you trust me?" And he said, "Yes."

MaryLinda Moss: But he's still thinking that they're gonna shoot him. So I looked at the other three …  and I say, "Should we go out together?" And they all three shake their head, "Yes. We'll go out together."
MaryLinda Moss: So I ask him if he's ready to be handcuffed, and he says, "Yes."
MaryLinda Moss: And then I ask him if I can take the gun, and he says, "Yes."
MaryLinda Moss: So I then ask him, "Are you ready?" He said, "Ah, I need a little bit more time."  As we're waiting, I heard a noise on the roof. … And it scared me.
MaryLinda Moss: So I didn't ask for permission.
MaryLinda Moss: I said, "It's time to do this now."
A PEACEFUL END
MaryLinda Moss: The negotiator said, "OK, we're ready." … I look to the other three. We all stand up together. I'm in front of him. The others kinda circle behind him.
KCAL CHOPPER AUDIO: They're close to getting him out. But I don't know …
KCAL CHOPPER AUDIO: I see some shadows…
MaryLinda Moss: We walked down and we get to the door, the door opens.
KCAL CHOPPER AUDIO: Here they come.
MaryLinda Moss: We take a step out.
Richard Winton: Everyone expected him to come last, on his own. But they kind of came with him. … Almost like making sure he was OK, 'cause he was bleeding.
MaryLinda Moss: We are descended upon. A lot of SWAT team members.
As the hostages were taken away, the gunman whose name is Gene Atkins, surrendered without a fight.
MaryLinda Moss: I was aware of them taking Gene over to handle him, but I was really like, it was done. … That's when I felt the relief.
But for Cory and the 20 others who were still hiding in the closet, it would take 15 long minutes before the SWAT team freed them.

Cory Page: I put my hands up and we filed out of the closet. … I just immediately started crying.  Every bit of emotion that I had bottled up because I didn't want to either make noise or I didn't want to express how I was really feeling while I was inside of there, it all came out.
Down the street waiting for Cory was his best friend Lexi, whose text messages kept him calm during his darkest moments.

Lexi Kavanaugh: We just held each other so close and that's when I cracked. … I could feel all of that hardened adrenaline … wear off and relax and I just sort of like melted and broke down a little bit. … I told him I loved him a million times.
KCAL ANCHOR: Well the good news is again it appears that this has been brought to a peaceful end. That suspect, we're told, emerged from the Trader Joe's …
It had been more than three grueling hours. MaryLinda, who had worked so hard to keep everyone safe, was free.

MaryLinda Moss: I saw my daughter, my husband and my son -- my daughter starts running toward me. …She runs into my arms and I hug her and then I hug my husband and he says, "I am so proud of you and so mad at you" [laughs].
The next day, an impromptu memorial was set up outside Trader Joe's to honor Mely Corado.
Mely Corado's friend: The Corado family has lost their sweet, funny and loving daughter, sister and friend.
Seven days later, her family held a public funeral.
Mely's Corado's father: I don't know where you go when you die, but I hope when I do, I end up with Mely.
Even though a police bullet killed Mely, Gene Atkins, now 29, was charged with her death for setting the events in motion.
Atkins was charged with a total of 51 felony counts including attempted murder and kidnapping.

Before this happened, Atkins had only minor scrapes with the law. He was raised by the very woman he's now accused of shooting – his grandmother, who survived. He's looking at a possible sentence of life in prison.
To work through their trauma, MaryLinda, Lynne, Cory and many of the other hostages from that day get together regularly to talk and to heal.
MaryLinda Moss: I'm just now starting to process it. Just now.
Cyrani Ackerman | Hostage survivor [at group meeting]: I'm shocked at some of the feelings that I have, in thinking about him and thinking about the incident.

Cory Page: The really remarkable part of this story, sort of the diamond in the rough … I have this whole group of like new best friends from different, you know, age ranges, different backgrounds that we just all happened to be at the place at the same time. … It's really been everything for me.

Lynne Westafer [at group meeting]: Just to feel whole again, it's kind of miraculous … I didn't actually think that was possible. There was a time when I thought, "there's – this is done, like who I am is gone."

Lynne Westafer: You have these moments where it's emotional and you think like, "God, I can't believe I'm alive" … And then there's other times where the sunlight will spike off of something and it's just beautiful and you think, "Oh, my god. I'm alive."

In October 2026, Gene Atkins was convicted of 41 counts including second-degree murder, assault with a semiautomatic firearm on a peace officer, attempted carjacking and mayhem for the July 2018 crime.

title: Gluesenkamp Perez wins competitive Washington race
summary: The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun in a district President Trump has won three times.
story: Washington — Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won a third term in Washington's 3rd Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Gluesenkamp Perez's victory, in a district President Trump has won three times, comes as she's flexed her independence over party loyalty. Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives in January, with stunning wins across the country.

The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun to win reelection in the rural district in the southwestern corner of the state. Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate, was a more mainstream Republican than Gluesenkamp Perez's prior opponent, far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Mr. Trump's counterterrorism chief before resigning in protest over the Iran war. But Braun, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump, also distanced himself from the president on some issues, including on tariffs, the Iran war and affirming that Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Though Gluesenkamp Perez angered her Democratic colleagues in September by helping Republicans on two party-line procedural votes that were struggling to pass, her win is a relief to Democrats, who needed to hold the highly competitive seat in their quest to retake the House majority.

Though House Democratic leaders initially called the split "a significant breach of trust" that "necessitates a serious response," the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — which is controlled by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York — continued to back Gluesenkamp Perez. In a coordinated ad with the DCCC in October, Gluesenkamp Perez said, "I don't answer to any political party or any president. I answer to you."
At a district event in September, Gluesenkamp Perez emphasized her loyalty to her community as she referenced her occasional defections.

"We have no form of representative democracy if we do not represent our districts, if we don't stand for a working waterfront, if we don't stand for people working in the trades, if we don't stand for right-to-repair, if we don't stand for our Ukrainian countrymen, we have nothing," she said. "All of democracy is predicated on representative government. That's the point."
Braun also sought to put space between himself and GOP leaders during the campaign.

While not criticizing the president directly on his handling of the Iran war, Braun said during an Oct. 13 debate, "I will not and I do not support a war without clear objectives and without a clear ending point."
"I think Congress has a very important role here — one they should exercise," he said.
Braun also lamented Congress ceding its powers to the president, especially its control over federal government spending and the ability to declare war.
"We have to take power back," he said.

On tariffs, Braun said, "with our allies, indiscriminate use of tariffs is not helpful and ultimately lead to an increase of prices for manufacturers and consumers." He called the administration's handling of immigration enforcement  a "mixed bag."

title: Black candidates for governor make history with midterm victories
summary: Americans elected the country's first Black woman, and four other Black candidates, into gubernatorial roles during Tuesday's record midterm races.
story: Americans elected their first Black woman into a gubernatorial role during the 2026 midterms, alongside four other Black candidates who won races for governor around the United States on Tuesday.

The races culminated, respectively, in victories for Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, in Georgia; Byron Donalds, a Republican, in Florida; David Crowley, a Democrat, in Wisconsin; Aaron Ford, a Democrat, in Nevada; and Wes Moore, also a Democrat, who was reelected to serve a second term as governor of Maryland. He became the state's first Black governor when he was elected in 2022.

Including Moore, only three Black Americans have previously been elected to serve as U.S. governors. Former New York Gov. David Paterson, who is also Black, became governor when Eliot Spitzer resigned in 2008.
Once Bottoms and Crowley were projected the winners in their races, Moore reflected on their wins to CBS News on Tuesday, calling the victories "incredibly important."

"This is exciting, because up until this moment, I was the only Black governor in America. And I was very clear that that's a title that I did not want to hold onto for very long," said Moore. "I'm only the third African American ever elected governor in the 250-year history of this country, and, now, in one cycle, we have at least doubled that number. I just think it's incredibly important. It's a historic moment."

Bottoms has been hailed as a trailblazer for more reasons than one, as she will become the first Black woman elected to a gubernatorial position in U.S. history. She will also be the first woman to serve as governor of Georgia when she joins the ranks of a record-high number of women — 17 — in governor's offices nationwide.
She told "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King on Wednesday that she had been trying to tune out the results when she learned that she won.

"I had put in my AirPods to work on my speech, and my husband was on the sofa near me, laying near me, and he kicked me," said Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor. "I went like, 'What?' He said, 'They called it.' And I said, 'Called what?' And so that's how I knew."

Donalds, who served as U.S. representative for Florida's 19th District after his election to that spot in 2020, is now also slated to become Florida's first Black governor. He is also the first Black Republican elected governor in the nation.

In Wisconsin, Crowley, a moderate Democrat, defeated Republican challenger Tom Tiffany in the culmination of a governor's race that played out in one of the country's most purple states. Tiffany, a U.S. representative, is also one of President Trump's top allies.

Ford, who was elected as Nevada's attorney general in 2018, won his state's gubernatorial race against Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, CBS News projected on Thursday. He will become Nevada's first Black governor and the first Black governor ever elected west of the Mississippi.

title: Dow posts biggest gain of the year after Democrats sweep Congress
summary: The Dow soared nearly 1,600 points, as Wall Street analysts predicted that political gridlock would limit Congress's ability to pass major tax and spending packages.
story: The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.
Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.

"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."

The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.
At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.
Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.

Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.
Gridlock good for stocks?

Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.

Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.

Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.

"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.
"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."

Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks.

"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.

"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

title: McDonald's plans to cook up new affordable menu bundles
summary: McDonald's CEO Christopher Kempczinski said the company is testing new value pairings at select U.S. locations.
story: McDonald's is testing new affordable menu bundles as it works to attract inflation-weary customers struggling with the cost of living.

McDonald's CEO Christopher Kempczinski said Wednesday during a call with Wall Street analysts that the fast-food chain recently launched an eight-week pilot program to test value-offerings at 1,900 U.S. locations. The company is testing different "mix and match bundles" and "fixed bundles"  to see which will drive sales, he said.
McDonald's plans to launch the bundles most popular with customers nationwide in 2027, Kempczinski said.

The news came after McDonald's earnings report, released Wednesday, showed comparable sales growth fell 0.2% at U.S. locations from July to September, after growing 2.4% during the same period last year. Overall foot traffic at the chain's U.S. stores was down 4.6% from a year ago, according to data from analytics platform Placer.ai.
Kempczinski acknowledged that the company has not done enough to meet the expectations of low-income diners, who are looking for "great entry-level value."
"We talked quite extensively about how [in] Q2 we didn't land that like we needed to," he told investors. "And so that's what we're in the midst of getting resolved right now and through testing."

His comments come the day after the U.S. midterms, where affordability concerns took center stage. Many candidates campaigned on addressing cost-of-living issues and bringing down gasoline prices, which have risen 38% since the start of the war in Iran, according to AAA data.

U.S. consumer spending has remained resilient even in the face of stubborn inflation, which remains stuck above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. However, economists note that lower-income consumers are feeling particularly strapped, as a larger share of their income goes toward expenses like gas.

Low-income consumers "are disproportionately feeling the effect of higher food and gasoline prices," Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, said on Wednesday during an event in New York City.

title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Thursday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. By midday Thursday, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,700 votes.
Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."
The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.
