title: Americans wary of AI for medical care and insurance claims
summary: Most Americans have qualms about using AI in healthcare for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment, Pew Research poll finds.
story: How much artificial intelligence is too much when you visit your doctor? Although patients are generally open to healthcare professionals using AI to handle administrative and some medical tasks, they want humans wielding the stethoscope, a recent survey suggests.

A solid majority of Americans are comfortable with AI translating patient notes or scheduling appointments, either on its own or with some human oversight, according to the Pew Research Center, which polled more than 3,400 U.S. adults in June. More than half the respondents were also open to using AI to analyze medical scans and lab test results, provided a healthcare professional supervised the process.

But people draw the line when it comes to AI driving diagnoses or making insurance decisions, Pew found. Almost half of those surveyed said they don't want an AI model deciding whether to accept or reject an insurance claim, while 41% said they don't want AI making a diagnosis on its own.

Galen Stocking, associate director of science and society research at Pew Research Center, said people see value in applying AI to healthcare. Still, patients want to know when and how healthcare providers and administrative staff are using the technology.
"Overall, people say it's extremely important that their healthcare provider tell them if they are using AI," he told CBS News.

"There is a lack of clarity on the side of the public," he added, noting Pew's finding that 46% of the survey respondents said they don't know if AI has ever been used in the course of them receiving care.
Indeed, 60% of respondents said they are uncomfortable with doctors using AI for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment; only 30% are OK with that, while 10% are unsure.
"People are concerned about patient-doctor relationships and the security of their own health information," Stocking said.

More broadly, Americans are split over whether AI will improve the quality of medical care. Some 37% of respondents said AI will improve health outcomes, while a nearly equal share think the technology could reduce the quality of care.

title: Escaped killer hid in shed, stole truck, left apology note before capture
summary: Authorities are still trying to piece together how a convicted murderer in Tennessee evaded capture for more than a week.
story: The convicted killer who broke out of a Tennessee prison went on to steal a truck, seek cover in a shed, drink beer and write an apology note before he was eventually apprehended near Kansas City, Missouri, officials revealed Wednesday.
Jacob Morley, 28, remained at large for more than a week before his capture, but authorities were still trying to figure out how he managed to evade law enforcement for as long as he did.

Morley was serving a life sentence for murder at the Northwest Correctional Complex in northwestern Tennessee when he slipped through a fence on the property and fled on the night of Oct. 25, the Tennessee Department of Correction said.
Morley was found after troopers used roadside cameras and a helicopter to track him down and his truck got stuck in the mud. Two rifles and a shotgun were recovered from the truck, authorities said.
They believe Morley found his way to a farm near Marion, Illinois — about 127 miles away — in the days after his escape, spending some time in a shed that was used periodically by hunters.

Investigators found evidence that he drank beer and prepared garlic bread and other food — and that he left behind an apologetic handwritten note after stealing a truck from the farm, according to Williamson County Sheriff Jeff Diederich. Morley is also suspected of stealing clothes and the three firearms from the property.

Diederich believes Morley walked about 3 miles to the farm after abandoning a different truck he had driven after his escape. Security cameras captured Morley walking away from the truck and at a couple of locations along Route 13, but the terrain — which includes fields and woods — would have made it tough for him to be spotted, Diederich said.
It's unclear why Morley traveled to Marion and why he was driving near Kansas City, more than 350 miles away.
"How he ended up in Marion is kind of a mystery," Diederich said.
Diederich said there's no evidence Morley had help from anyone.
After Morley's prison escape, surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned in Marion.

Kim Wheeler-Elder, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, wrote in a text message that all "available information" regarding Morley's whereabouts when he was on the run has been released.

The Missouri State Highway Patrol says it was informed Tuesday morning that Morley was possibly traveling west on Interstate 70 in the Kansas City area. Authorities said he was compliant when he was arrested.

Morley was transported to the Lafayette County jail in Lexington, Missouri, according to Justin Ewing, a spokesperson for the Missouri State Highway Patrol. The Lafayette County Sheriff's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. No charges have been filed against him in Missouri courts, according to online court records.

Before Morley was apprehended, he was charged in federal court in Tennessee with one count of unlawful flight to avoid prosecution, court documents show. Morley was also charged Tuesday in federal court in Missouri with one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm.

A deputy U.S. marshal interviewed Morley at the Lafayette County jail on Tuesday and Morley admitted to escaping the Tennessee prison, stealing the truck in Marion as well as the two rifles and shotgun, according to a probable cause affidavit.
District Attorney General Danny Goodman Jr. in Tennessee said in a phone interview that he plans to file additional charges but it's unclear when Morley will be returned to Tennessee.
Morley was convicted of killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home after he had been missing for a few weeks.

When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest.

title: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid
summary: Wendy's rebuffs unsolicited offer from Trian Partners, led by activist investor Nelson Peltz, and another group of investment firms.
story: Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.

"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.

The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.

In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.

The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.

"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."

Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

title: U.S. ID's remains of WWII soldier from iconic "Merrill's Marauders"
summary: The U.S. military said it has identified the remains of a soldier who fought with the iconic "Merrill's Marauders" unit during World War II.
story: The United States military announced Wednesday that it has identified the remains of a soldier who belonged to the iconic "Merrill's Marauders" unit during World War II, more than 80 years after his disappearance.

Joseph Gala, of Lynn, Massachusetts, was declared killed in action on July 14, 1944, two months after he went missing during a mission in what was then Burma, now Myanmar, according to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency.

Gala was 21 when he died. Although the circumstances of his death were never recorded, he was last seen advancing with his battalion toward a heavily-fortified Japanese area near the village of Mankrin, the military said.

Gala had fought alongside a volunteer infantry unit that came to be known as "Merrill's Marauders," named after its commander. The battalion was solicited by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to fulfill a "secret and dangerous mission" in the China-Burma-India Theater — the war's so-called "forgotten theater," as the Army described it in a 2016 article. About 3,000 young men volunteered for the mission, and just 200 returned home.
"Those that volunteered had no idea what the mission was going to be," Robert Passanisi, one of troops who did survive, told CBS New York in 2013.

Recalling his unit's 1,000-mile march through the Burmese jungle to disrupt Japanese supply lines, Passanisi added: "It's pretty well-known that nobody else ever did anything as strenuous, as enduring and as difficult in such miserable terrain."

The mission where Gala was last seen alive marked his unit's "final objective" overseas, the Army said in a 2016 article spotlighting surviving "Merrill's Marauders" troops. On May 17, 1944, the unit captured Burma's Myitkyina airstrip after defeating the elite, and much larger, Japanese army in five major battles and 30 minor ones.
"We were expendable," Sam Wilson, a former Marauder, told the Army in 2016. "A plan existed on paper to get us into Burma, but no plan existed to get us out."

Each soldier who was part of "Merrill's Marauders" was later awarded the bronze star by the U.S. military, and the Pentagon ordered that none would ever be placed in combat again. A dramatized version of their plight through the Burmese jungle came to life on the big screen in a 1962 war film named after the unit.

Gala's remains were buried at various U.S. military cemeteries in Burma and India. They were later transferred, alongside other unidentified remains of soldiers, to the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii.

DPAA said officials began to exhume unidenfied remains from the Punchbowl in efforts to identify more soldiers killed at Myitkyina in 2018. Scientists were eventually able to identify those belonging to Gala through dental and forensic tests, as well as "anthropological and circumstantial evidence," DPAA said.
Gala will be buried Thursday in his hometown, according to DPAA.

title: The biggest races Democrats won in the midterms
summary: Democrats won pivotal races in Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Michigan and elsewhere. Here are the biggest victories of the 2026 midterms.
story: Washington — Voters across the country delivered a stinging rebuke to Republicans in Congress and President Trump's agenda in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, with Democrats capturing House and Senate seats that had seemed out of reach just a few months ago.

CBS News projects Democrats will take control of both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January, with wide margins in each. Democrats are projected to control at least 54 Senate seats, with two races still unresolved. In the House, CBS News estimates the party could control between 251 and 268 when all the votes are counted.

Out of 11 Senate races that CBS News considered battlegrounds, Democrats were projected to win 10. The 11th race, in Alaska, is still rated a toss-up, with a lengthy ballot-counting process expected. The Mississippi Senate race is also unresolved and is unexpectedly close, with Democrat Scott Colom leading incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by only around 1,000 votes. CBS News has rated that race as a toss-up.
The victories weren't just limited to House and Senate races, either. Democrats captured the governor's mansion in Texas, a feat they haven't accomplished since 1990.
Here are the major races that propelled Democrats to victory on Tuesday, according to CBS News' projections:
Texas Senate: James Talarico
In the most expensive Senate race in Texas history, and one of the closest-watched matchups of the election cycle, Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who was elected to serve in the Texas House of Representatives in 2018.

Talarico's campaign focused on corruption and lowering costs. He told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that his victory sent a message to Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the race, that "Texas is not for sale."
"The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way," he said.
Paxton was backed by Mr. Trump, who endorsed the Republican attorney general over Sen. John Cornyn in the GOP Senate primary earlier this year.

Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary runoff in May, setting the race against Talarico. Paxton had weathered numerous controversies and was impeached by the state House in 2023 on allegations of bribery, obstruction of justice and abuse of trust. He was acquitted by the state Senate.
Texas governor: Gina Hinojosa

Hinojosa, a state lawmaker, bested Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democrat to win the governor's mansion in more than 30 years. Hinojosa will be the third woman to lead the state.

Abbott had been in office for more than a decade and was seeking a fourth term as governor, and the race against Hinojosa narrowed in the months leading up to the election. Hinojosa focused her campaign on affordability and public education. The fight over data centers also emerged as a major issue in the governor's race.
South Carolina Senate: Annie Andrews
Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Andrews, 45, made healthcare access and affordability the focuses of her campaign.

Graham was appointed to finish out the remainder of her late brother's Senate term following his unexpected death in July. President Trump swiftly threw his support behind Graham and campaigned for her in South Carolina in the lead-up to the midterms.
It has been nearly 30 years since a Democrat won the Senate in South Carolina, a state Mr. Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
Kansas Senate: Adam Hamilton

Hamilton, a fifth-generation Kansan, is the leader of the largest United Methodist church in the country and is a well-known author and speaker. The 62-year-old defeated Roger Marshall, a Republican, who was seeking his second term in the Senate.
Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 16 points in the last presidential election.

In the closing weeks of the Senate campaign, Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, came under scrutiny after the New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of his patients over outstanding medical bills, and 81 were arrested.
Georgia governor: Keisha Lance Bottoms

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will make history as the nation's first Black woman governor. The former Atlanta mayor and senior adviser in the Biden administration defeated Republican Rick Jackson and Libertarian Chase Oliver, CBS News projects.
With 99% of the vote counted, Bottoms had 54.3% of the vote, compared to 45.7% for Jackson.
Bottoms told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that she was surprised that the race was called as early as it was on election night.

"I thought that it was going to be a very long night. I knew that we had done the work, but Georgia has always, for the past few years, been a purple state, so I thought it would be much closer," she said.
Michigan Senate: Abdul El-Sayed
Michigan was viewed as Republicans' best chance to flip a Senate seat, but El-Sayed's victory over GOP opponent Mike Rogers keeps it in Democrats' hands.

The Senate race emerged as one of the most contentious of the midterm election cycle. Top Republicans, led by Mr. Trump, repeatedly leveled anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed, calling him a "jihadist" and claiming that he is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
El-Sayed told Fox News in an interview last month that he has "never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."
El-Sayed also came under scrutiny for his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and views on Israel raising questions as to whether he could win support from Jewish and Black voters.

There was a late twist in the Senate race in Michigan when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who sought the Democratic Senate nomination, endorsed Rogers and appeared alongside him at a Detroit church Sunday.
Maine Senate: Troy Jackson
Jackson was facing off against GOP Sen. Susan Collins, the only Republican running for reelection in a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.

Collins was first elected to represent Maine in the Senate in 1996 and had touted her ability to bring home benefits for the state as part of her pitch to voters. While she had survived difficult campaigns in the past, Collins was not able to fend off the challenge from Jackson.

Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who jumped into the Senate race late after Graham Platner, who initially won the Democratic Senate nomination, withdrew from the race after allegations of sexual misconduct. The former president of the Maine Senate unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for governor earlier this year.
Dozens of House seats across the country
Democrats are on track to flip dozens of House seats.
In Iowa, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats had a sweep of the most competitive seats.

Democrats defeated GOP incumbent Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, Zach Nunn of Iowa, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Brian Steil of Wisconsin and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin. They also flipped an open Iowa seat that is currently held by the GOP.

Redistricting helped Democrats win California's 1st District and Utah's 1st District. Redistricting was expected to hamper Democrats' chances in Texas' 15th District and 23rd District, but Democrats pulled off upsets.

In Ohio, embattled GOP Reps. Max Miller and Mike Carey both lost reelection, as did Tom Kean in New Jersey, Ann Wagner in Missouri, Gabe Evans in Colorado, Victoria Spartz in Indiana and Jen Kiggans in Virginia.
Democrats also flipped open seats in Kentucky's 6th District, Nebraska's 2nd District and North Carolina's 11th District.

title: Trump library plans on collision course with Democratic Congress
summary: President Trump is expected to spend time on plans for his presidential library, but Democrats in Congress have some questions about how it's being financed.
story: As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."
With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.
"The donors bankrolling his personal vanity project will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told CBS News.

In March, Mr. Trump shared renderings of a 47-story tower on a donated plot in downtown Miami. It showed golden escalators, a full-size Air Force One and a giant statue of him raising his fist, as he did after surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. But then he told reporters he does not "believe in building libraries or museums" and that the building is "most likely going to be a hotel," a departure from the traditional library his foundation described to the IRS last year.

The Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit, registered in Florida and run by Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, will fund the project. The foundation says it expects to raise $950 million by the end of 2027, including $600 million in 2027 alone, according to its October 2025 IRS application, obtained by CBS News. That far outpaces what Mr. Trump's predecessors had raised at this stage.

Tens of millions of dollars have already come from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. The nonprofit is also collecting donations through a payment processing company that has Donald Trump Jr. on its board, according to a fundraising portal page. And Mr. Trump has said the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave the U.S. last year — now in use as Air Force One — would go to the library, though Eric Trump and the White House have since said that plan is not final.

Some of the most recent money has come from people trying to stay in Mr. Trump's good graces. After the president threatened to cut ties with his top political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their consulting work for a pro-Russian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two men donated their fees from that work to the library, The New York Post reported.

A week later, The New York Times reported that Mr. Trump had told aides and allies that his former personal lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, should donate part of a contract worth more than $50 million to his library or another Trump-related entity. Habba Mildon's contract was with a company tied to the family of a Venezuelan businessman Mr. Trump pardoned in January, the outlet reported.

Asked by CBS News whether she planned to donate some of her fees to the library, Habba Mildon responded to the text message with a "haha" reaction. (She removed the reaction seconds later and declined to comment.)

A former Trump adviser, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the library is now where the fundraising action is, with the midterms over and donors already tapped for the America 250 celebrations and the White House ballroom. MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by Mr. Trump's allies, started September with more than $400 million to spend on Republicans in the midterms. Its filing due in December will show how much left it has in cash on hand.
"The library is one of the last few places he can squeeze people for money," the former adviser said. "That's what a businessman does. He just creates opportunities."

Fresh scrutiny of the library is expected after Democrats swept the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Starting in January, Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word warning on X to the administration after the election results: "Lawyer up."

"Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," Warren told CBS News, adding that she will be investigating the library "and any wrongdoing will be held accountable."

The library has already drawn scrutiny over Mr. Trump's stated plan to display the gifted jet. The plane's memorandum of understanding, signed in 2025 by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Qatar's Minister of State for Defense Affairs Soud bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, called it an "unconditional donation." But when questions were raised about the U.S. accepting and using the Qatari plane as Air Force One, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi concluded that the gift could be conditioned on transferring the plane to the library foundation by Jan. 1, 2029, about three weeks before Mr. Trump leaves office.
In August, Eric Trump told NBC News that displaying the plane was "not the plan at the moment," saying a retired Air Force One would be shown instead.

A Qatari official, speaking to CBS News on the condition of anonymity, said what happens to the plane after Mr. Trump leaves office is not Qatar's concern. "This is something the Americans need to deal with," the official said.
The White House referred questions about the library and whether any final decisions have been made about the plane or a hotel to the foundation, which did not respond to requests for comment.

"The Trump Presidential Library will be one of the most magnificent buildings in the world and a living testament to the indelible impact President Trump has made on America and its people," Davis Ingle, a spokesman for the White House, said in a statement.
Tens of millions from companies Mr. Trump sued

There have been two iterations of the library's nonprofit funding structure. The first, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund, was incorporated in Florida in December 2024, days after ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward the library to settle a defamation suit over anchor George Stephanopoulos' inaccurate on-air claim that Mr. Trump had been found civilly liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found him liable for sexual abuse.

Other settlements followed. Meta agreed to pay $22 million toward the library over the suspension of Mr. Trump's accounts after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Elon Musk's X paid $10 million to settle a similar suit by Mr. Trump and other plaintiffs. And Paramount paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.

By then, the current foundation had been incorporated in Florida in May 2025, listing Eric Trump, Boulos and James Kiley, an attorney who has represented Mr. Trump, as trustees. The original fund was dissolved that September after failing to file a required annual report. Jacob Roth, an attorney who incorporated the first fund, declined to comment.

In March, Sens. Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Melanie Stansbury asked the four companies for details of their payments. ABC said its $15 million was still in an escrow account held by a law firm representing Mr. Trump, where it had been since December 2024, awaiting release to the foundation. Paramount said it had paid $16 million but did not say to whom. Meta said $22 million had been "designated" for the library but did not say whether or where it was paid, and X, citing confidentiality, did not say how much of its $10 million settlement went there.

Mr. Trump's financial disclosure, filed in June, lists $56.5 million in settlement money from ABC, Meta and Paramount as paid to the foundation. It lists $8 million from X as paid to Mr. Trump himself, without saying whether some funds reached the foundation. The foundation's October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, which it labeled a proposed budget, projected $50 million in revenue and about $6 million in spending.

Meta and ABC declined to comment. X did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Skydance referred CBS News to the company's July 2025 statement announcing the settlement, which said the $16 million included the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs and that the remainder would go to Mr. Trump's future presidential library, with nothing paid to him personally.

The settlements are not the only large gifts. SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant, told Congress in July that it gave the foundation $50 million in January to support a library exhibit highlighting U.S.-Japan relations. Two months later, Mr. Trump's Energy Department announced it would lease federal land at a former uranium enrichment plant in Ohio to an affiliate of SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for a data center campus that the company says will be the world's largest for artificial intelligence.

A spokesperson for the Energy Department said the agency signed its lease agreement with the company on Feb. 26, about a month after SoftBank's donation to the library foundation. They added that a local development group first proposed the project in October 2024, before SoftBank acquired the lease rights in the fall of 2025. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment.
A library or a hotel?

The library foundation's filings offer few other details about how it operates. When it registered as a charity in Florida, the foundation said its officers did not expect to be paid. But in its application to the IRS, the foundation said it would pay its leaders. It projected spending $400,000 on compensation in 2025, rising to $1.2 million in 2027. The foundation's bylaws say trustees can't be paid, but other roles can come with compensation. Eric Trump is both a trustee and the foundation's president.
The foundation told CBS News it expects to file financial disclosures covering fiscal 2025 by Nov. 15. It did not respond to a question about whether Eric Trump will be paid.
Fundraising for the library is led by Meredith O'Rourke, who has worked with Mr. Trump since 2016.

The foundation also raises money through PSQ Impact, a donation platform run by PublicSquare, a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr. The foundation's donation page says contributions will "help preserve important archives, promote civic education, and inspire generations to come." Trump Jr. began receiving $42,000 a month in consulting fees from PublicSquare in August 2024, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he was not aware of the fundraising page and had no involvement in it. PublicSquare did not respond to questions about how much has been raised through the donation page or what fee, if any, it is charging for processing.

"This is just one example of many where the Trumps are set to possibly profit off something connected to Donald Trump's presidency," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen.

It remains unclear what form the library will ultimately take. Mr. Trump's suggestion that it could become a hotel is cited in a lawsuit filed in May by Miami residents, a local nonprofit and a Miami Dade College student. They argue that Florida's gift of the 2.63-acre parcel, a former college parking lot, violates a U.S. constitutional provision that bars states from giving the president financial benefits.

The land was appraised at more than $67 million, but the suit cites real estate experts who say its true market value is over $300 million. The plaintiffs note that the state's terms require only that the site include "components of a Presidential library, museum, and/or center" within five years, and do not preclude a hotel.

Other presidential libraries have been built on donated public land. Chicago leased parkland for Mr. Obama's center for $10, and Little Rock used eminent domain to assemble the site for Mr. Clinton's. But Florida conveyed its parcel outright.

The Justice Department has argued that Mr. Trump is immune from the suit. In September, U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II, a Trump appointee, halted discovery, writing that the defendants' arguments for dismissal, including presidential immunity, "may prove to be successful." He has not yet ruled on motions to dismiss the case, and a ruling may not come until March, according to Gerald E. Greenberg, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.
If the suit is dismissed, Greenberg said the plaintiffs are likely to appeal.

"This case is really about one of the core anti-corruption provisions," Greenberg told CBS News, saying the founders "understood the dangers of people currying favor with the sovereign by giving him gifts."
"It is extremely disturbing to think of our skyline and our downtown being blighted by this monument to corruption," he added.

title: Indiana carries out first of 3 U.S. executions set for Thursday
summary: An Indiana man was executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for Thursday in the U.S., which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. were put to death on the same day.
story: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13.
It would be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, but was the first this year in Indiana.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said.

Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit's case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," he said. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty."
The execution on tap in Florida

In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a "full and fair" hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.

Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama's scheduled execution

Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.

"If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today," said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

title: Midterm fallout begins after Democrats win control of Congress
summary: The impact of Democrats' sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections is already being felt in Washington. Follow live updates here.
story: Follow the latest developments in the wake of the midterm elections here. See earlier coverage and results below.
Updates on the 2026 midterm election results:

Democrats won sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday and will take control of the House and Senate next year, CBS News projects, as voters repudiated President Trump and GOP control. CBS News estimates Democrats will hold 251 to 268 House seats.Democrats have secured at least 54 Senate seats. Texas, Kansas and South Carolina elected their first Democratic senators in decades, and the party also flipped seats in Ohio, Iowa, North Carolina and Maine. Mississippi and Alaska remain toss-ups.The fallout has already begun. House Speaker Mike Johnson told staffers he would not seek another term as GOP leader, teeing up a fight over the conference's future. President Trump has been asking advisers whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay, multiple sources tell CBS News, although he later said he is not considering removing him. Previewing a possible intraparty debate ahead of 2028, Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war is "the reason we lost."Democrats have begun laying out their agenda for investigating the Trump administration. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said the party would "entangle [Mr. Trump] in legislative razor wire."Find updates on key House races here and Senate battleground races here.

Democrats won sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday and will take control of the House and Senate next year, CBS News projects, as voters repudiated President Trump and GOP control. CBS News estimates Democrats will hold 251 to 268 House seats.

Democrats have secured at least 54 Senate seats. Texas, Kansas and South Carolina elected their first Democratic senators in decades, and the party also flipped seats in Ohio, Iowa, North Carolina and Maine. Mississippi and Alaska remain toss-ups.

The fallout has already begun. House Speaker Mike Johnson told staffers he would not seek another term as GOP leader, teeing up a fight over the conference's future. President Trump has been asking advisers whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay, multiple sources tell CBS News, although he later said he is not considering removing him. Previewing a possible intraparty debate ahead of 2028, Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war is "the reason we lost."
Democrats have begun laying out their agenda for investigating the Trump administration. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said the party would "entangle [Mr. Trump] in legislative razor wire."

title: 2 Native American women make history in midterms
summary: In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
story: Two Native American women made history Tuesday night in the 2026 midterm elections, winning a Senate seat and a governorship — both firsts for Native women — as Democrats swept races across the country.

In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo, was already the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. She defeated Republican Gregg Hull, former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the race for governor.
Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and conservative commentator.
Who are they?

Haaland has notched many firsts. She became the first Native American woman to chair a state political party in 2015 when she was elected to lead the Democratic Party of New Mexico. In 2018, she became one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, alongside Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas, who was reelected Tuesday. Haaland later served as former President Joe Biden's Interior secretary from 2021 until January 2025.
On the trail, she spoke about raising her daughter alone, selling homemade salsa and relying at times on food stamps.
"My story is a lot like many New Mexicans — humble beginnings," she told a Rio Rancho congregation in October.

Flanagan got her start as an organizer, then served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children's Defense Fund Minnesota. She was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2015 and has been lieutenant governor since 2019, where she has helped reshape Minnesota's relationship with the state's 11 tribal nations.
Raised by a single mother in Section 8 housing, Flanagan had childhood asthma that kept her in and out of hospitals. She's been an outspoken supporter of Medicaid, saying that it "saved [her] life."
What do they stand for?

Haaland ran on the cost of living, protecting New Mexico's Universal Child Care program and overhauling its child welfare system. She also blamed President Trump for cuts to federal safety net programs. She has promised to issue an executive order on day one to pause the construction of new large-scale data centers until the state Legislature passes guardrails.
Flanagan drew on her own upbringing to connect with voters who are feeling financially squeezed. She ran as a progressive, backing "Medicare for All" and national paid family and medical leave.
"Minnesota, you just beat Donald Trump again," Flanagan told supporters on Tuesday night at her election watch party in St. Paul, where White Earth leaders played a victory song on a drum.
Why does it matter?

The National Congress of American Indians, the country's oldest and largest association of tribal governments, called the wins historic milestones for Indian Country. Native American women make up approximately 1% of the U.S. population, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, but have long been underrepresented in elected office.

"Long before Native women were welcomed into the halls of government, they were leading our Nations, protecting our families, and shaping the future of Indian Country," NCAI Executive Director Larry Wright Jr. said in a statement to CBS News.

"For young Native girls across Indian Country, these victories send an important message: their voices matter, their leadership is essential, and they belong wherever possibilities are reimagined," said Wright.

He added that he hopes that representation translates into "meaningful progress," in particular, protecting tribal lands and honoring treaty obligations between the U.S. government and tribal nations.

A third Native American woman could soon join Haaland and Flanagan in making history this midterm election. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, is in a Senate race with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan that remains a toss-up, according to CBS News estimates. The outcome may not be decided until ranked-choice tabulation later this month.

title: Tennessee murderer captured over a week after escaping prison
summary: Jacob Morley was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee when he escaped by slipping through a fence on the property.
story: Authorities have captured a convicted murderer who evaded law enforcement for more than a week after escaping from a Tennessee prison. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation announced Tuesday that Jacob Morley was back in custody. He was arrested near Kansas City, Missouri, investigators said.

"Thank you to the public for your assistance, vigilance, and the tips provided during this investigation," the bureau said in a statement. "We also thank all of our law enforcement partners for their continued efforts to safely bring this search to a successful conclusion."

Investigators got a tip Tuesday morning that Morley had been hiding in a shed at a hunting camp around Marion, Illinois, some 320 miles south of Chicago, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said in a statement. Authorities also learned a truck had been stolen from the property.

Missouri State Highway Patrol said it handled Morley's arrest alongside multiple partner agencies, after Tennessee authorities reported that Morley may be traveling through Missouri, based on footage obtained through Flock cameras. The arrest happened around 11:30 a.m. local time near Norborne, a small city about an hour's drive from Kansas City, the state agency said.
Authorities said they also recovered three firearms that had previously been reported stolen inside the truck.

Little information about the inmate's escape and the multi-state search for him has been made available since Morley broke out of prison. But investigators said more will be released as it becomes available.

Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in an isolated part of Tiptonville, a town roughly 90 miles from Memphis in northwestern Tennessee. He had been convicted of killing a coworker four years ago, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.

Correctional officers discovered Morley was missing from the prison at around 11:30 p.m. local time on Oct. 25, the department said. While parsing security cameras later on, investigators said they saw footage of Morley escaping the complex while wearing his prison uniform by slipping through a fence on the property.

Authorities released additional security footage that showed the inmate stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350, with Tennessee plates and a logo for Lindamood Planting Company on the side door, in the early hours of Oct. 26. It was stolen from Lake County, which includes Tiptonville, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said.
The truck was located the next day in Marion, Illinois, which is about 150 miles north of Tiptonville, the investigative bureau said. Morley's whereabouts were unknown at the time.

The bureau had said earlier in the week that Morley was on its "most wanted" list, as various agencies, including the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, the governor's office and U.S. Marshals, offered combined rewards of up to $17,500 for information leading to his arrest.
Investigators haven't shared details about how exactly the inmate escaped, beyond the fact that he breached a fence at the prison.

Morley received a lifetime prison sentence for murdering Cody Birchfield, his former coworker, in 2022. Authorities said Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home in Tennessee's Carter County after he had been missing for several weeks.

In addition to first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest, as he fled when deputies arrived at his home in 2022. Authorities said the manhunt for him at the time ended in North Carolina.

Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold 1,776 inmates under varying degrees of security, from the lowest level up to maximum, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction. It also houses minors who have been convicted of crimes as adults.

Multiple violent incidents have taken place inside the prison in recent years, some of which involved attacks between inmates and prison staff. In July, a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over the murders of five inmates, assaults against staff and other acts of violence. At a recent meeting of the Tennessee Inmate Disciplinary Oversight Board, members discussed ongoing problems in the prison and suggested issues with leadership played a role.

title: JetBlue hikes baggage fees for the second time this year
summary: Airlines have raised baggage fees and ticket prices to help offset the surging cost of jet fuel this year.
story: JetBlue on Tuesday said it is raising its checked bag fees for the second time in less than a year as the carrier moves to offset rising jet fuel and operating costs.

As of Tuesday, checking one piece of luggage for domestic, Caribbean and Latin American flights for most economy passengers will cost $50, up from $39 for off-peak periods, according to JetBlue. For peak travel periods, the fee will rise to $55, up from $49.
In March, the airline hiked its checked-bag fees by up to $9, citing "rising operating costs."
The airline told CBS News the baggage fee increase "helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
JetBlue also said it encourages customers to add their checked bags to their trips at least 24 hours before departure, enabling them to save up to $15 on the first checked bag.

JetBlue Plus, JetBlue Business and JetBlue Premier cardmembers can check one bag for free for the cardholder and up to three travel companions, according to the airline. TrueBlue Mosaic members may also check at least one bag for free. Mosaic 2, 3 and 4 members each get two free checked bags.

Surging global oil prices this year have sharply pushed up the cost of jet fuel, airlines' second-largest operational cost after labor. The price of jet fuel was $4.41 per gallon on Monday, up from just over $2 per gallon in January, according to Airlines for America's jet fuel price tracker.
Other carriers have also raised their baggage fees this year, including Delta, United and Southwest.

title: Mexican judge accused by U.S. of taking bribes in major drug case
summary: Luiz Benítez Alcántara is accused of releasing Andrew Clark from custody after accepting $2 million in bribe payments.
story: A Mexican judge has been arrested and accused of accepting $2 million in bribes in exchange for releasing a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody, U.S. officials said Thursday.

Luiz Benítez Alcántara was overseeing extradition proceedings in Mexico in 2024 for Canadian citizen Andrew Clark, who was charged in the U.S. with helping to run a billion-dollar drug trafficking group allegedly headed by former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, the Justice Department said in a statement. Benítez is accused of releasing Clark from custody after accepting the bribe payments, according to the statement.
Clark was arrested days after his release and removed to the United States, where he faces drug trafficking and murder charges.
The statement said Benítez, 49, was arrested Sunday in Colombia. He is charged in a nine-count indictment with being an accessory after the fact. It was not immediately known if he has a lawyer.
U.S. officials will request Benítez's extradition from Colombia, the statement said.

"Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement.

It's the latest arrest in the U.S. investigation into a multinational drug trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who became a top FBI fugitive accused of moving cocaine from Latin America into the United States and orchestrating several killings. Wedding was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges.

Dozens of people have been arrested in connection with the alleged drug network and authorities seized large volumes of drugs, weapons and cash, as well as millions of dollars worth of automobiles, motorcycles, artwork and jewelry in its investigation.
Clark's attorney, Matthew Lombard, did not immediately respond to messages Thursday.

After Wedding's arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel called the former Olympian "a modern-day 'El Chapo,'" — a reference to Joaquin Guzman, a one-time leader of the notorious Mexican drug ring known as the Sinaloa Cartel who is serving a life sentence in the U.S. According to the FBI, Wedding also used aliases, including "El Jefe," "Giant" and "Public Enemy."

Wedding, who competed in the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, has been accused of running a major drug trafficking network that moved cocaine from Colombia through Mexico to the U.S. and Canada. Patel said in a social media post Friday that Wedding was running his alleged operation as a member of the Sinaloa Cartel, and that Wedding was believed to have been hiding out in Mexico for over a decade.
Wedding was added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list last year, prior to his arrest.

title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
story: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."

British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
So far, it remains unclear who, if anyone, is behind any such coordinated action, and no authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats.

David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."

"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."

Kaminski-Morrow noted that, under an international aviation convention in place for more than 80 years, the pilot in command of a flight has the final authority over its safety, "and airlines always take threats to safety seriously. The business consequences alone of not doing so, even if the threat is proven to be a hoax, would be prohibitive – and you can imagine the cost if it turned out to be genuine."
The flights impacted on Thursday included:

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported. A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.  Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning. An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service." A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.

A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."

Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.

Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.

Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.

Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning.

An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service."

A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

The threats to commercial airliners Thursday came after at least seven other flights across Europe received bomb threats this week that prompted aircraft searches, diversions and in at least one other case an escort by an Italian fighter jet.
Some of the threats have been sent to airlines by email, but the nature of all of the messages has not been confirmed.
Hoaxes, but on an unusual scale

The British government described the incidents in a statement on Tuesday as hoaxes and stressed that the U.K. had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today," according to CBS News' partner network BBC.
Air transport security expert Paul Mason told BBC that threats to passenger planes "don't happen that frequently," making this week's spate of incidents "unusual."

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told the BBC's Radio 5 Live show. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
"There are a lot of processes" that airline crew members and ground staff go through "to validate the credibility of the threat," he said.

While no individual or group has claimed responsibility for any of this week's threats, and no government or security official has pointed the finger at any, the incidents come amid rising concern in Europe about state actors, chiefly Russia and Iran, orchestrating low-level sabotage operations to undermine security on the continent.
The growing "hybrid warfare" battlefield

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by the government, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."
"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said.

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad as the Polish prime minister said suspicious activity was seen on the Russian side, and that the fast security response may have prevented a "serious provocation."

The flight threats also come amid a wave of cyberattacks targeting European grocery store chains' refrigerators and freezers, and even French blood banks. The hacks have forced thousands of pounds of food to be discarded in several countries, but French authorities said security systems prevented the loss of any blood stored in cooling units.
Nobody has claimed responsibility for, or been blamed for the hacks on commercial refrigeration units as of Thursday.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
MI6 boss McCallum, in his remarks last month, said Iran in particular was "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.

McCallum noted in particular "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

Barry Andrews, an Irish Member of the European Parliament, referred to the diverted Aer Lingus flight to Rome on Thursday in a social media post, saying: "This after several hybrid threats and attacks across Europe, and ahead of the major European summit in #Dublin next week. Does anyone still deny Ireland faces serious security threats?"

title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
summary: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
story: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three other women on Thursday at his trial in London. Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand will be sentenced to prison.

Brand, 51, was initially accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. On Thursday, he was acquitted of two rape counts and the attempted indecent assault charge.

"You've been convicted of a number of offences including rape," Bennathan told Brand after reading Thursday's verdict, according to CBS News partner BBC. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."
Brand, who was denied bail and taken into custody, will be sentenced on Monday.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said, according to the Associated Press. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
The allegations, made by six women, spanned a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days. They found Brand guilty of grabbing a woman's breasts during a party at a bar in London's Soho neighborhood in the summer of 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at London radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005, and raping a woman at his home in Hampstead in 2009.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.
During the trial, a prosecutor accused Brand of being a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator."

Brand, who pleaded not guilty to the charges, testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man. He said he once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will, saying he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
He said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
During the trial, Brand suggested the reports were part of a coordinated attack because of his newfound prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator.

The women featured in the documentary said they only felt ready to share their stories after being approached by reporters, with some mentioning Brand's online fame as a factor in their decision to speak.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."
Brand's father, Ron Brand, told the BBC after the verdict and that he was "bemused and shocked."
"I just didn't expect this - it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating."

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

title: U.S. ID's remains of WWII soldier from iconic "Merrill's Marauders"
summary: The U.S. military said it has identified the remains of a soldier who fought with the iconic "Merrill's Marauders" unit during World War II.
story: The United States military announced Wednesday that it has identified the remains of a soldier who belonged to the iconic "Merrill's Marauders" unit during World War II, more than 80 years after his disappearance.

Joseph Gala, of Lynn, Massachusetts, was declared killed in action on July 14, 1944, two months after he went missing during a mission in what was then Burma, now Myanmar, according to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency.

Gala was 21 when he died. Although the circumstances of his death were never recorded, he was last seen advancing with his battalion toward a heavily-fortified Japanese area near the village of Mankrin, the military said.

Gala had fought alongside a volunteer infantry unit that came to be known as "Merrill's Marauders," named after its commander. The battalion was solicited by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to fulfill a "secret and dangerous mission" in the China-Burma-India Theater — the war's so-called "forgotten theater," as the Army described it in a 2016 article. About 3,000 young men volunteered for the mission, and just 200 returned home.
"Those that volunteered had no idea what the mission was going to be," Robert Passanisi, one of troops who did survive, told CBS New York in 2013.

Recalling his unit's 1,000-mile march through the Burmese jungle to disrupt Japanese supply lines, Passanisi added: "It's pretty well-known that nobody else ever did anything as strenuous, as enduring and as difficult in such miserable terrain."

The mission where Gala was last seen alive marked his unit's "final objective" overseas, the Army said in a 2016 article spotlighting surviving "Merrill's Marauders" troops. On May 17, 1944, the unit captured Burma's Myitkyina airstrip after defeating the elite, and much larger, Japanese army in five major battles and 30 minor ones.
"We were expendable," Sam Wilson, a former Marauder, told the Army in 2016. "A plan existed on paper to get us into Burma, but no plan existed to get us out."

Each soldier who was part of "Merrill's Marauders" was later awarded the bronze star by the U.S. military, and the Pentagon ordered that none would ever be placed in combat again. A dramatized version of their plight through the Burmese jungle came to life on the big screen in a 1962 war film named after the unit.

Gala's remains were buried at various U.S. military cemeteries in Burma and India. They were later transferred, alongside other unidentified remains of soldiers, to the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii.

DPAA said officials began to exhume unidenfied remains from the Punchbowl in efforts to identify more soldiers killed at Myitkyina in 2018. Scientists were eventually able to identify those belonging to Gala through dental and forensic tests, as well as "anthropological and circumstantial evidence," DPAA said.
Gala will be buried Thursday in his hometown, according to DPAA.
