title: Newly found prehistoric "giant rat" species named after princess
summary: The ancient creature offers new clues about how early rodents evolved to enormous sizes.
story: A giant rodent weighing around 66 pounds roamed what is now southern Thailand 33 to 35 million years ago, scientists said, after identifying a previously unknown species from two fossilized teeth.
The ancient animal, which one geologist on the team called a "giant rat," was among the largest known from the Paleogene period, offering new clues about how early rodents evolved to enormous sizes.
The findings, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports, were based on a molar and an incisor discovered in 2004 at a coal mine in southern Krabi province.
Pannipa Tian, a geologist with Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, who found the incisor, said she initially misidentified the fossil because of its "unusually large size."
"At first, I thought it was a bone. I showed it to my supervisor, who told me it was a giant rat's tooth," Pannipa, 51, told AFP on Thursday.
The cream-colored fossil stood out against the dark coal deposits, while another expedition member found the dark-colored molar the same day.
The Krabi basin has previously yielded fossils of ancient primates, carnivores and hoofed mammals.
But at the time of the discovery, the team lacked sufficient evidence and technology to identify the species.
More than two decades later, researchers from Thailand, France and Canada were able to do so through detailed analysis of the teeth.
The animal weighed around 30 kilograms — an estimated half as much as a large capybara, the world's largest living rodent, they said.
Unlike the South American capybara, however, the prehistoric rodent belonged to the now-extinct Ischyromyidae family, one of the earliest major groups of rodents.
"It tells a lot about the diversity of life in the past," Pannipa said, suggesting ancient rodents may have evolved in what is now Thailand before spreading to other parts of the world.
But with only two teeth recovered, the animal's appearance, diet and behavior remain unknown.
The species was named Yakamys sirindhornae in honor of Thailand's Princess Sirindhorn, a supporter of scientific and paleontological research.

While the new species may seem massive, other discoveries around the world have revealed even bigger rodents. In 2020, scientists announced the discovery of a prehistoric human-sized rat that lived in the Amazon rainforest 10 million years ago.

In 2008, Uruguayan scientists said they had uncovered fossil evidence of the biggest species of rodent ever found, a 1-ton creature that scurried across wooded areas of South America about 4 million years ago.
In 2003, researchers said they had found fossils for a 1,545-pound "Rat-zilla" that thrived millions of years ago in a swampy South American forest.

title: Ronaldo retires from Portugal national team
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo says he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.
story: Lisbon, Portugal — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.

The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."

While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.

Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country.

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said.
It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.
He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and has 985. Of those, a record 146 came in 234 appearances with Portugal.
Ronaldo became the first player in his sport to reach billionaire status, joining the ranks of the wealthiest athletes, Bloomberg reported in October 2025..

title: French blood banks hit by cyberattack days after European freezer hacks
summary: The cyberattack on several French blood banks comes after supermarkets across Europe reported their fridges​ and freezers​ were remotely taken over by hackers.
story: A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars.
The attacks have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology.

In the most recent cyberattack, the French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said in a statement released late Tuesday  "temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels" on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that "no blood products or samples were compromised," it said.

French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 22 Fahrenheit (minus 30 Celsius) to as high as 230 F (110 C).

The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the blood bank said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it "is aware" of the cybersecurity incident.

"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking "appropriate measures."
France's national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident. The ministry gave no indication of who might be behind the cyberattack.

This week's cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as $281 million (250 million euros), and crimp its operating income for the period by over $112 million (about 100 million euros).

"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said. "As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today," he said in a statement released with Delhaize's quarterly earnings.

The company had earlier blamed "malicious actions by others" and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

title: Ukraine says "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70
summary: Ukraine's president says an "insane attack" by Russia on an aid distribution center may have killed 70 people, as he renews his plea for air defenses.
story: Kyiv — The death toll from a Russian missile strike on a Ukrainian aid distribution center climbed to 40, President Zelenskyy said in a Wednesday post on social media. Zelenskyy said Russia dropped nine bombs on an old school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Ukraine's southeast Zaporizhzhia  region on Monday.

"They first struck people who had come to receive humanitarian aid, and then first responders and police officers who arrived at the scene," Zelenskyy wrote, noting that rescue efforts were still ongoing Wednesday afternoon, and "more than 30 people may still be under the rubble."

Russia's Defense Ministry said a strike in the area targeted Ukraine's military, and it claimed that as many as 25 Ukrainian service members were killed. Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians, despite strikes regularly hitting apartment buildings and other civilian infrastructure.
On Tuesday, Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the year on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting facilities in 10 different regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry.

The attacks affected the Ukrainian capital's water supply, with Kyiv residents losing running water in their homes for more than 16 hours. Kyivvodokanal, the city's water utility, said water supply and sewage pumping stations in Kyiv resumed operations on Wednesday afternoon.

Russian and Ukrainian representatives will visit the White House Friday to meet with Melania Trump, after the first lady brokered a temporary ceasefire last week to allow for civilian evacuations and humanitarian aid to move into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, officials in both Kyiv and Moscow said.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Davyd Arakhamiia, the leader of Zelenskyy's parliamentary faction, will attend the meeting, according to Ukrainian newspaper Ukrinform.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova planned to represent Russia at the meeting, but that visa complications could affect their travel.
Zelenskyy announced Wednesday that the U.S. first lady was to receive Ukraine's highest award for women, the Order of Princess Olga, 1st Class, for her role in brokering the limited ceasefire.

He also promised a Ukrainian response to the Russian attack on the Zaporizhzhia aid center, and a day after Democrats took control of both houses of the U.S. Congress, he renewed his plea for more missile interceptors and other key military support.

"Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered. We count on a response – Ukraine needs air defense support right now. I am grateful to the partners who are taking such steps."

title: Hackers can hijack grocery store freezers. What about our homes?
summary: Large-scale hacks targeting grocery stores in Europe and France's blood banks are renewing concerns about the vulnerabilities of everyday "smart" devices.
story: London — Cyberattacks on grocery store refrigeration systems across Europe sent temperatures soaring on Monday, spoiling food and causing significant financial losses in the second such incident in less than a month. In October, hundreds of French stores were targeted in a similar attack that sent temperatures in some units soaring to 122° Fahrenheit, destroying a huge amount of food.

On Wednesday, France's health service said the country's national emergency blood supply network had also been compromised by hackers this week, though alert and backup systems prevented cold storage facilities from being shut down, and no supplies were lost.

The incidents have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology. It is not just essential systems such as electricity grids, healthcare databases and grocery store chains' refrigeration, which can have multiple layers of security and redundancy built in, but everyday appliances that are now connected to the internet.
The concern among some experts is that devices pitched as time-saving conveniences for consumers could also create potential entry points for hackers.

CBS News spoke with several cybersecurity experts who warned that similar vulnerabilities to those exploited in the grocery store hacks could exist in our homes. From heating systems and smart TVs to security cameras, door locks and ovens, millions of household appliances are now online.
How vulnerable are our homes?

"Our homes may be more vulnerable than many people think. Smart fridges, TVs, cameras, and locks are small computers connected to the internet, and like any computer, they can have weaknesses," Dr. Manny Niri, a cybersecurity lecturer at Oxford Brookes University, told CBS News.
"Often the problem is simple: default or reused passwords, old software, or accounts with weak security," he said.

Professor George Loukas, head of the Centre for Sustainable Cyber Security at the University of Greenwich, said vulnerabilities in some mass-produced devices could potentially expose millions of households simultaneously.
"One flaw in a popular model opens the door to every home that owns it," he said.
What could hackers actually do?
The consequences could extend beyond hackers simply switching an appliance on or off remotely, to "anything the device is already allowed to do," Loukas said.

"If an app can turn off your heating, unlock your door or switch off your camera, so can a hacker. The physical harm comes from using the system as designed, just with malicious intent and controlled by someone other than you," he said.

"Unauthorized access to a camera or microphone could reveal when people are at home, what they are doing and, potentially, their conversations," said Niri. "A compromised device can sometimes give hackers access to other devices on the same network, potentially exposing personal or financial information. There can also be physical consequences, for example changing a fridge temperature, interfering with an alarm system, or opening a smart lock."

In 2025, U.S. cybersecurity officials identified a critical vulnerability in certain WiFi thermostats that could allow hackers to gain full administrative control of the units. Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission documented cases involving Ring security cameras in which hackers gained access to accounts and used cameras to spy on and harass homeowners.

Dr. Abdullahi Arabo, associate professor of cyberscience and network security at the University of the West of England, warned that a single compromised device could expose other systems within a household.
"A compromised device can sometimes give hackers access to other devices on the same network, potentially exposing personal or financial information," he said.
Could millions of homes be hacked simultaneously?
Experts say the greater danger may not be hackers targeting individual homes, but exploiting vulnerabilities across millions of identical devices.

In 2016, the Mirai malware infected hundreds of thousands of internet-connected devices, including household routers and security cameras, transforming them into a network capable of launching large-scale cyberattacks.
Artificial intelligence could make attacks like that significantly easier to pull off, Loukas told CBS News.
"With AI, an attack that once needed a skilled team working for weeks can now be run by one person," Loukas warned. "This lowers the bar for who can cause disruption at scale."
"When millions of homes rely on the same device, a single flaw becomes everyone's problem," he added.
How worried should we be?
The experts who spoke with CBS News emphasize that ordinary, individual households are unlikely to be deliberately targeted.

"I suggest awareness, not fear," Niri said, adding a warning that "comfort has a cost. Before buying a smart device, we should ask, 'Do I really need this to be online, and what happens if it is hacked?'"
He recommended changing default passwords on all devices, enabling two-factor authentication on those that allow it, regularly updating software, and retaining manual control over essential systems.

title: Mother, daughter dead in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
summary: Family members identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed.
story: A mother and daughter are dead in a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, British Columbia, devastating their family, according to the victims' relatives and B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
Family members identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed.
The victims were first reported missing on Nov. 1, after they failed to return from what was expected to be a short afternoon walk.

"The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them," said Josh Balcarras, Balcarras' brother, in an interview with CBS News Canadian partner CBC News. "That turns into a day, and then a night … then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing."

Balcarras' body was discovered in the Snooka West Trail area on Monday afternoon. Reed's remains were found on Tuesday. Agencies including the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and local search and rescue authorities took part in the investigation, said Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service. Tyre announced the discovery of the two sets of the remains on social media.

"Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time. We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident," Tyre said in one video.

Tyre said it is not clear how many bears were involved. Efforts to locate and capture any involved animals are underway, he said. Captured bears will be assessed. If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be "dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety," Tyre said. Tyre urged the public to avoid the Snooka West Trail area while this work is underway.
"Two peas in a pod"
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Josh Balcarras told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," Josh Balcarras told CBC.

The family has started a GoFundMe to cover funeral costs. Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and start a fresh chapter in her life, according to the fundraiser. Because of the move, she did not have savings, her family wrote. Balcarras leaves behind three young adult children and a grandchild.
Reed had "her whole life ahead of her," the family wrote, and "was only beginning her journey into adulthood."
Bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

A grizzly bear attacked a group of students and teachers in the Bella Coola valley in November 2025. Two people were critically injured, and two were seriously hurt. Others were treated on the scene and released, CBC News reported at the time. The bear was described as "aggressive," CBS News reported. The incident deeply shook the local community.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: How other countries are reacting to the U.S. election results
summary: Iran says the U.S. election results reflect a rejection of war and Spain's leader says it's another sign of a right-wing populist wave falling apart.
story: The Iranian regime was quick to label the resounding losses for President Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections as evidence of American voters rejecting the costly war he launched with Israel more than eight months ago.
Spain's leader called it a sign of a global, right-wing populist "wave" crumbling, and Russia acknowledged that it "could complicate relations with the U.S."
Below is a look at those statements and other reactions from foreign leaders and figures, including some hopeful leaders as elections loom in other countries.
Iran

A statement attributed to Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Wednesday made it clear that Tehran is not expecting the outcome of the U.S. elections to change Washington's approach more than eight months into its war with Iran:

"If there are still people who harbor even the slightest hope for a change in behavior or for party and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who believe that by making concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken," the statement published on Khamenei's official website said.
Earlier, Iran's chief negotiator said the results reflected Americans' rejection of the war with his country.

"Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X. He cited the increased cost of living, or "conscience," as two possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added as a warning.
Russia
In Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hoped President Trump would still be able to "continue his peace-making efforts" in the wake of the U.S. elections.
A new round of working-level talks between Russia and Ukraine, brokered by the U.S., is scheduled to take place Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

Mr. Trump has pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hard this year to accept a peace deal that many argue would strongly favor Moscow, with Kyiv likely having to allow Russia to maintain control over some of the territory it has occupied in Ukraine during the grueling four-year war.

Several previous rounds of U.S.-brokered talks have yielded prisoner exchanges, and a recent local ceasefire credited to first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo brought calm to one southern city occupied by Russia, but there has been no indication that Putin is prepared to abandon his demand to unilaterally seize Ukrainian territory as part of a deal to end the war.

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov noted Wednesday that Moscow has long had strained interactions with Democrats, saying the U.S. party's "core approach to relations with Russia is extremely negative."
Ryabkov said Russia's foreign policy would not be influenced by the election results, and its stance on Ukraine in particular would not change.
There was no immediate reaction from Ukraine's government to the U.S. election results.
Spain

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, among the most vocal European critics of the war with Iran and other Trump administration policies, welcomed the results, saying in a post on X that Americans had "voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hatred. Against sexism."

Sanchez, who will face his own country's electorate in a Nov. 29 election, called the U.S. results further evidence of a global right-wing populist wave crumbling, and he said he believed a similar result would follow in Spain.
"It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain," he predicted.
European Union

Top European Union diplomat Kaja Kallas voiced hope on Wednesday she that the new U.S. Congress would increase support for Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia with Democrats now in charge of both the House and the Senate.
Kallas said Europe and the United States "are much stronger together" in any efforts to push Russia to end its full-scale invasion.
European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose, in an earlier post on X, called the election results "wild."

"Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world," she said, adding that the EU "must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That's not up for debate."
United Kingdom
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's reaction to the walloping doled out to President Trump's Republican Party in the U.S. midterms was largely apolitical.

"President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living," Burnham told reporters in London on Wednesday, adding that prices could not be reduced until the U.S. war with Iran "is resolved."
South Africa
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters Wednesday that the U.S. election results would "introduce a new era in world relations."
"We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken," he said.

The Trump administration has had tense relations with South Africa, sanctioning officials it accuses of allowing the persecution of the country's White Afrikaner population and inviting its members to apply for refugee status in the U.S. — an opening that some 17,000 have sought to take advantage of.

Mr. Trump has alleged that Afrikaners face a "genocide" in South Africa. In a tense Oval Office meeting last year, he confronted Ramaphosa on the claims, showing him a video that spotlighted murders of farmers in the country.

The claims, long pushed by Elon Musk, have been strongly disputed. A 60 Minutes report in February featured Afrikaners who rejected the notion that they are facing a genocide and said murders on farms were linked to a broader crime problem in South Africa that harms people of all races.
Germany

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Wednesday that he expected cooperation between Europe's single largest economy and the U.S. to become "broader and perhaps more interesting" with the Democrats now in control of the House and Senate.

On U.S. support for Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, Wadephul said he was optimistic that both parties in the U.S. Congress would now engage more with each other to boost backing for Ukraine's government.
France

French Economy Minister Roland Lescure declined on Wednesday, during an interview with the BFM television network, to predict whether President Trump would "accept" the rebuke by American voters or stick to the policies widely perceived as having precipitated the midterm Republican defeat.

"Either he decides to rise above the fray — acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people — and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement; or he does not," said Lescure, adding that it was "something we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days."
Norway
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere on Wednesday called the U.S. election results "a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters."

"Voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."
This article will be updated with additional international reaction.

title: Stranded U.S. cruise ship departs Cambodia with no passengers
summary: The MV Odyssey had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs.
story: A U.S. cruise ship that forced all its passengers to disembark in Cambodia after suspending its operations last week has departed the Southeast Asian nation with only crew aboard, Cambodian officials said Wednesday.
The MV Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs.
It had been docked for a scheduled stop at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, when on Oct. 28 its 203 passengers were suddenly told they had to disembark within a few hours.

The ship left Sihanoukville late Tuesday with only crew and other personnel on board, said Tang Sochetkresna, director of the Tourism Department of Preah Sihanouk province. He said he didn't know the ship's next destination, but multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News the ship will be moved to Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned off.

The cruise ship is now under control of its lender, according to a message sent to residents and obtained by CBS News.  Company leadership, however, said they're optimistic they can get the ship back — if they find an operational partner.
"This is a 30- to 90-day process, and, during that process, we have time to get a restructure done," Mike Petterson, the company's founder and executive chairman, told CBS News.

Sochetkresna said that nearly 100 passengers remained in Sihanoukville, while others were visiting other parts of Cambodia or had traveled on to other countries. Most of the ship's passengers were Americans.
The ship, with its 650-passenger capacity, had 156 crew members on board, but it was not clear how many departed with the ship.

There has been no official announcement of future plans for the cruise ship. Media reports suggested that a creditor had taken over its management and was having it sailed to Singapore, Southeast Asia's main maritime hub.
The abrupt end to the ship's voyage has drawn widespread attention because it had touted itself as a floating home, combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
Several passengers said they had paid more than $300,000 for a suite for the lifetime of the vessel.
Villa Vie Residences said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.
The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.

Internal communications reviewed by CBS News showed the ship was in financial distress for at least three months prior to Cambodia. Now, additional documents show that the company had a sense of urgency in getting more residents to provide even more funds.

During a meeting that took place in early August, the company wrote in an internal PowerPoint presentation: "A significant new line of inquiry is the need to distinguish actual inability to contribute from unwillingness to contribute further."
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.

Passengers had said the company had been asking them for several months for contributions to keep the ship operating, and there has been an active debate on social media over whether its operation was ever financially viable.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.

Its current cruise began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise, along with the purchase of a second ship to operate in a similar capacity, had already been planned.

title: U.S. launches strikes on Iranian targets in Strait of Hormuz
summary: The U.S. launched limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft, a senior U.S. official told CBS News.
story: The U.S. military launched limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News.

The strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island, a senior U.S. official said. It came after two incidents on Monday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired at an American fighter jet, leading it to return fire, according to two U.S. military officials. Later Monday, Iran fired a missile from Qeshm Island that threatened shipping, the officials said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes, which came on the eve of Election Day in the U.S. President Trump has been floating the idea of restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms, at the same time as U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a possible U.S.-Iran deal.
Qeshm Island, in the northern Strait of Hormuz, is crucial to the Iranian regime's efforts to monitor and exert control over commercial traffic through the waterway.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday that Tehran retained "the right to legitimate self-defense" after the new U.S. strikes, and would do so "until the military aggression has been completely and permanently brought to an end."

Iran has retaliated for attacks on its territory throughout the war sparked by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28 by targeting commercial shipping traffic in the strait and U.S. allies and interests across the Persian Gulf region.

As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between suggesting he could strike a deal to end the war with Iran, to warning that he could resume major attacks against the country.
In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible."

Later Monday night, however, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with" the Israeli leader, but he did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.

The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
In Israel, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.
As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47.1 billion in military expenditure alone, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

CENTCOM said the cost of replacing spent munitions alone was about $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. Another $6.1 billion was needed to replace lost equipment, and there has been around $11.9 billion spent on incremental costs including support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which have been targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.

title: Poland launches major security operation along border with Russia
summary: Poland's prime minister says a rapid, major deployment of extra security forces to the border with Russia may have prevented "attempted acts of provocation."
story: Berlin — Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the country's national police chief said, and the Polish prime minister said the effort may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation targeting the NATO member.

Additional police and counterterrorism units, as well as troops from the elite military special forces unit GROM, have been deployed as part of the operation, which national police chief Marek Boroń said would run from Monday until at least Nov. 8.

Polish and allied intelligence agencies had warned of possible sabotage operations and provocations during the first half of November, particularly along Poland's border with Kaliningrad, and including possible border incursions by armed groups.
Those warnings had already put domestic security agencies on high alert even before the additional security forces were deployed to the northeast regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Tuesday that suspicious movements were observed overnight near Kaliningrad, including individuals carrying flashlights close to the border area.
He said the quick reaction by Polish security forces may have prevented an unspecified provocation this week.

"We very quickly mobilized the necessary security forces and means on site, and we successfully prevented any attempted acts of provocation, if that was the intention. Of course, we will never be able to completely confirm that," Tusk said Tuesday, adding that intelligence had pointed for weeks to possible "acts of diversion or more serious provocation" against the European Union, including "the intrusion of armed individuals into Polish territory."
A special command center was set up at Polish national police headquarters to coordinate the new security operation.
The goal is to protect the public, detect suspicious activities early, and prevent attacks on critical infrastructure, the police said Tuesday.

Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad, bordered only by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic Sea to the west, is of considerable military and strategic significance. It is widely believed that Russian security agencies, including the FSB and GRU intelligence agencies, have a presence in the territory in eastern Europe.

To the immediate east of Kaliningrad is the strategically important Suwałki Corridor — the only land border connecting the Baltic NATO states with the rest of the alliance, where Poland and Lithuania share a short border sandwiched between Russian and Belarusian territory.

Polish authorities had not published any evidence of specific plans for an act of sabotage or an attack originating from Kaliningrad by Tuesday afternoon, but the alert comes after months of sabotage, air incursion and other low-level incidents across Europe blamed largely on Russia.

During a joint news conference with Lithuania's prime minister on Oct. 13, Tusk referred to a conversation he had recently had with NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich, and said it had reinforced his own concerns about increasing threats of sabotage, including possible provocations involving aircraft or attacks on border crossings.

At about the same time, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture of the security threats facing the U.K. and Europe, and he said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one."

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Among the numerous incidents attributed to Russia across Europe this year alone, there was a fire in August at a Polish factory that produces drones and other military components, and an arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station that Polish officials blamed directly on Russia in September.

Russian drones have also crossed into NATO airspace in Eastern Europe repeatedly during the war in Ukraine, and just this week the U.K. Royal Navy said it had intercepted a Russian spy ship off the far northern coast of Scotland.
The navy said helicopters were dispatched to track the intelligence-gathering ship, which was "closely monitoring" a NATO exercise taking place near Scotland's Outer Hebrides islands.

title: 5 people rescued in South Pacific after months at sea, 4 still missing
summary: The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing in July.
story: Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing.

Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported, after they had drifted an estimated 3,355 miles east from the Federated States of Micronesia.

The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. The group had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo at the time, ABC reported.
A 10-day search covering 33,000 square miles followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said.
"Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care," the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email.
"Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them," the email added.
When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible.
A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island.
Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery.
"They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," she told the ABC.
The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. ABC said the group went missing after their boat was caught in a storm.
The governor of Micronesia's Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.
"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter.
"We continue to pray for their four companions," he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
Other rescues in the Pacific

There have been previous incidents where people have become lost at sea among the tiny island chains that stud the Pacific Ocean. An Australian man survived more than two months lost at sea in 2023 with his dog Bella after rough seas damaged their boat and its electronics system. Tim Shaddock, 51, had been traveling from Mexico to French Polynesia, but found himself drifting in the Pacific Ocean for more than two months. Shaddock and his canine companion survived by drinking rain water and eating raw fish that Shaddock caught, he said. They were spotted by a helicopter and rescued in July 2023.

Two American sailors and their two dogs were rescued after five months at sea in the Pacific in 2017. Jennifer Appel and Tasha Fuiaba were discovered 900 miles southeast of Japan by a Taiwanese fishing ship, the U.S. Navy said at the time. The vessel's engine died during bad weather, and they were unable to get to land using the ship's sails. The women said the boat drifted off course, and no ships were near enough to hear their distress calls. Water purifiers and a year's supply of food aboard the vessel kept them alive, the Navy said.
In 2024, three fishermen were stranded on a remote Micronesian island for more than a week. They were rescued after using palm leaves to spell out "HELP" in large letters on a beach.

title: 1 dead, 2 injured in helicopter crash near Mount Everest base camp
summary: The two helicopters were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season.
story: Two helicopters collided Tuesday while trying to land just below Mount Everest's base camp, killing at least one person and injuring two others, officials said.

The aircraft were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season. Heavy snow had covered the route before the weather improved Sunday and thousands of trekkers were able to move around.
There are no roads on Everest, and helicopters are the only way to bring down trekkers and guides who become sick or exhausted in the cold and high altitude.
The helicopters crashed at Pheriche village, which is at an altitude of 13,780 feet.

A 47-year-old tourist from India was killed in the crash, according to Bhupendra Thapa, a Solukhumbhu district administration officer. Arrangements were being made to airlift the tourist's remains to Kathmandu, the Agence France-Presse reported.
A passenger from New Zealand was injured and was being transported to the capital, Kathmandu, for treatment. A Nepali pilot sustained injuries but was treated locally.
The number of people on the two helicopters wasn't clear.

The Mount Everest base camp trek lasts up to two weeks and goes from the only airstrip in the area at Lukla to base camp located at 17,380 feet. Everest's summit is at an altitude of over 29,000 feet. The trek is popular during the fall season, right after the rainy season and before the harsh winter months.

The helicopter collision is the second incident along the route to Everest Base Camp this week. On Friday, Octo. 30, a fire broke out at a hotel in Dingboche, which is known as a stop for trekkers to pause while they acclimate to Everest's high altitude.

The fire may have been sparked by a cooking gas cylinder explosion, local media reported. Guests and hotel staff were safely evacuated. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Video obtained by CBS News shows the building in flames.
Dingboche is about 2 miles from Pheriche. The two destinations are about a 40-minute hike from each other, according to trail guides.

title: Soccer player dies following on-field collision in Spain
summary: Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision in a match.
story: A Spanish soccer player's death is now under investigation as possible involuntary manslaughter, after he suffered a fatal injury in an on-field collision during a match.
The country's National Police said Tuesday that proceedings were opened and prosecutors will also be involved.
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest from the on-field collision in a Spanish second-division match, his club said. He was 30 years old.
De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by the onrushing Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during added time.
Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

Tenerife said in a statement to Spanish media late Monday that De Miguel suffered cardiac arrest but that his pulse was restored in the ambulance to the hospital. However, it later said his condition had "worsened neurologically" and subsequently announced that De Miguel had died at 8 a.m.
The club, located on Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken."

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness," the club wrote, in part, in a statement announcing the death on social media. "The family of Jesús de Miguel thanks each and every one of the expressions of support received, and likewise requests, from the heart, the utmost respect for their privacy in these terrible moments."
De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."
The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina match to be held later on Tuesday.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun was playing for CSKA Moscow when he died from head injuries received in a collision during a match.

title: Stolen watch worth $290,000 returned to store with apology note
summary: The case of the stolen Audemars Piguet timepiece took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a note saying sorry.
story: A Swiss luxury watch worth about $290,000 that was stolen from a Tokyo store last week has been returned with an apology note, according to local media.
The theft occurred when a man posing as a customer tried on the Audemars Piguet timepiece and then fled the shop in the Japanese capital while it was still on his wrist.

But the case took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a handwritten note saying sorry, the Asahi Shimbun newspaper and other media reported on Monday, citing unnamed investigative sources.
The watch's serial number reportedly identified it as the stolen item.
A name and address were also written on the package, but police believe the information is fake, the Japan Times reported.
The shop declined to comment when contacted by AFP.
Tokyo police are still searching for the man on suspicion of theft, according to the Asahi Shumbun.

In August, four luxury watches worth 200 million yen ($1.3 million) were stolen from another store in the same shopping complex. Two Chilean nationals were arrested on suspicion of theft in connection with the incident and subsequently indicted, the Japan Times reported.

After that robbery, police conducted a crime prevention session for watch store owners, advising that they only display replicas, the Asahi Simbun reported. They were also taught how to use a special lining on display cases to make them difficult to break.

title: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
summary: The envoy will also meet with European and NATO allies to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine.
story: The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.

Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory seized over the course of the grueling war.

Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's land grab would set a dangerous precedent.

Witkoff's latest announcement of planned talks at the working level — which generally means discussions among technocrats, not at the senior diplomatic or national leadership level — comes after a rare, localized cease-fire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson ended on Sunday.
The brief truce allowed humanitarian supplies into the small Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and the evacuation of an undisclosed number of residents.

The cease-fire, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, has raised some hope for more diplomatic progress toward ending the war sparked by Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
Russia has continued pummeling the rest of Ukraine during and after the local ceasefire, however, with more strikes coming overnight into Tuesday across the country.
At least 29 people were killed in a village in the southeast Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia, authorities said Tuesday.
In the northeast city of Kharkiv, the regional administration said a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people and forcing the evacuation of around 200 patients.
Russia's defense ministry said Tuesday that it had carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine, and port infrastructure in the Odesa region.
Moscow's mayor said, meanwhile, that 500 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital were destroyed overnight.

title: U.K. man returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
summary: Karl Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998.
story: Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.

His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.

It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.

"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.

"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. We've had to create two world records just to get back here. And I couldn't have done it on my own. So it was a world, global effort."

Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998. He made his way north through Central America, the United States and Canada, then crossed the Bering Sea to Russia in the world's first recorded attempt. He then carried on through Central Asia and swam for 31 days across the Caspian Sea in another reported first, in order to circumvent the war in Ukraine.

Over the past few years, he crossed Europe, and just last month, he swam from France across the English Channel, setting foot on the country of his birth where British immigration officers had set up to check his passport.

"It's almost like arriving in a foreign country," Bushby told CBS News over the weekend as he neared home. "I've worked with dollars for 28 years. I don't know the brands in the stores. So I'm going around wondering what I'm going to be buying. A couple of times I got caught out crossing the road because I'm looking in the other direction because these people drive on the wrong side of the road."
His home stretch Monday, quite literally, was a roughly 3-mile brisk walk from near Hull's town center to a quiet, sprawling neighborhood to the north of two-story, red-brick terrace homes.
Children lined the turn to his mother's home and cheered while an honor guard led the way.
Bushby pushed the cart that had been with him for about 25 years the last few steps.
He then embraced his waiting mother on the street outside her home. The cheers quieted, and the two shared a moment in this homecoming.
Bushby said he feels like a man wondering what home truly means after spending a generation around the world.

"I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long. And it's an odd feeling. And I almost feel guilt," he said. "Like there are other parts of the world now that feel more like home to me. And now I'm going to be faced with this weird static thing."
Now, after more than 10,000 days away, Bushby faces a different task: processing it all.
Confronted with the question of whether the world had gotten better or worse, he acknowledged the troubles but did not give up on his optimism.

"The world's in a little bit messier time; there are more wars, you know," he told CBS News. "But it's all good. At the end of the day, we've been through worse. So we all need to breathe a little bit, get through the tough times; we're going to be just fine. My bet is on us, no matter what. My bet is on humanity."
His final advice for anyone wondering if they could also accomplish something extraordinary: dream bigger.
"Yeah, you can, because I'm nothing special. Maybe we need the art of dreaming big again. People seem to dream outside of a very confined space mentally at the world that they live in," he said.

"You've got to have that little confidence. You got to realize that you're more capable than you think you are. People constantly underestimate themselves. So that's the first step, I think. Dream big. Realize you're probably capable more than you'd think. If you take nothing else from this … take that!"

title: Matt Damon's wife had brain surgery days before Oscars, pulled off 'heroic' surprise for actor
summary: Matt Damon's regret over missing "The Departed" best picture win drove Luciana Barroso's bold decision just days after brain aneurysm surgery.
story: ‘Oppenheimer’ actors Matt Damon and Emily Blunt tell Fox News Digital one thing they’ll never do together as neighbors.
Matt Damon is sharing a frightening family health scare that nearly derailed one of Hollywood's biggest nights.
The actor revealed his wife, Luciana Barroso, had a brain aneurysm and had surgery a week before the 2024 Oscars.

MATT DAMON WAS 'PUSHED TO THE LIMIT' WHILE FILMING 'THE ODYSSEY,' DETAILS GRUELING PHYSICAL DISCOMFORTS

title: Russell Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault
summary: Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in a U.K. court on Thursday. He is expected to be sentenced on Monday.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports as Russell Brand faces trial in London over allegations of rape and sexual assault on 'America Reports.'

Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in the U.K. He denied the charges and was acquitted of two additional rape charges and attempted indecent assault.
He has been taken into custody and is due to be sentenced Monday, according to BBC.
Brand, 51, was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009.
RUSSELL BRAND ACCUSED OF RAPE, SEXUAL ABUSE OF 4 WOMEN; COMEDIAN DENIES ‘SERIOUS CRIMINAL ALLEGATIONS’
Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.  (Mike Marsland/WireImage)

According to Sky News, Brand acknowledged that he had been "reckless" and used his fame to pursue sexual relationships, but insisted that the encounters were consensual. He also told the jury that consent was "fundamental, essential and necessary."
Brand has denied forcing any of the women to engage in sexual activity against their will.
Last week, Brand's wife, Laura Brand, took the stand as a defense witness, one day after the comedian and actor testified.
During Laura's testimony, the mom of three — who first met her husband when she was 19, and he was 31 — opened up about the start of their relationship.

"When I met him, I was aware that he liked women, and I was aware toward the latter half of that year that he was engaging with other women," Laura told the court, per Sky News. "I was not interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. I was invested; we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."
The couple rekindled their relationship in 2015 and married in 2017. They share three children.

title: Paris Jackson demands $600M from father Michael Jackson's estate in legal war with longtime executor
summary: Paris Jackson accused executor John Branca of financial retaliation after she challenged his handling of Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate.
story: Victoria Price told Fox News Digital that as long as there is Halloween, people will listen to the horror icon's narration in the hit song.

Paris Jackson accused John Branca, the sole executor of her late father Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate, of financially retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the King of Pop's fortune.

Paris alleged in new court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, that she and her siblings experienced a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments while Branca maintained an "iron grip" over their inheritance.
She asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from her late father's estate into the family trust after accusing Branca of mismanaging the funds.
PARIS JACKSON SAYS DAD MICHAEL'S UNUSAL RULE HELPED PROTECT HER CHILDHOOD
Paris Jackson asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from Michael Jackson’s estate to the family trust. (Alan Chapman/Getty Images)
Branca has been the sole executor of Jackson's estate since 2009. The pop star died that year from acute propofol and sedative intoxication leading to cardiac arrest.

Branca's alleged mismanagement of estate funds included non-contractual gifts to colleagues, aggressive litigation, public attacks and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to Jackson's children.

"Without belaboring the point, when Paris began challenging the administration of the Estate last year through her objection to Executor Branca’s non-contractual gifts to his colleagues, her challenges were met with scorched earth litigation, public attacks, and a multimillion reduction in monies provided to her and her siblings by the Estate," her legal team wrote. "This course of conduct and administration should not continue."
Paris Jackson is the daughter of Michael Jackson and Debbie Rowe. (Swan Gallet/WWD/Getty Images)

In a separate filing obtained by Fox News Digital, Paris accused Branca of using estate resources for personal travel on private jets, improperly charging personal expenses to the estate and concealing the spending from beneficiaries.

She claimed Branca acknowledged taking multiple personal trips and reimbursed certain expenses only after she investigated them. Her attorneys characterized the conduct as "outright theft" and a breach of his fiduciary duties.
"Where the travel is of a purely personal nature, or in service of Mr. Branca's other clients or business affairs, it constitutes outright theft," the court filing stated.
Prince Jackson and Paris Jackson at the opening night of "MJ: the Musical," at Neil Simon Theatre on Feb. 1, 2022, in New York City. (Bruce Glikas/WireImage)

Paris also accused Branca of using estate funds for personal gifts, questioned more than $604,000 in credit card charges and reimbursements, and challenged $9.4 million in executor compensation, $1.4 million in payments to his law firm and roughly $835,000 in public relations expenses.

She further alleged that Branca mismanaged more than $440 million in estate cash while pursuing entertainment projects that benefited him financially, including the Michael Jackson biopic, which reportedly required tens of millions of dollars in reshoots and rewrites.
Her legal team urged the court to reject Branca's financial accounting and order him to provide a more detailed breakdown of the estate's spending.

"Once again, Ms. Jackson’s legal team raises the same hollow complaints and fails to acknowledge the unique structure of the Estate, which is operated as a dynamic business, with customary costs and expenses," a representative for the estate told Fox News Digital. "No rhetoric can hide the fact that the Executors have taken an Estate that was $500 million in debt when Michael died and turned it into the most successful Estate in history, producing $3 billion in revenue and the biggest biopic in movie history, with a box office exceeding $1 billion globally."

From left to right, Michael Jackson's kids Prince Jackson, Blanket Jackson and Paris Jackson, LaToya Jackson and Katherine Jackson attend Children's Hospital Los Angeles Receives Michael Jackson Artwork Donation ceremony on Aug. 8, 2011, in Los Angeles. (Valerie Macon/Getty Images)

A representative for Paris told Fox News Digital: "No rhetoric can hide the fact that Mr. Branca has used Estate funds to create a lavish lifestyle complete with charging personal trips on private jets to the Estate. This wasteful spending and financial mismanagement flies in the face of his fiduciary duty to the beneficiaries and has gone unchecked for too long."

As for the $600 million distribution, Paris argued that her father's estate plan entitled his children — Prince, Paris and Bigi — to trust income beginning at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at age 30. She claimed the executor had never funded the trust, despite Michael Jackson's death more than 17 years earlier.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Paris Jackson accused Michael Jackson's executor, John Branca, of retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the estate. (Rita Barros/Getty Images)

"Michael intended for his children to become the caretakers of his legacy," the petition read. "As each child reached certain ages, Executors were to increasingly provide for each child’s independence."

Paris' filing cited more than $2.5 billion in gross estate earnings and approximately $850 million in cash or cash equivalents as of December 2024. She argued that the estate could distribute $600 million while retaining enough money to cover outstanding liabilities.

"Ms. Jackson’s counsel is well aware that the Estate is prevented from fully funding the philanthropic giving and individual trusts for the beneficiaries until several legal hurdles have been removed, including in particular the ongoing IRS litigation where they sought $700 million in taxes and penalties from the Estate," a statement provided to Fox News Digital on behalf of Jackson's estate said. "The Estate was able to secure a ruling to significantly reduce that amount, but the matter has not been settled and could still change."

Paris Jackson claimed her father’s estate plan entitled his children to trust income starting at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at 30. Jackson died in 2009. (CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images)

"Further, the claim that the executor has withheld or ‘cut' payments is a complete fabrication," the statement added. "In fact, more than $200 million has already been distributed for the benefit of Paris and the other beneficiaries. Michael Jackson’s will is clear. None of his children receive a distribution until they are in their 30s. The Estate looks forward to the time when all issues are resolved so that their trusts can be fully funded as Michael wanted."

A representative for Paris told Fox News Digital: "The Estate is once again deflecting from its own incompetence. Paris called for the trust to be partially funded, something Mr. Branca had the ability and obligation to do long ago. After years of delay, Paris had no choice but to step in herself."
A court hearing on Paris' request to transfer $600 million into the family trust is scheduled for Dec. 4.

Paris Jackson's court filing cited more than $2.5 billion in gross estate earnings and about $850 million in cash or cash equivalents as of December 2024. (Dave M. Benett/Getty Images)

Paris previously spoke about her childhood as the daughter of Michael Jackson. Behind the glitz of Jackson’s larger-than-life world, Paris said her father enforced strict rules to protect his children’s sense of normalcy.

The 28-year-old model recalled in an interview on "Call Her Daddy" that her father required his children to finish their homework and chores before enjoying weekend activities, limited their television and movie viewing, and had them wear masks in public to shield their identities from the intense spotlight surrounding his fame.
Paris said she understood that her father was famous. What she didn’t grasp was the sheer magnitude of his celebrity.

"I just didn't know how famous ... There was definitely part of me that, like when I looked out my hotel window, and it was one of the times where, like, the alias didn't work and there's just like a sea of people with signs and stuff — I'm not so naive to think, yeah, everyone experiences this, you know?" Paris said. "I just didn't understand the lengths."

title: Tony Butala, voice behind 'The Way You Look Tonight' and The Lettermen co-founder, dead at 87
summary: Tony Butala co-founded The Lettermen in the late 1950s and performed for over 60 years, earning four Grammy nominations and a Hollywood Walk of Fame star.
story: Tony Butala died at the age of 87 Nov 1. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The Lettermen co-founder, Tony Butala, died Sunday, Nov. 1, at the age of 87.
Tracy Clark, the band's media coordinator, confirmed his death to The Associated Press with a statement, saying, "We have lost an integral member of The Lettermen family."

"It is with profound sadness that we announce the recent passing of Tony Butala, founding member of the international recording artists ‘The Lettermen,’ and recipient of a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame," the statement read.
"Our most heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with his children, grandchildren, siblings, the love of his life, the entire Lettermen organization and all who knew and loved him."
Tony Butala died at the age of 87 Nov. 1. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71
A cause of death was not disclosed, and there will be no public viewing. Details about celebrations of life in both Wisconsin and California will be announced at a later date.

He co-founded The Lettermen in the late 1950s with Jim Pike and Bob Engemann, and the group released its first hit, a rendition of Fred Astaire's "The Way You Look Tonight," in 1961, which earned the trio a Grammy nomination.
The Lettermen had 20 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 list. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The band recorded 20 hits that reached the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned four Grammy Award nominations.

Butala remained a member of the group for over 60 years, releasing hits such as "Goin' Out of My Head/Can't Take My Eyes off You," "Everything Is Good About You," "Come Back Silly Girl," "Theme from a Summer Place" and "Hurt So Bad."
Butala retired from performing in 2019. (Jean-Baptiste Lacroix/AFP via Getty Images)
He retired from performing with the band in 2019, the same year Pike died at the age of 82 from complications related to Parkinson's Disease. Engemann died in 2013.

A year after retiring, Butala attended the ceremony honoring the band with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. After his retirement, the band continued on with new faces, and the current lineup includes Donovan Tea, Bobby Poynton and Rob Gulack.
Butala attended the Walk of Fame ceremony honoring The Lettermen in 2020. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

"Tony never met a stranger," the official band statement continued. "His life was a living example of talent, perseverance, and refinement. But, above all, his true joy was entertaining and sharing his music with audiences worldwide."

Butala began his professional singing career as a child, performing on KDKA Radio in Pittsburgh at the age of 8 and moving to Los Angeles with his mother at 10 to further his career.
Butala began performing at 7 years old. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Once in Los Angeles, Butala joined the Mitchell Boys Choir, and it appeared in classic films like "White Christmas," "Peter Pan," "War of the Worlds" and "On Moonlight Bay."
