title: Ex-Alaska lawmaker details mystery recruiter as FBI, Congress widen 'Decoy Dan' scrutiny
summary: The FBI interviewed former Alaska Republican David Eastman after a Democratic operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter in the Senate race.
story: Article III Project attorney Will Chamberlain explains how an alleged effort to confuse Alaska voters by recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan could violate federal conspiracy-against-rights law, potentially exposing those involved to felony charges carrying up to 10 years in prison.

A former Alaska Republican lawmaker told Fox News Digital the FBI interviewed him after an apparent Democratic political operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter and tried to persuade him to enter the state's U.S. Senate race amid an intensifying congressional investigation into the controversial "Decoy Dan Sullivan" ballot scheme.

The allegations raise questions about potential federal criminal liability. Article III Project attorney Will Chamberlain argued that a coordinated effort to deceive voters about a candidate's identity could violate 18 U.S.C. § 241, the federal conspiracy-against-rights statute.

The revelations come after former campaign staff for Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola spoke to the New York Times about their knowledge of a reported scheme to stack Alaska’s four-person ballot with other "Dan Sullivans" to help siphon votes from incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.
MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The ballot ultimately included Peltola, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Republican Gerald Heikes and retired Petersburg teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Whether the similarly named candidate diverted votes or affected the outcome remains unproven.
Chamberlain told Fox News Digital the alleged operation could constitute a federal felony if prosecutors establish that participants conspired to interfere with voters' constitutional rights.
PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE
Dan J. Sullivan, who filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)
"The basic concept is you're not allowed to conspire to injure or harm people's constitutional rights. And one of those rights is to vote for the candidate of your choice," Chamberlain said.

"These people conspired to put a fake ‘Decoy Dan’ Sullivan on the ballot in order to trick people who were going into the ballot box intending to vote for the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan," he alleged. "There's a lot of good precedent on this that suggests that's a crime and a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison."

Chamberlain cited historical cases involving ballot manipulation, while acknowledging that the precise circumstances of recruiting a same-name candidate have not previously been addressed in an identical case.

"Nothing exactly like this has happened before in the sense of recruiting a same-name candidate to trick people in the ballot box," he said, adding that a lot of slanted electoral messaging is not illegal.
ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME

"If you want to pretend that another Republican is better than the current incumbent or pretend that the incumbent's not running and then persuade someone to vote for that candidate, that's not a ‘conspiracy against rights’ because the right to vote for the candidate of your choice has not been impinged upon," he said.

"It's the fact that when you're conspiring to put two people with the exact same name on the ballot to trick people who are going in there intending to vote for the incumbent and get them to vote for somebody else by deception."

Meanwhile, former state Rep. David Eastman, a Republican from the Matanuska-Susitna Valley, told Fox News Digital by phone from Wasilla that he was approached by an operative under what he later surmised were false pretenses to recruit him into the race. Eastman said he also received several "fake mailers" suggesting "Decoy Dan" Sullivan was the real or only Sullivan in the race.
The mailers, shared with Fox News Digital, are framed in a "meet the candidates" format and do omit Senator Sullivan.

Eastman told Fox News Digital he was approached in the Mat-Su by an operative he later identified in a blog post as Jerid Kurtz, who was named in the New York Times report. Eastman said the operative claimed to represent conservative donors and encouraged him to run for Senate.
"He approached me through a constituent. I sat down with him in April here in Wasilla," Eastman said.
"He pretended to represent conservative donors and was looking for conservative candidates to run for federal office; none of which was true," Eastman added.

Eastman alleged Kurtz "pretended" to represent conservative donors and used a false name, but said the operative never mentioned either Sullivan or disclosed an intention to confuse voters during their meeting.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DSCC, Peltola’s campaign and Wingspan Strategies — where Kurtz is named in congressional documents as a co-owner — for comment. Dan J. Sullivan reportedly "vanished" as investigators began knocking on doors in his remote community, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The allegations come as federal investigators examine whether Democratic political operatives improperly recruited Dan J. Sullivan in an effort to confuse voters who intended to support Senator Sullivan.

The controversy has also reached Capitol Hill. In an October 29 letter, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., requested that Kurtz appear for an in-person transcribed interview on November 6 concerning allegations that operatives associated with Mary Peltola's campaign sought to recruit similarly named candidates to confuse voters.
"As a Democrat operative who was allegedly tasked with assisting in this effort, you have information that will assist the Committee's investigation," Comer wrote.
"If you do not voluntarily appear for the interview, we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process," he warned.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Eastman said Kurtz did not mention either Sullivan or disclose an effort to confuse voters during their April meeting. He nevertheless questioned the operative's intentions after subsequent reporting connected Kurtz to the alleged candidate recruitment effort.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Eastman also confirmed the FBI has interviewed him. Fox News Digital reached out to the bureau for comment.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Gavin Newsom wipes out California's death row in historic mass commutation
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom will commute all 548 death sentences to life without parole, drawing sharp backlash from victims' rights advocates.
story: Decades after his daughter Polly Klaas was murdered, Marc Klaas speaks out against California Gov. Gavin Newsom's potential plan to commute California’s remaining death sentences, calling the move a betrayal of crime victims and voters.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will spare the lives of 548 inmates currently on the state’s death row, effectively clearing capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions.
In a letter to constituents, Newsom, a Democrat, declared the state's capital punishment system fundamentally flawed, error-prone, and morally incompatible with California’s core values.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."
EX-CHIEF SAYS CHRISTA PIKE WAS 'ALMOST GIDDY' DESCRIBING MURDER AS GOVERNOR WEIGHS IN AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he will commute the death sentences for all 548 of the state's death row inmates. (Fred Greaves/Reuters)
Under the executive action, all death sentences will be converted to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
The move comes amid renewed national conversations surrounding capital punishment following a botched execution in Tennessee involving death row inmate Christa Pike.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006. Shortly after taking office in 2019, Newsom placed an official moratorium on executions and ordered the dismantling of the execution chamber at San Quentin State Prison.
The decision drew immediate criticism from victims' rights advocates, including Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter, Polly, was kidnapped and murdered in 1993.
Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, remains on death row.
CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON

The father of Polly Klaas, Marc Klaas, heavily criticized California Gov. Gavin Newsom amid reports that he is considering a mass commutation of the state's death row inmates. Richard Allen Davis, who was convicted for the 1993 death of Polly Klaas, was sentenced to death by a judge. (Polly Klaas Foundation; AP)

"He just gave the gift of life to [hundreds of] people who took the gift of life from their victims," Klaas told Fox News Digital, expressing disappointment over the decision. "I don't understand his rationale behind it… but it's probably the same old tired stuff that he said when he did his moratorium."
"He has definitely secured the serial killer vote now," he added.
POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION

Lt. Sam Robinson calls to open a door at San Quentin State Prison's death row in San Quentin, Calif., on Aug. 15, 2016. The prison is California's oldest penitentiary and houses the state's only death row for men with 700 condemned inmates. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Conversely, anti-death penalty advocates strongly praised the move.

"The silence after the very breath of a human is violently wrestled out of them is deafening," Rev. Jeff Hood, a spiritual adviser to death row inmates, said in a statement reported by The Sacramento Bee.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I’ve heard it 14 times. Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence. These commutations represent the height of moral leadership," he added. "Cruelty laid down. Now, I’m left with one prayer: God, don’t let any of the governors in the other executing states get any sleep until they find the ethical stamina to follow Newsom’s lead."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Democrats ‘divorced from voters’ as 5 states back citizen-only voting, bolstering GOP push
summary: Voters in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved noncitizen voting bans by wide margins, but a key Supreme Court case looms.
story: Honest Elections Project Action Executive Director Jason Snead says voters overwhelmingly support proof-of-citizenship requirements and urges the Supreme Court to clear the way for states to verify voter registrations.

Voters in five states overwhelmingly approved ballot measures barring noncitizens from voting, including Kansas, where Democrats scored a major Senate upset, and Alaska, where the Senate race remains uncalled.

Federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, but measures approved in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia clarify or explicitly codify citizenship requirements for voting in state and local elections, with support exceeding 60% in each state.

Election integrity advocates pointed to the results as evidence supporting President Donald Trump and Republicans’ argument that their push to require proof of citizenship for federal voter registration has "overwhelming bipartisan support."
REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY
"I would absolutely agree that noncitizen voting bans are overwhelmingly popular," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. "They enjoy bipartisan support."
A 2024 Gallup poll found that 83% of Americans, including 66% of Democrats, support requiring first-time voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

A volunteer picks up a "Require Voter ID" sign at a news conference at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters March 2, 2026, as GOP lawmakers gather in support of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot.  (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)

The ballot measure wins also come as the conservative-majority Supreme Court prepares to consider a related dispute over whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship on its state voter registration form and remove suspected noncitizens from the rolls before an election, a ruling that could affect how states enforce citizenship requirements.

Related election measures failed in California and Arizona. California’s Proposition 39 was defeated 58.5% to 41.4%, a margin of roughly 17 percentage points; the measure would have required voter ID and additional citizenship-verification procedures.

"I would note that the unique thing there is not only that California is openly hostile to the idea of trying to prevent noncitizen voting in terms of its elected leadership, but also the left poured more than $30 million into the ballot measure campaign to defeat that," Snead told Fox News Digital.
Snead said Arizona’s measure was broader legislation that included several provisions beyond noncitizen voting, which may have contributed to its defeat.

The victories for the measures barring noncitizens from voting follow the Trump administration and congressional Republicans’ failed efforts to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.
ARIZONA VOTER LAW FIGHT REACHES SCOTUS AS ELECTION GROUPS WARN ‘ABSURD’ CONSEQUENCE COULD ENSUE
An election official sorts ballots during early voting Oct. 28, 2025, in Portland, Maine. (Robert F. Bukaty/AP)

The SAVE America Act also became a flashpoint in Congress, with Republicans and Democrats sparring over whether to attach it to a budget reconciliation package. Trump’s effort to tie the bill to Department of Homeland Security funding contributed to a prolonged standoff during the department’s shutdown.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans lacked the votes to pass it, while Democrats argued it would disenfranchise eligible voters.
Hans von Spakovsky, a former member of the Federal Election Commission and senior legal fellow of Advancing American Freedom, said the Democratic Party is completely "divorced" from its voters.
Snead agreed, saying Democrats took a "90-10 issue" and turned it into a highly politicized fight.
"The left is far out of step with the American public, and they really should be answering the question, 'Why are you opposed to something that 90% of the public is in favor of?" Snead said.

"Only citizens should vote in our elections. And if you believe, as the left claims to, in democracy, well then, we should start by making sure that we have free and fair elections that are decided only by American citizens."
But while Spakovsky applauded the passage of the ballot measures, he warned they could prove ineffective unless states are allowed to verify voters’ citizenship.
"Look, I'm glad those states passed that referendum, but those provisions aren't going to be much good unless states are able to do two things," Spakovsky said.

Spakovsky pointed to Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, a case in which the Supreme Court will decide whether federal law prevents Arizona from requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and from removing suspected noncitizens from its voter rolls.
He said the ruling could affect how effectively states can enforce citizenship requirements.
ELECTION EXPERT SOUNDS ALARM ON HOW NONCITIZENS ARE LANDING ON VOTER ROLLS
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks to reporters in the U.S. Capitol on Aug. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Snead said simply checking a box attesting to citizenship on a federal form has not been sufficient.

"As we have seen in a number of recent arrests by the Justice Department, with indictments going out against noncitizens, and with the failures of the automatic voter registration system in New Jersey, which added 6,600 noncitizens to the rolls, with almost 400 of them voting, we clearly have been let down by that check-a-box system," Snead said.
However, Spakovsky said a ruling in favor of Arizona would only go so far, arguing that proof of citizenship would only apply to future voter registrations.

"The only way for them to try to check the citizenship of people who are already registered is by using the SAVE database at the Department of Homeland Security, and with complete control of Congress, I have no doubt that one of the first things Democrats will do is try to defund the database so that states can't use it," Spakovsky said.

Snead applauded the Trump administration's efforts to expand states’ access to the SAVE database to clean up their voter rolls, arguing the previous process of tracking down ineligible voters was "cumbersome." He also voiced concerns that Democrats will gut the database.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"I would not be surprised if they try to defund the entire safe system or pass legislation to prevent its use for cleaning up voter rolls," Snead said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think that we are fast approaching the point where it is fair to say, 'Why are Democrats actively pushing for noncitizen voting?'" Snead continued. "I think that's the direction that we are going."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Hegseth demands $350B for military, fires back at Dem impeachment push
summary: War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve $350 billion in military funding and vowed to fight Democratic impeachment efforts.
story: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve at least $350 billion in additional funding, arguing the investment is needed to rebuild the military and keep the U.S. ahead in a dangerous world. (Credit: @SecWar)
War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress Thursday to approve at least $350 billion in defense funding while pushing back against efforts to impeach him.
In a video posted to X, Hegseth defended his Pentagon overhaul, including eliminating DEI initiatives, removing military leaders and rebuilding recruitment.
Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as political theater while defending his efforts to overhaul the Pentagon and advance President Donald Trump's military agenda.
HEGSETH FACES BIPARTISAN IMPEACHMENT THREAT AFTER IRAN WAR GETS BLAME FOR GOP MIDTERM SLAUGHTER
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testifies before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Capitol Hill, in Washington, D.C., April 30. (Cliff Owen/AP Photo, File)
"We need every vote from every patriotic member of Congress," Hegseth said, calling for a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion to strengthen the military and defense industrial base.

The impeachment effort is being led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced eight articles against Hegseth in September, accusing him of violating congressional war powers during the Iran conflict and abusing his authority in other military operations.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary in May, plans to renew the effort when Congress returns next week. The House has not voted on the articles.
Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling ABC News he intends to keep him in his Cabinet despite the impeachment push.
GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
Hegseth dismissed the effort as politically motivated.
"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly," Hegseth said.

He also took aim at former President Joe Biden and former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, accusing them of leaving the Pentagon in disarray and forcing the Trump administration to rebuild the military.
"We ended the weird and the woke and elevated patriots in strength," Hegseth said, defending his efforts to eliminate diversity initiatives and change military personnel policies.
HEGSETH'S LEADERSHIP QUESTIONED BY GOP MILITARY VETERAN AS DEMOCRATS TALK IMPEACHMENT
Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling ABC News he intends to keep him in his Cabinet despite the impeachment push. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images, File)
Hegseth also defended the administration's military operations against Iran, describing the campaign as a historic effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
The war secretary closed with a message to troops amid the political fight in Washington.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Don't blink. Ignore the noise. Never hesitate," Hegseth said."We will not back down. We put America and the warfighter first, always and without apology."
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: DOJ launches criminal probe into Supreme Court leak that exposed ruling overturning Roe v Wade
summary: Federal prosecutors are probing the Supreme Court leak after Chief Justice John Roberts' internal investigation failed to identify the leaker.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt has the latest on the DOJ launching a federal investigation into the 2022 leak of the Supreme Court's draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade on 'America Reports.'

The leak that exposed the U.S. Supreme Court’s (SCOTUS) draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade is under criminal investigation by the Department of Justice (DOJ), years after the court’s own hunt for the culprit came up empty.
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s Washington, D.C., office is leading the probe, multiple sources briefed on the matter told Fox News on Wednesday.
The investigation has been underway for at least a year, sources said, and comes three years after an investigation by SCOTUS failed to identify the culprit who leaked a draft of the 2022 decision.
Grand jury subpoenas have been issued during the probe, though it is unclear who received them.
SUPREME COURT LITIGATION FAILS TO IDENTIFY LEAKER OF DOBBS DRAFT DECISION
An investigation by the Supreme Court three years ago was unable to determine who leaked a draft opinion overturning the federal constitutional right to abortion. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images, File)
The New York Times first reported the investigation.
Politico published the draft before the June 2022 ruling, prompting Chief Justice John Roberts to order an internal investigation that failed to identify the leaker.

The DOJ and the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on the investigation. Fox News also reached out to the Supreme Court, asking whether the court or any justices have worked with outside investigators, including DOJ, or plan to do so.
The criminal probe comes as Justice Samuel Alito says he has an idea who was responsible but lacks sufficient evidence to publicly identify that person.
SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ROE V. WADE IN LANDMARK ABORTION DECISION
Chief Justice John Roberts had called upon the marshal of the court to investigate the leak. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)

"I do have an opinion. But the evidence available at this time is not strong enough for the court or for me to say this is the person who was responsible," Alito told Fox News chief legal correspondent and "Fox News Sunday" anchor Shannon Bream in an exclusive interview last month.
"It was a grave breach of the trust that everybody who worked in this building had before that point.
"And it very predictably made the five of us in the majority targets for assassination and nearly resulted in the assassination of my colleague Brett Kavanaugh."

Politico published the draft on May 2, 2022, revealing that at least five conservative justices were prepared to overturn Roe. The final decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization followed on June 24, 2022, ending the nationwide constitutional right to abortion.

Roberts tasked Court Marshal Gail Curley with investigating the leak. After months of forensic analysis and interviews with nearly 100 employees, the court announced in January 2023 that investigators were "unable to identify a person responsible by a preponderance of the evidence."
LATEST SCOTUS LEAK A GIFT TO LIBERALS ‘SALIVATING’ OVER CONTROL OF HIGH COURT NARRATIVE: EXPERTS
The probe comes as Justice Samuel Alito says he has an idea who was responsible.  (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo, File)

"No one confessed to publicly disclosing the document and none of the available forensic and other evidence provided a basis for identifying any individual as the source of the document," the marshal’s report concluded.

Multiple sources previously told Fox News that investigators had narrowed their inquiry into approximately 70 people who may have had access to the draft. Much of the initial focus was on roughly three dozen law clerks who worked directly with the justices.
Fox News was also told at the time that Curley asked several permanent court employees who may have had access to the draft to turn over their cellphones and electronic devices.
Supreme Court law clerks typically serve one-year terms for individual justices, meaning those who worked for the court when the draft leaked have since completed their clerkships.
SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES
The Supreme Court Jan. 13, 2026, in Washington.  (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)
Roberts brought in former Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff, a former federal appeals judge, to assess the court’s investigative methods. Chertoff concluded the investigation was thorough.
"At this time, I cannot identify any additional useful investigative measures," Chertoff said.

The marshal’s report also found it unlikely that someone outside the court had improperly accessed its computer systems. Investigators examined court devices, networks, printers and available call and text logs without finding forensic evidence identifying the source.

The report found that expanded work-from-home arrangements during the coronavirus pandemic and gaps in security policies made it easier to remove sensitive information from the building and the court’s networks.
Pro-abortion activists participate in the "Rally for Our Freedom" in Orlando, Fla. (Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images, File)
Some employees also admitted telling a spouse or partner about the draft, violating the court’s confidentiality rules, according to the report.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The leak prompted protests outside justices’ homes and deepened distrust inside the court. A California man was arrested near Kavanaugh’s Maryland home in 2022 and charged with attempting to assassinate him.

"When you lose that trust, especially in the institution that I’m in, it changes the institution fundamentally," Justice Clarence Thomas said shortly after the leak. "You begin to look over your shoulder."
Fox News Digital's Bradford Betz contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: House GOP launches defense plan to shield Trump from looming Democrat investigations
summary: House GOP leadership letter from Steve Scalise warns committee chairs to prepare defenses against expected Democrat-led probes of Trump allies.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports on Democratic lawmakers warning Trump administration officials of potential subpoenas and investigations, while party leaders emphasize affordability and downplay impeachment efforts.
FIRST ON FOX: House GOP leadership is giving Republican lawmakers a new playbook to go up against an expected barrage of Democrat-led investigations in the new Congress.

Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., wrote a letter to the current chairs of House committees on Thursday warning them to "maximize our remaining days in power to prepare for what is coming" with instructions on how to brace for those expected probes. A source sent a copy of that letter to Fox News Digital.

"House Democrats have signaled they intend to impeach President Trump, but they will not stop there. They will weaponize every single gavel to appease their radical base," Scalise said. "They will use their oversight authorities to harass the President, his family, cabinet officials, and they will seek to destroy our allies. You all will be a key line of defense in this fight."

The guidance includes three key points: "taking inventory" of current and likely future investigative efforts by Democrats while they are in the minority, identifying who is on Democrats' target list, and reviewing how recent Supreme Court rulings as well as a Department of Justice (DOJ) memo on executive privilege could factor into future investigations.
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMOCRATS, REPUBLICANS WASTE NO TIME IN SETTING SOCIAL MEDIA ABLAZE AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP
President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena on Oct. 30, 2026, in Daytona Beach, Fla. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Democrats' targets could include "administration officials, programs and authorities, and external allies, including conservative partners and industry leaders," Scalise said.
He added that his staff would meet with the relevant committees and others to further prepare.

"Please let me know if there are any additional tools or support you need from me as you undertake this important effort," Scalise wrote. "I have full confidence that we will be effective in our efforts to fight back as a team."
DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN
Democrats have signaled they are poised for a wide range of investigations targeting Trump's Cabinet, family, businesses, and allies as soon as they take over Congress next year.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next head of the House Oversight Committee, released a brief statement Tuesday night when it was projected Democrats would win the House: "Lawyer up."

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, joined by House Majority Whip Tom Emmer and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, holds a news conference after a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
DEMOCRAT IMMEDIATELY THREATENS SUBPOENAS FOR TECH EXECUTIVES IN WAKE OF MIDTERMS

The committee said in the statement, "Following this win, Garcia will become Chairman of the House Oversight Committee, where he has vowed to take on the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files. His statement can be found below."
House Homeland Security Committee Democrats have similarly signaled they are preparing to probe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
MIKE JOHNSON NOT RUNNING TO LEAD HOUSE GOP AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSSES

Meanwhile, a spokeswoman for House Judiciary Committee Democrats told Fox News Digital in response to Scalise's letter, "Sounds like Rep. Scalise is asking his fellow Republicans to compile a list of all the corruption, lawlessness, and abuse they’ve been protecting from congressional oversight. But the people have spoken, and the cover-up expires with the Republican majority. The days of invertebrate congressional submission are over."
The letter comes a day after Scalise launched a bid to become House minority leader in the new Congress.
He will be up against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, for the job.

title: Democrat drops out of race due to health concerns and still wins; opponent says, 'We deserve to know more'
summary: Democratic Iowa state House candidate Eric Armstrong, who announced in September that he was dropping his campaign due to health struggles, still won the election contest.
story: Pollster Justin Wallin joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze the significant midterm election results as Democrats take control of the House and Senate. Wallin breaks down key races, including James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate showdown.
A Democratic candidate who dropped his campaign for health reasons still defeated the Republican candidate in an Iowa state House race.
Democrat Eric Armstrong explained in a Sept. 7 Facebook post that he was abandoning his campaign due to health issues.

"Running a successful campaign requires immense physical and mental energy. Recently, I have been facing some personal health issues that require my full attention and immediate care," Armstrong wrote, in part.
"Because I must prioritize my health and recovery at this time, I am stepping down from my campaign, effective immediately. This was a deeply difficult choice. However, I know it is the right one.
3 INJURED IN SHOOTING AT DES MOINES, IOWA, POST OFFICE; SUSPECT DETAINED: POLICE
Eric Armstrong won the election after dropping his campaign due to his health. (Eric Armstrong for Iowa House District 20 on Facebook)

"Our District deserves a representative who can give 100 percent of their energy to this race. Right now, I must focus on healing so that I can continue to serve our community in other ways in the future."
Despite this announcement, Armstrong's name remained on the ballot, and voters still elected him.
Unofficial results indicate that Armstrong received 4,602 votes, while Republican Keith Jones, who is a member of the Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors, received 3,737 votes.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS' OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT
Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors member Keith Jones (pottcounty-ia.gov)
"I'm going to do my best to represent" the district, Armstrong said during a phone interview Wednesday with The New York Times. "But I still have health issues. That’s what I'm struggling with."
Armstrong did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment Thursday.
In part of a statement to Fox News Digital Thursday, Jones wrote, "I think we deserve to know more."

"Serious rumors were that he was hiding a background that could have disqualified him from office. People ‘could have’ donated to his campaign and subsequently voted for him based on a falsehood. I was a police officer for 29 years. There's absolutely something there that needs to be investigated by the media," Jones later wrote in part of another statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday.

"If he's truly sick, why did he reenter the race? Is he healthy enough to hold office? Did he lie about being sick to cover a damaging personal story? Public trust at that level is important. Is he qualified to be in public office?" Jones asked.
DEMS FLIP YET ANOTHER SENATE SEAT IN TRUMP COUNTRY AMID SWEEPING GOP UPSETS

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat and U.S. Senate candidate, during an election night event with Iowa Democrats in Des Moines, Iowa, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Scott Morgan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

title: North Korea's fake IT worker scheme takes dangerous turn as new threats emerge every day
summary: CrowdStrike says it uncovers one or two suspected North Korean fake IT worker cases daily, with operatives infiltrating defense contractors and AI firms.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent Rich Edson reports on North Korean cybercriminals using fake identities to secure remote jobs at U.S. companies on ‘Special Report.’

What began as a scheme to generate cash for North Korea by deploying fake IT workers at American companies has now turned into an opportunity to collect intelligence from high-value targets, cybersecurity researchers warn.

New details are emerging of the sprawling spy operation within U.S. borders, with cybersecurity tech company CrowdStrike claiming it is finding one or two suspected North Korea IT worker cases every day.

The scheme is creating a heightened espionage foothold inside American companies spanning multiple industries. And CrowdStrike claims it has seen remote IT workers hand off access to malware teams when North Korea identifies intelligence worth collecting. And federal cases show overseas workers gaining access to sensitive U.S. military technology.

"They don't discriminate," Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's head of counter adversary operations, told Fox News Digital, explaining that the workers apply broadly across industries, from consumer companies to defense contractors.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, center, and his daughter Ju Ae attend the inauguration ceremony of Saeppyol Street in Pyongyang. (KCNA via KNS/AFP via Getty Images)

But when they land inside a "particularly juicy target," Meyers said, CrowdStrike has seen the operation handed off to a malware team "because they realize that there's some intelligence value and something that they want to collect."
Meyers did not say whether the malware teams successfully collected sensitive information after those handoffs.
The FBI is now warning that the scheme poses a "significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat."
North Korean workers are targeting cleared defense contractors, jobs that require U.S. government security clearances, and even active-duty military personnel who can host company laptops.

Recent federal cases illustrate the stakes, from a worker who successfully accessed controlled technical information at an AI defense contractor to impostors who secured offers for jobs involving military AI and Top Secret intelligence.

In one case involving a network of U.S.-based "laptop farms" that helped overseas workers obtain remote jobs at more than 100 American companies, prosecutors identified a California defense contractor developing AI-powered equipment and technologies.
An overseas worker using a stolen American identity was hired as a full-time remote software engineer in January 2024, according to the indictment.

Instead of going to the purported employee, the company laptop was shipped to a conspirator in New Jersey and ultimately transferred to a laptop farm, where software allowed the overseas worker to operate it remotely.

For more than two months, prosecutors said, the worker accessed the contractor's systems and downloaded technical data, including material controlled under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR. The indictment said documents obtained from victim companies included information related to "sensitive U.S. military technology."

The same contractor hired two other overseas workers using stolen American identities within roughly six weeks, prosecutors said. Their laptops were also routed through U.S.-based facilitators for remote access.

Laptops and remote-access devices seized from Zhenxing Wang’s residence as part of a federal investigation into a North Korean IT worker scheme. Prosecutors said the setup allowed overseas workers to remotely access computers issued by U.S. companies. (U.S. Department of Justice)
A separate case unsealed last week shows operatives pursuing positions with even more explicit national security ties.
Overseas conspirators were allowed to use the identity of a Virginia man who worked for a cleared defense contractor and held an active top secret security clearance.

One impostor secured a $130,000 software engineering offer at a government contractor working on a generative AI project for a component of the U.S. military. The company shipped a laptop to the Virginia man's home before discovering during a video call that the purported employee did not match the person whose identity he was using.
HOW A FOREIGN GOVERNMENT HELPED ACCUSED SAUDI SPY'S FAMILY FLEE US AFTER OPENAI BUG SCANDAL
Another impostor using the same identity was offered a $170,000 senior software engineering position requiring top secret/sensitive compartmented information clearance.

That company caught the scheme before work began after a background investigation uncovered discrepancies and a video call revealed someone who appeared roughly 30 years younger than the man whose identity he was using.

Neither impostor ultimately performed the sensitive work. But the cases show how far the operation has reached into companies handling military technology and positions requiring some of the government's highest security clearances.

CrowdStrike began tracking the North Korean IT worker campaign it calls Famous Chollima in March 2024 after investigating what initially appeared to be a single malicious insider. Investigators soon identified dozens of other victims among its customers.
Unlike traditional espionage operations targeting specific organizations, Meyers said, the workers cast a wide net, applying for hundreds or thousands of remote IT jobs.

The primary objective is generating revenue for North Korea, according to CrowdStrike, which has linked Famous Chollima to the country's Munitions Industry Department. Meyers said the money helps fund North Korea's weapons program.
But access to a valuable target can create an additional intelligence opportunity.

Treasury last week sanctioned another North Korean IT-worker network, saying the regime takes most of the workers' wages and generates hundreds of millions of dollars to fund its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.
Treasury also warned that workers have exploited corporate access to deploy malware, steal proprietary information and remove sensitive data.

"The North Korean regime continues targeting and exploiting American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives who weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

Laptops and other devices seized during Operation Lonestar Roundup, an FBI operation targeting suspected North Korean IT worker "laptop farms" in Texas. Federal agents searched more than 40 homes and seized 187 laptops and remote-access devices. (U.S. Department of Justice)
The operation relies on stolen identities, increasingly sophisticated deception and U.S.-based facilitators who provide the physical footprint overseas workers lack.

After a worker is hired, a company laptop can be shipped to a facilitator's home and configured for remote operation, making it appear to company systems that the employee is working inside the United States.
Artificial intelligence is also making the deception more sophisticated.

Meyers said operatives use AI to create convincing LinkedIn profiles and resumes, answer interview questions and increasingly alter their appearance on video calls. Some also use AI to help perform the jobs after being hired.

The FBI says workers have purchased access to identity-verification services to test stolen identities, hired Americans to appear on camera or complete employment requirements and sometimes subcontracted entire jobs to other foreign workers.
The bureau also warned that workers "almost always" remove data from victim companies because many are required to record their screens to document daily work.
Federal authorities have intensified efforts to dismantle the infrastructure supporting the operation.

In October, the FBI searched more than 40 suspected laptop farms across Texas, seizing 187 laptops and other devices. The DOJ said coordinated actions announced that day affected more than 70 U.S. companies.

"This investigation is about far more than fraud," U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said. "It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders."
Meyers said CrowdStrike has identified laptop farms through patterns across multiple cases and passed information to the FBI, contributing to searches and arrests of U.S.-based facilitators.
North Korea has also exploited the other side of the hiring process, with operatives posing as recruiters to target employees already inside companies.

In a separate cryptocurrency theft investigation, Binance said a software engineer had been approached through a legitimate job platform by someone posing as an executive at a fictitious company, part of what it suspected was a North Korean effort to compromise employees through fake interviews.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Meyers said companies must treat identity verification as a security issue, not simply a hiring function, and train recruiters and security teams to recognize the tactics.
"They're an employee, so they have access to whatever an employee would have," Meyers said of workers who successfully get through the hiring process.
"And that could be ... the crown jewels."

title: Mexican judge arrested after U.S. charges him of accepting $2M bribe in case linked to former Olympian
summary: Luis Benítez Alcántara allegedly took a $2 million bribe to release Ryan Wedding's second-in-command in a billion-dollar cocaine enterprise.
story: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro joins DEA and Homeland Security Investigations officials to announce a superseding indictment charging 15 individuals in an alleged transnational methamphetamine and GBL trafficking operation.

Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexican judge accused of accepting a bribe to release a transnational cocaine smuggler, was arrested in Colombia on Sunday after the U.S. charged him with nine counts of being an accessory after the fact.

Benítez, according to a Thursday announcement from the U.S. Department of Justice, accepted a $2 million bribe from Canadian national Ryan Clark, who the DOJ alleges was second-in-command to former Olympic snowboarder Ryan J. Wedding in the latter's international drug dealing empire.

"Benítez Alcántara was a district judge in Mexico City who allegedly accepted $2 million in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of Wedding’s second in command, while Wedding was orchestrating a billion-dollar transnational criminal organization and the largest supplier of cocaine to Canada with connections in Colombia, Mexico, and the U.S.," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
US CHARGES MEXICAN GOVERNOR, TOP OFFICIALS IN CARTEL CONSPIRACY AS MEXICO FIRES BACK OVER PROOF

Clark was initially arrested in Guadalajara, Mexico on Oct. 8, 2024, according to a superseding indictment. He appeared in front of Benítez for extradition proceedings on Oct. 9 after the U.S. requested his extradition.
Judge Luis Benítez Alcántara in custody. (U.S. Department of Justice)

Beginning in Nov. 2024, Clark sent approximately $2.75 million to intermediaries over the course of four months, according to the indictment. On Feb. 24, 2025, Benítez received $2 million in payments from those intermediaries and granted Clark bond and release that same day, per the indictment.
Among the nine counts, Benítez is charged with being an accessory after the fact to aid and abet Clark.

Clark and Wedding are also charged with murder, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute a mixture and substance containing a detectable amount of cocaine and continuing a criminal enterprise, according to the indictment.
If convicted, Benítez faces up to 15 years in federal prison.
"Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

"Thanks to the work of the Homeland Security Task Force and our international law enforcement partners, Mr. Benítez will be held accountable. The Department of Justice will continue identifying and dismantling transnational criminal organizations that threaten the safety of the American people," Blanche concluded.
HIGHEST-RANKING TREN DE ARAGUA MEMBER EVER EXTRADITED TO US SET TO APPEAR IN HOUSTON COURTROOM: DOJ
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on April 7, 2026. (Getty Images)
Despite Benítez's role in granting Clark bond and release, Mexican law enforcement officers arrested Clark again days later and handed him over to U.S. authorities on Feb. 27, 2025.
Following Clark's arrest, he cooperated with FBI and U.S. officials in supplying information about his and Wedding's roles in their criminal enterprise, according to a DOJ indictment against Wedding.
KASH PATEL DEFENDS FBI'S ‘MOST WANTED’ BUSTS AMID MANIPULATION ACCUSATIONS, HIGHLIGHTS 'SUMMER HEAT' SUCCESS
Wedding, a former member of the FBI's Top 10 Most Wanted List, was arrested in Mexico in January 2026.

In addition to running a cocaine distribution empire that the indictment alleges imported the majority of illicit cocaine into Canada, Wedding is also accused of orchestrating the murders of numerous informants and other affiliates of his illicit activities.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS

Ryan Wedding, wanted by the FBI, was seen taking a practice run for the men's parallel giant slalom of the Salt Lake 2002 Winter Olympic Games in Park City, Feb. 13, 2002. (FBI | REUTERS/Jeff J Mitchell)
In January, he pleaded not guilty to federal charges of running a criminal enterprise, murder, conspiring to distribute cocaine and other crimes.
His empire allegedly worked in concert with the powerful Mexican Sinaloa Cartel to move and distribute cocaine through Colombia, Mexico and the rest of North America, according to the indictment.

"This individual and his organization and the Sinaloa cartel poured narcotics into the streets of North America and killed too many of our youth and corrupted too many of our citizens. And that ends today," FBI Director Kash Patel said in January after Wedding's arrest.

title: Schumer faces mutiny from newly elected Senate Dems as party prepares to seize power
summary: Senate Democrats face a leadership battle as Chuck Schumer seeks to keep his role, but several newly elected senators are pushing for new blood.
story: Several newly elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

Senate Democrats will soon decide who will lead them with their newly acquired grip on power in the upper chamber, and while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., appears to be the favorite, some in the caucus aren’t eager to back him.

Schumer has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, helming the caucus as both majority and minority leader since 2017. But many of the fresh crop of Democratic senators-elect, which spans the ideological gamut from moderate to progressive, are tepid, at best, in backing him for another term.
And some said throughout their campaigns that they wouldn’t support him at all.
DEM SENATE HOPEFUL REJECTS SCHUMER BUT BENEFITS FROM MILLIONS IN SPENDING BY HIS ALLIES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is confident he will continue to lead Senate Democrats, but newcomers to the caucus aren't on board with him at the helm.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership," Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton told CNN in September. "We need new younger leadership, young blood."

Hamilton is the moderate megachurch pastor who toppled Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., on Election Night, flipping the Sunflower State for the first time in nearly a century. He, like others this cycle, argued that Democrats needed "fresh ideas and fresh leadership."

"In Kansas, Chuck Schumer is a liability for Democrats, and we've got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together, not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems," he said. "And I think people are frustrated with the gridlock in the sense that people are not working together to solve problems."

Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections later this year, and Schumer will have to shore up support within his newly expanded caucus to stay at the top. But he will only need a majority of Senate Democrats to back him.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM
So far, Democrats’ majority in the upper chamber is at 54 seats and could further expand depending on the results in Mississippi and Alaska, which as of Thursday were leaning in their favor.

Schumer believed that he would still be the one to lead Democrats and contended to reporters on Wednesday that issues that incoming senators and their voters may have had with the direction of the Democratic Party in recent years were not about him.
"The issue is not me," Schumer said. "I'll be re-elected as majority leader, but the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want."

Still, there is a faction of newcomers, including senators-elect Troy Jackson in Maine, Julianna Stratton in Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, who aren’t all in for Schumer.
THUNE GOES ALL-IN ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS SCHUMER STAYS ON BENCH, FACES REJECTION FROM FELLOW DEMS
Former state Sen. Troy Jackson, a Democrat from Maine and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a Fighting Oligarchy event. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Jackson, speaking to reporters just before Election Day, said his position hadn’t changed on Schumer.
"I told Schumer that I’m going to, you know, support somebody else," Jackson said. "So it’s no different now."

That somebody else could be Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has been proposed as an alternative by progressives, like El-Sayed, to lead Senate Democrats instead of Schumer. Van Hollen may have his eyes elsewhere — he has said that he’s "kicking the tires" on a 2028 run.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A Democratic aide familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told Fox News Digital that before selecting a new leader, the lawmaker believed "the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people."
"He’s made it clear that the new Democratic majorities need to use their power to push a proactive, economic agenda," they said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Schumer, Jeffries sidestep questions on nuking filibuster, launching Elon Musk probe after blue wave
summary: Chuck Schumer ignored questions twice about abolishing the filibuster as Democrats prepare to take the Senate majority after midterm victories.
story: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., were pressed on looming questions over potential moves in Congress after flipping both chambers. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions about their potential first moves in Congress after the Democrats won back the majority in both chambers with sweeping victories in Tuesday’s elections.

Schumer was pressed on whether he plans to abolish the filibuster as speculation grows that Democrats could eliminate the filibuster after President Donald Trump urged Senate Republicans to terminate it numerous times to pass the SAVE America Act.
Trump previously warned that if Republicans didn’t act on it, the Democrats would if given the opportunity, which they now have.
Schumer ignored the question after being asked twice by Fox News Digital if he plans to eliminate it.
FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., hold a joint news conference at the U.S. Capitol Jan. 8, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Some Democrats have previously signaled openness to eliminating the filibuster if they regained the Senate.
During a news conference Wednesday morning, Schumer also refused to answer questions about some of his plans for the Senate as Democrats take back the majority, including eliminating the filibuster.

He also said he will be "re-elected as majority leader" by the Senate Democratic caucus despite opposition from newly elected Democrats. He quickly redirected the conversation to focus on the blue wave in the midterm elections and what the party plans to do with the "generational remake of the Senate map."
SCHUMER SAYS HE'S NOT GOING ANYWHERE, BUT HIS OWN CANDIDATES AREN'T READY TO BACK HIM

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

Jeffries was also asked by Fox News Digital about the looming question over whether Democrats will probe Elon Musk after the party has begun eyeing targets in discussed efforts to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
Jeffries gave Fox News Digital a thumbs-up when approached but did not respond when asked whether House Democrats would investigate Musk.

Musk has emerged as a potential target of Democratic oversight, with some lawmakers calling for scrutiny of his time as head of the Department of Government Efficiency. Democratic lawmakers have also suggested looking into his companies' multibillion-dollar contracts with the federal government and, more recently, his role in cutting internet access to the Ukrainian military.
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH
Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military. (Getty Images)
The House minority leader’s refusal to comment comes as Democrats are divided over whether they would select Jeffries as speaker of the house.

There was a petition started that has received over 550,000 to oust Jeffries from leading the House, arguing the party needs a speaker that represents "the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

With many of the newly elected congressional candidates hesitant, or outright opposed, to backing both Jeffries and Schumer as leaders, the decision over who will be the leaders of both chambers of Congress is still in limbo.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: New Jersey mayor who charged at resident during council meeting concedes election loss
summary: Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini was decisively defeated in a mayoral race following the spectacle at a township council meeting last month.
story: Video captures Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a heated council meeting before being restrained by others in attendance (Credit: Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful).

The Republican New Jersey mayor who was physically restrained while charging toward a resident during a Pemberton Township council meeting last month has conceded the mayoral race to his Democratic opponent.
Mayor Matthew Bianchini congratulated Belinda Fontanez in a Facebook post Wednesday.

"The voters of Pemberton Township have spoken, and the results are clear. I offer Belinda Fontanez my sincere congratulations on her victory. As she prepares to take on the responsibility of leading our community, she has my full support for a smooth transition," Bianchini wrote.
"I care deeply about the future of this township, and its success matters far more than any single election," he added.
Bianchini was decisively defeated, earning just over 30% of the vote, according to unofficial results.
'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING

Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini charged toward a resident during a heated council meeting in New Jersey before being restrained by others in attendance. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)
Bianchini, who was tapped to serve as mayor following the resignation of his predecessor, will remain in the role until the end of this year.

Video footage from an October Pemberton Township council meeting captured the mayor being restrained as he sought to advance toward resident Michael Sawka after Sawka appeared to give the middle-finger gesture at the mayor.
"I am f---in' gettin' you!" Bianchini can be heard declaring as another individual intervening in the tense situation pushed the mayor back.
"I should not have said that," Bianchini told WPVI, adding that it "was wrong" and that he is "not gonna get anybody."
NEW JERSEY PRE-K AIDE FACES 61 CHARGES, ACCUSED OF FILMING HIMSELF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING STUDENTS AT SCHOOL
"I will not apologize for my actions last night. If you attack my family, as that resident did last night, I will act," the mayor wrote on Facebook, according to the New York Post.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported the mayor's wife, who was in the audience during the meeting, noted in a Facebook comment on a Pine Barrens Tribune post, "I am not condoning my husbands [sic] actions but I will say as a parent and a spouse, I get his protection mode."

"He was saying verbally abusive comments about my wife and my daughter," Matthew Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune. "And then he did a hand gesture and looked at my daughter. To me, it appeared like he gave her the finger and that is when I stood up. He looked at me, smiled and gave me the finger and that is when I went out after him."
Bianchini and Sawka have a history of bad blood between them.
The mayor told WPVI, "I just basically snapped," noting, "I hate to put it this way, but ... it's a long time coming."
"Was it wrong? Absolutely. Was it justified? Absolutely. And I would do it again if I had to," the mayor told the outlet.
TRUMP BEDMINSTER GOLF COURSE FALLS TO DEMS AS REPUBLICANS LOSE KEY HOUSE SEAT
Video shows Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a council meeting before several people intervened. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Sawka, who according to WPVI denied making comments towards Bianchini's family, told the station, "All I've ever been trying to do is show that we're wasting money."
"His family, his stepdaughter, his stepson, his daughter, they all attack me online, and they just come after me just with personal attacks," Sawka told WPVI.
Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune that Sawka has been harassing his family "for a long time."
"Mr. Sawka has been a thorn in this township's side for a number of years," Bianchini told WPVI.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Ohio's most popular midterm Republican says election results hold a warning for Dems
summary: Frank LaRose says the Republican Party must refocus on human freedom and free market principles after GOP candidates struggled on Election Day.
story: Ohio's most popular midterm Republican has advice for Democrats now in power, while saying his party needs to refocus its message into a constructive appeal to voters if the GOP hopes to regain the ground it lost on Election Day.
Ohio's most popular midterm Republican says his party needs to refocus its message into a constructive appeal to voters if the GOP hopes to regain the ground it lost on Election Day.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose won his race to become Ohio State Auditor on Tuesday night, securing over 2.3 million votes, a total that easily eclipsed any other statewide Republican candidate.
Gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy secured just over 2 million votes in his race, and Sen. Jon Husted secured just under 2.1 million votes in his bid for re-election.
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'
Frank LaRose stands with other GOP candidates in Ohio prior to Election Day. (Dustin Franz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"There are, of course, cycles to American politics, but also I think we as a party need to focus on what we're for, not just what we're against," LaRose told Fox News Digital in an interview. "I mean, we know what we're against. The other side has a bunch of crazy ideas that are dangerous for the future of our states and our nation, but we need to get back to talking about what we're for. We're the party that stands for human freedom, that idea that we're endowed by our Creator with rights, those don't come from government."

"Protecting human freedom, protecting free market principles that people can prosper by, you know, the sweat of their own brow and working hard to build a business, those are really kind of the bread and butter conservative issues that drove me to become a Republican when I first started thinking about politics as a young man myself," he continued.
Sen. Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy endorsed each other on Monday night (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

LaRose went on to point to Ohio Issue 3, a ballot measure requiring Ohio voters to present voter ID when casting their ballots. The overwhelmingly Republican-backed measure sailed through Tuesday's election with over 65% of the vote, even as Republican candidates struggled.
LaRose argued that the measure presents a warning to the midterm election's victorious Democrats that Republican policies remain popular even if candidates fail in their messaging.
TRUMP COUNTRY SEES 20-YEAR GOP GRIP ON GOVERNOR'S MANSION SHATTERED

"Candidly, I wish more conservatives had showed up to vote yesterday, and I think the outcome might have come out a little different. But even among most people that consider themselves Democrats in Ohio, it doesn't compare to Democrats on the coast, right? The East Coast and the West Coast is more of that kind of, you know, woke DEI cuckoo wing of the party. But even in Ohio, most Democrats are pretty common sense people, and of course, showing your ID to vote is common sense," LaRose said.
More than a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

"Let this be a message to my friends from the other side of the aisle that won their elections in Ohio. Remember that Ohio is not a far left state when it comes to common sense kind of things," he added. "Govern like a Midwestern Democrat and maybe you'll be all right, but if you govern like a coastal Democrat, then I think your time in office is going to be short."
POLLSTERS MISSED THE MARK AGAIN — BUT THIS TIME, IT WASN'T REPUBLICANS THEY UNDERESTIMATED

As Ohio's secretary of state, LaRose had a front-row seat as election tallies started mounting. He said it became clear with around 60% of the vote tallied that Republicans were not going to have a good night.

Nevertheless, he thanked Ohio's 40,000 election workers for their professionalism throughout the election process. LaRose has served as Ohio's elections chief for eight years, and he says his move to state auditor will allow him to keep Ohio's politicians accountable for their spending.

"When they waste your money, we're going to make them infamous, and when they steal your money, we're going to lock them up," he said.

title: Hegseth faces bipartisan impeachment threat after Iran war gets blame for GOP midterm slaughter
summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth faces a bipartisan impeachment threat as House Republicans say a privileged resolution could pass when Congress returns.
story: A ‘FOX News Democracy 26’ panel discusses the impact of the war in Iran on the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration’s messaging on the conflict and more.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.
"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.
GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH
War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference on U.S. military action in Iran at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., on March 2, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.
7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.

That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.
GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS'
"If he introduces it, it'll pass," a second House Republican told Fox News Digital. Two more said they expected the same.

One GOP lawmaker said attendance could be a key factor in impeaching Hegseth. It's highly possible that many Republicans who lost re-election simply do not return for the final two months of the year, that person said. And with just a razor-thin majority, only a handful of absences would be enough for Hegseth to get impeached if all Democrats stuck together.

The Fox News Decision Desk projected Democrats taking the House shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Projections showed that the war in Iran, along with tariff policies, were key drivers in voters turning their backs on the GOP.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
And while President Donald Trump told reporters he believes Hegseth is doing "a good job," people in his circle appear to have their knives out.
"Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House official told Fox News Digital.

A current White House official said, "[Tuesday] would have looked very different without the Iran war. I believe you’ll ultimately see [Trump] hold Pete Hegseth accountable and that will play out in the lame duck."
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH
But the White House criticized the potential impeachment push on Thursday.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

And another White House official said, "If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Wednesday dismissed rumors that Trump could get rid of Hegseth himself.

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," he told Fox News Digital.
It's also worth noting that the majority of House Republicans will still oppose impeaching Hegseth — and many are still skeptical.
CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES
"I really doubt [it]," another House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Depends on if anyone wants to flip off the president walking out the door."
There is likely to be healthy support on the other side of the aisle for such a push as well.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker, has consistently criticized Hegseth. He posted on X Thursday morning, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?"

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic candidate Suzan DelBene celebrate at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee midterm election night watch party in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)
Even more moderate Democrats have signaled their support, given the administration did not seek the consent of Congress at any point during the ordeal.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I've said a long, long time ago that he's not qualified for the job, and he should be removed, and I think we're going to pursue that," Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to take over leadership of the House Armed Services Committee next year, told CNN's "This Morning" last month.
If Hegseth were impeached, he would not be removed before a trial in the U.S. Senate.
Fox News Digital reached out to the committee's Republican majority and the Pentagon for comment.
