Reuters contributed to this report.

title: EXCLUSIVE: State Department accuses politicians of endangering Afrikaner lives after gruesome farm attacks
summary: The State Department accused South African politicians of endangering Afrikaners' lives after a farmer was allegedly tortured and a woman beaten to death.
story: Anti-migrant protests take a violent turn in South Africa, as unrest spreads and the government pleads for calm.

FIRST ON FOX: The State Department has hit out strongly against South Africa and some of its politicians, accusing them of putting their people’s lives at risk after two attacks on White farmers believed to be Afrikaners — people of European descent — near Johannesburg.
A 50-year-old man was reportedly tortured, and a 55-year-old woman was allegedly beaten to death.
In exclusive comments to Fox News Digital, a State Department spokesperson said "the lives and property of Afrikaners have been endangered by politicians who incite race-based violence against them."

President Donald Trump, right, and Cyril Ramaphosa, South Africa's president, during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., May 21, 2025. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT

This is the latest volley from the administration in an increasingly bitter row, which first burst out of the Oval Office last year in a heated exchange between President Donald Trump and South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa on a range of the country’s policies and issues, including safety concerns for the Afrikaner community.
"This month’s attacks were appalling," said Ian Cameron, chair of South Africa’s Portfolio Committee on Police and a member of Parliament with the main opposition Democratic Alliance.
He detailed the attacks, starting with one involving Donovan Marx, a 50-year-old who was on his farm about 80 miles from Johannesburg.
Cameron told Fox News Digital there were reports Marx was shot, stabbed and had his ears cut off, describing the attack as "extraordinary cruelty."
He added that, in a separate attack in the same North West Province earlier this month, a female farmer, Hannetjie van Zyl, 55, was beaten to death while opening a gate.
President Donald Trump shows documents as he meets South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House May 21 in Washington. (AP/Evan Vucci)
Eyewitness reports claim she was approached from behind and hit repeatedly over the head with an iron bar.

In both attacks, the victims’ vehicles and belongings were reportedly stolen. But the alleged torture of Marx goes beyond straightforward crimes such as burglary, Corné Mulder, leader of the opposition party Freedom Front Plus, told Fox News Digital.

"Safety and farm attacks in South Africa remains a huge problem," Mulder said. "Donovan Marx was attacked this week. He's fighting for his life in hospital at the moment. The perpetrators not only attacked him, they tried to castrate him."
While both victims were White, there have been no accusations from public figures that the attacks were racially motivated.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa delivers the State of the Nation address in Cape Town, South Africa, Feb. 12, 2026. (Rodger Bosch/Pool via Reuters)

Cameron claimed the attacks were not isolated, noting he had "personally attended farm attack scenes in which people were tortured with boiling water, burnt with clothing irons and subjected to other horrific abuse."

"SAPS [South African Police Service] must put experienced investigators, forensic support and crime intelligence behind these cases," Cameron said. "Nobody should have to accept this level of violence as a normal part of life."

The reported torture of farmers is "unthinkable," Mulder said, adding "not one word from the President of South Africa to sympathize, not even acknowledging that this has happened, which is absolutely unbelievable."
"We have been pleading with [the] government to prioritize rural crime and farm attacks as a priority crime, they are not prepared to do so," he continued.
Fox News Digital reached out to the South African government for comment but was referred to police, who did not immediately respond.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa addresses the opening session of the G20 leaders' summit in Johannesburg, South Africa, Nov. 22, 2025. (Misper Apawu/ AP Phot/Pool)
SOUTH AFRICAN EX-POLICE CHIEF GETS TISSUE STUCK ON FOREHEAD WHILE SWEATING DURING CORRUPTION INQUIRY

Mulder claims the recent farm attacks were fueled by the South African president’s refusal to heed Trump’s demand last year to stop performances of the song "Kill the Boer, Kill the Farmer." The term "Boer" refers to a South African of Dutch or Huguenot descent, according to Merriam-Webster.
Ramaphosa said he could not stop the song being chanted in stadiums by crowds of up to 90,000 because the country’s highest court has said the lyrics are not hate speech.
THOUSANDS OF POLICE DEPLOYED ACROSS SOUTH AFRICA AS DEADLY ANTI-IMMIGRATION PROTESTS SPREAD TO MULTIPLE CITIES

"As long as [President Ramaphosa] does not stop the incitement to attack farmers with the singing of the song ‘Kill the Boer,’ the attacks will continue," Mulder wrote in a statement. "We see the practical reality when these things play out as happened with the last two farm attacks that we've seen."
Last month, U.S. Ambassador to South Africa Brent Bozell III told Fox News Digital Ramaphosa could ban the song despite a court ruling that it did not constitute hate speech.
"So, to say, ‘Well, you can’t do it because the court said it’s not,’ … you know, that’s poppycock," Bozell said. "If President Ramaphosa, if he wants to, he can do it. It’s just as simple as that."

The State Department doubled down on the administration’s demand that the singing of the song be banned, with a spokesperson telling Fox News Digital on Friday, "The United States asked senior government officials to condemn incitement to race-based violence, particularly the singing of "Kill the Farmer! Kill the Boer!"

U.S. Ambassador to South Africa Brent Bozell III, left, poses for a photograph after presenting letters of credence to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, right, at Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria April 8, 2026. (Phill Magakoe/AFP via Getty Images)

The spokesperson added that Trump has demanded South Africa formally designate rural crime as a priority crime and "expand alternatives to the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment ownership requirements, such as equity equivalent investment programs."

Regarding farmers, the State Department spokesperson said South African politicians "threaten to confiscate their farms without compensation and support a corrupt, race-based scoring system that discriminates against Afrikaners and other minorities in employment."

"The lack of a meaningful response to these requests made clear that the South African government does not want a constructive relationship with the United States and is willing to continue pursuing oppressive policies that disadvantage all South Africans," the spokesperson continued.
Nearly 13,000 South African refugees, most of them Afrikaners, have been flown to the U.S. during fiscal year 2026. That number is expected to increase by another 17,500 refugees in fiscal year 2027.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"As directed by President Trump, we are prioritizing the resettlement of Afrikaners in South Africa escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination," the State Department spokesperson said.
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Polish president turns plane around after 'coup' at nation’s top court
summary: Tensions between Poland’s president and prime minister intensified as demonstrators rally outside the country’s top court.
story: Protesters gathered outside Poland’s top court as a long-running political dispute involving President Karol Nawrocki and Donald Tusk’s government escalated.  (AP Video.)

While en route to Senegal, Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around and returned home after police entered Poland's top court, the Constitutional Tribunal, and the tribunal’s president was suspended."At such a moment, the President must be in Poland," Nawrocki posted on X. "I'm interrupting my flight to Senegal. I'm returning."Police say they secured the Tribunal after dozens of protesters gathered to demonstrate against what they called the wrongful suspension of the top court’s president by the current pro-European government.
Police said there were also dangerous objects thrown at officers outside the building.
Protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Court in Warsaw after police blocked access to the court building on Oct. 30, 2026  (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

Some protesters outside the court were seen praying, while others held posters reading "Tusk — a symbol of anti-Polish sentiment," "Down with the commies and Tusk’s regime," and "Stop destroying the state."Poland’s top judicial bodies, including the Constitutional Tribunal, have been a major bone of contention between the current pro-European government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which ruled the country from 2015 to 2023.
Critics accuse the PiS of imposing political control over key judicial institutions, with some reforms having led the EU to impose fines on Poland.

NATO ALLY PUSHES ‘FORT TRUMP’ US MILITARY BASE AS RUSSIAN HELICOPTER PENETRATES AIRSPACENawrocki, an ally of the PiS ​party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament earlier this year.

Constitutional Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski, ⁠who was appointed by the PiS government after also serving as a deputy justice minister, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties. According to the tribunal’s website, Święczkowski was suspended Friday.
Protesters rally outside Poland’s top court as tensions between President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government intensify. (AP)

"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," said Tusk, who returned to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the judiciary’s independence. He posted to X, "After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way." Since taking power, Tusk’s pro-European government’s efforts have been vetoed by two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki.

HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNRESTFormer Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, a former PiS member whose Rozwój Plus coalition is positioning itself as an alternative to Tusk's government ahead of next November’s parliamentary elections, also took to X to denounce "the forceful takeover of the Constitutional Tribunal."

Police officers stand behind the fence with a rosary hanging on it as protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Court in Warsaw after police blocked access to the court building on October 30, 2026 (Getty Images)

"Justice cannot be achieved through violence," Morawiecki said, adding that "Tusk will stop at nothing to cling to power… We do not consent to Belarusian methods in Poland!" "It’s true: a coup d’état is underway," former PiS Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X. "If someone were to forcibly break into the Prime Minister’s Office and take it over, we would all know what to call it… This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order… That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP"A judge whose oath was never accepted by the President Nawrocki has declared herself head of the Constitutional Tribunal and suspended its leadership, while police secured the building," added Morawiecki. "This is not how the rule of law is restored. The tribunal's crisis is real, but replacing one disputed set of rules with a more radical one only invites the next government to do the same."

U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose posted a statement on social media that read in part: "The events unfolding tonight at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal are very serious indeed. We appear to be witnessing an unprecedented confrontation over the government’s use of state power and the independence and authority of a constitutional institution. Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why. Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the Tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse. America is on Poland’s side. It is not our place to judge or interfere in its internal affairs. Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally."The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Netanyahu's bloc falls short as longtime allies reportedly weigh move that could end his rule
summary: Netanyahu's bloc secured only 53 Knesset seats as ultra-Orthodox allies reportedly explore breaking ranks to back Gadi Eisenkot's opposition.
story: With final election results leaving both major blocs short of a majority, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Israel on the negotiations that could determine the country's next government.

Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.

The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee, gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.

Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results.
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW

Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot, right, and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.

The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER

An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.

Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.

Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.

The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.

According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.

Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.

Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.

"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.

"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.

The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.
NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING

A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, of the Likud Party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Jack Guez / AFP via Getty Images)

A national unity government involving Likud and Yashar would offer a more straightforward mathematical route to a majority, but would require Eisenkot to reconsider his campaign pledge not to join a Netanyahu-led government.

For Netanyahu, the lengthy coalition formation process could provide additional opportunities. If Eisenkot receives the mandate to form a government but fails, President Isaac Herzog could assign the task to another candidate, potentially giving Netanyahu another chance to assemble a coalition. If successive efforts fail, Israel could face another election.
Despite the obstacles, the source familiar with opposition discussions pointed to Bennett and Lapid's experience navigating complex coalition negotiations as an important asset.
"They've both played this game many times. They know it, and they're not rattled," the source said, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language conversation.

The source suggested that Bennett's experience working with Netanyahu gives him a particular understanding of the prime minister's negotiating tactics, while Lapid brings additional experience in coalition-building.
Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, one of the opposition's senior figures, acknowledged Friday that forming a government would be considerably more difficult than campaigning against Netanyahu.

A combination picture shows Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as he attends a memorial service held for Ran Gvili, an off-duty police officer who was killed fighting militants that had infiltrated Israel during the deadly October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas, and the last hostage recovered from Gaza, in Meitar, Israel, January 28, 2026, and Israeli opposition leader and former military chief, Gadi Eisenkot, as he launches an election campaign for Yashar, his new political party, at an event near Hod Hasharon, Israel, June 30, 2026. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)
"Now comes the truly hard part: trying to form a government," Lapid wrote on X, urging supporters to remain patient.

"It takes place in small rooms, slowly, away from the cameras," he wrote, according to a translation of his Hebrew-language statement, emphasizing the importance of negotiations conducted out of public view.
The negotiations will also unfold against the backdrop of the Trump administration's Middle East agenda.

The source familiar with opposition discussions said understanding Washington's regional priorities could become an important consideration in shaping a future government, although no specific American role in coalition negotiations has been confirmed.
The election results are scheduled to be formally submitted to President Herzog on November 4, following remaining verification procedures. The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in November 10.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

U.S. President Donald Trump enters the Knesset, Israel's parliament, with Israeli President Isaac Herzog and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before he speaks on Oct. 13, 2025 in Jerusalem. (Evan Vucci - Pool/Getty Images)

For now, the election has settled the question of how Israelis voted, but not who will govern them. A source familiar with the negotiations concluded: "Whoever manages to forge new partnerships will move forward. Whoever doesn't will remain stuck."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass in the L.A. mayor’s race
summary: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.
story: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.

Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week.

Bass faced intense scrutiny over her response to a January 2025 wildfire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood, the most destructive in Los Angeles history. The blaze erupted while she was in the West African nation of Ghana attending a presidential inauguration. It went on to destroy thousands of homes and kill 12 people.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections.

Raman, a former urban planner and activist, accused Bass of mismanaging the city’s homelessness problem and rising housing prices. She blasted City Hall for what she characterized as “a reluctance to move forward with the transformative policy change that this city needs right now.”
Bass, for her part, argued Raman was “not ready for primetime” after six years on the City Council.

The two Democrats also differed sharply on Israel’s war in Gaza, highlighting a generational split in the party. Speaking at a September forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, Raman said she agreed with left-wing influencer Hasan Piker that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians; Bass rejected that label.

Raman’s candidacy drew comparisons to that of Mamdani, whose campaign rallied New York City voters dissatisfied with the political old guard. Raman touted her progressive bona fides while stressing her “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America.

The incoming mayor’s agenda will be defined in part by the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, a complex undertaking that will test the city’s physical infrastructure, public transportation services and security systems.

Raman endorsed Bass at the beginning of the year before she launched a last-minute bid of her own. Bass and Raman took the top two spots in a June 2 primary contest, advancing to a runoff over populist insurgent Spencer Pratt, a former reality television star who blasted the city’s political establishment with provocative social media videos.

On the City Council, Raman represents a district that ranges from the San Fernando Valley to the Santa Monica Mountains. She was born in India and moved to the U.S. with her family as a child, later attending Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

title: Head of DOJ Civil Rights Division resigns after GOP midterms loss
summary: WASHINGTON — Harmeet Dhillon, the Republican attorney who oversaw a massive overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation on Thursday.
story: WASHINGTON — Harmeet Dhillon, the Republican attorney who oversaw a massive overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation on Thursday.

Attorney General Todd Blanche posted on X that he has accepted Dhillon’s resignation. He wrote that she “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor” and that the DOJ “is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”
Dhillon posted on X Thursday that the job had been the “honor of a lifetime.”
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” she wrote.
The departure of Dhillon, who had a long history of working as an election lawyer for the GOP, comes just two days after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Under Dhillon’s leadership, the Civil Rights Division led some of the Trump administration’s most controversial legal maneuvers, including lawsuits that cited claims of discrimination at elite universities. The division declined to open a use-of-force investigation into the ICE officer who shot and killed Renee Nicole Good in Minnesota earlier this year.

Her office also filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., in an effort to obtain voter registration lists from the states in the months before the election, with federal judges dismissing 27 of those cases. Dhillon was a regular presence on conservative media in the run-up to Tuesday’s elections, promoting the work of the Civil Rights Division.
Dhillon is set to speak at the Donald Trump Ballroom at the Mar-a-Lago Club during the Conservative Political Action Committee’s Circle Retreat and Gala on Thursday.
Bloomberg Law first reported her resignation plans.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Dhillon’s office recently attempted to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former Trump administration official who testified before the House Jan. 6 committee about Trump’s actions during the Capitol siege.

Her office also brought a criminal case against former CNN journalist Don Lemon and protesters over a demonstration at a church in Minnesota under a statute historically used to protect reproductive rights facilities.

Stacey Young, the executive director of the group Justice Connection, called Dhillon “the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” and said in a statement that she “wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court.”

Dhillon “decimated” the Civil Rights Division, Young said, and called on the incoming Senate “to exercise its full advice and consent powers to ensure the next Assistant Attorney General fulfills the division’s congressional mandate to enforce all Americans’ civil rights diligently and fairly.”

Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and the former chief of the Civil Rights Division during the Biden administration, said Dhillon “abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department.”

Clarke said Dhillon “abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the Division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals,” and that the NAACP would demand that Dhillon’s replacement “respect the agency’s sacred mission, enforce the law fairly, and protect our civil rights.”

title: Wisconsin reports its first measles death in decades, the third in the U.S. this week
summary: An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the state health department said — the third measles-related death reported in the U.S. this week.
story: An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the state health department said Thursday — the third measles-related death reported in the U.S. this week.
It’s Wisconsin’s first measles-related death since 1990, the health department said, adding that a coroner had listed measles as the infant’s immediate cause of death.

The news came just one day after Pennsylvania’s health department reported a measles-associated death there — the state’s sixth this year. The department said Wednesday that an unvaccinated resident in Jefferson County who tested positive for measles had died.
For Subscribers
Two days before that, New York health officials announced that a child in Lewis County had died of measles. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency over measles in early October.
In total, the U.S. has recorded eight measles-associated deaths this year, according to state health department data. It’s the highest measles death toll in the country since 1991.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four of those deaths. The agency says it will update its count “as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.”

None of the eight people who have died were vaccinated, according to state health departments; some were ineligible because of their age or health status. Typically, the first dose of the vaccine is administered around a child’s first birthday.
Before the outbreaks in Wisconsin, New York and Pennsylvania, none of the states had recorded a measles death in more than 30 years.

Pennsylvania’s outbreak, which began in April, is by far the largest in the country, with a case total approaching 1,500 across 45 counties, according to the state health department. A Franklin County coroner reported an additional death last month possibly linked to measles, but the state health department said Wednesday that it has not yet confirmed any deaths as measles-associated in the county.
For Subscribers

Nationally, the CDC has confirmed 4,852 measles cases this year — more than double last year’s count and the highest number since 1991. The dramatic rise is linked, in part, to a decline in vaccination rates across the country. Two doses of the measles vaccine are 97% effective against the disease.

title: Photos: Celebration and gloom at watch parties across the U.S.
summary: Joy and despair punctuated election watch parties overnight after a blue tsunami swept the country’s midterm elections.
story: Joy and despair punctuated election watch parties overnight after a blue tsunami swept the country’s midterm elections.

In Detroit, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his victory over Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history. He was cheered on by a crowd of supporters — some wearing hijabs, others cowboy hats.

title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom commutes all death sentences
summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted all California death sentences on Thursday, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted all California death sentences on Thursday, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state.
In an open letter to constituents, Newsom said taking this step is “among the most difficult of my career.”
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values,” he said.
California has not put a prisoner to death since Jan. 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed via lethal injection.
Newsom said his executive action will impact the “548 people now under death sentence in California,” making for “the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.”
There were 561 inmates on death row as of Tuesday, according to Department of Corrections records.
California’s now-former death row prisoners include Richard Allen Davis, who was convicted in the murder of 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993.

Klaas had been abducted at knifepoint from her home in Petaluma, north of San Francisco, during a slumber party. The case drew national attention after it triggered a massive search that eventually led investigators to Davis, who then directed police to the girl’s body in a shallow grave.
Marc Klaas, Polly’s father, said Newsom’s decision is a “knife in the back” to him and other victims’ families who believe death row prisoners were lawfully sentenced.

“It’s unbelievably disappointing,” Klaas told NBC News. “I was told that when this guy was sentenced to death that this was a system we can trust. But here we are, 33 years later, and it’s a system we can’t trust.”
Newsom’s action was embraced by death penalty abolitionists, human rights advocates and faith communities.
“This is a day that will be remembered in California’s history and resonate globally for years to come,” Amnesty International USA Executive Director Nadia Daar said in a statement.
For Subscribers
“The death penalty should be abolished, everywhere. Today marks a significant moment for human rights in California and across the country,” Daar said.
For Subscribers

Since the U.S. Supreme Court ended a brief pause in capital punishment with its landmark 1976 ruling in Gregg v. Georgia, there have been 1,687 state executions, according to Death Penalty Information Center records.
Texas has carried out the most executions in that time, 603, while California has carried out a death sentence just 13 times.

“Governor Newsom’s announcement marks a decisive moment in the history of the death penalty in the United States,” Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher said in statement. “Though other governors have granted universal clemencies, none have been at this scale.”
Newsom’s decree, for most death row inmates, would still need the approval of the California Supreme Court.
Newsom is frequently mentioned as a possible presidential candidate for 2028, and the timing of this announcement isn’t lost on Klaas.

“We’re talking about serial killers, we’re talking about spree killers, we’re talking about cop killers, we’re talking about child killers,” Klaas said. “Why, two days after the midterms, does Gavin Newsom feel the need to commute these sentences? Who benefits from this?”
San Luis Obispo County DA Dan Dow said Newsom’s action is an affront the families of victims, whose killers were brought to justice by his office.

“Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California’s 548 condemned killers that the killers’ lives matter more,” Dow said in statement as immediate past president of the California District Attorneys Association.
“Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power.”

title: Trump’s D.C.-area arch expected to be approved, but without sniper or drone plans
summary: The National Capital Planning Commission is expected approve the president’s Triumphal Arch for Washington, D.C., with construction scheduled to begin almost immediately.
story: The National Capital Planning Commission is expected to vote Thursday to approve President Donald Trump’s massive — and controversial — “Triumphal Arch” for Washington, D.C., with construction scheduled to begin almost immediately.

The commission, led by Trump appointees, is considered likely to give the project a green light after a hearing in which scores of area residents had lined up to voice their opposition to the project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Mark Paoletta, the Office of Management and Budget general counsel who was appointed chairman of the commission in August, said in remarks at the meeting that it was a “national disgrace” that such a memorial had not already been built and praised Trump’s “monumental vision.”
He said it would be “the grandest arch ever built by mankind.”

The virtual meeting was interrupted for around 30 minutes during public comments by what Paoletta said was a “malicious attack” that caused the site to crash. He said it’s the “first time this has ever happened.”
Close to 130 members of the public were signed up to speak, with debate by committee members and a vote to follow.
“We’ll have this thing done, whether it’s past midnight or not,” Paoletta said.

Opponents of the project, including the governments of Virginia and the District of Columbia, are seeking an emergency court order blocking the construction from moving forward, arguing the project is illegal.

They’ve already asked a judge to immediately halt any construction in a bid to head off possible legal gamesmanship by the administration, citing its earlier destruction of the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom that includes national security measures.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan has asked to be notified after the commission’s vote.

Trump has said the arch would celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary and include a military complex with drones and snipers that he said would be important for national security. The final plans submitted to the commission, however, do not mention drones, ammunition storage or sniper positions.

Asked about the omission at the hearing, Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, said the current “design is capable of hosting national security functions,” but details of those functions aren’t public and have been filed under seal in the court case.
Preservationists and military veterans first filed suit to block the project earlier this year, arguing that it needed to be authorized by Congress and that the site was improper.

“Its location on Memorial Circle would situate the monument on an axis between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, obstructing a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the Nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century,” they said.

Testifying at the meeting Thursday, one of the plaintiffs, Vietnam War veteran Michael Lemmon, who served as U.S. ambassador to Armenia during the Clinton administration, called the planned arch “frankly blasphemous.”

Virginia and the District of Columbia filed their own action to stop the project last week, contending it “defies at least five federal statutes,” including one that “generally limits buildings in the District to a maximum height of 130 feet.”
The 250-foot arch “would exceed that limit almost twice over.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
They also argued it would harm both District of Columbia and Virginia residents.

“The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect,” their suit said.

“Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added.

In court filings, the administration countered that the city and state don’t have standing to sue and that the project was given the green light by Congress about a century ago, when it “authorized erecting and redesigning 166-foot-tall columns surmounted by statues — exceeding any applicable height limits — and those columns have not yet been built.”
Attorneys for the city and state called those arguments “implausible” and said those columns had initially been planned to be built with Memorial Bridge before the idea was dropped.
“As Defendants do not dispute, the Memorial Bridge Act nowhere mentions an arch,” they said.

title: Justice Department moves to toss Steve Bannon’s conviction tied to Congress’ Jan. 6 investigation
summary: The Trump administration moved to vacate the conviction of Steve Bannon on two counts of contempt of Congress in connection with its investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S.
story: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration moved Thursday to vacate the conviction of Steve Bannon on two counts of contempt of Congress in connection with its investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
Bannon, a White House chief strategist and senior counselor during President Donald Trump’s first term, served a four-month prison sentence after the conviction in 2022.

The Justice Department wrote in a court filing Thursday that it had determined “dismissal is in the interests of justice because, in an exercise of its prosecutorial discretion, the Executive Branch does not believe that it is appropriate to pursue contempt of Congress charges against a former advisor to the President who did not comply with a subpoena investigating the events of January 6, 2021, based on an asserted belief that he was protected by executive privilege.”
The administration “harbors significant doubts” about the trial’s fairness, it said in the motion, which was signed by Deputy Associate Attorney General Michael Weisbuch.

“President Trump has expressed grave concerns about the Biden Administration’s prosecutions related to the events of January 6, 2021, granting a large number of pardons and commutations,” the motion said.
The Justice Department filing added that in light of Trump’s actions, seeking to affirm Bannon’s conviction “is inconsistent with this Administration’s enforcement priorities.”
Bannon’s legal team did not oppose the motion.
For Subscribers
U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols previously denied a motion to dismiss the indictment, saying in August that the government had not adequately described why it wanted to do so.
For Subscribers
The Supreme Court had sent the case back to Nichols, wiping out an appeals court ruling that upheld the jury’s verdict.
Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter previously served as Bannon’s counsel. His name does not appear on the Justice Department’s court filing.
Trump had pardoned hundreds of Jan. 6 defendants on his first day back in office.

title: The Met’s Costume Institute pivots after scrapping controversial Galliano show
summary: A new theme for next year’s Met Gala exhibit was announced Thursday, two months after event organizers scrapped their original idea to honor British designer John Galliano following backlash over his past anti-Jewish and anti-Asian remarks.
story: A new theme for next year’s Met Gala exhibit was announced Thursday, two months after event organizers scrapped their original idea to honor British designer John Galliano following backlash over his past anti-Jewish and anti-Asian remarks.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City, which hosts the annual star-studded event commonly known as fashion’s biggest night, said the replacement exhibit will examine how fashion designers transform conventional objects and everyday clothing to create new garments.

“From jeans, T-shirts, and puffer coats to paper, plastic, and metal, the exhibition will reveal how the seemingly unremarkable can inspire delight, surprise, and wonder,” the museum said in a press release Thursday. “The exhibition will examine how craft, construction, material experimentation, and conceptual wit give these ordinary forms extraordinary possibilities.”

Titled “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” the exhibit is being assembled by the Met’s Costume Institute, which curates the exhibit and theme of the Met Gala, an annual fundraiser for the institute.
The exhibit’s theme typically determines the dress code for the Met Gala, which traditionally falls on the first Monday in May.
Andrew Bolton, head curator at the Costume Institute, spoke to The Associated Press this week about the challenges he faced coming up with a new idea following the cancellation of the Galliano show.
“I had no Plan B, to be honest,” Bolton said. “There wasn’t another exhibition already researched and ready to go.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

With little time to come up with a new idea, Bolton said he relied on a passing thought he had while working on the last Met Gala exhibition, which explored the relationship different types of bodies have with clothing.

That previous show “sort of led me to think more about how we experience clothing in everyday life,” Bolton said. “We have a favorite T-shirt, we have a favorite pair of jeans, and we wear them until they literally fall apart.”
“Everyday clothes carry extraordinary amounts of meaning,” he added. “I like the idea that designers turn these familiar things into these incredible sources of wonder.”
Before changing course, the Costume Institute had already been collecting Galliano designs for the original show, which was announced in late July.

As controversy ensued, the museum said it would not shy away from confronting the designer’s “derogatory conduct that fundamentally altered his career and public reception,” but the exhibit in his honor was ultimately canceled in August.
At the time, museum director Max Hollein said the institution and Galliano decided together not to proceed with the original show.

The influential Galliano spent years as the creative director of Christian Dior. He was fired in 2011 over a series of racist and antisemitic comments that went viral online. That same year, the designer was convicted of antisemitic abuse in France after berating a couple at a cafe in Paris. Galliano blamed the behavior on substance abuse and testified in court that he had no recollection of the events.
Galliano later made a comeback in 2014 when he was hired by Paris fashion house Maison Margiela, where he remained for a decade.
If left unchanged, the unveiling of the Galliano exhibit would have coincided with Holocaust Remembrance Day on May 3, 2027.
Longtime Met Gala chair Anna Wintour, who is also Vogue’s global editorial director and a longtime supporter of Galliano, supported Hollein’s and Galliano’s joint decision to cancel the show.

“John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” Wintour said in an August statement. “I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support.”

title: ‘Married At First Sight UK’ dropped by network after women say they were raped during show
summary: The U.K. version of the “Married At First Sight” reality franchise has canceled its season after allegations that two women were raped during the production of the show.
story: The U.K. version of the “Married At First Sight” reality franchise will no longer air on Channel 4 after allegations that two women were raped during the production of the show.

Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra confirmed in a statement Thursday the network was cutting ties with the reality series following an external review of the allegations made while filming its sixth season.
The review found no wrongdoing by the network or the show’s production company, CPL, but Dogra said that the “right course was to bring Married At First Sight UK on Channel 4 to an end.”

“Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that ... the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format,” Dogra said.

The rape allegations were first revealed this summer in a BBC Panorama investigation. One of the two women alleged that the husband she was matched with raped her and threatened her with an acid attack, according to the BBC.
A third woman accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.
All three men involved denied the allegations.

The premise of “Married At First Sight” is that a group of contestants agree to be matched with complete strangers and meet at the altar. Couples are then followed by the cameras as they navigate their relationship and discuss their problems on air with the show’s counselors. Version of the show have aired across the world, including the U.S., Australia, France, and Spain.

Channel 4 hired a law firm to review safety protocols at the time of the alleged sexual misconduct and how the production company handled them once they were raised, the company said in a press release. The network’s review did not seek “to adjudicate” the allegations, which it said “remain a matter for the relevant authorities.”

More than 30,000 documents were reviewed by law firm Clyde & Co in addition to hours of footage, according to Channel 4. The review found that the production company and network were compliant with regulations from the U.K.’s Office of Communications.
A full version of the review was not made available but Channel 4 did provide a summary of findings, noting that the report was a “legally privileged and confidential review.”

There was no overall breach of the broadcasting code, though the full “welfare framework” was not applied in some incidents, the review found. One of the incidents included contributors who broke rules regarding “prohibited substances” but were given a warning rather than being removed.

A report from former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey, who was asked to examine if any protocols should be changed, said that there are elements of the show that could put pressure on individuals to be physically intimate. She recommended that the show consider discontinuing events such as Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.
Heggessey’s report said that the show’s stars could “become dependent on production and lose touch with reality,” which could affect decision-making.

She also recommended the show consider changing the mechanism in place that forces a couple to remain for another week if one person in a couple wants to leave but the other asks to stay during their weekly commitment ceremonies.

Among some of the recommendations were to install video and recording equipment in couple’s apartments to be monitored 24/7, provide couple’s separate bedrooms, provide “panic buttons,” and allow contributors to have at least one unsupervised visit back home during production.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The network said the full implementation of the recommendations “would entail a materially greater level of intervention, monitoring and supervision that would fundamentally alter the format and editorial proposition of the programme.”

“The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over ten years,” Dogra said.

Dogra said that the money budgeted for the series would be reinvested into finding “the next generation of distinctive and disruptive British television.” She thanked the staff who worked on the series and credited them for their “significant efforts to protect the welfare of contributors.”

The production company, CPL, said it understood Channel 4’s decision to part ways with the reality program, according to Sky News. It emphasized in its statement that Heggessey’s report found the welfare protocols to be “extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard.”
“CPL has always put contributor welfare at the heart of its programme making and will continue to do so,” the company said.
This is not the franchise’s first controversy.

The show’s Australia series has been criticized for subjecting contestants to potentially harmful situations, including a man who had a history of domestic abuse allegations. While the allegations were dismissed before filming began, the woman who was matched with him told The Guardian in June that the show “obviously needed a better vetting process.”
“We are strangers sleeping in a bedroom on our own on the first night, you’ve got no security, you’re by yourselves,” Awhina Rutene told the outlet.
She added that she was not subjected to abuse, but noted that the environment felt invasive and that physical intimacy felt “forced.”
“Every morning (in interviews) they’d be like, ‘Why aren’t you having sex?’” Rutene said.
The Australian Communications and Media Authority has conducted 10 investigations, according to the Guardian, and no breaches of its code of practice were found.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help. Confidential chats are available in English and in Spanish.

title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass in the L.A. mayor’s race
summary: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.
story: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.

Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week.

Bass faced intense scrutiny over her response to a January 2025 wildfire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood, the most destructive in Los Angeles history. The blaze erupted while she was in the West African nation of Ghana attending a presidential inauguration. It went on to destroy thousands of homes and kill 12 people.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections.

Raman, a former urban planner and activist, accused Bass of mismanaging the city’s homelessness problem and rising housing prices. She blasted City Hall for what she characterized as “a reluctance to move forward with the transformative policy change that this city needs right now.”
Bass, for her part, argued Raman was “not ready for primetime” after six years on the City Council.

The two Democrats also differed sharply on Israel’s war in Gaza, highlighting a generational split in the party. Speaking at a September forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, Raman said she agreed with left-wing influencer Hasan Piker that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians; Bass rejected that label.

Raman’s candidacy drew comparisons to that of Mamdani, whose campaign rallied New York City voters dissatisfied with the political old guard. Raman touted her progressive bona fides while stressing her “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America.

The incoming mayor’s agenda will be defined in part by the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, a complex undertaking that will test the city’s physical infrastructure, public transportation services and security systems.

Raman endorsed Bass at the beginning of the year before she launched a last-minute bid of her own. Bass and Raman took the top two spots in a June 2 primary contest, advancing to a runoff over populist insurgent Spencer Pratt, a former reality television star who blasted the city’s political establishment with provocative social media videos.

On the City Council, Raman represents a district that ranges from the San Fernando Valley to the Santa Monica Mountains. She was born in India and moved to the U.S. with her family as a child, later attending Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

title: LIV Golf plans to shut down
summary: LIV Golf, the breakaway golf tour backed by Saudi royalty and some of the biggest names in the game, said Thursday it planned to wind down — a stunning conclusion to an effort that had received billions of dollars in backing.
story: LIV Golf, the breakaway golf tour backed by Saudi royalty and some of the biggest names in the game, said Thursday it planned to wind down — a stunning conclusion to an effort that had received billions of dollars in backing.
In a statement, LIV said discussions with financial backer BC Partners had failed to produce an agreement to keep the league going.
“In light of the current circumstances, we believe shifting toward an orderly wind-down is the most responsible path forward for the League at this time,” LIV said in the statement.

Formed in 2021 by a group of golfers led by Phil Mickleson and Greg Norman who expressed dissatisfaction with the long-running PGA Tour, LIV attracted numerous bold-faced names including Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson with millions in guaranteed payouts.
Since 2022, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the league’s primary backer, has invested more than $5 billion.

Its creation set off a civil war of sorts in the game between LIV players and others committed to sticking with the PGA Tour, whose tournaments were seen as more competitive. By contrast, LIV’s events were accused of lacking drama because players’ payouts were guaranteed.
While LIV tournaments attracted healthy audiences overseas, they failed to land a long-term TV partner in the U.S., hampering their visibility and revenue streams.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
An earlier hearing in New Jersey bankruptcy court indicated LIV planned to shut down operations as it sought relief from creditors. It was not immediately clear how much it owed.

The Financial Times reported earlier this week that LIV had sought a last-minute investment with a large private equity group, only to see the deal fall apart. Sports media outlet The Athletic reported the group, BC Partners, did not receive enough commitments from golfers interested in reviving the tour, which had seen multiple events canceled this year, including a team championship.

title: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
summary: U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers.
story: U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers.
The Justice Department was ordered to respond to the allegations, made by the ship’s Russian owner, Burevestmarin LLC, by 9 a.m. Friday.

The tanker, Bella 1, was seized by the U.S. military in the North Atlantic in early January after a weekslong chase on the high seas. U.S. authorities said the ship, which they believed was carrying illegal Iranian oil, was caught fleeing an American blockade of Venezuela. Attorneys for Burevestmarin dispute the claim that the vessel was carrying Iranian oil.
The ship was sold to a scrap dealer for $9.1 million, the company’s lawyers said, well below the $21 million that the Bella 1 would fetch as scrap metal alone.
Even a proper scrap metal price tag would understate its worth, they added, because the ship has “substantially greater value” as “an operating commercial vessel.”

“As discussed and previously briefed, the Government posits a world in which it can — while withholding notice to known interested parties and while aware of challenges to the Court’s jurisdiction — engage in precisely this kind of economically irrational sale for its own convenience,”  the owner’s lawyers wrote.
They said the sale was conducted “behind closed doors” as part of the government’s “self-interested and unreasonable decisions.”
Representatives for the Justice Department and the scrap dealer named in court documents could not be immediately reached for comment Thursday.

Previously, DOJ attorneys have argued that seized ships put the government in a financial bind, so selling these vessels is necessary to avoid tens of millions of dollars in maintenance and repair costs.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
DOJ attorney Rajbir Datta told the court in July that “the government has spent $60 million in maintaining this and doing all kinds of mechanical fixes to the asset itself.”
A root issue in the ongoing court battle is whether American authorities are right to argue that transporting Iranian oil benefits the sanctioned Islamic Revolutionary Guards Force.
That question is further complicated by the Trump administration permitting international sale of Iranian oil to help relieve domestic fuel prices.

Attorneys representing Bella 1’s owner are also fighting the Justice Department’s efforts to seize other ships that they own, citing what they believe is a legal double standard invoked by the government, court records show.

In the case of the vessel Galileo attorneys for the ship owner argued that “on March 20, 2026, the same day that the Government (under seal and ex parte) alleged that the Galileo was a source of influence over the IRGC and IRGC-QF, it expressly licensed the international sale of Iranian oil — an action that would be illegal under multiple statutes were the shipment of Iranian oil in itself necessarily the equivalent of providing a means of support to the IRGC or IRGC-QF or becoming the property of the IRGC or IRGC-QF.”

In the case of another vessel, Skipper, attorneys for Burevestmarin LLC said the Justice Department did not establish the correct venue and may have improperly seized that vessel. The Skipper was on the “high seas” thus meaning it was outside of the U.S. or a foreign country’s territorial waters.

title: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
summary: Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
story: PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike.

Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas.
Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police.
Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).

“Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added.

In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans.

title: How to prevent your pipes from freezing this winter, according to plumbers
summary: Frozen pipes can burst and cause costly water damage. Plumbers share how to keep your pipes from freezing and what to do if one bursts.
story: Nothing ruins a winter morning quite like turning on the faucet and getting nothing but a sputter, or worse, finding water pouring through your ceiling. When temperatures plunge, the water inside your pipes can freeze and expand, putting enough pressure on them to crack or even burst. The result is water damage, a hefty repair bill and a big headache. The good news is that frozen pipes are largely preventable, and most of the fixes are cheap, quick and easy enough to handle yourself.

To find out how to keep the water flowing all winter, I spoke to two plumbing experts about how frozen pipes happen, what you can do to protect yours before the next cold snap and how to handle the situation if your pipes do freeze.
What causes pipes to freeze?

Pipes freeze when the water inside them gets cold enough to turn to ice — and some parts of your plumbing are far more vulnerable than others. “Pipes can freeze when they’re exposed to cold temperatures without enough insulation or heat to protect them,” says Steve Clemente, president and COO at Benjamin Franklin Plumbing. “This is especially a concern for outdoor plumbing and pipes that run through unheated areas of the home, like an attic or basement.”

The real danger isn’t the ice itself but rather what happens when water freezes. “As water freezes, it expands,” says Mike Rippel, owner of Quality Pro Services, a plumbing and heating company in Middlesex, New Jersey.  And according to Clemente, “a frozen pipe can burst, leaving you with water damage and potentially costly repairs.”

The first sign of a frozen pipe is usually a faucet that won’t run, or only trickles, when you turn it on. You might also notice frost on exposed pipes or hear unusual sounds when water tries to move through them. A frozen pipe isn’t always a disaster, but it’s a warning sign you shouldn’t ignore.
What can help you prevent frozen pipes?
To find out which products are worth considering, I asked Clemente and Rippel what they recommend homeowners use to protect their pipes from freezing. Here are the types of products they suggested.

“Smart sensors can provide another layer of protection by detecting drastic temperature changes or water where it shouldn’t be,” says Clemente. This one attaches to your main water supply pipe and tracks the temperature of the water inside. If the water gets cold enough to put your pipes at risk, it can automatically shut off your water supply and send an alert to your phone. It also monitors water flow to flag leaks. You can install it yourself, though Moen recommends hiring a professional.
Other things you can do to prevent frozen pipes
Beyond buying products that can help prevent your pipes from freezing, experts say there are a few other things you can do to mitigate the risk.

Prep your outdoor plumbing. “Start before cold weather arrives by disconnecting garden hoses or other faucets and draining outdoor water lines you won’t use during the winter,” says Clemente.Insulate exposed pipes. “Insulate exposed pipes, especially those outdoors or in unheated spaces like attics and basements,” says Clemente.Keep the heat on. “Have your heating system serviced, and keep the heat on low even when you’re away so the temperature inside your home doesn’t drop too low,” says Clemente.Let your faucets drip. During especially cold nights, “run the faucet at a slow but steady drip to prevent the water from freezing,” says Rippel.
Prep your outdoor plumbing. “Start before cold weather arrives by disconnecting garden hoses or other faucets and draining outdoor water lines you won’t use during the winter,” says Clemente.
Insulate exposed pipes. “Insulate exposed pipes, especially those outdoors or in unheated spaces like attics and basements,” says Clemente.
Keep the heat on. “Have your heating system serviced, and keep the heat on low even when you’re away so the temperature inside your home doesn’t drop too low,” says Clemente.
Let your faucets drip. During especially cold nights, “run the faucet at a slow but steady drip to prevent the water from freezing,” says Rippel.
How cold does it need to be for your pipes to freeze?

“Exposure to temperatures below 32 degrees [Fahrenheit} can cause pipes to freeze and potentially burst,” says Clementes. But pipes don’t necessarily freeze the moment temperatures dip below that mark. How quickly it happens depends on how cold it gets, how long the cold lasts and how well your pipes are protected. “Pipes outdoors or in unheated, poorly insulated areas are particularly vulnerable because they stay cold for longer, so protect those lines before freezing weather arrives,” says Clemente.
How can you tell if your pipes are frozen?

If water freezes and expands in your pipes it can cause cracks or even cause the pipe to burst. And because the water is frozen, the leak may not start until the ice thaws and water begins flowing through the damaged section again, says Rippel.

If a pipe does burst, where that pipe is located may determine how much damage you have to deal with.  Depending on the location, that water can soak into drywall, flooring and insulation before you even realize there’s a leak, which is why it’s important to act quickly if you suspect a pipe has frozen.
What should you do if a pipe does burst?

The most important thing is to stop the flow of water as quickly as possible. “Shut down the incoming water system so that when the line does thaw, you don’t have consistent running water causing major flooding,” says Rippel. This is why it pays to plan ahead. “It’s also a good idea to know where your main water shutoff valve is and make sure it works so you’re prepared if a pipe does burst,” says Clemente.

Once the water is off, call a licensed plumber to assess and repair the damaged pipe. If water is near outlets, appliances or your electrical panel, turn off power to the affected area before you start cleaning up. It’s also a good idea to take photos of the damage and contact your homeowners insurance company, since many policies cover sudden water damage from a burst pipe.
